metadata.title: No Surprises Act & IDR Updates | What Healthcare Payers & Providers Need to Know
metadata.author: Zelis Healthcare
metadata.shortDescription:
The Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process remains one of the most critical — and evolving — elements of the No Surprises Act (NSA). In this video, we break down the latest regulatory developments, legislative actions, and policy shifts shaping the future of surprise billing dispute resolution.

Key Topics Covered:
• Why the IDR process is challenging — and why the government is prioritizing its improvement
• Recent bipartisan Congressional activity, including new bills and information requests
• Funding updates and proposed federal rules designed to reform the IDR system
• How ongoing litigation continues to influence policy and compliance
• Acknowledged challenges within the current IDR framework and stakeholder engagement

Whether you work in healthcare payer administration, provider operations, compliance, or revenue cycle management — understanding these developments is crucial for navigating the NSA landscape and minimizing surprise billing risk.

 Stay Ahead of Policy & Compliance Changes
This video equips you with actionable insights into the future of the No Surprises Act and IDR process — and what it means for your organization.

Learn More About Zelis NSA Solutions: https://bit.ly/3MElvHI

metadata.title: No Surprises Act Check-In: The Latest Changes to the IDR Process
metadata.author: KLGatesLaw
metadata.shortDescription: In this episode, Gabe Scott, Kevin Alonso, and Cindy Laura Ortega Ramos unpack recent updates to the federal independent dispute resolution (IDR) process under the No Surprises Act. They discuss the operational changes introduced in May by the Departments of Health and Human Services, Labor, and the Treasury, along with the Office of Personnel Management, and what these updates mean for how payment disputes are processed and resolved.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to Triage, timely
conversations for healthcare
professionals, a podcast created and
produced by K&L Gates. Each episode is
designed to highlight important
developments in health law and analyze
the impact on our clients and friends of
the firm. We hope you enjoy this
podcast.
>> Welcome to another episode of Triage. My
name is Gabe Scott and I'm a healthcare
partner in K&L Gates healthcare and FDA
practice.
Today we're going to be discussing a
significant update to the federal
independent dispute resolution or IDR
process under the No Surprises Act. So,
on May 28th, 2026, departments of Health
and Human Services, Labor, and Treasury,
together with the Office of Personnel
Management, issued a final rule making a
number of operational changes to the
federal IDR process. I'm joined by two
of my colleagues from K&L Gates
healthcare practice group. Tim Alonso is
a partner in our Nashville office and
Cindy Ortega Ramos is an associate in
our Chicago office.
>> Thanks for having us.
>> Great. So, before we dive into the
specific changes here, let's start with
some basics. Cindy, you know, first off,
what is the federal IDR process?
And why did the agencies feel the need
to issue this rule?
>> Yeah, so that Thank you so much for
having us, Gabe. And the federal IDR
process is the mechanism established
under the No Surprises Act to resolve
certain payment disputes between payers
and out-of-network providers.
And since its implementation in 2022,
out-of-network providers have submitted
hundreds of thousands of claims under
the current baseball style arbitration
process, which is significantly higher
than the agencies originally
anticipated. And so, as with any new
process, not everything has gone
smoothly.
Over the last several years, the
agencies have had to contend not only
with a number of administrative burdens
and operational challenges, but also
with litigation.
So, this final rule is largely aimed at
at improving how the system functions,
rather than changing the substantive
standards used to resolve payment
disputes.
>> Got it. Thanks, Cindy. So,
of the changes that were made, what are
some of the most significant ones?
>> So, some of the most notable changes
relate to improving communication
between providers and payers. So, now
payers will be required to communicate
information to out-of-network providers
using specific claim adjustment reason
codes and remittance advice remark
codes,
which is intended to help identify
whether a claim is or is not subject to
the federal IDR process.
Um that requirement, although effective
on August 3rd, 2026, does not become
operational immediately. The agencies
intend to issue future guidance
implementing those provisions. And
payers will also be required to submit
additional information about the payer
with their payment denials, as
historically providers have sometimes
found it difficult to identify the
correct payer contact information in
order to initiate the open negotiation
process as well.
>> Thanks, Cindy. And one more interesting
change in relation to that last point
that's worth mentioning is that in the
future the agencies actually plan to
have an IDR registry. Payers will have
to register and receive a registration
number and include that registration
number with their payment denials. That
should make it a lot easier for
providers to initiate open negotiation
and cut down on disputes being initiated
against the wrong party.
This is a work in progress, however. The
IDR registry requirements won't go into
effect until the agencies provide
further guidance.
>> Thanks, Kevin. So, you know, what about
the sort of open negotiation process
itself? As I understand it, providers
can
really initiate the open negotiation
process, and then they may never
actually receive a response from the
payer.
>> Yeah, that's right. The 30 business day
open negotiation period is an
opportunity to settle things before
getting too deep into the federal IDR
process. And the agencies really want to
encourage actual negotiations.
In light of that, the final rule
actually requires the non-initiating
party, which is often the payer, to
issue a response by the 15th business
day of the open negotiation period.
>> Right. So, so it's really putting an
onus on the on the payers to provide
some sort of response and knowledge that
the you know, the process has begun.
Cindy, you know, there are obviously a
lot of changes in this final rule, more
than you know, we have time to discuss
here, but you know, what are sort of two
or three other notable changes that that
you think folks should care about?
>> Yeah, so I think there is uh maybe three
changes that are definitely worth
mentioning. The first one would be that
existing regulations do not say any time
frame for the certified IDR entities to
make eligibility determinations.
Um the final rule will require them to
make eligibility determinations within
five business days of their selection.
So, I think that's that's important. The
second one would be that the agencies
are making the federal IDR process more
accessible by reducing the
administrative fee from $115 to $15. And
that was effective as of uh June 11,
2026. And I think lastly, the third one
would be that batching will be limited
to 50 items and services in a single
dispute to help certified IDR entities
more easily make timely eligibility and
payment determinations.
The definition of a batch dispute
applies to disputes with open
negotiation periods beginning 90 days
after the effective day of these final
rules. So, I think those would be my key
three changes to highlight.
>> Kevin, what should stakeholders be doing
now given the final rule here as folks,
you know, look to adjust their processes
to accommodate the changes under the
final rule. What should they care about?
>> Yeah, so stakeholders should start
evaluating existing workflows now to
identify where operational changes are
needed in light of the rulemaking. I
think the new claim adjustment reason
codes and remittent advice remark codes
will help providers identify eligible
claims with greater speed and accuracy.
So, incorporating these new codes into
existing workflows will be pretty
important.
Furthermore, if the $150 administrative
fee previously dissuaded providers from
the IDR process for low-dollar claims,
it might be worth a second look at this
point given that the fee has dropped to
Finally, given that many changes will
require additional agency input, it's
really important to continue monitoring
the agency's publications for relevant
guidance over the coming months.
>> Very interesting. Kevin and Cindy, you
know, thanks to you both for joining us
today and thanks to our listeners for
engaging with another episode of Triage.
These IDR process changes could really
meaningfully reshape the negotiation
process and how claims are handled under
the No Surprises Act. And so, we will
continue to monitor further developments
on this issue.
In the meantime, if you have questions
about IDR issues or other healthcare
regulatory matters, please contact Cindy
or Kevin or your current Cano Health
attorney.
In the meantime, we'll be back with
another episode of Triage. Thanks again
for listening.
>> Thanks again for listening to Triage,
timely conversations for healthcare
professionals. New episodes are
available for download through Apple
Podcasts, Google Podcasts, and Spotify.
By subscribing to Triage, you will
receive timely notifications for each
new episode. Also, if you have any
topics you would like to hear discussed
on Triage, please don't hesitate to
email triage.support@klgates.com.
We would love to hear from you.

metadata.title: No Surprises Act Independent Dispute Resolution Drives Up Healthcare Costs in America
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
No Surprises Act Independent Dispute Resolution Drives Up Healthcare Costs in America.

The No Surprises Act stopped out-of-network physicians from billing patients who received care at  in-network hospitals.  

This situation most typically applies to Radiologists, ER doctors, Anesthesiologists, Pathologists and Assistant Surgeons who are out-of-network practicing at in-network hospitals.

Currently, the physicians and the insurance companies must agree on a payment amount or take their dispute to an Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process set up by the Federal Government.

About 300,000 cases per month go through the IDR process with doctors winning 80-85% of the time.  These physicians are winning amounts that are 4.5X the median in-network reimbursement rate on average.

IDR cases are filed by a relatively small number of private equity-own physician practices.  The majority of IDR cases are also in the select few states of TX, FL, NJ, NY, AZ, TN and GA.

There are approximately 15 arbitration companies contracted with the Federal Government to settle these disputes.

What can self-funded employers do about this high out-of-network physician win rate and high award amount?
1.  Ask their carrier to share and identify claims data that had gone through the IDR process to quantify the amount and identify offending provider groups and their associated hospitals.
2.  Lobby their congress person to hold public hearings with the arbitrators about the seemingly 'lopsided' judgements in favor of out-of-network physicians.
3.   Steer plan members away from hospitals that have these out-of-network provider groups that are receiving high out-of-network reimbursements through plan design, direct primary care referrals and direct contracting.

metadata.title: An Overview of the Independent Dispute Resolution Process for Disputing Parties, Part II
metadata.author: CMSHHSgov
metadata.shortDescription: Training session on the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process for disputing parties (health care providers, emergency facilities, providers of air ambulance services, group health plans, health insurance issuers, and Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB) Carriers).

segments.text: [Amanda Brander] Okay, we can now begin our session. Again, welcome.

And thank you for joining this call today. We plan to review the IDR process for disputing parties and answer questions that we've received as we go through each step in the process. We’ll save time at the end to try to answer additional questions if
we are able, but if we don't have time, we'll make sure to follow up after the meeting with further questions.
So, today this information provided is intended only to be general information
in the summary of technical legal standards. It’s not intended to take place of statutes or regs or formal policy guidance, upon which it is based. The presentation is a summary of current operations
and we encourage everyone on the call

to reach out if you have questions. The content of the document does not have the force and effect of law and are not permitted to bind the public in any way. This communication was created at the expense of US tax dollars.
So again, today we're going to take a look at Department Announcements, and then walk through that process and Q&A that I just spoke about.

As a reminder, many of you were on the IDR training that the Departments held on Friday the 8th. But for those who are unable to attend, we wanted to have a quick update on recent announcements from the Department. On February 23rd, the US District Court of the Eastern District of Texas invalidated portions of the interim final rule, Requirements Related to Surprise Billing, Part II,

that was issued by the Departments and governs the IDR process. Due to the decision, the Departments announced steps we’re taking to conform to the court’s order and specifically, the Departments withdrew guidance documents that were based on, or that referred to, portions of the rule
that the court invalidated. Yesterday we updated the guidance and reposted that to conform to the court’s order, so you'll find new guidance documents at CMS.gov.
In addition, on April 5th, the Departments announced that the online IDR portal is planned to launch this week.
In the near future, we plan to host a webinar to take an in-depth look at the IDR process and give a demo of the Federal IDR portal.
Let's get started with the steps preceding the IDR process. There are several steps parties must go through prior to the start of the Federal IDR process.

The first starts when a furnished covered item or service results in a charge for emergency items or services from an out-of-network provider or facility, for non-emergency items or services from an out-of-network provider at an in-network facility, or
for air ambulance services from an out-of-network provider of air ambulance services.

And each of these boxes, in the graph you see on the slide, represents a sort of step in this process. So in Step 2, within 30 calendar days, the initial payment or notice of denial of payment must be sent by the plan issuer or carrier.

The plan must include with its initial payment or denial of payment, the appropriate person or office to contact if provider facility or provider of air ambulance services wishes to initiate open negotiations.
They must also include a statement that if the open negotiation period does not result in an agreement on the out-of-network rate, either party
to the open negotiation may initiate the Federal IDR process. The applicable qualified payment amount for each item or service must also be included by the plan.

In Step 3 of this process, the parties must initiate open negotiation period, if that's the desire, within 30 business days beginning on the day the out-of-network provider receives either an initial payment or the notice of denial of payment.

So, again, either party may initiate open negotiation, but both parties must in good faith actively participate in the open negotiation period and provide all the required information that's necessary if the open negotiation is unsuccessful
and the parties choose to use the Federal IDR process.
So, the initiating party in the open negotiation must provide written notice to the other party of its intent to negotiate.
This is referred to as the open negotiation notice, and it must include information sufficient to identify the items and services that are subject to negotiation.
These items that must be included are: the date that items or services were furnished; corresponding service codes for the items or services;
the initial payment amount or notice of denial of payment, as applicable;
an offer for the out-of-network rate; and contact information of the party sending the open negotiation.
And again, these things should have been found in the payment or denial of payment by the plan.

And so the Departments have received several questions regarding applicability of the Federal IDR process and the open negotiation period that we'd like to try to clarify before moving to our IDR initiation. [background noise]
The first question is: How does the nominating party know
if the items or services are eligible under the No Surprises Act if there's no way to know anything other than the services and CPT codes? I'll turn it over to you, Matt, for a response.

[Matt Meidell] Yeah, thanks Amanda. So, with the initial payment or the denial of payment that payers are sending it’s required to include a statement that the QPA applies for the purpose of the recognized amount.

And so the interim final rules require that a statement from the plan or issuer that the QPA applies for purposes of the recognized amount so that providers and facilities will understand that the plan or issuer has determined that neither an all-payer
model agreement or specified state law applies for purposes of calculating a participant’s cost sharing amount, but rather this cost sharing amount would be calculated using the QPA.

So the Departments expect that in most, if not all cases, the QPA will serve as the basis for determining the recognized amount, and the Federal IDR process will govern a dispute over the payment instead of a specified state law or process.
[Amanda Brander] Thanks, Matt. The next question is: Many people calculate QPA differently.
Does the party have to provide details on how it is calculated?

[Matt Meidell] Absolutely. Thanks Amanda. So, the first surprise billing interim final rules set forth how the QPA must be calculated and require that plans and issuers make certain disclosures with each initial payment or notice of denial of payment and
plans and issuers must provide additional information, upon request of the provider or facility,
and this information must be provided in writing, either on paper or electronically, to a non-participating provider or emergency facility or provider of air ambulance
services is applicable where the QPA serves as the recognized amount.
This information should be provided by the initiating party with the notice of IDR initiation.
[Amanda Brander] Thanks, Matt.

And the last question in this section that we received that we will go over today is: Will the Departments be giving guidance on adding sufficient information to identify the customer and claim? From our experience with negotiations, there is not sufficient information
to identify the customer or claim on the form as it exists today.

We have found providers are solving that by adding their own fields to the form by doing [inaudible] or email with the identifying information, or by including information with the form, such as an EOB that will help to identify the customer.
In some cases, we are having to reach back out for information if the provider hasn't proactively provided that to us.

[Matt Meidell] Yeah, thanks Amanda. So, the current open negotiation notice requires a description of the item or service, which would include information that sufficiently identifies the item or services that are being disputed.

And then also I want to note that updated guidance that the Departments have posted notes that as part of open negotiations, the non-initiating party can request that the initiating party provide additional information that will identify the claim that's in the dispute. So this would includes things such as a claim reference number or the location of the service. [Amanda Brander] Thank you, Matt, for
providing those responses. Now let's take a look at the Federal IDR process after the open negotiation period.

The Federal IDR process may be initiated within four days after the last day of open negotiation period if parties do not reach an agreement on an out-of-network rate. The Departments will open the Federal IDR portal this week, and make available
the online web form to initiate IDR.
When the initiating party submits the IDR initiation form, the initiation is sent to the Department by the Federal IDR portal or our online system.

If your open negotiation period ended prior to the IDR portal opening, the Department will permit submission of a notice of initiation of the IDR process within 15 business days following the opening of the IDR portal.

The initiating party is also required to provide a copy of the initiative form to the non-initiating party. It can be done electronically, if they have a good faith belief that the other party will receive the electronic communication, and they must also
provide it in paper form at no cost, if requested.
The IDR initiation form is another step in this process for which we've received questions. So we'll try to provide clarification by answering a few of those questions now.
The first question says: We are following the guidance for the No Surprises Act, but are not clear on how to initiate arbitration, and the open negotiation
period is now passing.

I'll ask Alper to please respond to this question. [Alper Ozinal] Hi, yes, hello. Thank you, Amanda. So, the Departments announced that the portal will be going live the week of April 11 on the No Surprises website. So, for disputes for which the open negotiation period
has expired, the Departments will permit submission and notice of initiation of the IDR process within 15 business days following the opening of the IDR portal.
For example, if the portal opens on April 15, then parties whose open negotiation period expired before April 15 will have until May 6 to initiate, May 6 being 15 business days.
Thank you.
[Amanda Brander] Thanks Alper. The next question:
Plan detail should be included on the initiation web form. Plan details that need to be included are funding, whether it's fully insured or self-insured, and contract information for each state.
This information is needed for the IDRE to determine eligibility of a claim or service under a state law or the federal law. Without this level of detail, eligibility cannot be determined.
And Matt if I could ask you to answer that?

[Matt Meidell] Yeah, sure, Amanda. So, the location of where the items and services are furnished is required to be provided on the notice of IDR initiation form. And information on the QPA, which only applies again if a specified state law or all-payer model agreement doesn't
apply, it must also be provided as well.

Also, parties to dispute, or excuse me, if parties dispute the applicability of the IDR process, they'll provide the certified IDR entity with information disputing that the claims are eligible with their notice of selection of failure to select a certified
IDR entity.
This information will help IDREs figure out if an all-payer model agreement or specified state law applies and therefore the Federal IDR process would not apply.
Thanks.

[Amanda Brander] Thanks, Matt. And the final question on this step is: Will the IDR notice, that is created by the initiating party, be available through the portal, or is the only way for the non-initiating party to receive it is for the initiating party to send it?
Alper, if you could respond?

[Alper Ozinal] Sure, thanks Amanda. Yes, so the initiating party has to send a copy of the initiation web form directly to the non-initiating party. The notice will not be available in the portal for the other party to access.
So, it must be sent - a copy of the initiation web form must be sent directly to the non-initiating party. Thank you, Amanda.
[Amanda Brander] Thank you.

Now let's look at the second step in the Federal IDR process, which is selection of the IDR entity. The non-initiating party will receive an email from the Federal IDR portal, notifying them of the initiating party’s preferred certified

IDR entity that also includes a secure link to agree with the selection or make an alternative selection. You'll also have to attest to a conflict-of-interest statement and attest to the applicability of the Federal IDR process. The non-initiating
party must respond on this form within three business days.

If they cannot not agree on the selection of a certified IDR entity within those three business days after initiation, and the Departments will randomly select a certified IDR entity, no later than six business days after the date of initiation of the Federal
IDR Process and will notify the parties of the selection by email from the Federal IDR portal.

Once a certified IDR entity is selected, a notice will be sent to the certified IDR entity from the IDR portal, and the entity will review the dispute to make its eligibility for the IDR process determination as well as attest to conflicts of interest

within three business days. Making an eligibility determination requires the certified IDR entity to review whether any specified state laws or all-payer model agreements apply to the dispute in question. Because we have several questions on eligibility,

it's important to remember that the Federal IDR process will be applicable in all states for certain plans. Some states allow self-funded plans to opt into their state process, but it is not required that a self-funded plan opt into that state’s process.
Therefore, the Federal process will be available to all self-insured plans who have not opted into their state’s process.

Similarly, the Federal process will be available in all states for FEHB carriers, who do not have a contract with the Office of Personnel Management, that directs the carrier to use the state process.
Other questions we received on this step
and the IDR process are as follows, and I will ask Matt again to respond. The first question: If the eligibility is in dispute,

how would that be handled? Is there a way to dispute eligibility prior to the IDRE being assigned and fees incurred? Or should eligibility disputes be sent to IDREs for them to resolve and make a determination?
[Matt Meidell] Thanks Amanda. So, currently the Departments and the certified IDR entities will review for Federal IDR process eligibility before any fees are collected.
Thanks.
[Amanda Brander] Question says: If the IDRE agrees that claims are not eligible, will the parties’ IDRE fees be returned?
Will this be established in guidance?
[Matt Meidell] So again, currently the certified IDR entity must conclude that the Federal IDR process applies before administrative fees and certified IDR entity fees are paid.
[Amanda Brander] And then the next question: What if initiating and non-initiating parties enter different QPAs
onto the forms that we have received at this point?

Thank you.

Thank you.

entity, including a notice of offer form requesting each party respond to the email and again, include documentation. Guidance posted yesterday

The presentation is a summary of current operations and we encourage everyone on the call to reach out if you have questions. The content of the document does not have the force and effect of law and are not permitted to bind the public in any way. This communication was created at the expense of US tax dollars. On February 23rd, the US District Court of the Eastern District of Texas invalidated portions of the interim final rule, Requirements Related to Surprise Billing, Part II, that was issued by the Departments and governs the IDR process. Due to the decision, the Departments announced steps we’re taking to conform to the court’s order and specifically, the Departments withdrew guidance documents that were based on, or that referred to, portions of the rule that the court invalidated. Yesterday we updated the guidance and reposted that to conform to the court’s order, so you'll find new guidance documents at CMS.gov. In addition, on April 5th, the Departments announced that the online IDR portal is planned to launch this week. In the near future, we plan to host a webinar to take an in-depth look at the IDR process and give a demo of the Federal IDR portal. Let's get started with the steps preceding the IDR process. There are several steps parties must go through prior to the start of the Federal IDR process. The first starts when a furnished covered item or service results in a charge for emergency items or services from an out-of-network provider or facility, for non-emergency items or services from an out-of-network provider at an in-network facility, or for air ambulance services from an out-of-network provider of air ambulance services. And each of these boxes, in the graph you see on the slide, represents a sort of step in this process. So in Step 2, within 30 calendar days, the initial payment or notice of denial of payment must be sent by the plan issuer or carrier. The plan must include with its initial payment or denial of payment, the appropriate person or office to contact if provider facility or provider of air ambulance services wishes to initiate open negotiations. They must also include a statement that if the open negotiation period does not result in an agreement on the out-of-network rate, either party to the open negotiation may initiate the Federal IDR process. The applicable qualified payment amount for each item or service must also be included by the plan. In Step 3 of this process, the parties must initiate open negotiation period, if that's the desire, within 30 business days beginning on the day the out-of-network provider receives either an initial payment or the notice of denial of payment. So, again, either party may initiate open negotiation, but both parties must in good faith actively participate in the open negotiation period and provide all the required information that's necessary if the open negotiation is unsuccessful and the parties choose to use the Federal IDR process. So, the initiating party in the open negotiation must provide written notice to the other party of its intent to negotiate. This is referred to as the open negotiation notice, and it must include information sufficient to identify the items and services that are subject to negotiation. These items that must be included are: the date that items or services were furnished; corresponding service codes for the items or services; the initial payment amount or notice of denial of payment, as applicable; an offer for the out-of-network rate; and contact information of the party sending the open negotiation. And again, these things should have been found in the payment or denial of payment by the plan. And so the Departments have received several questions regarding applicability of the Federal IDR process and the open negotiation period that we'd like to try to clarify before moving to our IDR initiation. [background noise] The first question is: How does the nominating party know if the items or services are eligible under the No Surprises Act if there's no way to know anything other than the services and CPT codes? I'll turn it over to you, Matt, for a response. [Matt Meidell] Yeah, thanks Amanda. So, with the initial payment or the denial of payment that payers are sending it’s required to include a statement that the QPA applies for the purpose of the recognized amount. And so the interim final rules require that a statement from the plan or issuer that the QPA applies for purposes of the recognized amount so that providers and facilities will understand that the plan or issuer has determined that neither an all-payer model agreement or specified state law applies for purposes of calculating a participant’s cost sharing amount, but rather this cost sharing amount would be calculated using the QPA. So the Departments expect that in most, if not all cases, the QPA will serve as the basis for determining the recognized amount, and the Federal IDR process will govern a dispute over the payment instead of a specified state law or process. [Amanda Brander] Thanks, Matt. The next question is: Many people calculate QPA differently. Does the party have to provide details on how it is calculated? [Matt Meidell] Absolutely. Thanks Amanda. So, the first surprise billing interim final rules set forth how the QPA must be calculated and require that plans and issuers make certain disclosures with each initial payment or notice of denial of payment and plans and issuers must provide additional information, upon request of the provider or facility, and this information must be provided in writing, either on paper or electronically, to a non-participating provider or emergency facility or provider of air ambulance services is applicable where the QPA serves as the recognized amount. This information should be provided by the initiating party with the notice of IDR initiation. [Amanda Brander] Thanks, Matt. And the last question in this section that we received that we will go over today is: Will the Departments be giving guidance on adding sufficient information to identify the customer and claim? Similarly, the Federal process will be available in all states for FEHB carriers, who do not have a contract with the Office of Personnel Management, that directs the carrier to use the state process. metadata.author: AJR Radiology

Christensen, PhD discusses his research that assesses the fraction of out-of-network claims for which radiologists and other hospital-based specialists can expect to at least break even when challenging payer-determined payments through the No Surprises Act independent dispute resolution process, as a measure of the process's financial viability.

metadata.title: Is This Claim Eligible for IDR? How to Check Before You File (No Surprises Act)
metadata.author: Lido
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you determine if a claim is eligible for No Surprises Act IDR? Confirm the claim falls under the federal NSA and not a state process, make sure you have the documents that prove it (CMS-1500, 835/ERA and EOB), and check the plan funding type, because that decides whether the dispute goes to federal IDR or state arbitration. Then decide if the expected award is worth filing.

In this video, Andres from Lido walks through how we run an IDR eligibility audit on a sample claim in a Lido IDR (lidoidr.com) demo environment (no real patient data).

How to check NSA / IDR eligibility:
1. Gather the claim documents: CMS-1500, 835 (ERA), EOB and insurance card.
2. Read the remark codes. N877 or N876 point to federal NSA. N871 or N944 point to a state process. N872-N875 mean the claim is closed. N943 or N885 mean the payer says the NSA doesn't apply, which is worth rechecking.
3. Check the plan funding type. Self-funded ERISA plans go to federal IDR. Fully insured plans can fall under state law, like Texas SB 1264.
4. Request missing documents before the clock runs out. Open negotiation must start within 30 business days of the initial payment or denial, and IDR must be initiated within 4 business days after negotiation ends.
5. Estimate the expected award before you file. Eligible doesn't always mean worth it.

Why this matters: 17% of federal disputes in H1 2025 were ruled ineligible, mostly over data and deadline errors. Source: [CMS LINK]


Common questions
Which remark codes mean federal IDR? N877 and N876.
The payer says the NSA doesn't apply (N943/N885). Is that final? No, recheck it against the plan type and service.
Does a self-funded plan go to federal IDR? Yes, self-funded ERISA plans go to federal IDR.

Sources: CMS No Surprises Act: https://www.cms.gov/nosurprises | Texas SB 1264: [TDI LINK]

Made by the Lido team. Lido runs No Surprises Act IDR end to end for providers, RCMs and law firms: intake, eligibility, open negotiation, IDR filing, entity selection and fees, offer and brief, and decision and payment tracking. SOC 2 Type 2 and HIPAA compliant, and we sign BAAs. Flat software cost, no share of recovery.

Get free IDR eligibility audit or book a demo: lidoidr.com

This video is educational and is not legal advice. NSA rules, deadlines and fees change, so check CMS and your state regulator before filing.

metadata.title: Out-of-network payment process under the No Surprises Act
metadata.author: American Medical Association (AMA)
metadata.shortDescription: As a follow-up to the AMA’s January webinar (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zyTkKRTBBEg) on the No Surprises Act (NSA), this webinar focuses on the payment process for physicians and other providers in surprise medical billing situations. Joel Ario and Michael Kolber from Manatt Health join the chair of the AMA Board of Trustees Bobby Mukkamala, MD, to discuss provisions of the NSA, such as the initial payment, open negotiations period and Independent Dispute Resolution process.The speakers also discuss the different ways that state regulators are choosing to enforce the NSA’s surprise billing provisions, including in those states with existing surprise medical billing laws.

metadata.title: How the No Surprises Act Impacts Employers + Navigating the IDR Payment System with Tia Goss Sawhney
metadata.author: Payerset
metadata.shortDescription:
Join Andrew Gordon as he interviews Tia Goss Sawhney, a healthcare data and policy expert, to break down the real-world impact and current issues surrounding the No Surprises Act. Get a direct look into the independent dispute resolution process and its effects on employers, providers, and patients.

In this episode…

-How the No Surprises Act protects consumers from unexpected medical bills
-The mechanics and flaws of the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process
-What Qualified Payment Amounts (QPAs) are and why they’re controversial
-How certain providers and vendors exploit loopholes for exorbitant payments
-Concrete steps employers can take to uncover and address excessive IDR costs

Or the physician could not hand me the form or the physician could hand me the form and I say and I could say, "I'm not signing this. I don't want to pay this bill." Then, if the surgery if my elective breast reduction surgery is at at an in-network facility, that physician who didn't give me the form or who gave me the form and I didn't sign it can then file for file for payment under IDR. I consider that to be a mistake. Um um an then consequence or something to be corrected in the current idea rules. Because if the patient knowingly selects a provider who's out of network, then that is not a surprise. The second scenario is Let's say with breast reductions for the moment. The physician decides that they want a assistant surgery in a assistant surgeon in the operating room. Now, the patient has not selected the assistant surgeon. So, one could argue that is a surprise. But, here's where it's not as much of a surprise. What if the assistant surgeon is from the same practice as the lead surgeon? Or what if the assistant surgeon is the buddy of the lead surgeon, but from from from another practice? Um, is that a surprise? Or is that um, or is that stuff in the operating room to maximize billings? I have seen cases, I've worked cases where where I I can and I can see it in the data where the assistant surgeon, lead surgeon are from the same practice. The anesthesiologist, um, did the surgeon select the the anesthesiologist? Or is the facility where the in-network facility where the procedure's happening knowingly putting out of network anesthesiologist into their ORs? For an elective surgery, there should be no surprise about who's in the operating room. Is Is Is that a summary of what I'm saying? Yet, the surgeon, the assistant surgeon, and the anesthesiologist, and I must I must forget the neuro monitoring company which is not so an issue for breast reduction as much as for spinal surgeries which are often elective, too. Are all are all coming into the IDR process. >> So in in a lot of these cases, Tia, that you're saying the facility itself typically would be in network and then these folks who are supporting, providing the operation at the individual level, most of them are out of network. Just so that I'm understanding it correctly. >> Well, I mean most people most surgeries most days for are are all in network. But for IDR cases where where where is one provider out of network, there's often a whole cast of care of a providers who are out of network. And and in they're interconnected with each other. They're from the same they're from the same medical practice or or they've got or they've otherwise have connections to each other. So you will you will see you will see the the the the same anesthesiologist working with the same surgeons, the same neuro monitoring company. Sometimes the neuro monitoring company may be a a sister sister group to the to the to the a medical group. >> I see. Okay, and I guess that makes sense because they would be supporting each other for these services or these operations and they probably end up working together in a variety of different aspects. But I guess could you help us understand and break down from a lead surgeon versus an assistant surgeon standpoint versus some of these other characters as you mentioned, how that plays into either exorbitant awards or this IDR process and and what people are getting paid. Help us kind of understand why these different roles are important to segment. >> Each of those out-of-network providers providing providing one or more services to that related to that surgery if the surgery is in it in-network facility. It can can go through the IDR process. And um so therefore a surgery that all the professionals combined may have been paid 20 30 40 thousand dollars can net costing 500,000 600 700 800,000. And it's it's And I've I've actually been working this data for the last few months and it's it's astounding. >> Many multiples above as you mentioned what a typical reimbursement expectation would look like. You had mentioned before that there is little or no appeal processes or kind of accountability measures in place to prevent some of these exorbitant awards from happening. Talk to us a little bit about what's there, what exists, what doesn't exist. >> Um I put a disclaimer here. I am not a lawyer. So any lawyer listening, please forgive me. Um this this but the way the NSA was written, there was it was written without any private right of action. So the IDR entity awards have the force of a government decision. They do not and they do not have private right of action. And this has been um this has been this has been challenged in the courts multiple times. So at the moment the only recourse is to go to a CMS website and write about your complaint. Well >> [clears throat] >> I shouldn't use the word complaint cuz complaint we think of complaints as something that gets filed in in a lawsuit. Um it's not that. It's like it's it's it's go to the CMS right website and write about your gripe. And with and you'll probably never hear from CMS and there and there's and um and they don't have to do anything. They may do something over time if they get enough gripes about the same topic. >> Fascinating. So for the thinking about some of these modifications going beyond just accountability or other processes that may or may not be present there. What would you say with the NSA IDR process being recently amended? What do you think with these changes that have become recently effective? Are they Are they helping or hurting the process? What are you seeing? >> It's we don't see anything yet. The the the amendments for the process were effective in August and um it will be uh next March or April before data will before um before aggregate data will come out. Um so what what the amendments did though was make the IDR process more accessible to providers. Cheaper, faster. So it does it did not it in fact address the issues that we've been talking about. It in fact one can reasonably expect it will mean that the number of IDR disputes will continue to grow. >> I did also just want to jump in and and make a comment possibly also cycle over a question to you just relative to incentives and thinking about as these supportive clinicians and characters in these different services as more of them either fall out of network or maintain out of network status, what incentive given what we've talked about today with these exorbitant awards and the massive win rates that we're seeing on the provider side, what incentive would these clinicians and folks have to maintain or work to be in network with various insurance carriers? >> Well, I firmly believe that most uh most medical professionals want to be paid a reasonable amount for their work, and they want it to be as they want the payments to be fast as fast and as frictionless as possible. So, to those to those professionals, thank you. There are, however, a subset of professionals and the and more importantly, the medical groups that they work for, who are in to maximizing revenue. And it and if that is the game that the that the medical group is playing, then then they should not be in a network. They should um and if if they if And they do and they do and they do um and they and if they can do their surgeries or procedures at an in-network facility, they then they have lots of incentive to stay out of network and play the IDR game. >> So, there was recently, just going back to as well the amendments and some of the latest things happening in the media and news relative to this this process, there was a major court decision regarding qualified payment amounts. What do you see in terms of the results of that and the decision going back to helping or hurting, pros and cons relative to where we've been and where we're going? >> The the the qualified payment amount um decision was sound. But it was But it was it was brought The case was brought by providers in Texas. And um so as such it it was it was it was to fix the problems that providers perceive with QPAs. Topping the Topping the list was the use of ghost rates. So a ghost rate is when a negotiated rate exists um between a payer and a provider, but either it's minimally it's it The expectation is that it's never going to be used. So for example, um an OBGYN medical practice that that in their contract with the provider has has negotiated rates for heart surgery. The OBGYN doctors never go to Doctors are never going to do heart surgery. But when when the when the when the rates were negotiated, what they did is they created a rate set for all possible physician services. And the OBGYN medical practice said, "Well, do these do the do the OBGYN prac- services seem to have good rates for us?" And they said yes, and they signed off on it. So their contract actually includes cardiac surgeries. But that's a ghost rate, right? The other thing is that the the decision said that the rates have to include incentive and bonus payments. So not all medical services are paid on a fee for service basis. So fee for service refers to when a specific service is is rendered, there's a specific rate for that service, and it's paid. But there could also be payments associated with quality and bonuses so that um the specific fee is paid for that service, but at the end of the year if the doctor or the medical group has has done a good job overall, they get an extra 20%. So, to get rid of ghost rates and to include the bonus payments in the market rate calculation makes sense. Um what it doesn't does not change however is is what it is that the 2019 is the base and no one can verify the 20 Well, not I shouldn't say no one. Uh most entities can't verify the 2019 rates. Since 20 Since 2022, rates have been public. So, we can I can go today um and look and see um what Aetna is paying in a market for uh for cardi- cardiac surgery services. And that's available today. It's and it was available starting in 2022. There were problems early on with the files and newer files are getting better, but we're still stuck on 2019 and we're under trending. >> So, we're still stuck on 2019 and the the idea is that we are going to have a lot more visibility and then accountability too with everybody being able to see the rates as of 2022 and the transparency and coverage files being released. That is really where we can start to see a little bit more of the rubber meets the road if I'm hearing you correctly. >> Well, and I wouldn't use the 2022 files either. I would Yeah, if I was creating the rule today, I would be using today's files. So. >> For sure. Makes a lot of sense. I want to look into the future a little bit and just thinking about where change is going to come from, where the evolution of this is going to continue to go. We talked about with no appeal process and just challenging these individual exorbitant awards. Now, how does that How are How are people How might people challenge these kind of moving forward? Talked a little bit about how folks historically have or have not been able to challenge them. What are we looking at when it comes to the system change here? >> First and foremost, let me say again, not a lawyer. Um but I we need system change. The people paying these bills, which is the largely employers, um and among employers, it's largely self-funded employers, need to understand what's happening and they need to bring forth change, in my mind. I believe, I hope, pray that there are opportunities for them to do so. So, there is no private right of action against an IDR award. But, are there other possibilities? Perhaps, but certainly one can make political noise. And I really advocate for that. And and of course, political noise is most effective when when employers and other organizations band together. So, employer groups um and coalitions um need to be on top of this. Um I believe that there may be other opportunities also. So, you can't if you can't take action against the award, can you get take action against the provider or or or the vendor, either one, because these exorbitant awards are not justifiable. So, but they put forth a justification. So, how to how to break the veil of secrecy and get those justifications? And and then if they are if they're making false statements within the justifications, that is a problem. And at which point there is action that can be taken. So, is there enough circumstantial evidence to cause to break the veil of secrecy on the justifications and see what's being written and challenge what's been written. For example, there's a case right now that Emblem Health um um ha- has against Dr. Norman Rowe um who uh who does um breast reductions. Uh he uh he he and his multiple um um provider groups uh do um breast reduction surgeries primarily in New York and New Jersey and Florida. And um Emblem Health has um has filed a ca- case against um on on just the gr- on just these grounds. Another way of going at it is for self-funded employers, states can't regulate self-funded employers. So, but it's can and do regulate providers. So, is are the providers following state law? Um so, for for example, New Jersey has a particularly has a version of the federal Stark Law that it's much more powerful than the uh federal Stark Law. And according to my read, not a lawyer, it would it it is providers cannot self-refer. So, um a a New Jersey surgeon who puts a assistant surgeon from the same practice in the operating room, that may be illegal. Not a lawyer. Um also in um in New Jersey, New Jersey has an NSA type law, no surprises um act type law that pre- predates the federal No Surprises Act. And that and that seemingly prevents surgeons who the lead surgeons who provide an elective uh service from seeking payment in excess of the of the payers normal out-of-network payment. So, if the patient selected the lead surgeon, the lead surgeon can't under Georgia law, according to my reading. So, can it could could those payments be challenged under New Jersey law? >> So, you see a lot of these D A as opportunities for employers to challenge it. Just want to make sure that I'm receiving that right and that is there anything else that you would say that employers might be able to do as it comes to and realizing how much of these awards they're funding. >> Well, if you look at the commercial market, the commercial market is just by employers. Now, it's it's not the employers often have insurance companies as their administrators. So, when Emblem brings a suit against um Norman Rowe, the the actual cases that were that that are described in the suit are actually cases um where this the surgery was provided to employees and dependents of New York City. Um of a New York City's benefit plan. So, which brings me to another point. Public funded employers are a special class. So, false claims made against public employers, whether they're state or federal, um are subject to if that if it's a federal if it's a federal employer, it's subject to a federal false claims acts. And and and many states have have a equivalent at the state level. So, when you um uh had they have state level of false claims acts. So, when to the extent that the these awards are being made against public employers, they have they have they have the power of the of the federal or state and or state false claims acts, they also have potentially the power of the of the of the state level um judiciary and um legal system. They have the power of the state attorney general. >> I was going to say, is there anything that I neglected to ask you that you'd like to share with the audience? I feel like we've had a really great conversation thinking about what's happening right now, understanding where do we stand, what's been the evolution to date, where it's kind of been breaking, what are some ways and changes that are coming down the pipe, as well as just some changes that could help to make things operate a little bit more smoother with more accountability and transparency. Anything else that you wanted to add for the audience today? >> I would encourage every every employer, not just self-funded employers, to find out exactly what they have been paying with respect to NSA IDR claims. If you don't know, you need to know. And self-funded is coming directly from your bank account. But, if you uh any employer over 50 employees, in some states 100 employees, then you're experience rated, and these exorbitant awards are going into your experience rating. So, therefore, ignorance is expensive. Go find out what you're paying, and then and then work toward change. Make political noise with politicians, with the press, via lawsuits. Um and work together. Work with the co- uh work with associations and coalitions. Um propose legislative change. Demand transparency. Demand an appeal process. >> So, I wanted to actually dive in a little bit on your comment about looking at the claims, figuring out and understanding where this is happening. Could you add a little bit of color as to I assume there's not some massive sign that says this is an NSA IDR determination or what have you when going through the claims data. So, could you help us understand how that might emerge or how that would become clear to an employer that is doing exactly that. They're diving into their claims data. They're looking through the information. What are they What are they looking for as it relates to these specific things? >> So, just excuse me if I get a little technical here. Um there are there are multiple paths to find the IDR claims or at least the probable IDR claims. Um keep in mind IDR gets initiated after an initial payment. So, what you're looking for is a claim that was paid at a reasonable amount that two to six months later typically is paid at a much larger amount. So, and the way it works is the claim is paid and then in the data you'll see that the claim the payment was reversed and then a much bigger payment was made. Um Now, when claims are reversed in a in a in a and the much bigger payment's made there is hopefully a reason code and hopefully one of the reasons code is IDR decision. That's the best case scenario. Um unfortunately, the data that's often distributed doesn't include reason codes. So, if your data doesn't have reason codes, you're still looking for that pattern. Was a Was there a claim paid that several months later was repaid at a much, much larger amount? And that that is a clue to probable idea. >> So, with these claim adjustment reason codes and the possibility that those codes are there, but you said that sometimes they're not, I don't want to open too much of a can of worms, but I am curious, why might the data streams that folks are reviewing or having access to not be able to include these reason codes? And is it that sometimes they're just not included in it? Is it that these codes are often times there? They're just behind the scenes and not not commonly shared in the feed that goes to, whether it's employers or the folks who are reviewing these claims on behalf of employers? How would you How would you explain share that? >> Oh, well, the codes are definitely there in the claims administrator system, which is often an insurance company's system. Um so, but yes, it's not distributed out um because remember historically claims data wasn't shared with employers and and now that it's being shared, it's it the exact fields that get shared are a matter of negotiation and maybe no one and so the reason reason codes um have not been part of the request, a part of what's been distributed. Um so um but they they are available, they can be produced. >> I see. And so, just also to recap for the audience and to make a clarification, these exorbitant awards, when they're being paid there is no added expense to the member, to the patient when these determinations and these claim adjustment reason codes are put in to say, "Well, the clinician was paid $5,000, 6 months down the pipe that's changed to $50,000. My out-of-pocket as a patient on that specific service is not going to waiver. Is that correct? >> It will. I mean, it could actually benefit the patient. Um because if it was originally paid as an out-of-network claim, remember, it originally it gets paid initially as It could It could initially it could have been paid one of two ways. Initially it could It could have been paid as an out-of-network claim adjudicated as an in-network adjudicated at the in-network level. Um but at which point it's It's not going to It's It's probably not going to change. But in it It would initially it could have been adjudicated or alternatively it could have been adjudicated as an out-of-network claim at an out-of-network level. So, in that case, um then, um then, you know, the patient could actually benefit. And you might say, "But wait, why would, given the NSA, why wouldn't the Why wouldn't the payer have adjudicated it up front at the in-network level?" The other thing that has been found and documented is that claims go into the have gone into IDR as substantial percentage, in fact, of the IDR claims that go into IDR and have awards are, in fact, claims that should never have gone in. So, the payer may have adjudicated quite appropriately as an out-of-network claim, but it went into IDR, at which point and and the IDR entity decided that IDR applied, at which point it has to be re-adjudicated as an in-network claim. >> So, there wouldn't be a situation or at least it wouldn't become into have a situation then where from a patient cost-sharing perspective, they're actually going to be expected to pay more or they would be impacted in a negative manner. >> Overall, patients are being well protected, but payers are not being well protected. >> The reason why I'm asking these questions to you is as we're familiar with the the cases against Wells Fargo and Johnson & Johnson and just some of these other major companies that was originally brought a lot of the times by employees for exorbitant amounts of money paid or not being able to get competitive rates for certain things. I mean, as we talk about fiduciary liability and for the audience who may or may not be familiar with the Consolidated Appropriations Act originally in 2021 and has since been going through a lot of updates as well to strengthen it. It's very important for people, the employers who are funding and and providing for and looking over and offering competitive benefits to their people to make sure that they're getting the best rates possible and to make sure that they're really targeting and finding value in those contracts and in the partnerships and the claims that they're paying. How does the IDR process impact that? When we talk about fiduciary responsibility and then you have these exorbitant awards that they're paying. Granted, a lot of it is not hurting the patient necessarily as we said, but when you think about the high expense of health care and the damage to salaries or benefits because of this larger and larger expense growing on the employer's book of a book of accounting book, how do you how do you kind of justify or where does or does not fiduciary liability play a role in this conversation? >> Once again, I'm not a lawyer and the courts have been working on this. I would argue that it's a very important part of fiduciary responsibility. Um, let's look at it from a few perspectives. First of all, a lot of times employee employee contributions um, employee premiums for their benefits are are I are pegged at a at a percentage of the expected costs. So, if So, the if it's 20% of the expected total cost, then every dollar extra that's being paid is being paid 20 cents of that is being paid by employees in their employee premiums. So, even even if the employee is being protected vis-a-vis their cost sharing, they're paying for it in their premiums. Second of all, total cost of care affects what employers can pay in wages. It also affects whether an employer can even offer a plan. So, I mean, do we want to be paying three-quarters of a million dollars for for the for all the professionals who who attended a surgery where the you know, they reasonably collectively should have been paid under $50,000? Um, you know, that's so $700,000 spread. Well, that's that's more employees that employers paying that that that's more employees that an employer could could could hire. That's more raises that employer could give. Um, sudden spikes in in healthcare benefits, which benefit costs, which a lot of employers are experience right now, may determine whether they even continue to offer a plan or whether or whether they change the cost sharing on the plan or whether they up the percentage of the plan costs that the employee has to pay for premiums. I mean, ultimately, ultimately, you know, employees pay. >> Bringing this home for us, talking about how we've seen cases grow year-over-year. We've seen these awards be dozens or hundreds of times higher than fair market rates for services. Thinking about what's coming down the chain, anything else that you want to share as we round this out in terms of what people should be aware of and what their action items should be specifically for sounds like employers and policy makers and also few other stakeholders. >> My very short summary is get involved. Look at the data, get involved, ask questions, challenge. Uh there's There are many other topics I could talk about um including um including more details of IDR. So, I hope you will invite me back for further discussions. >> For sure, absolutely. It's been a really good conversation. Now, for those of uh for those in the audience who are interested in reaching out to you to continue the conversation privately, where would you direct them? >> Um reach out to me by email. My email address is Tia G as in Tia Ghose Sawhney S A W H N E Y @tsteushealth.com. >> Excellent. Tia, thanks so much for coming on today. It was a pleasure having you. >> Thank you, Angel. My pleasure. >> That's a wrap for this episode of The Price of Healthcare. We appreciate you tuning in and we'll see you on the next one. >> [music]

metadata.title: Panel - Fixing the No Surprises Act’s Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) Process
metadata.author: Coalition for Affordable Hospitals
metadata.shortDescription:
The current arbitration process for determining out-of-network payments threatens healthcare affordability, leaving employers and union health funds on the hook for exponentially increasing out-out-network costs. Experts will dissect IDR’s unintended consequences and explain how purchasers can work with advocates to demand regulatory relief—and ultimately, reform. 

Speakers:
Melanie Evans is a reporter and producer for Tradeoffs. She spent eight years at The Wall Street Journal, where she reported on hospital costs, healthcare quality and the Covid-19 pandemic. Before the Journal, Melanie covered health policy and business for Modern Healthcare and began her career at the Duluth News Tribune in Minnesota, her home state. Her coverage has won awards from the New York Press Club, Society for Advancing Business Editing and Writing and Association of Health Care Journalists. She lives in New York.

Maya Holmes is the Senior Director of Health Policy for the Culinary Health Fund, a multi-employer Taft-Hartley Fund that provides health benefits to workers represented by the Culinary Worker, Bartender, and Stage Technician unions in Las Vegas, Nevada, and their dependents, approximately 145,000 lives.

As the health care lobbyist for the AFL-CIO, Tom Leibfried works with Congress to improve health care coverage for America’s working families. His work focuses on employment- based health insurance, the Affordable Care Act, Medicare, Medicaid, and the Children’s Health Insurance Program.

To learn more visit our website: https://coalitionforaffordablehospitals.org

metadata.title: “No Surprises Act  The New Independent Dispute Resolution Process”   CPE Webinar
metadata.author: PYA, PC
metadata.shortDescription:
The Federal No Surprises Act took effect on January 1, 2022. It includes such provisions as balance billing protections and the payment of defined out-of-network services using the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process.

PYA Principal Bob Paskowski and Senior Manager Dave Hall, along with Crux Strategies CEO Tim Gary, provided background on the No Surprises Act, the new IDR process, and some practical experiences based on initial learnings. Specifically, they provided:

A No Surprises Act overview
The establishment of the qualifying payment amount
A step-by-step overview of the IDR process
Initial learnings
Potential IDR strategies


This complimentary one-hour webinar took place on September 28, 2022.

This webinar is part of PYA’s twice-monthly “Healthcare Regulatory Roundup” series in which experts from across the firm provide practical insights on the latest regulatory developments.

To learn more about our “Healthcare Regulatory Roundup” series visit us at: https://www.pyapc.com/healthcare-regulatory-roundup-webinars/
To download the slides from this webinar visit us at: https://www.pyapc.com/insights/webinar-cpe-hcrr36-no-surprises-act-the-new-independent-dispute-resolution-process/

To learn more about PYA: https://www.pyapc.com/
To learn more about Crux Strategies: https://cruxstrategies.com/

metadata.title: Trends & Insights from 2024 CMS IDR Data | What’s Changing in No Surprises Act Disputes
metadata.author: Zelis Healthcare
metadata.shortDescription:
The 2024 CMS Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) public use file reveals major shifts across the No Surprises Act landscape — and the implications are significant for both payers and providers. This video breaks down the most important trends, challenges, and regulatory considerations emerging from the latest federal data.

Key Insights from 2024 CMS IDR Data:
• 115% increase in disputes, signaling continued strain on the IDR system
• Ongoing delays in dispute resolution that impact payer and provider operations
• A growing perception of a provider-friendly environment within IDR outcomes
• Concentration of disputes among a small group of high-volume organizations
• Early signs of improvement in case closure rates, following recent system enhancements
• Persistent inconsistencies among certified IDR entities, complicating forecasting and strategy
• Forthcoming regulatory updates aimed at addressing gaps in process clarity and consistency

As IDR volumes rise and the regulatory landscape evolves, organizations must adopt a more strategic, data-driven approach to managing No Surprises Act disputes. This video explores how upcoming changes may reshape workflows — and why strategic partnerships are becoming essential to success.

Learn More About Navigating NSA & IDR with Zelis: https://bit.ly/4alaJzU
