segments.text: Unger: Hello.
This is the AMA Update video and podcast.
Today's topic is what physicians need
to know about the No Surprises Act.
We're joined today by Emily Carroll, a senior attorney
for the AMA's Advocacy Resource Center in Chicago and George
Cox, the AMA's director of legislative counsel
in Washington, DC.
I'm Todd Unger, AMA's chief experience officer in Chicago.
Emily, George, thanks for joining us today.
Carroll: Thanks for having us.
Cox: Glad to be here.
Thank you.
Unger: Emily, you joined us in December
to talk about the No Surprises Act.
And I know a lot's happened since then
but let's just kind of start with a baseline, very
quick, high-level overview of the act
and what it's supposed to accomplish.
Carroll: Great.
Thanks, Todd.
So the No Surprises Act was signed into law
back in December of 2020 and it took effect January 1
of this year.
It was intended to address unexpected gaps
in insurance coverage that result
in surprise medical bills when patients unknowingly
obtain medical services from physicians
and other providers outside of their health care network.
The bill prohibits out-of-network billing
by physicians, hospitals and other providers in emergency
situations, and then also in certain non-emergency
situations at in-network hospitals
when a patient might have not typically been
able to pick their provider.
The law also sets up a payment process
for physicians and the plan potentially
ending with arbitration.
So it's really important for physicians
to be aware of these changes and the new prohibitions
and requirements in their out-of-network billing.
Unger: Well, I know the AMA supports the goal of the act
to protect patients from surprise bills
but there have been some concern about the independent dispute
resolution process that's outlined within the act.
Can you remind us of how that resolution
process is supposed to work and what the concerns are, Emily?
Carroll: Great.
Yeah, thanks, Todd.
You're right.
The AMA has long supported protections
for patients against surprise medical billing.
And we have always thought they should be kept out
of the middle of those disputes between physicians
and other health care providers and plans.
So when the law was being debated,
we did support those protections and worked
to help set up a independent dispute resolution
process between the plans and the providers.
The idea was that this arbitration process would
be structured in a baseball-style arbitration
way, where each physician or provider would submit
their own offer with supporting information
and the plan would do the same.
And the arbiter would essentially
pick one of the offers.
As the implementing rules have been released,
there has been a emphasis by the administration
to really focus on what is called the qualifying payment
amount, which is supposed to be the in-network median rate
for physicians or other providers for that service
in that area.
And there's been less of an emphasis
on these other supporting factors,
like the complexity of care or the education and experience
of the physician.
When the first set of rules was released,
there was generally no way or very little way
that some of that supporting information
could be used in the decisions by the arbiter,
and the qualifying payment amount sort of
became the de facto payment rate for physicians.
And as the additional rules have rolled out
over the last couple of years, which
I'm sure we'll talk more about, unfortunately, the emphasis
has continued on that qualifying payment amount, which
essentially creates a de facto payment
rate not only in arbitration but in the market in general
for physician services.
So we're very concerned about the way this arbitration
process has been established.
Unger: And we'll return to talk more about how, then,
the AMA has been advocating for a resolution
around that process.
George, let's ask you a question here.
Back in August of this year, the HHS Labor and Treasury
departments issued final rules addressing
some of these issues.
What were the highlights of those decisions?
Cox: Yes, so on August 19, the departments
issued final rules addressing the provisions
of the independent dispute resolution payment process.
These rules and the supporting FAQs
responded to several concerns directly raised
by the AMA and other state and specialty federation members.
First, they clarified that the parties initiating
open negotiations are always permitted
to use the standard federal initiation notice.
That is, a plan cannot require a physician to use
the plan's proprietary portals to initiate open negotiations.
The rules also reflect the language
that the AMA and other physician associations
advocated for to address the lack of transparency
when a plan downcodes a service and calculates a QPA based
on the down service code.
Now if a plan downcodes a claim, it
must provide additional information
on why the claim was downcoded, including
an explanation of why it was downcoded
and which service codes were adjusted.
This will help physicians in the open negotiation and the IDR
process, primarily because without this information,
physicians are disadvantaged in dispute payment processes
since the QPA doesn't reflect the original claim.
The rules also address our concerns
that non-negotiated contracted rates, also known
as ghost rates, were being included in the QPA calculation
and contributing to the artificially low QPAs.
Plans must now calculate a median contracted rate
separately for each specialty when the plan's contracted
rates for service codes vary based on physician specialty.
One other important change I'll highlight
is a direct result, also, of the successful Texas Medical
Association's lawsuit on the interim final rule.
As a result of the court decision in that lawsuit,
the final rules removed the rebuttable presumption
requirement whereby an arbiter presumed
that the qualifying payment amount is
the appropriate out-of-network rate.
The arbiter now must select the party's offer
that best represents the value of the service
after considering the QPA and information submitted
by the parties.
As we've considered this new language,
however, we're very concerned that it
falls far short of what Congress intended and still weighs
the QPA to the advantage of health plans.
Unger: Well, these are all positive steps
that you've talked about.
But, obviously, as you said, still some concerns.
Let's talk a little bit more about the remaining challenges.
I know that the AMA has taken legal action in response.
George, how are we approaching this from a legal perspective?
Cox: Sure.
So just to take a quick step back,
when the interim final rule was released last fall,
it included a provision that the IDR entity, or the arbiter,
presumed that the QPA is the correct out-of-network payment
rate, and required it to select the offer that
was closest to the QPA, unless there was credible information
that the QPA was materially different than what was
otherwise an appropriate rate.
The AMA expressed significant concern
with this rebuttable presumption that
was in favor of the QPA and the impact
that it would have on physician's ability
to negotiate fair contracts with health plans.
So the AMA joined with the American Hospital Association
in a lawsuit that we filed in the Federal District Court
in the District of Columbia here in DC asking the court
to vacate this rebuttable presumption that weighed
in favor of health plans as contrary
to the clear intent of Congress.
Around the same time, the Texas Medical Association
filed a similar lawsuit in the U.S. District Court
for the Eastern District of Texas.
In February of this year, the Texas Court
found in favor of the TMA case and vacated
the provision in the IFR, or the Interim Final
Rule, that created the rebuttable presumption in favor
of the QPA in the IDR process.
As a result, the departments had to go back and rewrite
the IDR regulations, which are reflected now
in the final rules.
Thus, since the final rules vacate the provisions
in the interim final rule that were the basis of the AMA
and the AHA's lawsuit, our lawsuit became moot.
However, as I mentioned a moment ago,
the final rule still, in our opinion,
depart from the intent of Congress
and still place a thumb on the scale in favor of health plans.
So on September 22, the Texas Medical Association
filed a new lawsuit in the same federal court in Texas
arguing that the final rules still
suffer from the same problems as the interim final rules.
And we wholeheartedly agree.
And rather than file a new lawsuit of our own
in the DC Federal Court, we decided,
along with the American Hospital Association,
that we would be a force multiplier in the Texas case
and make our voice heard by filing an amicus brief.
In the latest final rule, CMS explains
that the QPA presumably already factors in most other data,
and that, therefore, the IDR entity, or the arbiter,
is directed not to, quote, double count or consider
all other data that were required to be considered
by Congress unless they find that a physician demonstrates
that their data was so exceptional and unusual that it
wasn't already included in the QPA calculation.
The final rule also requires arbiters
to provide written decisions to the departments
at the end of the IDR process.
And if the IDRE, or the arbiter, does not
choose the offer that's closest to the QPA,
it must include a detailed explanation
of additional considerations relied upon,
whether the information submitted by the parties
was credible and the basis upon which the IDRE determined
that the credible information demonstrated that the QPA is
materially different from the appropriate out-of-network
rate.
We emphasize in our amicus brief that these requirements, viewed
in whole, looks more like a fist rather than
a thumb on the scale in favor of the health plans.
So, in other words, when all of the extra statutory
requirements are viewed as a whole,
we argue that the final rules elevate the QPA
above the other factors that Congress requires the arbiter
to consider, and that it's in violation
of the plain word of the statute.
Unger: So still a lot of work to be done here on that dispute
resolution process.
Emily, from what we understand, a lot
of concern about the final rule in this
regard from private practices.
Can you give us a little more information about the concern
here about how this will impact private practices
if things don't change?
Carroll: Absolutely.
So, as you mentioned, the QPA, because of the weight
that the rules give this QPA or this median in-network rate,
it becomes the rate that not only out-of-network physicians
are paid in just that independent dispute resolution
process but it becomes the rate that enters into contract
negotiations for all physicians when
they're having these negotiations with plans
to be in-network.
We've been hearing not only that these rates have been--
contract rates that are offered to physicians
are lowering as a result of these final rules
and the interim final rules before that
but we're also hearing a lot about physician practices being
cut from networks as a result of this.
So the plans can take it or leave it
in terms of contracts with physicians at this point
and still have the benefits of having
patients receive in-network rates for their care.
So without greater protections in place and without a more
robust IDR process, we're going to continue to see
these contracting issues.
And particularly for small or independent practices,
the results are going to be long-lasting.
These are often plans that they've
had multi-year, decades-long contracts with that they're now
seeing rate cuts or removals from these networks.
And the long-term impact on patients is an access issue.
Some of these practices will simply not
be able to keep their doors open.
And we're not going to be seeing in-network access for patients
in the long run.
Unger: Those are huge concerns.
And, obviously, much more work continuing to address these.
Emily, when you look into the future,
do you expect more provisions as the No Surprises Act evolves?
Carroll: Yeah.
The No Surprises Act was not actually
just focused on surprise billing,
although that's been the focus for many over the last year.
But there were a lot of other provisions
in the law that passed that are in the process
are being implemented now.
Several of those focus on price transparency requirements.
We saw implementation last year of a price transparency
requirement, which has been sort of dubbed the good faith
estimate provisions for either self-pay or uninsured patients.
And this requires physicians or other health care providers
who are scheduling care with a patient who
is self-pay to collect estimates from other providers involved
in the care and submit that information to the patient
prior to care being provided.
The AMA certainly supports price transparency and providing
patients with meaningful price information
prior to care so they can make informed cost decisions.
But it's really important that as these provisions are
implemented, we're not putting unnecessary administrative
burdens on already strapped physician practices
to do some of these price transparency requirements,
especially when lots of states have price transparency
requirements such as these in place already.
So some of these rules may be duplicative.
And next year, we're anticipating the implementation
of what's being called the Advanced Explanation
of Benefits Provision.
So this is the sort of sister provision to that good faith
estimate one that implements price transparency
and a cost information prior to care for insured patients.
So we're anticipating a lot of comment letters
over the next couple of months on these provisions.
And we're also really advocating for meaningful price
transparency that really recognizes that all of this
is happening in a much larger ecosystem of data exchange
and the workflow of physician practice,
and really urging the administration
to keep the administrative burden that's being placed
on physician practices in mind as they implement
these provisions.
Unger: And I think that's just a really important point.
You can really take away a couple of key things here.
One is this is very complicated.
And, two, just how important the role of organized medicine,
AMA, the Federation are in being able to address
some of these things, particularly
in the legal front.
Got to be very confusing to physicians.
George, how do we help physicians
navigate what are these really complicated issues?
Cox: Well, we've put together a number of documents
and guidance materials that help physicians understand
the implementation of the No Surprises Act.
This includes a summary of the August final rule
that we've been talking about, as well as
the toolkit that walks through the steps
that physicians or their practice managers
need to take when disputing and out-of-network payment.
And we're currently in the process
of updating our toolkit and other resources
to reflect the changes that were made in the final rule.
And we're going to be posting these revised
resources on our website when they're finalized.
Also, I should point out that the Centers
for Medicare and Medicaid Services,
as well as the Department of Labor, also
has resources for physicians on their websites.
And the link to those resources are in our toolkit.
And we've also held two national webinars on the No Surprises
Act implementation.
The first is on the implementation itself
and the second one focuses on the out-of-network payment
process under the law.
Those are currently on our website.
We also continue to revise our resources
and create new ones as developments arise.
And that will include the changes,
if there are any, to the final rule that
relate to the independent dispute resolution process
as a result of the outcome of the current lawsuit in Texas.
Unger: Thank you so much, George.
All the links for the resources that George talked about,
you can find them in the description of this episode.
And, again, what a great example of the power
of organized medicine and just how important
it is to support the AMA and your state societies.
That wraps up today's episode.
Again, thank you, Emily, George, for all the
work that you and the advocacy team at the AMA
are doing on this important concern for physicians
and patients.
We'll be back with another AMA video and podcast soon.
You can find all our videos and podcasts
at ama-assn.org/podcasts.
Thanks for joining us today.
Please take care.
[MUSIC PLAYING]

segments.text: You went to the emergency room. You had
no choice. Now you're holding a bill for
thousands of dollars and your insurance
is refusing to pay. If this happened to
you, what I'm about to tell you could
save you everything. If you're dealing
with a denied ER bill right now, I
created a complete insurance appeal kit
with every letter and template you need.
Link is in the description. Get it
before you pay a single dollar. In 2022,
a federal law called the No Surprises
Act went into effect. It was designed
specifically for situations like yours.
Here's what it says. If you go to an
emergency room, even an out-of-network
one, your insurance company cannot make
you pay more than your in-network
cost-sharing amount. Not more. Not even
if the hospital was out of network. Not
even if you had no time to check.
Emergencies don't come with a directory.
The law recognizes that. Your insurance
company is counting on the fact that you
don't. There are three common ways
insurers illegally deny ER claims.
First, they claim the visit wasn't a
true emergency. Under federal law, the
standard is the prudent layperson
standard. Meaning if a reasonable person
in your situation would have gone to the
ER, it qualifies. Your subjective fear
of a serious condition is enough.
Second, they apply out-of-network rates
to an emergency visit. This is illegal
under the No Surprises Act for most
plans. Period. Third, balance billing.
This is when a provider bills you
directly for the difference between
their charge and what insurance paid.
For emergency services, this is banned
under federal law. Here is what you do
immediately. Step one, do not pay the
bill yet. Paying can be interpreted as
accepting the charges.
Step two, request an itemized bill from
the hospital. Billing errors are found
in up to 80% of medical bills. Errors
alone can reduce or eliminate your
balance. Step three, file an appeal with
your insurance company citing the No
Surprises Act by name. Your letter must
state that the visit meets the prudent
layperson standard and that federal law
requires in-network cost-sharing to
apply. Step four, if the insurer
refuses, file a complaint with the
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid
Services. This is free and often
resolves the issue without further
escalation. Step five, request an
external review. An independent reviewer
will assess whether federal law was
followed. This process works, but it
only works if you start it before the
deadline. You have 120 days from the
date of the denial to file your appeal
in most cases. The clock is already
running. The insurance appeal kit in the
description has the exact letter
template for ER denials, the No
Surprises Act language to quote, and a
step-by-step checklist. Click the link
below. Do not pay that bill until you've
read it.

metadata.title: No Surprises Act: Nearly 30% of Awards Unpaid by Insurers
metadata.author: Long Reads, Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
Health insurers led by Anthem are refusing to pay arbitration awards won by doctors under the No Surprises Act, leaving nearly 30 percent unpaid since 2024. Learn why insurers say the system is being gamed, how providers are squeezed, and what Congress may do.

Based on “Flouting Consumer Law, Insurers Refuse to Pay Medical Bills for Emergency Care” · The New York Times, November 3, 2026

Chapters
0:00 Opening
0:19 A Faucet Shut Off
2:25 How the Law Works
4:45 The Unpaid Awards
7:02 The Insurers' Case
10:50 No Enforcement
13:20 Providers Squeezed
15:55 Anthem and HaloMD
17:46 Fixing the Law
19:32 Bottom Line

Long Reads, Explained: the day's most important long reads, narrated and illustrated.
Subscribe for new explainers every day: https://www.youtube.com/@LongReadsExplained?sub_confirmation=1

#Healthcare #Insurance #Congress

segments.text: A federal law meant to protect patients from surprise medical bills has turned
into a standoff, and health insurers are now simply refusing to pay what
arbitrators say they owe. The New York Times found that nearly thirty percent of
those awards have gone unpaid since twenty twenty-four.
Start with one story. Flight for Life is a medical helicopter service in southeastern
Wisconsin. Over the past two years it has airlifted car crash victims,
premature babies, and adults struggling to breathe to hospitals across the region.
Anthem, the major health insurer, covered dozens of those patients.
But it has refused to pay two point one million dollars that it owes the company
for their helicopter rides.
The amounts due for each flight range from nine thousand three hundred eighty-two
dollars to sixty-two thousand three hundred seventy-three dollars.
Anthem had historically paid its bills. Then, late last year, it suddenly stopped.
Leif Erickson, Flight for Life's executive director, described the moment plainly.
In his words, it was like a faucet they just shut off.
Anthem's explanation, which comes later in the story,
is that the medevac service broke the arbitration system's complex procedural
rules. Flight for Life disputes that. But first,
it helps to understand how the money is supposed to flow.
The Times frames Anthem's willful nonpayment as the latest in a cascade of
unintended consequences. They flow from a widely supported law that was meant to
protect patients from surprise medical bills.
That law, which took effect in twenty twenty-two,
calls for arbitrators to decide appropriate levels of reimbursement.
It has already triggered millions of disputes between medical providers and
insurers. Doctors have prevailed overwhelmingly,
sometimes winning settlements far above the usual insurer rates.
And now, fed up with what they consider unfair outcomes,
insurers are fighting back in the bluntest way available.
They are refusing to pay.
The law is called the No Surprises Act.
Congress enacted it with a large bipartisan majority.
Its purpose was to make sure patients never got excessive bills in situations,
like emergencies, where they could not choose their doctors.
Here is how it handles a disagreement, in three steps.
First, when a health care provider and an insurer cannot agree on a price,
each side submits a proposed dollar amount.
Second, an arbitrator reviews the two proposals and decides which one is most
reasonable. There is no splitting the difference.
Third, the insurer is required to pay that amount within thirty days.
And billing the patient for anything beyond it is prohibited.
That last part is the consumer protection at the heart of the law.
Lawmakers expected this system to be used rarely.
They expected it to produce reasonable payments,
settling the occasional hard case.
That is not what happened. Doctors and other providers have swamped arbitrators
with millions of claims. Those claims are often for amounts that far exceed what is
customarily paid for a service. And providers
have won the vast majority of their cases.
The Times gives three examples of what winning can look like.
The largest is four hundred forty thousand dollars for a breast reduction.
Another is one hundred twenty-five thousand dollars,
for assisting on prostate surgery.
And the third is seventy-three thousand dollars for an ankle X-ray.
Sums like these are the backdrop to everything insurers are now doing.
Insurers first tried the conventional routes.
They sued doctors, and they lobbied Congress to change the law.
Their argument was that the large awards and lopsided results are driving up health
insurance premiums for everyone.
But Washington has moved slowly. So insurers adopted a simpler strategy.
They just decline to pay. That brings us to the numbers on how often that happens.
A major medical billing firm called HaloMD gave The Times an analysis of four hundred
thousand arbitration awards. It shows that nearly thirty percent of awards have gone
unpaid since twenty twenty-four.
Anthem's nonpayment rate was the highest by far, at seventy-four percent.
Other large insurers, including Cigna, UnitedHealthcare and Aetna,
have also declined to pay a significant portion,
though the article does not give their exact rates.
And Anthem is accelerating. This year, according to the HaloMD data,
it has not paid eighty-three percent of arbitration claims.
That is a substantial jump from previous years.
These figures come with caveats, and the article spells them out.
First, the four hundred thousand claims make up around two-thirds of the total
cases HaloMD has won since twenty twenty-four.
Second, the data set only includes cases where
HaloMD could reliably track payments to doctors.
Third, the source itself is controversial.
Health plans, Anthem among them, criticize HaloMD for business tactics that exploit
the arbitration system and result in large payouts.
Finally, only one of the major insurers The Times contacted disputed the accuracy
of the data. A Cigna spokeswoman said a significantly smaller share went unpaid in
twenty twenty-six than the Halo data showed.
The result, the article says, is dysfunction and lawlessness in a system
that a growing number of lawmakers and administration officials say needs
changing. Katie Keith directs Georgetown
University's Center for Health Policy and the Law.
She put it this way. The providers are succeeding in what feel like egregious
award levels, and then the insurers are also doing some of this egregious behavior
by not paying. But there's not accountability on either side.
So how do insurers justify their side of it?
Most large health insurers told The Times they have a policy.
They will not pay an award if they believe the claim should never have qualified for
arbitration. That holds even when the arbitrator determined it was eligible.
That is the reasoning in the Flight for Life case.
Anthem says it will not pay because the medevac service violated the system's
complex procedural rules. Flight for Life disputes that assessment.
Ariel Bayewitz is vice president of health economics at Elevance Health,
Anthem's parent company. He said the company believes strongly in paying
eligible awards on time. But Anthem estimates that most claims moving through
arbitration should have been found ineligible,
either because they broke the rules or because
they fell outside the consumer protection law.
Bayewitz summed up the insurer view in a single sentence.
More providers are submitting ineligible cases, he said,
because ineligible cases aren't being dismissed like they should be.
In other words, from Anthem's side, the problem starts with arbitrators letting
bad claims through, and nonpayment is the response.
To weigh that argument, it helps to know what makes a claim eligible at all.
The law limits access to the system in several ways.
First, it sets a series of deadlines and procedures that doctors need to follow.
Second, cases where the patient has a government plan,
like Medicare or Medicaid, are not eligible.
Third, neither are situations where the doctor
already has a contract with the health plan.
And insurers raise one more complaint. They say they sometimes see doctors
winning twice for the same care. First in a state-level system for resolving billing
disputes, and then again through federal arbitration.
Josh Goldberg is executive director of health policy at Health Care Service
Corporation, which covers twenty-seven million
people through six Blue Cross affiliates.
On double awards, he was blunt. We're not going to pay it twice, he said.
This is just a situation where we're a
little bit between a rock and a hard place.
Katie Keith, the Georgetown expert, rejects the premise.
The insurer, she said, is not the final decider.
She described Anthem's strategy as high-risk,
because it flouts binding arbitration decisions.
Insurers answer that the system is tilted.
Arbitrators are paid a flat fee for each dispute they resolve.
But if they rule a case ineligible, they earn nothing.
So, insurers argue, the incentive pushes arbitrators to find claims eligible.
Smaller health plans are withholding too, in cases where they think the award is
unreasonable. Some even have form letters they
send to doctors whose awards they won't pay.
One such letter comes from EmblemHealth, a New York insurer.
It declines to pay an award ninety-nine times the plan's usual rate for a breast
reconstruction. The determination, it says, is not merely high.
It is legally defective.
Alex Gomez, a spokesman for the plan,
said EmblemHealth has recently observed a significant increase in very high-dollar
claims, which it is actively reviewing and challenging as appropriate.
So what happens to an unpaid award? Formally, the answer is clear.
A spokeswoman for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services,
which oversees the arbitration system, said
the law always requires insurers to pay.
In practice, it is murkier. Doctors and air ambulance companies have filed
hundreds of lawsuits to enforce arbitrators' decisions.
But three federal appeals courts have ruled that the No Surprises Act does not
include a right to sue.
Stephen Ware, a law professor at the University of Kansas, explained why.
Unlike most arbitration situations, he said, the No Surprises Act does not
explain how a ruling can be enforced.
One appeals court decision suggested the government itself could sue to force
insurers to pay. So far, the Trump
administration has not exercised that power.
The law does give the government a tool.
It authorizes the Trump administration to fine health insurers one hundred dollars
for each day they do not pay an arbitration award.
So far, it has not issued a single penalty.
Doctors have sent hundreds of complaints about unpaid awards to the Centers for
Medicare and Medicaid Services. Those The Times spoke with said they had rarely
received a response. Health plans say the agency has also failed to respond to
thousands of their complaints about ineligible claims.
Thomas LaGreca, a partner at Callagy Law, which files claims for providers,
estimates that twenty-seven percent of his clients' claims remain unpaid six months
after arbitration decisions. There has to be some enforcement, he said.
Spokespeople for both the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and the
Labor Department declined to respond to questions
about why they had not issued penalties.
In July, a Trump administration spokesman told The Times that the system is being
gamed by doctors, and that the government was actively working to clean it up.
But the administration has not yet announced any policy changes.
Meanwhile, the people waiting on the money are feeling it.
Doctors say nonpayment makes it hard to manage their practices.
Some who built their businesses around the arbitration system and its high payouts
have taken on debt to stay afloat.
Doctor Jennifer Raley is a managing partner at Wake Emergency Physicians,
which serves patients in central and eastern North Carolina.
She said the practice has one point two million dollars in outstanding awards.
It won one thousand thirty-two arbitration cases in twenty twenty-five.
Its average award was around four times what insurers typically pay.
And in January, the practice had to take out a line of credit to make payroll.
Doctor Raley framed it in terms of the staff on her payroll.
We just want to get paid, she said, what we
need to pay the people who saw the patients.
For an air ambulance company, the consequences can reach all the way to
whether a community keeps its service.
PHI, a national air ambulance company, recently closed a base in Red Bluff,
California, a small city between Sacramento and the Oregon border.
Its chief executive, Scott McCarty, cited sixteen point three million dollars in
outstanding payments from Anthem as the cause.
In his words, the insurance companies cannot unilaterally decide to breach a
federal law if they don't like the end result.
That's essentially what they are doing.
Anthem tells it differently. Spokeswoman Janey Kiryluik said the insurer was
actively trying to bring PHI Air Medical into its network.
But she said the company had requested unreasonably high rates,
typically asking for fifty-six thousand dollars per flight in arbitration.
Doctor Brian McHugh is a neurosurgeon from Long Island, New York.
According to federal data, he often wins arbitration awards that are forty times
higher than what Anthem typically pays.
He has repeatedly received letters from Anthem challenging those awards on the
grounds that they are too expensive.
He said other doctors at his practice have stopped seeing Anthem patients.
For its part, Anthem said it does not use a financial threshold as a basis for
holding payment, and that it no longer uses the letter Doctor McHugh received.
Anthem's position has shifted over time. Like all major insurers,
it supported the No Surprises Act when Congress was writing it during the first
Trump administration.
But over the last six years, its executives soured on the arbitration
system, saying it encourages abusive billing.
Many of the high awards, the article notes, have been for scheduled procedures,
not the emergency care the law was written to address.
Anthem defends its nonpayment as intentional.
In a thirteen-page report, it estimated that sixty percent of its cases decided by
arbitrators should never have qualified.
This year, it has not paid eighty-three percent of arbitration claims.
And according to documents The Times obtained, the Labor Department,
which oversees large employer health plans,
is investigating Anthem's failure to pay. Anthem says it is cooperating.
Insurers say HaloMD, the firm behind the data, is part of the problem.
They say it typically submits unreasonably high bids,
sometimes winning one hundred thirteen times typical insurer payments.
It has also been accused of filing a high volume of ineligible claims.
Five insurers have sued Halo, accusing it of fraud.
Three of those suits, including Anthem's, were dismissed in federal court,
on the grounds that courts can't review arbitrators' decisions.
HaloMD spokesman Patrick Velliky pushed back.
He called the insurers' lawsuits an attempt to intimidate physicians and
clinicians out of seeking fair and sustainable reimbursement.
With both sides dug in, attention is turning to Congress.
Congress has recently taken greater interest in reform,
with a Senate committee hosting round table meetings and new legislation in the
House. Three lawmakers stand out.
First, Representative Greg Murphy, Republican of North Carolina,
who worked as a urologist before running for office.
He admits there are problems on both sides.
But he believes the majority of abuses come from insurers who do not pay,
and he has introduced a bill to stiffen penalties for nonpayment.
Second, Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana,
who chairs the Senate Health Committee and was an architect of the law.
He has told those involved that he sees fixing its problems before he leaves
office in January as a legacy project.
Third, Representative Frank Pallone Junior, Democrat of New Jersey,
also an author of the original law. Last month he introduced a bill to abolish the
arbitration system altogether, and instead set a flat payment for doctors at the
level insurers typically pay.
Murphy speaks from his own experience as a doctor.
I ran a small business, he said. If I don't have income,
guess what happens to the business? It dies.
Pallone had always been skeptical of arbitration.
He supported it only as a compromise to get the surprise billing ban passed.
He said the reality turned out even more chaotic than he had predicted.
We have the proof with the facts, he said,
that shows that this arbitration system is out of hand.
Put it all together. The No Surprises Act still does its core job of keeping
surprise bills away from patients. But its arbitration system has become a
battleground between providers and insurers.
Providers win large awards, sometimes many times typical rates.
Insurers, led by Anthem, refuse to pay a large share of them.
And the government has issued no penalties,
while the courts say providers cannot sue.
Until the administration or Congress acts, the dysfunction continues.
And it falls on medevac crews, emergency practices, and the patients they serve.
That was a summary of The New York Times report, Flouting Consumer Law,
Insurers Refuse to Pay Medical Bills for Emergency Care.
As Katie Keith put it, the insurer is not the final decider.
For now, though, no one else is deciding either.

It authorizes the Trump administration to fine health insurers one hundred dollars for each day they do not pay an arbitration award. So far, it has not issued a single penalty. Doctors have sent hundreds of complaints about unpaid awards to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Those The Times spoke with said they had rarely received a response. Health plans say the agency has also failed to respond to thousands of their complaints about ineligible claims. Thomas LaGreca, a partner at Callagy Law, which files claims for providers, estimates that twenty-seven percent of his clients' claims remain unpaid six months after arbitration decisions. There has to be some enforcement, he said. Spokespeople for both the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and the Labor Department declined to respond to questions about why they had not issued penalties. In July, a Trump administration spokesman told The Times that the system is being gamed by doctors, and that the government was actively working to clean it up. But the administration has not yet announced any policy changes. Meanwhile, the people waiting on the money are feeling it. Doctors say nonpayment makes it hard to manage their practices. Some who built their businesses around the arbitration system and its high payouts have taken on debt to stay afloat. Doctor Jennifer Raley is a managing partner at Wake Emergency Physicians, which serves patients in central and eastern North Carolina. She said the practice has one point two million dollars in outstanding awards. It won one thousand thirty-two arbitration cases in twenty twenty-five. Its average award was around four times what insurers typically pay. And in January, the practice had to take out a line of credit to make payroll. Doctor Raley framed it in terms of the staff on her payroll. We just want to get paid, she said, what we need to pay the people who saw the patients. For an air ambulance company, the consequences can reach all the way to whether a community keeps its service. PHI, a national air ambulance company, recently closed a base in Red Bluff, California, a small city between Sacramento and the Oregon border. Its chief executive, Scott McCarty, cited sixteen point three million dollars in outstanding payments from Anthem as the cause. In his words, the insurance companies cannot unilaterally decide to breach a federal law if they don't like the end result. That's essentially what they are doing. Anthem tells it differently. Spokeswoman Janey Kiryluik said the insurer was actively trying to bring PHI Air Medical into its network. But she said the company had requested unreasonably high rates, typically asking for fifty-six thousand dollars per flight in arbitration. Doctor Brian McHugh is a neurosurgeon from Long Island, New York. According to federal data, he often wins arbitration awards that are forty times higher than what Anthem typically pays. He has repeatedly received letters from Anthem challenging those awards on the grounds that they are too expensive. He said other doctors at his practice have stopped seeing Anthem patients. For its part, Anthem said it does not use a financial threshold as a basis for holding payment, and that it no longer uses the letter Doctor McHugh received. Anthem's position has shifted over time. Like all major insurers, it supported the No Surprises Act when Congress was writing it during the first Trump administration. But over the last six years, its executives soured on the arbitration system, saying it encourages abusive billing. Many of the high awards, the article notes, have been for scheduled procedures, not the emergency care the law was written to address. Anthem defends its nonpayment as intentional. In a thirteen-page report, it estimated that sixty percent of its cases decided by arbitrators should never have qualified. This year, it has not paid eighty-three percent of arbitration claims. And according to documents The Times obtained, the Labor Department, which oversees large employer health plans, is investigating Anthem's failure to pay. Anthem says it is cooperating. Insurers say HaloMD, the firm behind the data, is part of the problem. They say it typically submits unreasonably high bids, sometimes winning one hundred thirteen times typical insurer payments. It has also been accused of filing a high volume of ineligible claims. Five insurers have sued Halo, accusing it of fraud. Three of those suits, including Anthem's, were dismissed in federal court, on the grounds that courts can't review arbitrators' decisions. HaloMD spokesman Patrick Velliky pushed back. He called the insurers' lawsuits an attempt to intimidate physicians and clinicians out of seeking fair and sustainable reimbursement. With both sides dug in, attention is turning to Congress. Congress has recently taken greater interest in reform, with a Senate committee hosting round table meetings and new legislation in the House. Three lawmakers stand out. First, Representative Greg Murphy, Republican of North Carolina, who worked as a urologist before running for office. He admits there are problems on both sides. But he believes the majority of abuses come from insurers who do not pay, and he has introduced a bill to stiffen penalties for nonpayment. Second, Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, who chairs the Senate Health Committee and was an architect of the law. He has told those involved that he sees fixing its problems before he leaves office in January as a legacy project. Third, Representative Frank Pallone Junior, Democrat of New Jersey, also an author of the original law. Last month he introduced a bill to abolish the arbitration system altogether, and instead set a flat payment for doctors at the level insurers typically pay. Murphy speaks from his own experience as a doctor. I ran a small business, he said. If I don't have income, guess what happens to the business? It dies. Pallone had always been skeptical of arbitration. He supported it only as a compromise to get the surprise billing ban passed. He said the reality turned out even more chaotic than he had predicted. We have the proof with the facts, he said, that shows that this arbitration system is out of hand. Put it all together. The No Surprises Act still does its core job of keeping surprise bills away from patients. But its arbitration system has become a battleground between providers and insurers. Providers win large awards, sometimes many times typical rates. Insurers, led by Anthem, refuse to pay a large share of them. And the government has issued no penalties, while the courts say providers cannot sue. Until the administration or Congress acts, the dysfunction continues. And it falls on medevac crews, emergency practices, and the patients they serve. That was a summary of The New York Times report, Flouting Consumer Law, Insurers Refuse to Pay Medical Bills for Emergency Care. As Katie Keith put it, the insurer is not the final decider. For now, though, no one else is deciding either.

metadata.title: You Won Arbitration – So Why Is the Money Still Missing? | Enforcement Push for No Surprises Act
metadata.author: Apex IONM Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
Providers are struggling to get paid. They’re losing out on thousands—and in some cases, even millions.

Even though the No Surprises Act created a process for resolving payment disputes through arbitration, many providers are still dealing with delays or outright non-payment even after they win.

Laura Trotter, the host of the show, breaks down the No Surprises Act Enforcement Act and what it’s trying to change, including stronger accountability for health plans and making sure arbitration decisions are actually enforced.

We also talk about how these gaps are impacting day-to-day cash flow, especially for IONM providers who rely on timely reimbursement to keep operations running smoothly.

On top of that, we discuss the grassroots effort Apex is leading to push for change—calling on providers and industry professionals to take action by sending a letter to their local representatives.

You can participate here:
https://secure.legisletter.org/campaign/cmosmp7b80000kv04tnc85iub

If you’re in the space, this gives you a clearer look at what’s happening behind the scenes and why enforcement is becoming such a major focus right now.

metadata.title: No Surprises Act arbitration is driving 2027 premium spike
metadata.author: Long Reads, Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
Rogé Karma of The Atlantic explains why employer health premiums could rise by as much as 11 percent in 2027. GLP-1s and AI billing play a part, but the biggest driver may be the No Surprises Act's arbitration process, where providers win about 85 percent of disputes.

Based on “The Perverse Reason Health-Care Costs Are About to Surge” by Rogé Karma · The Atlantic, November 11, 2026

Chapters
0:00 The Coming Spike
2:04 Old Pressures
3:16 Three Culprits
5:39 A Law Backfires
7:47 Gaming the System
9:52 Who Wins
11:39 Bad Faith?
12:49 Arbitrators' Incentives
14:51 The Bill Comes Due
16:39 Employers React
17:37 The Fix

Long Reads, Explained: the day's most important long reads, narrated and illustrated.
Subscribe for new explainers every day: https://www.youtube.com/@LongReadsExplained?sub_confirmation=1

#HealthCare #Insurance #Economy

segments.text: If twenty twenty-six was the year of gas prices,
twenty twenty-seven will be the year of health-insurance premiums.
And the biggest reason, Rogé Karma argues in The Atlantic,
is a law that was meant to protect patients from surprise medical bills.
Start with the scale. One hundred sixty million Americans get their health
insurance through an employer. That is the kind of coverage this story is about.
The cost of that coverage is expected to rise by as much as eleven percent next
year. That is roughly double the average annual increase over the past decade.
In other words, a normal year's increase, twice over.
Ellen Kelsay is the president and chief executive of the Business Group on Health,
an organization that lobbies on behalf of large employers.
She told Karma, in her words, these are the highest numbers we've ever seen.
And she added a warning. The current projections, Kelsay said,
are likely an understatement. So the eleven percent figure may turn out to be a
floor rather than a ceiling.
Who pays for all this? According to Karma, much
of the increase will be passed on to employees.
That happens in two ways. Directly, workers face higher premiums,
co-pays and deductibles. Indirectly, they get reduced benefits,
smaller raises and slower hiring.
And here is the article's central claim. The biggest reason this is happening is,
in Karma's word, deeply perverse. It is a
law designed to end surprise medical billing.
That law, he argues, has turned into a tool for squeezing even more money out of
insurers, and raising the cost of care for everyone else.
Before getting to how that happened, it helps to see the trend it is making worse.
The coming spike, Karma writes, is a bad situation getting worse.
Over the past decade, the cost of employer-sponsored health insurance has
increased by fifty percent. That is much higher than overall inflation.
A twenty twenty-six survey by K-F-F found that the average yearly cost of coverage
for a family of four was about twenty-eight
thousand three hundred dollars.
Of that, employees paid about seven thousand four hundred dollars themselves.
The employer covered the rest, which is why
rising costs also squeeze wages and hiring.
The reasons for that long-running climb are well documented, and there are three.
First, an aging workforce that needs more care.
Second, an increase in the prevalence of chronic illness.
And third, a dramatic consolidation of the hospital sector.
These are slow, structural forces. But they do not explain why next year's jump
is so sudden. For that, the article points to three newer culprits.
The first is a class of drugs known as G-L-P-ones.
Projections from Marsh, a health-care consulting firm,
imply that these drugs will account for up to a quarter of next year's rise in costs,
compared with the preexisting trend.
The second explanation, Karma writes, appears to be A-I,
specifically tools that change how doctors bill.
The third, and likely the largest, is also the most surprising and, in his word,
infuriating. It is that law about surprise billing.
Let's take the A-I story first.
Over the past few years, providers have begun adopting A-I tools that record and
transcribe their meetings with patients. The ostensible justification is to give
the doctor more time talking with the
patient and less time filling out paperwork.
But according to Karma, these products are designed to hunt for and maximize revenue
from moments a doctor ordinarily might not bill for.
One example is noting a patient's chronic disease during a routine checkup.
That turns an ordinary visit into a more billable one.
The companies that make these tools are very open about this purpose.
Ambience Healthcare, one of the makers, urges doctors to use its products to,
quote, protect your bottom line with stronger documentation.
The same company promises to, quote, capture every dollar earned,
automatically. That is a sales pitch about revenue, not about bedside manner.
Another company, Suki, claims that its A-I scribes generate up to six thousand five
hundred sixty-six dollars in revenue per clinician per year.
They do it by increasing the share of patient
visits classified at more complex billing rates.
Add that up across the system, and analyses from Marsh and the Business Group
on Health imply that A-I coding inflation will explain up to a quarter of next
year's extra health-insurance inflation. Still, Karma says the largest factor lies
elsewhere, in a law passed by Congress.
First, the problem the law was meant to solve.
Before twenty twenty-two, a patient might visit an in-network hospital but receive
care from an out-of-network provider. Insurance would typically cover only the
in-network rate, and the patient would get an unexpected bill for the rest.
The No Surprises Act, passed in twenty twenty and in effect two years later,
made that practice illegal. Its solution seemed simple.
Patients would be responsible only for their portion of the in-network cost.
On the back end, though, things were more complicated.
The out-of-network provider and the insurer would have to negotiate any
further payment among themselves.
If they couldn't agree, they would enter a process called independent dispute
resolution, or I-D-R. Each side submits its desired payment to a third-party
arbitrator. So the question became how often that would happen.
Government agencies estimated that the law would give rise to only about seventeen
thousand disputes a year. Their logic was that both sides would want to avoid the
risk of having to accept the other's number.
They were wrong. Providers began submitting far more requests than
expected, often demanding far more than any insurer would pay.
The trend started slowly in twenty twenty-two and grew each year.
In twenty twenty-five, providers filed two point six million disputes.
Technically either side can start arbitration.
But it happens only once an insurer refuses the requested amount,
so providers trigger it more than ninety-nine percent of the time.
And it is accelerating. Claim volume in the first half of twenty twenty-six was
fifty percent higher than a year earlier, and experts expect it to rise even faster
next year. So who is filing all these claims?
According to a report from Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance
Reforms, half of those disputes came from just two provider practices.
The first is Radiology Partners, which is
majority-owned by private equity and venture capital.
The second is TeamHealth, owned by the private-equity giant Blackstone.
Together, those two account for half of all disputes.
Another twenty-seven percent came from HaloMD.
As the publication Stat has reported, that company was founded in twenty twenty-two
specifically to help providers earn as
much money as possible from I-D-R disputes.
Jack Hoadley is a professor emeritus at Georgetown and a co-author of that report.
He rejects the idea that this is about ordinary physicians.
In his words, this really isn't about your average doctor trying to get a fair rate.
It's an active strategy by a few companies with a lot of money trying to game the
system. The companies, unsurprisingly, see it differently.
The entities using the process tend to point the finger at insurers.
A HaloMD spokesperson wrote that the health insurance lobby's false narrative
that the I-D-R process has increased medical
spending is not supported by the data.
A TeamHealth spokesperson wrote that the company supports the law and its dispute
process because it works. Patients are protected, the spokesperson said,
and providers can challenge insurers' attempts to deny,
delay or lower fair reimbursement.
And Radiology Partners sent a document arguing that Congress thoughtfully
designed the law to protect patients while preserving sustainable payment rates.
Unfortunately, it said, some insurers have disrupted that goal.
The numbers on outcomes, though, tell their own story.
Since the law was enacted, providers have won
about eighty-five percent of submitted disputes.
And the wins are large. In twenty twenty-five,
the median award providers earned was more than four times the typical in-network
cost for the service in question.
HaloMD advertises even better numbers. Its website says it wins more than
eighty-eight percent of the time.
And it says the average award is more than five times the qualifying payment amount,
which is the benchmark rate used in these disputes.
Individual cases make those multiples concrete.
In one case reviewed by The New York Times,
a Dallas surgeon who had accepted a patient's insurance was paid one thousand
eight hundred forty-three dollars for a prostate-removal operation.
The surgeon's assistant, who had not accepted the insurance,
went through arbitration and made fifty thousand four hundred fifty-six dollars
for the same procedure.
The Times also found that a single plastic-surgery practice had submitted
more than six thousand arbitration claims.
They earned the practice as much as four hundred forty thousand dollars for a
single breast-reduction surgery. The typical cost of that surgery in the United
States ranges from nine thousand to fifteen thousand dollars.
Those are extreme examples. But they sit on top of the system-wide pattern,
a median award of more than four times the in-network cost,
and HaloMD's own claim of more than five times.
Providers have an explanation for why.
Some providers argue they win so often because insurers refuse to negotiate in
good faith. An analysis by a group of physicians' lobbies points out that in
eight percent of disputes, insurers submitted claims of one dollar or less.
And in about twenty-five percent of cases, the insurer didn't submit a counter at
all, which means an automatic win for the provider.
But in a forthcoming analysis, Hoadley finds that ninety percent of insurer
offers are either at or above the qualifying payment amount.
When insurers don't submit a claim, he argues,
that's likely because they can't keep up with the volume.
How heavy is that volume? An executive at the Health Care Service Corporation,
a large health-insurance plan, recently gave a conference audience a sense of it.
He said his company currently had, quote, well over four hundred people just working
I-D-R disputes. Still, overwhelmed insurers don't fully explain the lopsided
results. For that, scholars look at the referees.
Several recent papers by health-policy scholars offer what Karma calls a
compelling explanation. The arbitrators have strong financial incentives to rule
for providers. Four facts build the case. First,
arbitrators are not public servants at a federal agency.
They work for a handful of for-profit companies and nonprofit organizations.
Second, those organizations are paid based on the number of claims they process.
Third, that means arbitrators get paid only if providers submit cases.
And providers are more likely to submit cases if they expect to win.
Finally, in many cases, providers get to choose which arbitration company will hear
their case. Put those together, and the incentive points one way.
Christopher Whaley, a health economist at Brown University, spelled out the logic.
In his words, the more these arbitrators rule on behalf of providers,
the more money they ultimately make. So what you end up with is a competition
between arbitrators to be the most provider-friendly.
And the data appear to bear that out.
Hoadley and his co-author, Kennah Watts, point out that in the first half of twenty
twenty-four, the arbitration company that received the most cases decided more than
ninety percent of them in favor of providers.
Meanwhile, the entity with the fewest cases, less than one percent of the total,
decided in favor of providers only a third of the time.
Making matters even more ethically dubious,
according to the Private Equity Stakeholder Project,
some private-equity firms have invested both in the arbitration companies that
hear claims and in the practices submitting them.
All of this has a price.
Take one employer. The New York Department of Civil Service has incurred more than
two hundred million dollars in additional claim payments from I-D-R for its
state-employee health plan. The agency called this a primary contributor to the
nearly ten percent increase in premium rates in twenty twenty-five.
Nationally, Hoadley and Watts estimate that administrative costs plus payments
above the in-network rate added up to about one point six billion dollars a year
from twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-four.
In twenty twenty-five, that number spiked to sixteen point six billion dollars,
more than ten times as much. Experts expect it to be even higher in twenty
twenty-seven, as more providers take advantage of a system that, Karma writes,
is basically handing out money.
Projections by consulting firms imply that the arbitration process could account for
twenty-five to forty percent of the extra rise
in employer health-insurance costs next year.
Compare that with the other two culprits. G-L-P-one drugs and A-I coding are each
projected to explain up to a quarter. That is why Karma calls the No Surprises Act
the likely largest explanation.
Whaley, the Brown economist, does not think the peak has arrived.
He told Karma, I don't think we've seen the worst of it yet, not even close.
This is a tidal wave that could totally wipe out health-care affordability if it
isn't fixed. Employers, meanwhile, are already reacting.
Three examples show how. Disney recently announced that next year it will drop
health coverage for working spouses who have access to their own coverage.
Starbucks is one of several major companies
ending coverage of G-L-P-ones for weight loss.
And Deloitte is rolling back its parental-leave and I-V-F funding benefits
for certain employees. But Karma says these tactics will go only so far.
Higher premiums appear inevitable. According to K-F-F,
employee premiums for family coverage
increased by nine percent in twenty twenty-six.
That was the fastest rate since twenty ten.
If current projections are correct, next year's figure will be even higher,
and will likely come with higher deductibles and co-pays.

Karma says there is good news. Unlike the structural factors driving up health-care

Congress should start by solving the problems of its own making.
That was The Perverse Reason Health-Care Costs Are About to Surge, by Rogé Karma,
published in The Atlantic on November eleventh, twenty twenty-six.

metadata.title: New Final Rule on No Surprises Act - Explained
metadata.author: HealthWatch Wisconsin
metadata.shortDescription:
On August 19, the US Departments of Health and Human Services, Labor, and Treasury issued a new Final Rule to implement pieces of the No Surprises Act specific to independent dispute resolution processes within the law. The No Surprises Act, signed into law in late 2021, took effect January 1, 2022. Pieces of the law impacting how providers and insurers interact have been in dispute, but all of the consumer protections of the No Surprises Act are unchanged. We explain this new Rule.
---
0:00 Overview
0:35 Old Rule
1:11 New Rule 
1:52 Sources
---
Read the new Rule:
https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/08/26/2022-18202/requirements-related-to-surprise-billing

Read the CMS Fact Sheet:
https://www.cms.gov/nosurprises/policies-and-resources/overview-of-rules-fact-sheets  

If you believe you have been billed in violation of the No Surprises Act, you can call the No Surprises Act helpline at 1-800-985-3059

Support HealthWatch Wisconsin with a tax deductible donation:
https://www.paypal.me/healthwatchwisconsin

Visit our official website:
https://healthwatchwisconsin.org

Want to get in touch with us? Send an email:
info@healthwatchwisconsin.org

About HealthWatch Wisconsin:
HealthWatch Wisconsin is a nonprofit subsidiary of ABC for Health, Inc. working to promote improved access to health care coverage and services. HealthWatch Wisconsin actively shares materials, education, and trainings with health care professionals and consumers.

On our YouTube channel, you will find content about health insurance and coverage programs like Medicaid, social security programs, and private health insurance. We stay on top of current events, policy, and rule changes. We also cover topics that intersect with health coverage for vulnerable populations, such as food, energy, and housing assistance programs. You will also find content on programs specific to Wisconsin such as: BadgerCare Plus eligibility, enrollment, and program rules and disability program rules and features for adults as well as children with special health care needs (CYSHCN). Finally, we share some tips and advocacy strategies.

metadata.title: The No Surprises Act Is Working — Here's How
metadata.author: IndeMed
metadata.shortDescription:
The NSA's Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process lets independent arbitrators determine fair, market-based payments for physicians while protecting patients. 

IndeMed is a physician-led organization working to preserve the autonomy of independent medical practices across the U.S. and keep the NSA strong for the patients and physicians who depend on it.

Join the movement: 
www.indemed.org

metadata.title: The No Surprises Act Created a Monster
metadata.author: About The Rest
metadata.shortDescription: When the No Surprises Act passed, the federal government predicted about 17,000 independent dispute resolution (IDR) cases per year. The actual run rate? Five million and it's about to surge further as the filing fee drops from $115 to $15. Randy breaks down how we got here: insurance companies used NSA rules to hammer down reimbursement rates, so sophisticated anesthesia groups fought back through IDR arbitration and they're winning 85–88% of cases. Now the commercials are suing everyone to stop the bleeding, losing in court, and watching their leverage evaporate. The result is a widening divide: well-resourced anesthesia groups with IDR infrastructure are clawing back rates, while smaller groups without that capability are falling further behind.

metadata.title: Runaway Costs: Getting the No Surprises Act Back on Track
metadata.author: Center on Health Insurance Reforms
metadata.shortDescription: On Thursday, November 12, 2026, Georgetown’s Center on Health Insurance Reforms (CHIR) hosted a discussion of practical strategies to fix the No Surprises Act and get its cost-saving measures back on track. The discussion featured expert perspectives from ERIC’s Melissa Bartlett; Paragon Health Institute’s Jackson Hammond; Families USA’s Sophia Tripoli; and Georgetown CHIR’s Jack Hoadley and Kennah Watts, in a conversation moderated by Washington Post Intelligence’s Rebecca Adams.

segments.text: Good morning, everybody.
Good morning, and welcome to Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public
Policy. My name is Kevin Lucia, and I'm a research professor and co-director of the
Center on Health Insurance Reforms.
For those of you who are not familiar with us, CHIR is a team of leading health
policy researchers dedicated to studying advancing evidence-based solutions at both
the federal and the state levels. Our mission is to strengthen health insurance,
increase affordability, and ensure everyone can get the coverage and the care that
they need at a price that they can afford.
We're delighted to have you to at today's briefing, Runaway Costs: Getting the No
Surprises Act Back on Track.
When the No Surprises Act passed with broad bipartisan support and was signed into
law by President Trump in December 2020, the goal was twofold: uniformly protect
the 177 million Americans with private health insurance, including those with
employer-sponsored coverage from balance billing, while simultaneously containing
healthcare spending. In the years since enactment, the consumer protection side has
been very successful.
Tens of millions of surprise medical bills have been avoided in the emergency room,
the air ambulance, and in network hospital settings, shielding consumers from these
unexpected and sometimes financially ruinous charges.
However, the cost containment side of the equation has been severely undermined by
outcomes associated with the No Surprises Act independent dispute resolution
process. Through various guardrails and a three-step process of initial payment,
open negotiation, and then arbitration, actually intended to serve as a last resort
and anchor around in-network rates, the IDR process was designed to encourage fair
payment and to resolve disputes between payers and out-of-network providers and
facilities. Our team at CHIR documented in
a recent Health Affairs Forefront analysis, spending associated with the IDR
process exploded to more than $22.4 billion
over its first four years, and all this driven by an avalanche of filings and
arbitration awards that, in many cases, far exceed in-network market rates.
While individual consumers are being protected from surprise balance bills, there
are growing concerns that the runaway costs associated with the IDR process are
flowing directly into overall costs of healthcare coverage, basically shifting from
balance bills into higher monthly premiums paid by everyday consumers, including
workers, families, and employers.
Today, we are here to unpack why the No Surprises Act IDR process is falling short
of congressional intent to protect consumers from balance billing while containing
costs, and share actionable bipartisan strategies to rein in excessive arbitration
spending, and basically to try to get the law back on track.
I want to thank the sponsors of today's event, Arnold Ventures, for their deep
commitment to improving healthcare affordability and taking on this complicated
challenge ahead. Okay,
a few quick logistical notes before we begin.
Recording, the event is being recorded, and we'll be posting the recording to
our website, and we'll email the links to all attendees.
Second, there will be an opportunity for you to ask questions at the end of our
panel,
at the end of the morning.
When the time comes, simply raise your hand, and someone with a microphone will
come over and straight to you. Okay.
To kick off our morning, we're fortunate to hear directly from a key congressional
staffer who is working on the frontline of healthcare policy, including protecting
consumers from balance billing. I'd like to welcome Romney Propato, Health Policy
Advisor for the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pension.
Romney advises Chairman Bill Cassidy.
As many of you know, Senator Cassidy was deeply involved in authoring the original
No Surprises Act, and his office continues to be actively conducting oversight on
how the IDR process is being implemented, on understanding its impact on
consumers and costs, and exploring ways to ensure that the NSA meets its goal
of protecting consumers from balance billing in a way that doesn't increase costs.
Romney?
Panel is yes.
Good morning, everybody. It's exciting to see such a large crowd here to talk about
the No Surprises Act today. I just wanted to say a quick thank you to Georgetown
for the opportunity to participate, and I'm excited to share some of the work that
Senator Cassidy and the Help Committee have been working on over the past couple of
months. Like we said earlier, when Congress passed the No Surprises Act in 2020,
there were three fundamental goals.
The first was to protect patients from balance billing and unexpected medical
bills. The second was to encourage in-network participation.
And lastly, we wanted to lower overall healthcare costs.
The law has been successful in protecting patients from surprise bills, but nearly
five years into implementation, we do experience some challenges in the other two
areas. What was designed to be a backstop for resolving occasional payment disputes
has become an increasingly expensive and heavily utilized arbitration system.
And those costs aren't simply disappearing.
They're being passed on to employers, patients, and families through higher
healthcare spending. We've heard concerns through our extensive roundtables that
we've hosted recently from insurers, employers, and patient groups, as well as the
large insurers, about the operational challenges that are facing the system,
inconsistent payment determinations from IDREs, ineligible claims reaching the
system, the payment calculations, and also delays in reimbursement.
The volume of disputes that we've experienced has far exceeded what Congress had
anticipated, and rather than encouraging meaningful negotiations and in-network
contracting, the system can continue to create incentives that rely solely on
arbitration if reform is not heeded.
We cannot continue to allow the law to operate in a way that does not lower
healthcare costs and simply becomes a driver of increased spending.
Over the past several months, like I said, Senator Cassidy and I have been hosting
roundtable conversations, and thank you to those of you who are in the room who
participated in those. Our team has been working on comprehensive legislation to
restore the three core pillars of the No Surprises Act.
Our proposal, which will be released soon, focuses on strengthening program
integrity, improving oversight of IDREs, restoring accountability, increasing
transparency around the entire dispute resolution process, and ensuring that the
dispute resolution process is fair and predictable for those involved.
We're also focused on protecting employers from unnecessary costs, ensuring that
providers are compensated in a timely fashion, and addressing the incentives that
might be driving increased utilization of arbitration.
We're encouraged by the administration's recent work and are excited to continue
building on that. We wanted to say a quick thank you to the administration for the
efforts that they've done to improve the IDR process, including the most recent
rulemaking they've done, the establishment of the IDR gateway, and the increased
oversight that they have done of IDREs.
Just last week, the Trump administration announced that it would deny the
recertification of two IDR entities that failed to meet some performance
requirements. We're excited to see that positive momentum and want to continue to
work with the administration on ensuring the law operates as intended.
Throughout this process, like I said, we've engaged extensively with stakeholders,
providers, insurers, and the federal agencies.
While these stakeholders don't always agree, and there's millions of dollars on the
line in disputes between them, we look forward to finding a pathway where we can
have common sense bipartisan consensus.
The No Surprises Act was a strong bipartisan product, and we are excited to
continue to work on that in that way.
Fixing the implementation should be something that is common sense and bipartisan.
Our goal isn't to reopen the fundamental patient protections that Congress
established. It's to ensure that the law fully delivers on its promises, protecting
patients, encouraging in-network participation and fair negotiations, and overall
lowering healthcare costs. Thanks for having me, and I'm very excited to hear the
conversations that continue to happen today, and are excited for you all to share
feedback once our text comes out soon. Thank you, guys.
Thank you so much for those remarks, and for your ongoing work on Capitol Hill.
Next, I'd like to introduce my colleague, at CHAIR, Kenna Watts.
Kenna is a research fellow where her research centers on issues related to
commercial health insurance affordability, including implementation of the No
Surprises Act. Kenna has analyzed the federal data, this is federal data out of the
puff files on the IDR system, and its cost implications.
And she is going to walk us through
what the numbers tell us about arbitration, and especially volume and spending.
Kenna, the podium is yours. Thank you.
Good morning. Thank you all for joining us here today.
As Kevin mentioned, I'm going to walk through some of our analysis of the public
use file data to show the trends we've been seeing in IDR, and I'll also describe
some of the potential incentives that we think might be contributing to these
trends.
So I'll start with the reason why we're all here today, the cost of the IDR system.
As Kevin mentioned, we estimate that since the system's implementation, it has
generated more than $22 billion in total costs, and these costs are rapidly
growing. In 2025 alone, IDR costs reached more than $16 billion, nearly
3.5 times that of the previous year.
And these totals reflect award amounts that exceed the QPA, as well as the fees and
administrative costs associated with arbitration.
And these costs are partly a result of eroded guardrails that originally intended
to incentivize private negotiation, and in instances where negotiation failed,
encourage the parties to submit modest offers in IDR.
Instead, we've seen the process and parties' incentives have not played out as
expected. For example, we see that providers might be incentivized to repeatedly
pursue IDR and to submit higher award amounts or offer amounts.
IDR entities, in turn, may have financial incentives to determine disputes
ineligible and to arbitrate a higher volume of disputes, and we see that insurers
may be unable or unmotivated to affect provider win rates.
Various groups have raised concerns about insurers' financial interests when acting
as a TPA on behalf of their self-funded plans, and the potential incursion of
shared savings fees in IDR disputes.
And these incentives can help explain the IDR system we see today.
While we don't know if or how often the parties act on these incentives, the clear
trends in volume, award amounts, and ultimately costs are not what Congress
anticipated when drafting the NSA.
And I'll walk through these trends in more detail.
Starting with volume, you can see that the number of disputes submitted each
quarter continues to steadily grow and far outpaces agency estimates.
While the agency has expected about 17,000 emergency and non-emergency disputes to
be resolved annually, in 2025, we saw more than 2.6 million disputes filed.
That's more than 7,000 disputes a day.
So the assumption that IDR would serve as a backstop or this last resort measure
has not played out. Instead, we see that IDR seems to be a routine practice for
some provider groups.
In fact, we see that five provider groups account for roughly three-quarters of all
disputes, and that their volume continues to grow each year.
Four of these groups are private equity-backed physician staffing organizations who
were also frequent balance billers prior to the No Surprises Act.
And the fifth group, HailMD, is an intermediary company that handles IDR disputes
on behalf of providers. And while HailMD is a top filer of disputes, they're only
one of a new cottage industry of IDR intermediaries that profit from this process.
In fact, new research from Harvard estimates that up to $1.4 billion of provider
awards ultimately went to middlemen as contingency fees.
And not only are these groups the top filers of disputes, but they're also among
the most successful. As you can see on this slide, these groups win awards well
above the QPA, and some win awards six to ten times median in-network rates.
I also want to add that the four physician staffing groups also have win rates
between 90 and 96%, which is higher than the overall provider win rate of 85%.
And recently, we've begun to see that certain specialties are becoming
exceptionally successful in IDR.
So from 2023 to 2025, the median awards for neurology and plastic surgery more than
doubled, and now the awards for these specialties range from 24 to 30 times
median in-network rates. And for some services, such as breast reductions, these
awards are more than 80 times Medicare rates.
And these trends may partly be attributable to IDR entity behavior.
In a fair standard arbitration process, one would expect outcomes to be relatively
