videos.full_text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, and welcome to Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy. My name is Kevin Lucia, and I'm a research professor and co-director of the Center on Health Insurance Reforms. For those of you who are not familiar with us, CHIR is a team of leading health policy researchers dedicated to studying advancing evidence-based solutions at both the federal and the state levels. Our mission is to strengthen health insurance, increase affordability, and ensure everyone can get the coverage and the care that they need at a price that they can afford. We're delighted to have you to at today's briefing, Runaway Costs: Getting the No Surprises Act Back on Track. When the No Surprises Act passed with broad bipartisan support and was signed into law by President Trump in December 2020, the goal was twofold: uniformly protect the 177 million Americans with private health insurance, including those with employer-sponsored coverage from balance billing, while simultaneously containing healthcare spending. In the years since enactment, the consumer protection side has been very successful. Tens of millions of surprise medical bills have been avoided in the emergency room, the air ambulance, and in network hospital settings, shielding consumers from these unexpected and sometimes financially ruinous charges. However, the cost containment side of the equation has been severely undermined by outcomes associated with the No Surprises Act independent dispute resolution process. Through various guardrails and a three-step process of initial payment, open negotiation, and then arbitration, actually intended to serve as a last resort and anchor around in-network rates, the IDR process was designed to encourage fair payment and to resolve disputes between payers and out-of-network providers and facilities. Our team at CHIR documented in a recent Health Affairs Forefront analysis, spending associated with the IDR process exploded to more than $22.4 billion over its first four years, and all this driven by an avalanche of filings and arbitration awards that, in many cases, far exceed in-network market rates. While individual consumers are being protected from surprise balance bills, there are growing concerns that the runaway costs associated with the IDR process are flowing directly into overall costs of healthcare coverage, basically shifting from balance bills into higher monthly premiums paid by everyday consumers, including workers, families, and employers. Today, we are here to unpack why the No Surprises Act IDR process is falling short of congressional intent to protect consumers from balance billing while containing costs, and share actionable bipartisan strategies to rein in excessive arbitration spending, and basically to try to get the law back on track. I want to thank the sponsors of today's event, Arnold Ventures, for their deep commitment to improving healthcare affordability and taking on this complicated challenge ahead. Okay, a few quick logistical notes before we begin. Recording, the event is being recorded, and we'll be posting the recording to our website, and we'll email the links to all attendees. Second, there will be an opportunity for you to ask questions at the end of our panel, at the end of the morning. When the time comes, simply raise your hand, and someone with a microphone will come over and straight to you. Okay. To kick off our morning, we're fortunate to hear directly from a key congressional staffer who is working on the frontline of healthcare policy, including protecting consumers from balance billing. I'd like to welcome Romney Propato, Health Policy Advisor for the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pension. Romney advises Chairman Bill Cassidy. As many of you know, Senator Cassidy was deeply involved in authoring the original No Surprises Act, and his office continues to be actively conducting oversight on how the IDR process is being implemented, on understanding its impact on consumers and costs, and exploring ways to ensure that the NSA meets its goal of protecting consumers from balance billing in a way that doesn't increase costs. Romney? Panel is yes. Good morning, everybody. It's exciting to see such a large crowd here to talk about the No Surprises Act today. I just wanted to say a quick thank you to Georgetown for the opportunity to participate, and I'm excited to share some of the work that Senator Cassidy and the Help Committee have been working on over the past couple of months. Like we said earlier, when Congress passed the No Surprises Act in 2020, there were three fundamental goals. The first was to protect patients from balance billing and unexpected medical bills. The second was to encourage in-network participation. And lastly, we wanted to lower overall healthcare costs. The law has been successful in protecting patients from surprise bills, but nearly five years into implementation, we do experience some challenges in the other two areas. What was designed to be a backstop for resolving occasional payment disputes has become an increasingly expensive and heavily utilized arbitration system. And those costs aren't simply disappearing. They're being passed on to employers, patients, and families through higher healthcare spending. We've heard concerns through our extensive roundtables that we've hosted recently from insurers, employers, and patient groups, as well as the large insurers, about the operational challenges that are facing the system, inconsistent payment determinations from IDREs, ineligible claims reaching the system, the payment calculations, and also delays in reimbursement. The volume of disputes that we've experienced has far exceeded what Congress had anticipated, and rather than encouraging meaningful negotiations and in-network contracting, the system can continue to create incentives that rely solely on arbitration if reform is not heeded. We cannot continue to allow the law to operate in a way that does not lower healthcare costs and simply becomes a driver of increased spending. Over the past several months, like I said, Senator Cassidy and I have been hosting roundtable conversations, and thank you to those of you who are in the room who participated in those. Our team has been working on comprehensive legislation to restore the three core pillars of the No Surprises Act. Our proposal, which will be released soon, focuses on strengthening program integrity, improving oversight of IDREs, restoring accountability, increasing transparency around the entire dispute resolution process, and ensuring that the dispute resolution process is fair and predictable for those involved. We're also focused on protecting employers from unnecessary costs, ensuring that providers are compensated in a timely fashion, and addressing the incentives that might be driving increased utilization of arbitration. We're encouraged by the administration's recent work and are excited to continue building on that. We wanted to say a quick thank you to the administration for the efforts that they've done to improve the IDR process, including the most recent rulemaking they've done, the establishment of the IDR gateway, and the increased oversight that they have done of IDREs. Just last week, the Trump administration announced that it would deny the recertification of two IDR entities that failed to meet some performance requirements. We're excited to see that positive momentum and want to continue to work with the administration on ensuring the law operates as intended. Throughout this process, like I said, we've engaged extensively with stakeholders, providers, insurers, and the federal agencies. While these stakeholders don't always agree, and there's millions of dollars on the line in disputes between them, we look forward to finding a pathway where we can have common sense bipartisan consensus. The No Surprises Act was a strong bipartisan product, and we are excited to continue to work on that in that way. Fixing the implementation should be something that is common sense and bipartisan. Our goal isn't to reopen the fundamental patient protections that Congress established. It's to ensure that the law fully delivers on its promises, protecting patients, encouraging in-network participation and fair negotiations, and overall lowering healthcare costs. Thanks for having me, and I'm very excited to hear the conversations that continue to happen today, and are excited for you all to share feedback once our text comes out soon. Thank you, guys. Thank you so much for those remarks, and for your ongoing work on Capitol Hill. Next, I'd like to introduce my colleague, at CHAIR, Kenna Watts. Kenna is a research fellow where her research centers on issues related to commercial health insurance affordability, including implementation of the No Surprises Act. Kenna has analyzed the federal data, this is federal data out of the puff files on the IDR system, and its cost implications. And she is going to walk us through what the numbers tell us about arbitration, and especially volume and spending. Kenna, the podium is yours. Thank you. Good morning. Thank you all for joining us here today. As Kevin mentioned, I'm going to walk through some of our analysis of the public use file data to show the trends we've been seeing in IDR, and I'll also describe some of the potential incentives that we think might be contributing to these trends. So I'll start with the reason why we're all here today, the cost of the IDR system. As Kevin mentioned, we estimate that since the system's implementation, it has generated more than $22 billion in total costs, and these costs are rapidly growing. In 2025 alone, IDR costs reached more than $16 billion, nearly 3.5 times that of the previous year. And these totals reflect award amounts that exceed the QPA, as well as the fees and administrative costs associated with arbitration. And these costs are partly a result of eroded guardrails that originally intended to incentivize private negotiation, and in instances where negotiation failed, encourage the parties to submit modest offers in IDR. Instead, we've seen the process and parties' incentives have not played out as expected. For example, we see that providers might be incentivized to repeatedly pursue IDR and to submit higher award amounts or offer amounts. IDR entities, in turn, may have financial incentives to determine disputes ineligible and to arbitrate a higher volume of disputes, and we see that insurers may be unable or unmotivated to affect provider win rates. Various groups have raised concerns about insurers' financial interests when acting as a TPA on behalf of their self-funded plans, and the potential incursion of shared savings fees in IDR disputes. And these incentives can help explain the IDR system we see today. While we don't know if or how often the parties act on these incentives, the clear trends in volume, award amounts, and ultimately costs are not what Congress anticipated when drafting the NSA. And I'll walk through these trends in more detail. Starting with volume, you can see that the number of disputes submitted each quarter continues to steadily grow and far outpaces agency estimates. While the agency has expected about 17,000 emergency and non-emergency disputes to be resolved annually, in 2025, we saw more than 2.6 million disputes filed. That's more than 7,000 disputes a day. So the assumption that IDR would serve as a backstop or this last resort measure has not played out. Instead, we see that IDR seems to be a routine practice for some provider groups. In fact, we see that five provider groups account for roughly three-quarters of all disputes, and that their volume continues to grow each year. Four of these groups are private equity-backed physician staffing organizations who were also frequent balance billers prior to the No Surprises Act. And the fifth group, HailMD, is an intermediary company that handles IDR disputes on behalf of providers. And while HailMD is a top filer of disputes, they're only one of a new cottage industry of IDR intermediaries that profit from this process. In fact, new research from Harvard estimates that up to $1.4 billion of provider awards ultimately went to middlemen as contingency fees. And not only are these groups the top filers of disputes, but they're also among the most successful. As you can see on this slide, these groups win awards well above the QPA, and some win awards six to ten times median in-network rates. I also want to add that the four physician staffing groups also have win rates between 90 and 96%, which is higher than the overall provider win rate of 85%. And recently, we've begun to see that certain specialties are becoming exceptionally successful in IDR. So from 2023 to 2025, the median awards for neurology and plastic surgery more than doubled, and now the awards for these specialties range from 24 to 30 times median in-network rates. And for some services, such as breast reductions, these awards are more than 80 times Medicare rates. And these trends may partly be attributable to IDR entity behavior. In a fair standard arbitration process, one would expect outcomes to be relatively consistent amongst the entities, but instead, we see vast variation. In fact, we see that the IDR entities that more often rule in favor of providers also tend to award providers higher amounts and have a higher volume of disputes. And as I mentioned earlier, these trends may be influenced by IDR entities' financial incentives to find disputes eligible and to arbitrate higher volumes of disputes. And so despite the unexpected outcomes and costs we've seen in the IDR process, I really want to end with a reminder that the majority of NSA-covered claims are not entering arbitration. Data indicates that insurers' initial payments often center around the QPA, and that in the majority of cases, providers accept this initial payment or the parties reach an agreed-upon rate in open negotiation. Only a small share of claims, approximately 6%, actually enter IDR. And while the cost of IDR are more easily estimated, the potential savings on this other side of the ledger is a bit more difficult to calculate, but is equally important to consider. So thank you all so much for your time. I look forward to the panel discussion and connecting with you all after the event. Thank you. Thank you, Kenna, for all of your work and dedication to understanding this data. It's really been impressive. At this time, I'd like to ask our moderator and panelists to please come and take your places on the stage. I'm delighted to introduce today's superstar panel, guided by our moderator, Rebecca Adams. Rebecca is the lead healthcare analyst for WP Intelligence with "The Washington Post," where she examines policy and industry trends, including coverage and cost drivers. Prior to WP Intelligence, she served as a newsroom liaison at Kaiser Health News, collaborating with national outlets including "The Washington Post," NPR, CNN, ABC, CBS News, and previously reported for CQ Roll Call. She is an exceptional journalist, and we are so pleased to have her guide our discussion today. Thank you. Thanks. metadata.title: Do You Have to Pay a Surprise Medical Bill? (The No Surprises Act Explained)
metadata.author: Law Unpacked
metadata.shortDescription:
Got a surprise medical bill from a doctor you never chose? Since January 1, 2022, the federal No Surprises Act bans most surprise out-of-network bills. For emergency care, out-of-network hospitals and doctors can't bill you more than your in-network cost-sharing (42 U.S.C. § 300gg-131). At in-network hospitals and surgery centers, out-of-network anesthesiologists, radiologists, pathologists, lab services and other doctors you don't choose generally can't balance bill you, and they can't ask you to waive your rights (45 CFR § 149.420). Air ambulances are covered; ground ambulances generally aren't. If you're uninsured or self-pay, you can get a good faith estimate and dispute a bill that's at least $400 over it, within 120 days. Plus the 2017 $108,951 heart attack bill that helped spark the law, and what to do if you get a surprise bill.

Chapters
0:00 The surprise bill
0:32 The No Surprises Act
0:52 Emergencies
1:14 The doctor you never chose
1:42 The consent form trap
2:12 Ambulances
2:28 No insurance?
2:56 What to do
3:30 Recap

Sources
- 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-131 (emergency services balance billing): https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/300gg-131
- 42 U.S.C. § 300gg-132 (non-emergency services at in-network facilities): https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/300gg-132
- 45 CFR § 149.420 (notice and consent, ancillary services): https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/149.420
- CMS, Know your medical bill rights: https://www.cms.gov/medical-bill-rights/know-your-rights
- CMS, rights when not using insurance (good faith estimates, $400 dispute): https://www.cms.gov/medical-bill-rights/know-your-rights/no-insurance
- NPR / KFF Health News, the $109K heart attack bill (2018): https://kffhealthnews.org/news/the-109k-heart-attack-bill-is-down-to-332-what-about-other-surprise-bills/

This video is for general education only and is not legal advice. Laws vary by state and change over time; for advice about your situation, consult a licensed attorney in your state. Researched and scripted with the help of AI tools; narrated with a synthetic voice.

metadata.title: Insurers Say the No Surprises Act Is Paying Providers Too Much
metadata.author: Apex IONM Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
Insurance companies say providers are getting paid too much under the No Surprises Act. But are they telling the whole story?

The controversy centers on payments awarded through the No Surprises Act's Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process, where some insurers argue that neuromonitoring providers are receiving excessive reimbursement.

But here's what those numbers may be leaving out: A 15-minute outpatient neurological test and hours of complex intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) can share the same billing codes, despite involving very different clinical circumstances.

In this episode of The Revenue Fix: Unboxed, Apex CEO Laura Trotter challenges the overpayment narrative and explains why understanding what's being compared matters just as much as the numbers themselves.

Before you cry overpayment, make sure you know what you're comparing.

About The Revenue Fix: Unboxed

The business of IONM, from the people who know it best.

Join the subject matter experts at Apex IONM Solutions as they unpack the hot takes, industry controversies, and challenges shaping healthcare revenue cycle management.

Subscribe for more conversations about the No Surprises Act, IONM reimbursement, medical billing, and healthcare revenue cycle management.

Can you get an out-of-network doctor paid at in-network rates? The answer might surprise you! In this video, I’ll explain what ‘in-network’ and ‘out-of-network’ really mean, how they affect your medical bills, and when your insurance is required to pay more than they claim.

I’ll also break down key laws—like the No Surprises Act—that can protect you from unexpected medical bills. Plus, I’ll share tips on how to fight for lower costs and make sure you’re not overpaying.

If you’ve ever been hit with a huge medical bill, this video is for you! Don’t forget to like, comment, and subscribe for more ways to save on healthcare.

More and more medical provider refuse to deal with insurance companies. They have no contract or financial agreement with your plan and can bill patients directly. Considered "Out of Network", their services can be pricey, with little or no insurance reimbursements. Unless... Let's explore how some OON services can be reimbursement at the higher In Network rate and save you $.

In this video, Martine Brousse, the Medical Bill Whisperer, shares practical tips on how to get your insurance to pay for out-of-network care. Martine explains six important reasons why you might need to go out of network, like needing a specialist, not having a suitable in-network provider, or continuing care with an out-of-network doctor. You'll also learn simple steps to make your case stronger, such as documenting your reasons and getting a referral from your primary care doctor. Watch this video to find out how to save money and get the care you need without worrying about your insurance saying no.

There are 6 good reasons why you may have to use out of network providers. Today we explore the 3 most common ones, and I'll tell you how your insurance can be forced to pay the highest rate for those services, saving you $.

metadata.title: CoGenetix & ANS Solutions- OON IDR Webinar
metadata.author: Ben Martin
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you leaving revenue on the table with underpaid or denied out-of-network claims? In this webinar, we break down how healthcare providers are shifting the balance of power back in their favor using the federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process established by the No Surprises Act (NSA).

Stop accepting payer-dictated rates. Learn how to leverage strategic arbitration to move beyond the Qualified Payment Amount (QPA) and secure fair compensation for your clinical expertise.

In this video, we cover:
The IDR Advantage: How "baseball-style" arbitration works and why the QPA is not the payment ceiling.
Proven Results: Discover how we have maintained a 90–95% win rate and recovered over $3.85 million for our clients.
Winning Strategy: Why our proprietary provider profile-building process helps us win disputes against the nation’s largest insurers, including Aetna, UnitedHealthcare, and Blue Cross Blue Shield.
Scalable Solutions: Specialized approaches for Ambulatory Surgery Centers (ASCs), Large Orthopedic Groups, and Health Systems.
Low-Risk Implementation: How our performance-based model ensures our incentives are perfectly aligned with your bottom line—we only make money when you do.
Ready to identify the hidden revenue in your out-of-network claims?

Contact us today for a complimentary assessment of your payer mix and denial trends.

#HealthcareRevenue #NoSurprisesAct #IDR #MedicalBilling #RevenueCycleManagement #ProviderCompensation #Orthopedics #ASC #HealthSystems

segments.text: Welcome to this video on the out of
network billing unlock through the No
Surprises Act Independent Dispute
Resolution process. Our partnership with
CoGenetics and ANS Solutions is
currently achieving a win rate of over
90% for providers.
The No Surprises Act was enacted to
protect patients from unexpected
out-of-network bills. For providers, it
establishes a federal IDR process,
providing a structured enforceable
pathway to contest underpayments and
shift the balance of power.
Before this act, payers often dictated
payments with little recourse for
providers. The new IDR process levels
the playing field with binding
arbitration, allowing providers to
submit their own payment offers and
contest rates based on factors beyond
just the qualifying payment amount.
The IDR process follows a specific
six-step timeline, typically spanning 90
to 120 days from claim to final payment.
We manage every step of this process on
your behalf to ensure deadlines are met
and submissions are optimized.
Understanding the qualifying payment
amount, or QPA, is crucial. It is often
set well below market value by insurers.
Our strategy is to request significantly
higher rates from the arbitrator based
on legitimate practice costs, a practice
that is fully legal under the current
regulations.
Industry data shows the efficacy of the
IDR process with approximately 86% of
decisions favoring providers. Our own
clients have recovered over $3.85
million,
consistently demonstrating that those
who use the IDR process strategically
are achieving significant results.
Our success stems from a comprehensive
approach. For every client, we build
detailed provider profiles that include
credentials, service complexity, and
regional market benchmarks, ensuring our
submissions to the arbitrator are robust
and compelling. Our workflow is designed
for seamless integration with your team.
Whether through a dedicated billing
queue or custom file exports, we
proactively audit, flag, and identify
opportunities for recovery, ensuring
your claims are managed efficiently.
IDR filing fees are a necessary
component, but because our win rate is
so high, these costs are typically
reimbursed by the payer. This makes the
IDR program a low-risk, high-reward
strategy for your practice.
Our track record speaks for itself, with
a 90% to 95% win rate and millions
recovered. Our consistent success is
driven by individualized profiles,
strategic positioning, and a deep
command of the regulatory landscape.
We have successfully challenged many of
the nation's largest commercial payers,
covering 58 unique CPT codes. This
demonstrates our ability to achieve
significant recoveries across a wide
range of specialties and regional
markets.
For ambulatory surgery centers, the
recovery potential is particularly high.
We manage both facility and professional
fee claims simultaneously, transforming
underpaid facility fees into a
significant revenue opportunity through
strategic IDR management.
Large orthopedic groups benefit greatly
from our process. Fellowship training
and surgical complexity are powerful
tools in arbitration. By systematically
routing claims, these groups can turn
OON volume into a predictable and
reliable revenue stream.
For large health systems, our
integration services ensure IDR becomes
a scalable and compliant operation. We
design custom workflows and provide
regular reporting, allowing you to
maximize collections across every
department and service line.
Our pricing model is strictly
performance-based, meaning we only
succeed when you do. With no upfront
costs, our tiered structure ensures our
interests are fully aligned with yours
as we work to maximize your recoveries.
This final section covers common
questions regarding the process.
Regarding patient liability, patients
are fully protected under the No
Surprises Act. They only pay normal
in-network cost sharing as the IDR
process exists to resolve payment gaps
between providers and insurers.
To address operational concerns, know
that IDR determinations are legally
binding. Payers cannot initiate
clawbacks and they are required to pay
awarded amounts within 30 days.
Furthermore, your billing staff workload
remains minimal as our system is
designed for simple, efficient routing.
To begin, we offer a complimentary OON
assessment to identify your potential
recovery opportunities. We then move
through a strategy session, onboarding,
and consistent revenue recovery. Reach
out to learn how we can help your
practice secure the revenue it is owed.

metadata.title: How to Improve Out-of-Network Reimbursement and IDR Recovery
metadata.author: Vee Healthtek
metadata.shortDescription:
Out-of-network recovery can be lost before arbitration begins when payment variances go unnoticed, deadlines expire, or evidence arrives too late. This video explains how one accountable recovery workflow can connect payment review, negotiation, dispute preparation, and posted cash while directing specialist effort toward the strongest net recovery opportunities.

In this video, you will learn:

Why each eligible claim needs clear ownership from initial payment through final recovery
How expected recovery, collection costs, evidence strength, and approaching deadlines guide prioritization
Why clean intake, reusable evidence, and payer-level history support a more resilient recovery program

Read the full article: https://www.veehealthtek.com/why-us/points-of-view/out-of-network-reimbursement-idr-recovery

Relevant Vee Healthtek capabilities:

Underpayment Recovery and Payer Variance Resolution : https://www.veehealthtek.com/how-we-deliver/back-office/underpayment-recovery-and-payer-variance-resolution
Accounts Receivable Follow-Up : https://www.veehealthtek.com/how-we-deliver/back-office/accounts-receivable-follow-up
RevAmp : https://www.veehealthtek.com/how-we-deliver/technology/revamp

About Vee Healthtek
Vee Healthtek is a practitioner-led, technology-powered revenue cycle partner helping healthcare providers turn out-of-network payment variances into accountable recovery work. We connect specialist expertise, evidence preparation, deadline management, and AI-enabled prioritization to improve recovery visibility and reimbursement predictability.

#OutOfNetworkReimbursement #IDRRecovery #UnderpaymentRecovery #RevenueCycleManagement #VeeHealthtek

segments.text: Out of network recovery can fail before
arbitration begins.
A low payment [music] posts is final, a
variance waits for review, and an
opportunity closes before anyone takes
responsibility. [music]
Improving recovery starts with an
operating change.
Treat each eligible claim as time
sensitive work with a known next action
[music] rather than another balance
aging in AR.
First, give one owner the complete
recovery path.
That owner coordinates payment review,
evidence, [music] negotiation, filing
decisions, and award reconciliation.
[music] Specialists still perform their
roles, but one person remains
accountable for the claims position,
[music]
deadline, and unresolved barriers.
Begin at remittance.
Compare the payment with the available
supporting information [music] and flag
potential shortfalls promptly.
Confirm the appropriate recovery pathway
before the account moves into a generic
follow-up queue. Keep evidence
preparation upstream.
Waiting until a filing decision can
leave too little time to assemble a
defensible submission.
Next, prioritize by net recoverable
value.
Consider the likely additional payment,
filing expense, specialist effort, and
time remaining.
A large balance is not automatically the
best opportunity.
Strong evidence, a credible recovery
path, and manageable collection costs
may make another claim more valuable.
Include recurrence in that decision.
A repeated payer methodology affecting
hundreds of similar claims deserves
attention beyond a single dispute.
Investigate whether negotiation, payment
validation, or an upstream correction
can address the pattern instead of
repeatedly recovering the same type of
shortfall.
Use automation to rank inventory and
surface approaching deadlines.
Keep expert review for eligibility,
evidence, and complex decisions.
The objective is fewer missed
opportunities, not simply more filings.
Build a process that can as requirements
change.
Maintain clean intake, claim level
evidence, payer history, and documented
decisions.
Review applicable requirements before
acting rather than relying on an
outdated checklist.
Finally, follow the award through
payment.
Compare the determination with the
amount received, escalate unresolved
differences, and reconcile the final
cash.
Keep eligible dollars, submitted
disputes, awards, and posted payments
separate in reporting.
This gives finance a clearer view of
recovery yield, collection effort, and
expected timing while showing exactly
where value remains at risk.
Manage the clock from the first payment
and turn supported recovery
opportunities into collected revenue.

metadata.title: No Surprises Act: Notice of IDR Initiation - Resubmission Web Form Demo
metadata.author: CMSHHSgov
metadata.shortDescription: A demonstration of the Notice of IDR Initiation – Resubmission web form, which the initiating party may be prompted to complete as part of the Federal IDR process.

segments.text: This demonstration will cover how to complete and submit the Notice of IDR Initiation – Resubmission
web form.
For the demonstration today, we are going to look at this form in a test environment.
All of the data that I will be entering or the data that has been prepopulated is made
up test data.
Access to this form will be through a unique link that will be emailed to the initiating
party from the Federal IDR portal when a dispute has been determined as eligible for resubmission.
The subject line of the email will read, "Notice of IDR Initiation – Resubmission form due".
Upon selecting the link provided in the email, you will land on the Notice of IDR Initiation
– Resubmission welcome page as you can see here.
On this page, there are a few notes and reminders that the initiating parties will want to review,
including some general information about the overall process and instructions to completing
the web form.
If you have any questions, you can reach out to the IDR questions mailbox at FederalIDRQuestions@cms.hhs.gov.
There is also a reminder here letting you know that you must compute the form in a single
session and that your session will time out after 60 minutes of inactivity.
After reviewing the information at the top of this page, the initiating party should
read this warning message and the security and privacy agreement.
At the bottom of this page, select the checkbox next to the Security and Privacy Agreement.
And select Continue.
The dispute reference number listed in the subject line or body text of the email should
be entered in dispute reference number field.
Before selecting Continue.
Then we get to the next screen, which would look familiar as this form is an abbreviated
version of the Notice of IDR Initiation form.
Many of the fields on this form will be prepopulated based on the information that was entered
in the original dispute.
As you can see, the "I am a," "Tax ID," and "Health Plan Type" fields are prepopulated.
The "I am a" field will not be editable, but the "Tax ID," "National Provider Identifier,"
and "Health Plan Type" fields are editable if that information requires updating.
Selecting Continue will take us to the next page.
The point of contact page contains contact information for the parties, which will also
be prepopulated based on the original dispute.
The fields for party type and name will be uneditable, but the fields for address, contact
information, and primary and secondary contacts are editable in case that information needs
to be updated.
For this demo, no information here needs to be updated, so I will select Continue.
On this page, the Assigned Certified IDR entity will prepopulate to the original IDR entity
on the original dispute and will not be editable.
This is so that when this form is submitted, this new dispute will be automatically assigned
to the same IDR entity that was assigned to the original dispute.
The summary of qualified items and or services table will display all the line items that
were sent for resubmission in this specific grouping.
Please note that certified IDR entities may send all dispute line items and or services
eligible for resubmission in one grouping, or they may send multiple groupings for resubmission.
In the case of multiple groupings, the initiating party will receive separate emails with separate
unique links to the Notice of IDR Initiation – Resubmission web form.
It is the responsibility of the initiating party to review all line items and or services
in a particular grouping and ensure that any line items or services being resubmitted together
are compliant with federal IDR batching and bundling criteria.
You may click on each line item link to view more detailed information about the item.
The fields here will be prepopulated with the information that was entered in the original
dispute but are editable so you may update information as required.
The documentation of the claim and QPA that was attached to the original dispute will
be referenced in the payment information section.
The initiating party should refer back to their internal files to determine what documentation
they had submitted in the original dispute.
And also determine if additional documentation should be uploaded.
If so, you may select the upload files button or drag and drop files into this area.
Before moving forward, ensure that all required fields marked with the red asterisk are completed
and select the Save and Continue button at the bottom of the page.
The initiating party should take the time to review the detailed information for all
line items in the table.
From the table, the initiating party will have the option to save line items for later.
Saving items for later will remove the line items from the current dispute, and there
will be an opportunity to submit another dispute or disputes for those items later.
There is more information about saving for later in the text above.
For the purpose of this demonstration, I will save 2 line items for later by selecting the
checkbox next to the line item and selecting the Save for Later button.
A pop-up window will appear with an important note and a question asking if you would like
to proceed.
I will select Yes, and now you can see that the items have been removed from the table
and we will be able to review them again later.
If any line items were removed in error at this point, you may either refresh or re-enter
the form and the items will reappear.
Moving along, additional supporting documentation can be uploaded in this section as long as
the file size is less than 500 MB.
And to proceed forward, the initiating party will select the checkbox next to this statement
in the Sign and Submit section, and enter their name in the initiating party field to
sign the web form.
The date will automatically populate to today's date.
And then we can select Continue.
Now we have the question of "What are you disputing today?"
There is the option to submit as a single, bundled, or batched dispute, and there's information
in the section above to guide the initiating party on what type of dispute they are submitting.
If the original dispute is batched, the batched option will automatically be selected as you
can see here.
However, this option will not display if there is only one line item being resubmitted.
If the dispute type is single, there is a secondary question asking if you are submitting
a bundled arrangement.
Because this dispute contains more than one line item, the Yes radio button is automatically
selected and cannot be changed to No.
I'll continue by indicating that this dispute is a batched dispute.
Select Submit, and you will see the confirmation page that outlines next steps.
Now that the web form has been submitted, it is the responsibility of the initiating
party to download and print a copy of the Notice of IDR Initiation Resubmission web
form by selecting the Print PDF button and saving this file for their records.
It is also the responsibility of the initiating party to send a copy of this PDF to the non-initiating
party.
Both parties will receive confirmation emails from the Federal IDR portal letting you know
that the web form has been submitted.
If you saved any items for later, you will see the Continue Submitting button.
Please note that you must first select Print PDF to download a copy of the form as required
as you will not be able to return to this page afterwards.
Once you do, selecting Continue Submitting will redirect you back to the summary of qualified
items table to review the line items you saved for later and you may proceed to resubmit
the line items as appropriate.
You also have the option to exit this form and come back to the items saved for later
at a later time using the same web form link in the email from the Federal IDR portal.
I'll go ahead and click Continue Submitting.
And now we are back to the page with a summary of qualified items table with the 2 line items
that we previously saved for later.
I will use these line items now to demonstrate an alternate scenario where we have a batched
original dispute that will be resubmitted as a single bundled dispute so you can see
how the system guides initiating parties through the form for this specific process.
So we will continue through the form as we did previously by reviewing the table, uploading
additional documentation as necessary, and completing the sign and submit section.
We land again on the question of "What are you disputing today?"
Because the original dispute was submitted as batched, the batched option will automatically
be selected.
But to demonstrate an alternate scenario, I am going to change the dispute type from
batched to single.
Because this dispute contains more than one line item, the Yes radio button is automatically
selected for the question of whether we are submitting a bundled payment arrangement.
I'll select Continue.
Because we are resubmitting as a bundled dispute, we will have to review the line items, identify
the item or service type, and ensure that all required fields are completed.
In the item or service type field, the initiating party will identify if the line item will
be the bundled item or service or the component item or service.
I'll indicate test item 3 as the bundled item.
You will then want to verify and ensure that all required fields marked with the red asterisk
are completed before selecting Save and Continue.
Once a line item is identified as the bundled item, the remaining line items of the dispute
will automatically be updated as the component item or service.
Review that all required fields are completed and select Save and Continue to progress through
each line item.
You will be able to review all changes again here in the summary of qualified items and
or services table where you can now see that the line item type column is populated.
Continue through the additional supporting documentation and sign and submit sections
and select Continue.
You will reconfirm the dispute type you are submitting and select Submit.
We have now submitted the web form as you can see from this confirmation page.
As detailed in the next steps, the initiating party is required to download and print a
copy of the web form by selecting the Print PDF button and saving this file for their
records.
It is also the responsibility of the initiating party to send a copy of this PDF to the non-initiating
party.
And once they are ready to exit the form, they can select the Exit button.
This concludes the demonstration of the "Notice of IDR Initiation - Resubmission" web form.

metadata.title: Decoding The Federal IDR Operations Final Rule: Access, Process and Timing
metadata.author: HaloMD
metadata.shortDescription:
The Federal IDR Operations Final Rule (CMS-9897-F), released May 28, 2026, makes the most significant operational changes to the Federal independent dispute resolution process since the No Surprises Act took effect. In this webinar, HaloMD breaks down what is changing, what it means for providers and the timeline for compliance.

What we cover:

The administrative fee reduction from $115 to $15 per party per dispute, applicable to disputes initiated on or after June 11, 2026
New payer disclosure requirements, including standardized CARC and RARC codes on out-of-network remittances
Changes to open negotiation, including initiation through the Federal IDR portal and a required response notice by the 15th business day
Expanded batching criteria and the new 50 line item cap per dispute
The 5 business day eligibility determination requirement for certified IDR entities
The new Federal IDR Registry and payer registration numbers
Phased applicability dates and what providers need to prepare for now

HaloMD is the #1 provider of IDR services as indicated by CMS PUF, backed by industry leading technology infrastructure and data intelligence. We support more than 20,000 healthcare providers across 50 states and Washington, D.C. under the No Surprises Act and state balance-billing laws.
Learn more at www.halomd.com or contact us to request your personalized Federal IDR Benchmark Report.

metadata.title: Notice of IDR Initiation Web Form Demo
metadata.author: CMSHHSgov
metadata.shortDescription: This video demonstrates how initiating parties will complete the Notice of Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) Initiation web form to create a dispute and start the Federal IDR Process.

segments.text: The demonstration will cover how to complete and submit the Notice of IDR Initiation web form.
Initiating parties can start the Federal IDR Process within four business days after the end of the 30-business-day
open negotiation period if an agreement is not reached between the disputing parties, unless the dispute qualifies for an exception.
For the demonstration today, we are going to look at the Notice of IDR Initiation web form in a test environment.
All of the data that you see being entered on this form is made up test data.
As you can see on the welcome page, there are a few notes and reminders that the initiating parties will want to review,
including some general information about the overall process and instructions to completing the web form.
There is a section that lists all of the information you will need to provide and use to fill out this form.
If you have any questions, you can reach out to the IDR questions mailbox at FederalIDRQuestions@cms.hhs.gov.
There is also a reminder here letting you know that you must complete the form in a single session
and that your session will time out after 60 minutes of inactivity.
After reviewing the information at the top of this page, the initiating party should read this warning message
and the security and privacy agreement.
At the bottom of this page, select the checkbox next to the security and privacy agreement
and select Continue.
The following qualification questions pages will ask a series of questions to confirm your eligibility for the Federal IDR Process.
All required fields are marked with an asterisk.
If you are completing the form as a third-party administrator, you will need to indicate which party you are working on behalf of.
For additional guidance, there is a glossary of insurance terms and definitions that is linked at the top of the form.
The first qualification question asks if the service in question was provided prior to January 1st of 2022.
Select the radio button next to yes or no.
If the plan renewal date is after the date of service, the dispute will not be eligible for the Federal IDR Process.
I will select No and continue to the next question,
where I will select the party type I am or am acting on behalf of.
I will select that I am a Health Care Provider and enter either a Tax ID or a National Provider Identifier number.
From the drop down, I will select the health plan type.
Depending on the health plan type selected, there may be additional follow-up questions that require completion.
For the purpose of the demo, I will select "Non-federal governmental plan".
Before moving forward, ensure that all required fields marked with the red asterisks are completed
and select Continue at the bottom of the page.
If any of the required fields are not completed, you will get an error when you try to continue to the next page.
The next qualification question asks when the open negotiation period started.
Either enter the date or use the calendar to select the day that the open negotiation started.
The 30-business-day open negotiation period must elapse before starting the Federal IDR Process.
At least one file must be uploaded as evidence of the open negotiation period start date.
Select Upload Files to choose files or drag and drop files into this area here.
However, if the date entered is more than 34 business days prior to the current date,
you will need to upload evidence of the open negotiation period start date
and you will be prompted to select an extension justification.
If the first reason is selected, you will be prompted to upload evidence of the extension approval.
If the second reason is selected, you will be prompted to enter the Dispute Reference Number that triggered the cooling off period
and upload evidence of the payment determinations that initiated the cooling off period.
For the purpose of this demonstration, I will indicate that the open negotiation period did start within the standard window.
Next, indicate whether the health care provider or health care facility received consent from the
from the participant, beneficiary, or enrollee to waive surprise billing protections.
If surprise billing protections were waived, the dispute will not be eligible.
I will select No, then select Continue.
The next qualification question asks what you are disputing today. You may select a single dispute,
which means I'm disputing either A. One service code that represents one item or service,
or B. One service code that represents multiple items or services.
Or you may select a batched dispute,
which means I am disputing multiple items or services, all of which are related to the treatment of a similar condition.
When selecting a single dispute, a secondary question appears regarding whether you're disputing a bundled payment arrangement,
where there are multiple items or services, bills, or reimbursed, under one service code.
When selecting a batched dispute, a modal will appear with a list of criteria that will help determine if
the disputes qualify for the batching process.
Select Yes or No to make your selection.
For the purpose of the demonstration, I will select a batched dispute, review the criteria, and select Yes.
On this page, you will be entering information for both the initiating and non-initiating parties involved in the dispute.
The initiating party information will be entered first.
Note that the section will vary depending on who the initiating party is completing the form as.
Because I am completing this form as a health care provider, as you can see here,
I will enter the test contact information for the health care provider name,
the hospital, healthcare facility, or group name
mailing address,
city, state, zip code,
email, and a phone number.
Information for an alternative primary point of contact, such as a third-party administrator, can be entered into this section.
As well as information of an optional secondary point of contact.
Scrolling down, I will now enter the contact information of the non-initiating party.
I will select group health plan as the insurance provider type and enter the health insurance or company name,
mailing address,
city, state, zip code,
email and phone number.
And again, there is the option to provide different primary and secondary points of contact.
Ensure that all required fields marked with a red asterisk are completed and select Continue at the bottom of the page.
Next in the Notice of IDR Initiation form, you are going to provide information on the items or services included in the dispute.
Enter a claim number and date of qualified item or service.
Note that the form will verify that the date entered for each dispute line item
is prior to the open negotiation start date provided at the beginning of the web form.
If the entered date is after the open negotiation date, this error message will appear.
In the payment information section, enter a description of the item or service and what the qualifying payment amount was.
Next, at least one file must be uploaded as documentation of the claim and QPA.
Select Upload Files to choose a file or drag and drop files into this area here.
Also enter the Cost Sharing Amount and what the initial payment was if applicable.
In the type of qualified item or service section, indicate the item or service type by selecting the checkbox next to the relevant option
and enter the service code.
Optionally, enter one or more service code modifiers if applicable.
Service code modifiers must be two alpha-numeric characters and up to four separate service code modifiers can be entered.
When more than one service code modifier is entered, the modifiers will be automatically separated by a semicolon as you can see here.
Then enter the place of service code and select the location of service from the drop down list.
If this service was in a state with state-specific eligibility criteria further screening for dispute eligibility is required.
An attestation statement will appear where you must select the checkbox to attest that you have reviewed the state-specific criteria
and attest the item or service is eligible for the Federal IDR Process.
And before continuing, this is a reminder that you will not be able to submit duplicate dispute line items with
the same claim number, date of service, service code, and if applicable, service code modifiers
as another previously entered dispute line item except for in the following situations:
First, if the previously submitted dispute was subject to the cooling off period and
was closed as ineligible due to submission prior to the end of the cooling off period.
Or if the newly submitted dispute received approval for an extension from the Federal IDR team.
The form will verify if the line item exists in the Federal IDR Portal and will prevent you from submitting a duplicate line item.
To add another item or service to this batched dispute, I will select Save & Add Another.
You will be prompted to enter another claim number and date of service,
along with the description, QPA, documentation of the claim and QPA, and cost sharing amount allowed.
And again, select the item or service type and enter a service code, service code modifier, place of service code, and location of service.
As outlined in the criteria for a batched dispute in this section,
the form will also verify that the date of service entered for each item or service is within 30 business days of all items and services
in the batched dispute, unless the 90-calendar-day cooling off period applies.
And if the 90-calendar-day cooling off period applies,
the items and services in the batched dispute are not subject to the 30-business-day date of service requirement.
Once you have entered all items or services, select Save.
A modal will appear asking if you are ready to submit the form.
Select Back to add more items or services or select Continue to move on to the next page.
Select Save & Add Another to continue entering dispute line items.
If you need to remove an item or service from the dispute, select Cancel Dispute Line Item.
You will be asked to confirm if you want to discard the line item.
On the summary of qualified items or services page, you can review all the dispute line item information entered.
Select the item hyperlink to go back and edit the information that was entered.
You can select Add Another Item to add another item or service.
And from this table, you also have the option to delete an item by selecting the trash can icon.
If you need to add supporting information, you can upload additional documents in this section here.
Once I have added all the information needed, select Sign & Submit.
From the drop-down list, select the preferred certified IDR entity that you would like to handle this dispute.
For this demonstration, I will select this test IDR entity.
In the conflict of interest attestation section, first indicate whether the person completing this form
is a third-party administrator, or other service provider, initiating on behalf of the initiating party.
Then select the checkbox next to the statement below to attest that you do not have any conflict of interest with the certified IDR entity.
Enter the initiating party name, and the date field will be automatically populated with the date of submission.
Select Submit, and you will see the confirmation page that confirms that the web form has been submitted and outlines next steps.
It is the responsibility of the initiating party to download and print a copy of the Notice of IDR Initiation web form
by selecting the Print PDF button and saving this file for their records.
It is also the responsibility of the initiating party
to send a copy of this PDF to the non-initiating party on the same day the form is submitted.
Both parties will receive confirmation emails from the Federal IDR Portal
letting you know that the web form has been submitted and will include further information on the next steps.
Once you are ready to exit the form, select the Exit button.
This concludes the demonstration of the Notice of IDR Initiation web form.

metadata.title: No Surprises Act Update - October 2026: Pallone, Cassidy, CMS Meeting
metadata.author: Gottlieb and Greenspan, LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
Rep. Pallone introduced the “Lower Premiums, Faster Payments Act”, which would eliminate IDR for services starting in 2028 and make the carrier-calculated QPA the out-of-network payment, with no judicial review. I walk through what is in the bill, why physician groups came out against it within hours, and why I think it is unlikely to pass this year.

Senator Cassidy, the retiring HELP Committee chair, says there is “common ground” for a narrower NSA fix before he leaves and is reportedly aiming for the year-end package. The focus is ineligible disputes and timely payment of awards, but watch what the carriers try to attach to it.

CMS brought all 17 certified IDR entities to Washington on October 1 to discuss “increasingly high IDR-associated costs.” I break down CMS’s framing, what it signals for providers, and the one item on CMS’s list that actually helps us.

segments.text: Hey everyone, James Greenspan from Gottlieb and Greenspan here with another no surprise
act update. We had a big bill uh get proposed down in Washington DC. Recently, Congressman
Palone proposed essentially something that would end NSA arbitration as we know it. He is proposing
doing away with the arbitration system and instead switching to a national fee schedule based on the
QPA. This is something he proposed before back in 2019 when the parties were negotiating as to
how the NSA itself would be structured. This is exactly what he wanted at that time, but
fortunately he was overruled and ultimately signed on to the bill which included the arbitration
process. So this just seems like he's proposing something that he already lost on. From what
I'm hearing, there's not a lot of appetite on the Hill to support this bill. There's not currently
any co-sponsors and it seems like if anything it's potentially just an anchoring technique
which is going to be gearing up for negotiations in the next Congress about what tweaks, if any,
are potentially required for the NSA. Speaking of those tweaks, Senator Cassidy is someone to
keep an eye on because he is one of the original architects of the NSA and he has indicated that he
would like to make some tweaks. He recently lost his uh re-election campaign. he lost his primary,
so he's going to be out of Congress at the end of this session in just a couple of weeks
from now. He's indicated that he does think there's some common ground with respect to
at least eligibility and accountability where the everyone might be able to get together to
pass some kind of legacy bill. I'm hearing that it would not limit the types of cases
that are eligible. it would merely clarify the eligibility process and move it more towards
the beginning of the entire timeline and make it binding rather than you know having to face
continual challenges like we're seeing. The last thing I wanted to mention is that uh CMS recently
called all 17 IDR entities into headquarters and had a closed dooror meeting with them. We're not
entirely sure what was discussed there, but it doesn't necessarily seem like it's great
for providers if CMS and you know the carrier the carriers and their media propaganda are putting
all this pressure on theres. So keep an eye on that as well. I dive into all these topics in
uh much greater depth in my blog and in the in the video that's linked here as well. So as always,
I hope you find these helpful. Please like and subscribe and have a great day.

I hear that you you go in and you get a nice blanket and there's no waiting and they're going to they're going to sponsor your kids baseball team and um you know, they they are out in our fire stations and and police substations and and and building a community um and uh you know, we we want providers that that have a relationship with our employees. We just want to make sure that uh they're charging us a reasonable fee for doing that. Um somebody asked in the questions if if we had talked thought about uh direct primary care. That is something also that we are going to be exploring this next year. >> Yeah. Um one of the things I'll emphasize once once more and Mary Ann, if you want to come on uh and close us out here, but uh I I it's was really will help us in Texas and beyond if employers will be willing to speak up. Uh, to speak to reporters, to speak to legislators, uh um, to to to visit with uh, with Senator Cruz's office as an example. Uh, these are opportunities that uh um, are are worth their their weight in gold. Um, they need to hear from employers and the more we can have employers voicing concern over this and all the craziness that is healthcare delivery today, uh by employers, uh, that that would be of of help. So, uh, Mary Ann, do you want to uh, provide a closing comment and >> I totally agree. This was a very comprehensive and very informative webinar today. I I mean I'm taking notes. And I think the key issue right now for employers who are overwhelmed with a zillion other things is to try to get to capture their attention, especially when you describe the cost to the employers for for this um losing the IDR cases.
