metadata.title: No Surprises Act: Understanding Good Faith Estimates & Patient Provider Dispute Resolution Reqs
metadata.author: CMSHHSgov
metadata.shortDescription: Information for providers and facilities on the No Surprises Act requirements to provide good faith estimates to uninsured/self-pay patients, and information on the patient-provider dispute resolution process.

segments.text: Jeananne Sciabarra: Hello and welcome to CMS' webinar on no surprises next, Good Faith Estimate and patient provider dispute resolution
requirements. My name is Jean Sciabarra and I will provide some background information before turning it over to my colleague to go into details on the provider requirements.
Jeananne Sciabarra: Here's our agenda for today's presentation, we will provide some background information, including an overview of the no surprises act protections
for uninsured or self-pay individuals. We will discuss the good faith estimate requirements,
and we will describe the patient provider dispute resolution process.
Jeananne Sciabarra: Please note that the information provided in this presentation is intended only to be a
general informal summary of technical legal standards. It is not intended to take the place of the statutes, regulations, or formal
policy guidance upon which it is based. This presentation summarizes current policy and operations as
of the date it was presented, we encourage readers to refer to the applicable statutes, regulations, and other interpretive materials
for complete and current information.
Jeananne Sciabarra: The contents of this document do not have the force and effect of law and are not meant to bind the public in any way,
unless specifically incorporated into a contract. This document is intended only to provide clarity to the public regarding published or produced and disseminated at US taxpayer expense.
existing requirements under the law. This communication was printed,
Jeananne Sciabarra: And now we will begin our webinar.
Jeananne Sciabarra: Let's begin with an overview of the No Surprises Act. The No Surprises Act introduced new requirements for providers, facilities
and providers of air ambulance services to protect individuals from surprise medical bills. These requirements prohibit providers
and facilities from directly billing individuals for the difference between the amount they charged and the amount that the individual's
plan or coverage will pay plus the individual's cost sharing amounts, i.e. balanced billing in certain
circumstances; require providers and facilities to provide good faith estimates of charges for care to uninsured or self-pay
individuals upon scheduling care or on request, and for individuals with certain types of coverage to submit good faith estimates
to the individual's plan or issuer; Create a patient provider dispute resolution process for uninsured or self-pay individuals
to contest charges that are substantially in excess of the good faith estimates;
require certain providers and facilities publicly disclose restrictions on balance billing,
and limit billed amounts in situations where a provider's network status changes mid treatment or individuals act
on inaccurate provider directory information.
Jeananne Sciabarra: The scope of individuals protected under the No Surprises Act, beginning January 1, 2022.
These No Surprises Act requirements will apply to items and services provided to most individuals enrolled
in private or commercial health coverage, such as employment based group health plans, both self-insured and fully insured
individual or group health coverage on or outside the federal or state based exchanges. Federal Employee Health Benefit
or FEHB health plans nonfederal governmental plans sponsored by state and local government employers
certain church plans with IRS jurisdiction and student health insurance coverage
as defined at 45 CFR 147 point 145.
Jeananne Sciabarra: Some requirements also apply to providers and facilities with respect to uninsured or self-pay individuals like
requirements that providers and facilities provide good faith estimates for scheduled care or upon request.
Requirements under the No Surprises Act don't apply to beneficiaries or enrollees in Medicare, Medicaid, Indian Health Services,
Veterans Affairs health care or TRICARE. These programs have other protections against high medical bills.
So, protections also don't apply to short term limited duration insurance, excepted benefits or retiree only plans
or account based group health plans.
Jeananne Sciabarra: This is one of a series of presentations of No Surprises Act. Other slide decks in this series can be found on the
No Surprises Act website, CMS.gov/nosurprises.
Jeananne Sciabarra: Overview of the No Surprises Act's protections for uninsured for self-pay individuals.
Effective January 1, 2022, the No Surprises Act protects uninsured or self-paid individuals from many
unexpectedly high medical bills. If an individual does not have certain types of health insurance or does not plan to use that insurance
to pay for health care items or services, they are eligible to receive a good faith estimate of what they may be charged before they receive the item
or service. A new patient provider dispute resolution process is available for uninsured or self-pay individuals who get
a bill from a provider that is substantially in excess of the expected charges on the good faith estimate.
Under the PPDR process, and uninsured or self-pay individual or their authorized representative, they initiate the PPDR
Process to seek a determination from an independent third party certified by HHS,
a selected dispute resolution or SDR entity for the amount the individual has to pay.
This process can provide the uninsured or self-pay individual important consumer protections
from paying billed charges that are significantly more than the expected charges in the good faith estimate.
Jeananne Sciabarra: And now I will hand it over to my colleague Jamie Hermanson who will present information on
the good faith estimate requirements.
Jaime Hermansen: My name is Jaime Hermansen and I'm providing an overview of the no surprises act protections for uninsured
or self-pay individuals. On October 7, 2021, HHS published interim
final rules titled requirements related to surprise billing part two, implemented various provisions of the
No Surprises Act, including good faith estimates and the PPDR process for payment determinations.
This presentation will focus on what information must be included in the GFE and the PPDR process.
Jaime Hermansen: Good Faith estimates for uninsured or self-pay individuals.
The Good Faith Estimate, also referred to as the GFE is a notification that outlines an uninsured or
self-pay individuals expected charges for a scheduled or requested item or service. Providers and facilities
must give this estimate to an uninsured or self-pay individual or their authorized representative who
requests it or who schedules an item or service. The good faith estimate will also include items or services reasonably
expected to be provided along with the primary items or service, even if the individual will receive the
Items or services from another provider or another facility. These requirements are applicable for good faith estimates
requested on or after January 1, 2022 or for good faith estimates required to be provided
in connection with items or services scheduled on or after January 1, 2022.
Jaime Hermansen: Scope of providers that must comply
with the no surprises Act requirements pertaining to protections for uninsured or self-pay individuals. For the
purposes of the good faith estimate. a health care provider means a physician or other health care provider who is acting within
the scope of practice of that providers license or certification under applicable state law,
including a provider of air ambulance services. The following types of health care providers must comply with the NSA's
good faith estimate and PPD are requirements. Physicians other health care providers who are acting
within their scope of practice under applicable state law and providers of air ambulance services.
Jaime Hermansen: Public Facilities that must comply with NSA requirements pertaining to protections for uninsured or self-pay
individuals. All healthcare institutions licensed under applicable state or local law are treated
as healthcare facilities that must comply with the No Surprises Act GFE and PPDR
requirements, including, for example hospitals, outpatient hospital departments, critical access
hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, rural health centers, federally qualified health centers, laboratory
centers, and imaging centers.
Jaime Hermansen: Scope of care included in good faith estimates. Under the NSA, uninsured or self-pay
individuals should receive a single comprehensive GFE that includes expected charges
before the primary item or service that will be furnished by the convening provider or convening facility and that
is the initial reason for the visit. All items and services that are reasonably expected to be provided in conjunction
with the primary item or service provided during a defined period of these items or services can include
any of the following encounters, procedures, medical tests, supplies, prescription drugs,
durable medical equipment, or fees including facility fees.
Jaime Hermansen: An example we made a good faith estimate for knee surgery.
If an individual schedules a knee surgery with their orthopedic surgeon, a good faith estimate
could include an itemized list of items or services in conjunction with and including the actual knee surgery,
such as physician professional fees, assistant surgeon professional fees, anesthesiologist
professional fees, facility fees, prescription drugs, durable medical equipment fees.
Jaime Hermansen: All the items and services that are reasonably expected to be to be provided from admission
through discharge are part of that scheduled knee surgery period of care, these services or items should be included
in the good faith estimate. Separate good faith estimates would be provided upon scheduling or upon request for any items or
services that are necessary prior to or following provision of the primary item
or service beyond the period of such as preoperative laboratory test, or post discharge physical therapy.
Jaime Hermansen: How expected charges are determined for a good faith estimate.
Expected charges included on a good faith estimate should be the cash pay rate or rate that the
uninsured or self-pay individual would be expected to pay for items or services listed on the good faith estimate.
The expected charges should reflect true anticipated billed charges, including any anticipated discounts or
adjustments that a provider or facility would anticipate applying to the uninsured or self-pay individual. For example,
the expected charges provided by a federally tax exempt nonprofit hospital should apply any adjustments
to billed charges that would be applied to an individual under the hospital's financial assistance policy.
In determining expense expected
charges, providers and facilities are expected to use the coding that best describes each item or service listed in
the good faith estimate. When a single service code is available that captures reporting and billing for the component parts of an item
or service. The same of service code and expected charge for that single service code would be reported in the good faith
estimate to capture the most comprehensive coding level. The component parts would not be included in the good faith estimate
as they would not be separately reported or billed.
Jaime Hermansen: Convening provider or facility and Co-provider or facility. A convenient provider or facility
must provide a good faith estimate for the uninsured individual, including any item or service but is reasonably expected
to be provided in conjunction with a scheduled or requested item or service, another provider or
facility also refer to as a co provider or co-facility. As a result, the good faith estimate
could contain expected charges from multiple providers; the convening provider, and co-providers or co-facilities
that furnish items and services that are customarily provided in conjunction with a primary item or service.
For instance, if a patient scheduled the surgery that convenient provider or facility might include in the good faith estimates
Cost of surgery in the co provider or co-facility might include the cost of any labs, tests or
anesthesia that may be used during the operation.
Jaime Hermansen: We now move on to a knowledge check.
A provider is deciding which CPT codes to use for laboratory tests. The provider is choosing
between CPT code 85027 for individual CPT codes for each component parts of the
service represented by CPT code 85027. In order to remain compliant
with the NSA, which option would best describe the item or service for use in the GFE?
Jaime Hermansen: Knowledge Check Answer, HHS expects that the GFE
would include expected charges for CPT code 85027 not expected charges for each
component part since there is a single CPT code available that better captures reporting for all of the component parts
of the laboratory service. And a single service code is available that captures reporting and billing
for the component parts of an item or service. The spin off service code
and expect to charge for that single service code would be reported in the gap to capture the most comprehensive coding level.
Jaime Hermansen: Informing uninsured or self-pay individuals. A convening provider or facility must
inform all uninsured or self-paid individuals of the availability of a good faith estimate of charges
upon scheduling an item or service or upon request. To determine if someone is an uninsured or self-pay individual
the provider or facility must ask if the individual is enrolled in a group health plan, group health insurance
coverage offered by a health insurance issuer, a federal health care program, a health or
a health benefits plan under a Federal Employees Health Benefits.
Jaime Hermansen: If not involved in any of the above, the individual is considered uninsured for the
purposes of the good faith estimate. The individual is enrolled in a group health plan, group or individual health insurance
coverage offered by health insurance issuer or an FEHB health benefits plan. The convening provider
or facility must ask if the individual is seeking to have a claim submitted for the items or services with such plan
coverage. If not, the individual is considered self-pay for the purposes of the good faith estimate.
Jaime Hermansen: Distribution and display of the good faith estimate to individuals. information
regarding the availability of good faith estimates for uninsured or self-pay individuals must be written in a clear and understandable manner
prominently displayed and easily searchable from a public search engine, on the convening providers or convening facilities website,
in the office and on site where scheduling or questions about the cost of items or services.
Convening providers and facilities must also give information about the good faith estimate for uninsured or self-pay individuals. When
scheduling an item or service or when questions about the cost of items or services occur. Convening providers and convening
facilities must consider any discussion or inquiry regarding the potential cost of items and services under
consideration as a request for a good faith estimate.
Jaime Hermansen: Timeframe. Upon receiving a request for a good faith estimate from an uninsured or self-pay
individual or upon scheduling a primary item or service for an uninsured or self-pay individual, the convening
provider or convening facility must contact all co-providers and co facilities are reasonably expected to provide
items or services in conjunction with and in support of the primary item or service no later than one business day after scheduling
or receiving the request. The convening provider or convening facility must request that the co-providers or co facilities
submit Good Faith Estimate information to the convening provider or facility.
Convening providers and facilities must provide a good faith estimate to uninsured or self-pay individual
within the following timeframes. When a primary item or service is scheduled at least three business days
before the date, the item or service is scheduled to be furnished. The GFE must be provided no later than one
business day after the date of scheduling. When a primary item or service is scheduled at least 10 business days before such items
are furnished, the GFE must be provided no later than three business days after the data scheduling.
When a GFE is requested by an uninsured or self-pay individual, the GFE must be provided
no later than three business days after the date of the request.
Jaime Hermansen: HHS recognizes that some providers or facilities may need to establish efficient and secure
communication channels for transmission of good faith estimate information between convening providers or facilities and
co-providers and co facilities. It is also understood that it may take time for providers and facilities to develop systems and processes
for receiving and providing the required information from co-providers and co facilities.
Therefore, for good faith estimates provided uninsured or self-paid individuals from January 1, 2022
through December 31, 2022, HHS will exercise its enforcement discretion in situations where a GFE
provided to an uninsured or self-pay individual does not include expected charges from co-providers or co facilities.
Jaime Hermansen: A co provider or co-facility is not prohibited from furnishing the information before
December 31, 2022, and nothing would prevent the uninsured or self-pay individual from separately requesting
a good faith estimate directly from the co-provider or co-facility, in which case the co-provider and co-facility would be required to provide a
good faith estimate for such items or services. Otherwise during this period, HHS encourages convening providers
and convening facilities to include a range of expected charges for items and services reasonably expected to be provided and
billed by co-providers and co-facilities.
Jaime Hermansen: Changes to the scope of the GFE. If a convening provider, convening facility, co-provider or co-facility anticipates
or is notified of any changes to the scope of a GFE, such as anticipated changes to the expected charges,
items, services, frequency recurrences, duration providers or facilities previously furnished at the
time of scheduling, the convening provider or competing facility must provide the individual with a new GFE no later than one business day
before the items or services are scheduled to be furnished. If any changes and expected providers or facilities represented
in the GFE occurred less than one business day before the item or service is scheduled to be furnished. The replacement
provider or facility must accept the GFE for the relevant items or services being furnished
that was provided by the replaced provider or facility.
Jaime Hermansen: For good faith estimates provided upon request of an uninsured or self-paying individual upon scheduling
of the requested items or services. That convening provider or convening facility must provide the individual with a
new GFE for the scheduled item or service within the standard timeframes specified in the timeframe section of this presentation.
Good faith estimates for recurring primary items or services.
A convening provider or convening facility may issue a single GFE for recurring
primary items or services if both of the following requirements are met. The GFE for recurring items or services
includes in a clear and understandable manner. The expected scope of the recurring primary items or services such as
timeframes, frequency, and total number of recurring items and services. The scope of a good faith estimate for recurring
primary items or services does not exceed 12 months.
Requirements For co-providers and co-facilities. Co-providers and co-facilities must submit
GFE information upon the request of the convening provider or convening facility, the co-provider or co-facility
must provide and the convening provider or convening facility must receive the GFE information no later than one
business day after the co-provider or co-facility receives the request from the convening provider or convening facility.
Co-providers and co-facilities must notify and provide new GFE information to a convening
provider or convening facility if the co-provider or co-facility anticipates any changes to the scope of the
GFE information previously submitted to the convening provider or facility, such as anticipated changes
to the expected charges, items, services, frequency recurrences, duration providers, or facilities.
Jaime Hermansen: If any changes to the co-providers or co-facilities listed in the good faith estimate occur less than one business
day, before the item or service is scheduled to be furnished, replacement co-providers or co-facility
must accept as its good faith estimate of expected charges the GFE for the relevant items or services included
in the GFE provided by the replaced provider or facility. In the event and uninsured or self-pay individual
separately schedules or request a GFE from a provider or facility that would otherwise be considered a co-provider or
co-facility, that provider or facility must meet all requirements that apply to convening providers
and convening facilities for issuing a GFE to the individual.
Jaime Hermansen: Content requirements for a GFE issued to an uninsured or self-pay individual.
A GFE issued must include the patient name, date of birth,
description of the primary item or service and clear and understandable language and, if applicable, the date the primary item or service
is scheduled. An itemized list of items and services grouped by each provider or facility reasonably expected
to be furnished for the primary item or service and items or services reasonably expected to be furnished in conjunction
with the primary item or service for that period of care, including both items and services
reasonably expected to be furnished by the convening provider, or convening facility for the period of care, and items or
services reasonably expected to be furnished by co-providers or co-facilities.
Jaime Hermansen: GFE also includes the applicable diagnosis codes, expected
service codes and expected charges associated with each listed item or service. Along with the name,
National Provider Identifier and tax identification number of each provider or facility represented in the GFE
and the states and office or facility locations where the items or services are expected to be
furnished by such provider or facility.
Jaime Hermansen: The GFE also includes a list of items or services that the convening provider or convening facility anticipates will require a separate scheduling and
that are expected to occur before or following the expected period of care for the primary item or service. The GFE must
include a disclaimer directly above this list that includes all the following information.
Separate good faith estimates will be issued to an uninsured or self-pay individual upon scheduling
or upon request of the list of items or services. Notification that for items and services
included in this list, information such as diagnosis codes, service codes, expected charges and provider or facility identifiers
do not need to be included as that information will be provided and separate GFEs upon scheduling
or upon request of such items or services. Along with instructions for how an uninsured
or self-pay individual can obtain GFEs for such items or services.
Jaime Hermansen: GFEs also include a disclaimer informs the uninsured or self-pay individuals
that there may be additional items or services that the convening provider or convening facility recommends, as part of the course of care
that must be scheduled or requested separately and are not reflected in the good faith estimate.
An additional disclaimer that informs the individual that the information provided in the good faith estimate
is only an estimate regarding items or services reasonably expected to be furnished at the time the GFE is issued
to the uninsured or self-pay individual and that actual items, services or charges may differ from the GFE.
Jaime Hermansen: A disclaimer that informs the
uninsured or self-pay individual that the individual's right to initiate the patient provider dispute resolution process
or if the actual billed charges are substantially in excess of the expected charges included in the
good faith estimate. This disclaimer must include instructions for where the individual can find information about how to initiate
the PPDR process and state that the initiation of the PPDR process will not adversely
affect the quality of health care services furnished to the individual by provider or a facility.
And then disclaimer that a good faith estimate is not a contract and does not require the uninsured or self-pay individual
to obtain items or services from any of the providers or facilities identified in the GFE.
Jaime Hermansen: HHS has developed a model template and notice that providers and facilities may use to
Jaime Hermansen: or self-pay individuals of the availability of a GFE. Use of this model notice is not required
and is only provided as a means to facilitate compliance with applicable notice
requirement. This model notice and template were published as part of CMS form 10791 and are available for download.
Jaime Hermansen: And here we show an image of the HHS model notice and template.
Jaime Hermansen: Content requirements for GFE information submitted by co-providers or co-facilities
to convening providers or convening facilities. To get the information submitted to convening providers
or convenient facilities by co-providers or co-facilities for inclusion in GFE must include patient name
and date of birth, a list of items or services expected to be provided by the co-provider or co-facility that are reasonably expected
to be furnished in conjunction with the primary item or service as part of the period of care. Applicable
diagnosis codes, expected service codes, unexpected charges associated with each listed item or service.
A disclaimer that the GFE is not a contract and does not require the uninsured or self-pay individual to
obtain the items or services from any of the co-providers or co-facilities identified in the GFE.
Jaime Hermansen: Required methods for providing GFE for uninsured or self-pay individuals. A GFE
must be provided in written form either on paper or electronically pursuant to the uninsured or self-pay individual’s
requested method of delivery and within the timeframes described above. GFEs provided
electronically must be provided in a manner that the uninsured or self-pay individual can both save and print.
GFE is provided to uninsured or self-pay individuals by paper mail may be postmarked by the
timelines specified in the timeframe section of this presentation. A GFE must be provided and written using clear and understandable language.
Jaime Hermansen: Additional requirements. A GFE issued to an uninsured or self-pay individual under
Meaning providers and convening facilities must provide a copy of any previously issued GFE
furnished within the last six years to an uninsured or self-pay individual on request by the individual.
if those state processes and rules do not meet federal Good Faith Estimate requirements, those providers and facilities have failed to comply with federal Good Faith Estimate.
Jaime Hermansen: A provider or facility will not fail to comply with federal GFE requirements solely because despite acting
in good faith, and with reasonable due diligence, the provider or facility makes an error or omission any required
GFE provided that the provider or facility corrects information as soon as practicable.
If items or services are furnished before an error in the gap is addressed, the provider or facility
may be subject to PPDR if the actual billed charges are substantially in excess of the GFE.
Jaime Hermansen: To the extent that compliance with federal GFE requirements requires a provider or facility
to obtain information from any other entity or individual, the provider or facility will not be able to comply
with this section if it relied in good faith on the information from the other entity, unless the provider or facility
knows or reasonably should have known that the information is incomplete or inaccurate. If the provider or facility
learns that the information is incomplete or inaccurate, the provider or facility must provide corrected information to the uninsured
or self-pay individual as soon as practicable. If items or services are furnished before an error
in an in a GFE is addressed, the provider or facility may be subject to PPDR if the actual billed charges are substantially in excess of the GFE.
Jaime Hermansen: Here we show an example of how items itemized list of expected items and services could be displayed in a gap.
Jaime Hermansen: In addition, this second slide provides another example of how items or services could be displayed in a GFE.
I will now hand the presentation over to my colleague Janny Frimpong to discuss the patient provider dispute resolution process.
Janny Frimpong: Patient provider dispute resolution process. Beginning January 1, 2022. The patient provider
dispute resolution process will be available for uninsured or self-pay individuals who get a bill for an item
or service that is substantially in excess of the expected charges on the GFE. Under the PPDR process
the individual has to pay. This process can provide an uninsured or self-pay individual important consumer protections
from billed charges that are substantially in excess of the expected charges in their good faith estimate.
Janny Frimpong: Items or services eligible for PPDR. The PPDR process can apply to any item
or self-pay individual for the total billed charges are substantially in excess of the total expected charges
in the good faith estimate. HHS regulations established that when the billed charges for any provider or facility
in excess of the good faith estimate for that provider or facility by $400 or more, the item or service
may be eligible for payment determination by an SDR entity through the PPDR process, as each
Good Faith Estimate could potentially contain expected charges for multiple providers and facilities, the substantially
in excess determination is made separately for each specific provider, or facility listed on the good faith estimate.
Items or services eligible for PPDR continued. If a co-provider
or co-facility that provided an estimate of the expected charge for an item or service in a good faith estimate is replaced
by a different co-provider or co-facility, less than one business day before that item or service is scheduled
to be provided, an item or service filled by the replacement code provider or co-facility is eligible for dispute resolution
if the billed charge was $400 or more than the total expected charges included in the good faith estimate
for the original co-provider or co-facility. If the replacement provider or facility provides the uninsured or
self-pay individual with a new Good Faith Estimate within the timeframes HHS is shared, then the determination
of whether an item or service bill by the replacement co-provider co-facility is eligible for dispute resolution is based on whether
the total billed charges for the replacement co-provider or co-facility is $400 or more than the total expected
charges included in the good faith estimate provided by the replacement co-provider for co-facility.
Joshua Annas: Knowledge check Tonya is 40 year old female with a long history of right knee pain. She does not have any form of health insurance
Tonya scheduled an appointment with her orthopedist to receive a cortisone injection underneath. Upon scheduling the appointment her orthopedist
sends her a good faith estimate. The good faith estimate lists the total expected charges of $300 for the procedure. Tonya undergoes
the injection and subsequent subsequently received a bill from the orthopedist. The total bill charges $850. Would Tonya
be eligible to pursue the PPDR process.
Joshua Annas: Knowledge check answer. Yes, Tanya would be eligible to pursue the PDR. Tonya is uninsured and the total bill charge
is considered substantially in excess of the good faith estimate, since the difference between the total expected and total billed charges is greater than
or equivalent to $400. Under the NSA in order to be eligible to pursue the PPDR process, an individual must
be considered uninsured or self-pay, the total bill charges by the particular convening provider, convening facility, co-provider,
or co-facility must be substantially in excess of the total expected charges for that specific provider or facility listed in
the good faith estimate, and the date of the bill must be within 120 days.
co-provider or co-facility. For good faith estimates provided to uninsured or self-pay individuals on or after
where the good faith estimate does not include expected charges for items and services from a co-provider or co-facility.
If expected charges for a co-provider and co-facility do appear on the good faith estimate those items
or services will be eligible for the patient provider dispute resolution process as normal. This particular application for PPDR
eligibility would only apply in 2022. During the period of enforcement discretion, items or services to be
provided by co-provider or co-facility that appears on the good faith estimate that do not include an estimate of the expected charges
or that appear as a range of expected charges would not be eligible for the PPDR process for the item or service
provided by the co-provider or co-facility.
Janny Frimpong: Would a provider or facility be subject to requirements for the PPDR process but not requirements
for the good faith estimates? Good Faith Estimate requirements work together with the PPDR requirements to establish
important consumer protections for uninsured or self-pay individuals who see bill charges that are $400 or more
than the good faith estimate they received prior to scheduling or upon request of items or services.
As a result, the requirements for the PPDR process apply to all providers or facilities subject to the good faith estimate requirements.
Janny Frimpong: How is PPDR eligibility determined when there are different providers or facilities listed on the same
good faith estimate? Eligibility for PPDR is determined separately for each unique provider or facility listed
on the good faith estimate. For each provider or facility, the total expected charges for each item or service
should be added up. The total amount is then compared to the total of all billed charges for that provider or facility, including
billed charges for items and services that were furnished but not included in the good faith estimate to determine eligibility for PPDR.
Janny Frimpong: How is PPDR eligibility determined when there are different providers or facilities listed on the same Good Faith Estimate,
continued. Example one. In example one the good faith estimate contains two providers Provider A
and Provider B. The total expected charges for both providers a and b equal $2,625.
However, for purposes of PPDR the total of expected charges is separated by provider.
In this case, the total expected charges for Provider A are $2,125.
And the total expected charges for Provider B are $500. The billed charges for providers A and B are compared with
their total expected charges to determine whether the bill charges are eligible for PPDR as shown an example two.
Janny Frimpong: How is PPDR eligibility determined when there are different providers or facilities listed on the same Good Faith Estimate,

Joshua Annas: What about items not originally on the good faith estimate? For billed items or services not listed on the good faith estimate, if the SDR entity determines the provider or facility did not provide credible information that demonstrates the difference between the billed charge for the new item or service, and the good faith estimate reflects the cost of a medically necessary item or service and is based on unforeseen circumstances that could not have reasonably been anticipated by the provider or facility when the good faith estimate was provided then the SDR entity must determine that the amount to be paid for the new item or service to be equal to $0. Joshua Annas: What about items not originally on the good faith estimate, continued. If the SDR entity determines that a provider or facility has provided credible information, that the billed charge for new items or services that did not appear on a good faith estimate does reflect the cost of a medically necessary item or service and is based on unforeseen circumstances it could not have been reasonably anticipated by the provider or facility, when the good faith estimate was provided, then the SDR entity must determine the charge to be paid by the uninsured or self-pay individual for the new item or service as the lesser of one the billed charge or to the median payment amount paid by a plan or issuer for the same or similar service by the same or similar provider in the geographic area as defined in Section 149.140(a)(7) where the services were provided as reflected in an independent database as defined section 149.140(a)(3) using the methodology described in Section 149.140(c)(3). When comparing the billed charge with the amounts contained in an independent database, the SDR entity should account for any discounts offered by the provider or facility. Joshua Annas: What about items not originally on a good faith estimate, continued. After making a determination about each item and service subject to the PPDR, the SDR entity will add together the amount to be paid for all items and services subject to this determination. In cases where the final amount determined by the SDR entity is lower than the build charge, the SDR entity will reduce the final amount by the administrative fee ow paid by the individual for any item or service that does not appear on the good faith estimate. For example, a new item or service they see the table below. Joshua Annas: Can providers and facilities settle their payment dispute with uninsured or self-pay individuals during the PDR process? Yes, HHS recognizes that the two parties to the PDR process, the uninsured or self-pay individual and the provider or facility may agree to resolve the dispute by settling on a payment amount. At any point after the PPDR process has been initiated but before the date on which a determination is made by the SDR entity. The parties can settle the payment amount through either an offer a financial assistance or an offer to accept a lower amount or an agreement by the uninsured or self-paid individual to pay the bill charges in full. Joshua Annas: Can providers in facility settle their payment dispute with uninsured or self to individual during the PPDR process, continued. In the event that the parties agree to settle on a payment about the provider facility should notify the SDR entity through the federal IDR portal electronically or in paper form as soon as possible no later than three business days after the date of the agreement. Once the SDR entity receives the notification of the settlement the SDR entity must close the dispute resolution case as settled and the agreed upon payment amount will apply. Jaime Hermansen: Knowledge Check. Maria the 25 year old female self-pay individual she has an appointment with her gynecologist to discuss long acting reversible contraceptives. Maria decides to schedule a procedure to have an intrauterine device placed. Upon scheduling the appointment, the gynecologist sends her a good faith estimate, which includes a total expected charge of $400. Maria undergoes that procedure. Several weeks later she received a bill for $850. Maria submits the initiation notice to HHS. However, before the SDR entity makes a determination, Maria instead agrees to pay the bill charges in full. Are parties allowed to settle a dispute outside of the PPDR process? Jaime Hermansen: Knowledge Check Answer. Yes, parties are allowed to settle the payment amount after the PPDR process has been initiated but before a determination is made, the parties can settle the payment amount through an offer financial assistance, an offer to accept a lower amount or an agreement by the uninsured herself pay individuals to pay the bill charges in full. If the parties agree to settle the provider facility must provide a settlement notification to the SDR entity no later than three business days after the date of the agreement. Joshua Annas: Treatment of payments made prior to the determination. Payment of the billed charges or a portion of the bill charges by the uninsured or self-pay individual or by another party on behalf of the uninsured or self the individual prior to a determination does not demonstrate agreement by the individual to settle at that amount or any other amount. Joshua Annas: Deferral to state PPDR processes. If HHS determines that a state law provides the process to determine the amount to be paid by uninsured or self-pay individual to a provider or facility and that such process meets or exceeds minimum federal requirements HHS shall defer to the state process and direct any PPDR requests proceed from uninsured or self-pay individuals in such state to the state process to adjudicate the dispute resolution initiation request. Joshua Annas: Extension of time periods for extenuating circumstances. The time periods specified throughout the PPDR process, other than the timing of all payments, including payment of the administrative fees may be extended in extenuating circumstances at HHS discretion if an extension is necessary to address delays due to matters beyond the control of the party or for good cause, and the parties attests that prompt action will be taken to ensure that determination under this section is made as soon as administratively practicable under the circumstances. Any party may request an extension by submitting a request for extension to extenuating circumstances through the federal IDR portal, or electronic or paper mail. If the extension is necessary to address delays due to matters beyond the control of the party, or for good cause. Joshua Annas: HHS model notices. HHS has developed a model notice the SDR entities may use to provide the determination notice to providers or facilities and a model notice that providers or facilities may use to notify the SDR entity and HHS that all parties agree to settle on a payment amount. These model notices were published as part of CMS form number 10791 and are available for download. Joshua Annas: HHS model notices, continued. Joshua Annas: HHS model notices continued two. Joshua Annas: Summary of the PPDR process. Areas of particular applicability to providers and facilities have been underlined for emphasis. Timeline. Within 120 days, calendar days. Process step. Initiation notice and administrative fee. The uninsured or self-pay individuals submit the initiation notice and other relevant information to the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services. The initiation notice must be sent with within 120 calendar days from when the uninsured or self-pay individual receives their initial bill for items and services from their service provider or facility. HHS will choose and notify the selected dispute resolution entity. Once HHS has chosen the SDR entity the uninsured or self-pay individual must pay an administrative fee to the SDR entity. Timeline. Within three business days. Process step. SDR entity conflict of interest identification. Should a conflict of interest exist, HHS will select a new SDR entity to conduct the PPR process. If no SDR entities are available to resolve the dispute, the initially selected SDR entity will be required to initiate their entity level conflict of interest mitigation plan, which may include identifying a subcontractor whom they have verified that not have a conflict of interest and submit notice to HHS related to the implementation of the mitigation plan no later than three business days following selection by HHS. HHS will then assign the case to the identified alternative SDR entity to conduct the PPDR process. Joshua Annas: Summary of the PPDR process, continued. Timeline. Within 21 calendar days. Process step. Eligibility determination and additional information. After the SDR entity receives information submitted by the uninsured or self-pay individual, they will notify them regarding whether or not they're eligible for PPDR and if additional information is needed to determine eligibility, or if the patient can proceed to dispute resolution. If additional information is required, the patient has 21 calendar day to furnish it after being notified of the information deficiency. Process step four. PPDR initiation. If the SDR entity determines that the item or service meets the eligibility criteria, and the initiation notice contains the required information. The SDR entity will notify the uninsured or self-pay individual and the provider or facility that the item or service has been determined eligible for dispute resolution. Joshua Annas: Summary of the PPDR process, continued. Timeline. Within three business days. Process step. Parties’ conflict of interest identification. The uninsured or self-pay individual and provider or facility may attest to having a conflict of interest with the SDR entity. Joshua Annas: Summary of the PPDR process, continued. Timeline. Within three business days. Process step. Patient provider negotiation. If the parties to a PPDR process agree on a payment amount to either an offer a financial assistance or an offer of a lower amount or an agreement by the uninsured or self-pay individual to pay the billed charges in full after the PPDR process has been initiated but before the date on which a determination is made, the provider or facility will notify the SDR entity through the federal IDR portal electronically or in paper form as soon as possible, but no later than three business days after the date of the agreement. The settlement notice notification must contain at a minimum a settlement amount, the date of such settlement and documentation demonstrating that the provider or facility and uninsured or self-pay individual have agreed to the settlement. The settlement notice must also document that the provider or facility has applied a reduction to the uninsured or self-pay individual's settlement amount equal to at least half the amount of the administrative fee paid. Jeananne Sciabarra: Now I'd like to provide a recap of today's main takeaways. The No surprises Act protects uninsured or self-pay individuals from unexpectedly high medical bills in two ways. If an individual does not have certain types of health insurance or does not plan to use that insurance to pay for health care items or services, they are eligible to receive a good faith estimate of what they may be charged before they receive the item or service. When the billed charges for any provider or facility are in excess of the good faith estimate for that provider or facility by $400 or more, the item or service may be eligible for payment determination by an SDR entity through the PPDR process. A convening provider must provide a good faith estimate to the uninsured individual, including any item or service that is reasonably expected to be provided in conjunction with a scheduled or requested item or service by another provider or facility. A co-provider or co-facility is a provider or facility other than a convening provider or convening facility that furnishes items or services that are customarily provided in conjunction with a primary item or service. Jeananne Sciabarra: Providers' and facilities' main responsibilities in the PPDR process include: the provider or facility should submit any required information to the SDR entity within 10 business days of receipt of the selection notice. While the PPDR process is pending, the provider or facility must not move the bill for the disputed item or service into collection or threaten to do so. Or, if the bill has already moved into collection, the provider or facility should cease collection efforts. The provider or facility must also suspend the approval of any late fees on unpaid bill amounts until after the PPDR process has concluded. In the event that the parties agree to settle on a payment amount, the provider or facility should notify the SDR entity through the federal IDR portal electronically or in paper form as soon as possible but no later than three business days after the date of the agreement. The determination made by the SDR entity will be binding upon the parties involved. Jeananne Sciabarra: This slide provides additional resources including links to the rule and published guidance, a sample disclaimer and model notice, a link to the No Surprises Act website, and contact information for the No Surprises help desk, which is staffed from 8am to 8pm eastern time seven days a week. Jeananne Sciabarra: Providers who have questions about the No surprises Act provisions can email Provider_enforcement@CMS.HHS.gov. Jeananne Sciabarra: The rest of the slide deck is a glossary of terms used in the presentation. Please review at your leisure and thank you for viewing this presentation.

metadata.title: ANESTHESIOLOGY® 2026: No Surprises Act, IDR, and Out-of-Network Spending
metadata.author: TopMedTalk
metadata.shortDescription:
Recorded at ASA Anesthesiology 2026 in San Diego, hosts Andy Cumpstey and Harriet Hopf speak with Patrick Velliky, Chief External Affairs Officer and Senior Vice President for Government Affairs at HaloMD, about misconceptions around the No Surprises Act (NSA) independent dispute resolution (IDR) process and its cost impact.

 Velliky argues many studies cite total arbitration awards without a pre-NSA baseline, and his emergency medicine analysis comparing like-for-like out-of-network (OON) claims found OON spending is 13%–50% lower post-NSA, with modeled savings depending on assumptions about payments for the ~90% of eligible claims not going to IDR.

 He discusses the qualifying payment amount (QPA), recent litigation finding unlawful QPA manipulation, and concerns about third-party administrators (TPAs), including lack of transparency, shared-savings fees, and a reported ~35% nonpayment rate of binding IDR awards.

 The conversation links these issues to anesthesia, subsidies, consolidation, employer oversight, and pending bipartisan legislation to penalize nonpayment and improve accountability.

videos.full_text: Topmed talk. >> [music] >> Welcome to Topmed talk. I'm Andy Comstock. I'm your host here at Anesthesiology 2026 in the wonderful San Diego. And the answer, I think, for that probably depends probably what researchers measure as well as what they compare it with. So, it's a real pleasure to welcome Patrick Velicky from Halo MD, who's going to discuss his work analyzing out-of-network spending before and after the No Surprises Act. Halo MD represents more physicians than any other organization within that dispute resolution process. I'm responsible for about 22% of all initiations in the the dispute resolution process or the IDR process. And what prompted you to examine the cost of this differently? >> Yeah, so there's a lot of existing research and a lot of commentary on how the IDR process, the dispute resolution process, is is working. And I think, frankly, a lot of misinformation about the costs associated with that process. Largely because for essentially all of the research that's been that's been done so far, they're missing a pretty crucial piece and that's a a baseline. You really can't compare or assess how something is affecting cost if you don't know how you paid for the thing before it went into effect. So, really set out to create that comparison and develop a baseline that we could look at to really see how things are changing. >> So, I would always be curious about the baseline. So, how did it come to be that the baseline wasn't part of the conversation to begin with? >> So, a lot of the research that exists really treats the total cost of arbitration as though it were new cost, right? It they look at the total award amounts, the the dollars associated with the arbitration process, and then just sort of report out those dollars without at all like like I said, looking at a baseline. >> So, the baseline would be malpractice resolution or like what Yeah. Or or um bill resolution or >> Yeah. So, basically what what we set out to use as a baseline is you can trying to go for apples-to-apples like you ought to when in any sort of comparative analysis, what did we pay for out-of-network care prior to the No Surprises Act and the arbitration process, and what do we now pay for that same out-of-network care after arbitration? >> Thank you. >> And so, I guess that's what makes this approach more complete than just looking at reimbursement purely through the independent the IDR itself. Is it that is the whole package is that's the difference? >> Yeah, the way I like to think about it it's like if you were told that the steering wheel in your car cost about $800. And then using that $800 steering wheel, you were supposed to somehow into it whether the cost of cars had increased or decreased based on what you're now paying for steering wheels, right? You don't have the picture. You're only looking at this little piece of the total cost of the car and don't even have the context as to well, were steering wheels $200 5 years ago or were they $1,000, right? All you're seeing is well, steering wheels cost $800. That's the same as true when you look at the arbitration process and you're told well, the cost of care that went through arbitration was $22.4 billion over the the 5-year period which is what Georgetown reports. Well, you're just looking at this little snapshot of what's being paid for this care without any sort of meaningful analysis as to its place in the larger system or comparison to what you would have paid for that exact same care prior to the No Surprises Act. >> And so I guess the next obvious question is what did your analysis of this show? >> Yeah. So, as you might imagine when you bring in a real baseline and start comparing apples to apples, the findings are very very different. And what we actually found and and this research focused primarily on emergency medicine because that's where we had the most data. We would love to recreate it for additional specialties and would really love to look at anesthesia. I think there are a lot of inferences you can take even just from the emergency medicine approach, but worth noting again, we looked at emergency medicine. So, we found effectively once you considered all the the care the effect of the IDR process and post-NSA, we're paying somewhere between 13% to 50% less for out-of-network emergency medicine than we were prior to the No Surprises Act for the exact same volume of of claims. >> That's a significant drop. >> Yes. >> Yeah. >> And a real conflict in the narrative. Yeah, the narrative is that it is adding cost and even misinterpretation of of again, the Georgetown research is probably the most well-cited. >> Yeah. >> $22 billion over over 5 years. A lot of news outlets report that as an additional 22 billion over 5 years. Which is simply not the case. >> So, you represent physicians. >> Correct. >> I'm curious where that savings comes from. Guessing that it's not coming by the original plan was which is well, we're just not going to pay you for that care. >> Right. Yeah, so it's a great question. One of the big pieces that's been missing from from research in addition to a missing baseline is the context around where the arbitration process fits in the larger out-of-network puzzle. So, one of the key aspects of the research that I did is that I really wanted to use adversarial data, right? That was a really important piece that's missing again from essentially all the research. What the health plans actually reported was that in 2024, only 6.2% of claims that could have gone to arbitration did. But then the rest, we had to make at least a couple of assumptions, right? That remaining 90-ish percent. We think those assumptions are pretty strong and and based in experience and and data. But if you assume that that remaining 90% is reimbursed at roughly the out-of-network benchmark that the plans have been reporting, then you end up with the savings numbers that that we calculated, right? It's like, what if we're wrong? What if we're underestimating the amount that the plans are paying? They're actually paying more than that the benchmark. Let's say they're paying 1 and 1/2 times the benchmark. Well, you still save around 30 30%. And if they're paying double the benchmark, which we know is overly conservative, >> [laughter] >> right? You still save about 13% year-over-year. So, we're pretty confident in in the math there. It's meant to be based on an individual plan's 2019 in-network rates. Right, so they look at their contracts in 2019, find the median through each different specialty and and code, and and that's your QPA. And then annually it's supposed to be updated for inflation. Uh there was actually litigation brought by the Texas Medical Association. It's colloquially known as TMA 3. That importantly found what a lot of physicians already knew, there was a lot of opportunity for manipulation of that QPA calculation. I'm really, I guess, intrigued by what you're saying. I get from your more broader research, does does the way the law is in in the USA at the moment here lead to increased costs overall, or is it actually reducing the costs overall? >> Yeah, the evidence suggests if you actually again look at you know, apples to apples and and compared to a benchmark, the effect of the No Surprises Act is very, very likely a reduction in overall medical spend. That has been contrary to what the health insurers, the No Surprises would like folks to believe. I I think that is a really important part of of examining outcomes here as well. Plans are saying that premiums are going up at least in part because of the No Surprises Act. So, I mean, you talk about the third-party administrators sort of setting the prices for this, but is there anything that they can miss or that they they get overlooked in that process? >> The reality is there's a real lack of transparency between the TPA and the employer sponsor. That's been a problem for a very long time. The third-party administrators go out of their way to make it very very difficult to really understand the specifics of how they are administering the plan. You hear horror stories about employer sponsors attempting to audit their TPAs and their their claims process and it it becoming just a an exercise in frustration where you really can't get the transparency you can need. So, I think there is a need for reform of the No Surprises Act and the the independent dispute resolution process, but where those reforms can be the most effective, one, compelling and and creating real mandates around payment of arbitration awards. Insurers have just notoriously not paid these binding awards, but the other really important piece is creating some mandatory transparency from TPAs to employer sponsors. Yeah, they can't legally do it, but they are they are doing We have roughly 35% non-payment rate. It depends on the insurer. Some insurers are are very intentionally choosing to not pay. Think others it's There are some honest mistakes in there, but there are several major insurers that have at this point disclosed that they don't intend to pay legally binding awards. >> So, can you walk us through what happens when an administrator charges a a particular saving fee or but before that reimbursement is then transferred and paid across? >> Yeah, you go through the arbitration process. It's a year on the physician side and you prevail. Arbiter decides that you know, the insurer owes additional Let's call it $500. That's supposed to be binding, right? The insurer is supposed to have 30 days to make payment for that award. The reality is that many plans either don't pay timely, let the 30-day deadline come and go, and and get around to paying when they feel like it. But, increasingly, there are plans that simply don't pay at all. We've got examples where physician clients have been waiting over a year for award payments, and they are simply not forthcoming. But, where there's that extra layer, that sort of employer and TPA interaction, some of those fee structures that I I mentioned a little bit before, and then you mentioned shared savings. Shared savings is a practice that actually New York Times did a big exposé on maybe 5 or or 6 years ago. Front page of the the Sunday edition of the Times, right? And it's a process by which insurers charge a fee to the employer sponsors for allegedly negotiating down or reducing the final payment amount for out-of-network claim. They take the bill charge amount, and then whatever the payment amount that the insurer ends up paying, they take a cut, a percentage cut of that that delta. So, let's say bill charge is $1,000, the allowed amount ends up being $100, the insurer will take 40% of that $900 delta. And that was a borderline predatory practice prior to the No Surprises Act. It is really, really hard to defend at all post No Surprises Act, when there is now a process for determining those out-of-network payments. There are instances, and New York Times reported this, in which the shared savings fee that the insurer takes from processing those claims was several times greater than the amount paid to the physician who actually provided the care. It is just a predatory practice that is driving up costs. >> So, maybe now that moves us on to the employer and the impact on the employer. So, I think to start with, are the employers who are paying for this insurance, and there's sort of several steps beyond them, like they are not actually involved in that negotiation between the insurance company and the Are they asking these kind of questions? Have they become interested in this problem? >> They should be. It's not clear. I think there is an understanding in the employer space that there should be more transparency between employers and NTPAs. And you've seen this fight play itself out in in different settings as well between those two parties. There was the Patients Deserve Price Tags Act. It was a a bill that Senator Marshall had been leading on. And it one point there was considerable controversy in the committee process where the TPAs were fighting very hard to reduce the amount of disclosure that they would have to make. Basically carving out employer groups with fewer than 50 employees from the TPAs responsibility to disclose claims information. So, it's an active fight, right? And TPAs are trying very very hard to keep what they do on behalf of their employer clients out of view of those same employer clients despite the fact the employer is ultimately the fiduciary responsible for the administration. >> There must be the laws the employees can call I mean those lawsuits not impacted this discussion at all in any way or >> Yeah, to this day employers are having to fight very very hard to get access to detailed claims information. And some of this is really common sense reform that would go a long way toward making the process work better. If you required the TPA to provide on a quarterly basis to their employer sponsor how frequently they lost in arbitration by default, right? 24% of insurer losses in the arbitration process are because the insurer didn't show up and submit an offer at all. 24% of the time. I think an employer sponsor ought to be appalled if they learned that they were paying more in arbitration a quarter of the time because the person they're or the organization they're they're paying to administer the process didn't even show up. Another 9 and 1/2% of insurer losses are because they made an offer of $1 or less in the arbitration process. And that's not an additional dollar, right? They're not saying we we're willing to pay one more dollar. They're saying we believe the total value of this service is $1 or less. 9 and 1/2% of the time, right? So, disclosing that to employer sponsors, really how are you calculating the QPA? Are there contracts that you turned down? Right? Are any of the physician organizations that we went through arbitration with, did any of them offer you a contracted rate? Would it have cost my employees and the employer less money had you accepted that contract? This is all information that employers don't have access to right now. And if they did, one, I think they would be very, very concerned with the way that their plans are being administered, but two, you would restore some of those incentives that were designed in the arbitration process and the No Surprises Act in the first place to actually work together toward fair reimbursement and toward durable, sustainable, in-network arrangements. >> So, is there some movement toward allowing employers who are sponsoring healthcare to be a part of that arbitration then? >> Yeah, so there's currently legislation led by Congressman Murphy in the US House. It's bipartisan, bicameral. The original co-sponsors were Murphy and Jimmy Panetta, a Democrat from California, but there's a companion bill in the Senate led by Senator Marshall and Senator Bennet. And it's got co-sponsors in the House from folks on the Energy and Commerce Committee, Ways and Means Committee, Education and Workforce, basically the committees that really matter for healthcare issues. And it would do a couple of things. First and foremost, ensure that the same penalties that exist on the physician side when a patient gets balance billed illegally, well, apply those same penalties to insurers if they don't correctly adjudicate a claim and instruct a physician to pass on dollars to patients. But it would also create a penalty for non-payment in the arbitration process. I think there's an opportunity to further amend that proposed legislation. The Ways and Means Committee is likely to mark up that bill, basically put it through the committee process in November. I think a really meaningful improvement to that legislation would be some of these transparency and disclosure requirements that TPAs, you know, just aren't sharing with their employer sponsors. >> So, I guess bringing this back to anesthesia practice, anesthesia providers, and ultimately patients trying to have their operations, right? I mean, do those transparency gaps Does that maybe partially explain or help explain why some anesthesia practices are getting delays and not experiencing the payments through? Is that >> Yeah, I think so. >> Yeah, so I think look, like I said, the IDR process was really designed to find that economic equilibrium between what insurers are are offering and what physicians are are asking for and then bring them together to not have to use the arbitration process every single time. Find that in-network arrangement. You know, when it comes to anesthesia, if the process starts working the way it's supposed to, it significantly improves the ability for physician groups who want to be in network with major payers in their market to find a sustainable rate. And look, have more certain and predictable cash flow, not have to go through Look, the IDR process is long and complicated. No one would choose to go to IDR instead of network, right? It it takes 60 to 90 days at a minimum and creates uncertainty and you may or may not get paid at the back end, right? Everyone would rather be in network where you could have a predictable and reasonable rate of reimbursement. >> So, I think about anesthesiologists, there's lots of different ways to practice, different kinds of practices, which I assume are all affected differently. And so, I think what should leaders of those practices, the varying kinds of practices, and honestly, what should anesthesiologists who are not in charge of their finances be taking away from this conversation? >> You know, one of the really interesting things about anesthesiology is it's one of the very heavily subsidized specialties. I'd say most anesthesia practices rely on some form of hospital subsidy in order to make up the gap between what it costs to provide the care and what reimbursement actually brings in. One of the big opportunities here is utilization of the IDR process creates an opportunity to bring more transparency into the cost of care. Better that it be shown through reimbursement and sustainable contracts than through of opaque through facility fee and and seeking subsidy and and all that sort of additional complexity within the reimbursement system. So, I think look looking at the arbitration process as a way of ensuring that you've got contracts that are sustainable and that you can actually provide the coverage and access to care that you want to provide and then really using that as a pathway toward a more sustainable in-network approach over time. So, there's a real opportunity there and I think it's likely that most practices don't realize quite how much volume they have that could be subject to the NSA and in the IDR process and it's worth taking a look at that and understanding what what's that opportunity there and kind of use that to really get in network sustainably. >> And when I think about the subsidies we get, a lot of it's associated with the cost of care of being available. Like, it's the billing rate for us, we're fortunate be okay for when we're actually providing care, but you need you know, we're level one trauma center, all this stuff that you need people there who would like to be paid for their time in the hospital and that's really where the subsidies come from. Is that something that you can get addressed in this IDR process? >> Yeah, you know >> or or some other process affiliated with it. >> I think kind of sort of, right? Ultimately, it is strange to most people, especially anyone not in the health care space, right? When you tell a layman the reimbursement for anesthesia or for any other specialty for that matter, you know, obstetricians is another, you know, area where folks don't realize not making money on the reimbursement, right? That's heavily subsidized parts of facility-based care. I think that's surprising for most laymen and I think the real answer to the question is, well we really ought to have more of the total cost of care reflected in reimbursement. metadata.title: Anesthesia IDR Is a Knife Fight. Who Walks Away?
metadata.author: About The Rest
metadata.shortDescription:
Anesthesia IDR is a knife fight, and in 2026 both sides finally have a knife. Providers are winning most No Surprises Act disputes. Payers are answering with canceled contracts and warnings to hospitals. Who walks away?

Host Joseph Rodriguez (Co-Founder and Chief Growth Officer, Guide Anesthesia) is joined by Randy Moore (Chief Anesthetist Officer, NorthStar Anesthesia) and Brian Schmutzler, MD, PhD (Executive Vice President of Medical Affairs, CCI Anesthesia). They don't agree on all of it. That's the point.


Anesthesia reimbursement. Randy explains why the math stopped working. Labor costs keep climbing while reimbursement falls, and a divided specialty looks like easy pickings to payers. Brian says the cuts don't reduce the cost of care, they shift it to hospitals and ASCs, and rural hospitals can't absorb it. He also shares a surprise: Elevance raised its Indiana anesthesia rates about 26% this year.


The IDR knife fight. Brian walks through how independent dispute resolution works and why mediators side with anesthesia providers most of the time. Joe counters with the fine print: nine to twelve months to get paid, the fees, and some groups whose win rates are losing them money. Randy predicts that companies winning contracts on 100% IDR assumptions will be in trouble within 18 to 24 months.


ASC anesthesia stipends. From Tenet's USPI to Ascension's AmSurg deal to the Surgery Partners sale, surgical volume keeps moving to ASCs, and stipends follow it. Brian explains how one center cut a $20K-a-month subsidy to nearly zero by billing surgeon-owners for unused block time. Randy breaks down why ASC contracts turn over faster than hospital contracts.


CRNA and anesthesiologist workforce. Randy sees early stabilization in metro markets, while rural sites still depend on locums. Brian warns that wages won't come down and that an anesthesiologist cliff is coming. Joe argues the real competition is between organizations that get the most out of both professions.


Plus: how each leader responded internally to the Nashville spinal medication tragedy, and the hardest professional lesson each of them learned in 2026.


Takeaways

IDR is leverage, not free money. Payment takes nine to twelve months, the fees come first, and a weak win rate turns the whole process into a loss.

Payment cuts don't lower the cost of anesthesia. They shift it to hospitals and ASCs. In rural markets, a few hundred thousand dollars of shifted cost can close a hospital.

Many ASC subsidies are an efficiency problem with a price tag. When surgeon-owners pay for their unused block time, the subsidy can drop to zero.

The CRNA shortage is no longer uniform. Metro markets with training programs are stabilizing, while rural and exurban sites still run on locums. The anesthesiologist pipeline is the bigger long-term risk.

The competition that matters isn't CRNA versus anesthesiologist. It's which organizations get the most value out of both.
