Mm-hmm. Uh, you're seeing a, a moderation of locum demand, and you're seeing a moderation in, in locum rates- Mm-hmm as well. And you're actually starting to see some employer discipline and, and, and you're seeing some decisions around, well, we could bring in a locum to open up- Hmm … this point of service, but it's not making sense, which was unheard of, you know, even three years ago. People was like, "Just open, blow the doors out, bring in whoever you need to bring in. We'll pay whatever." That's-- those conversations are starting to change. So the net result of that is you're starting to see some, some stabilization and some early stage stabilization. But it's like anything else. This is super complicated- And you know, what I, I tend to see is like in the markets that are kind of metro or metro adjacent, so think of s- markets that are arguably kind of more attractive to live and work, you-- who also happen to be well-resourced with nurse anesthesia programs, uh, that you're seeing those stabilize. And, and so, and you're seeing W2 hiring go up, W2 staffing go up. You're seeing the locum tenem utilization going down. But it's, you know, there are sites that are rural and underserved that aren't necessarily as geographically attractive. They are still, and will for a while, continue to have very high locum utilization. And so you're seeing in the metro markets some people having to make some hard decisions. Mm-hmm. Uh, locum providers who were not locum providers in 2018. They weren't locum providers in 2019, but they saw the world shift and like, "Hey, I can sleep in my own bed, and I can be a locum at the facility I was a W2 at for the last five years." Those folks are gonna have to make some decisions and are increasingly having to make decisions about whether they wanna convert back to a 1099-- uh, a W2 or a more moderate, uh, 1099 rate, or what if they wanna continue to play the locum game, then you're really gonna have to work in less attractive areas or in sites that have, you know, that are, you know, really on fire and not particularly attractive to work at. Yeah. I think we're gonna see that trend over time. You know, I think 18 to 24 months, it's gonna look even more stable. Uh, on the physician side, you know, w- we are, we're the highest staffed than we've ever been in terms of, um, or I should say it, our vacancy rate is the lowest it's ever been since I've been in the company on physician staffing. It's, it's really-- it's improved significantly on the CRNA side, but we are pre-COVID levels of physician staffing. So, uh, you know, that feels good. Uh, and we have some hotspots on physician staffing, but we, we are, uh, doing really well. Now, the question is: What does that look like three or four or five years from now when you look at the, the physician age demographics relative to the year over year, uh, physician resident graduates? That might be a bit of a different story, but that's where I tend to be more bullish on the CRNA side than- Yeah … than on the physician side. Yeah. And Reuben, we'll take Brian. What are you seeing? Yeah, I agree with that. Um, I guess what, what we're seeing is the rate of increase is decreasing, right? So we used to be, you know, having an increase in our- Yes, that's a great way to say it. Yeah. Right. That, that's what we see. I, I don't think wages are ever gonna come down. Um, you know, locums going away maybe makes the entire industry look like, like wages came down, but I don't think you're ever gonna see, you know, I as a W2 CRNA am making, you know, 300K right now, um, and I'm gonna make 270 next year, right? I just don't think that's ever gonna happen, but I think that rate of increase is, is, uh, declining a bit. Um, we are seeing s- uh, anesthesiologist, um, vacancy rates decrease in metro markets. The problem I have are these sort of not truly rural, but not suburban or metro either, kinda that middle area. Um- 30 to 45 minutes outside the metro, it gets harder. Exactly. And, and a lot of these facilities still need an anesthesiologist, at least according to their bylaws, and so that, that's our biggest issue right now is that sort of middle area. How do I get an anesthesiologist to go to… Like, for instance, Terre Haute, Indiana, is one of our, our bigger contracts. Right. Um, you know, how do I get an anesthesiologist to go out there? Um, and so those rates are, are increasing, you know, at a huge, huge rate, uh, those W2 rates for anesthesiologists. Um, so I mean, I, I think that's gonna be a problem, and we're gonna hit a cliff. You know, we're not making any more anesthesiologists. Uh, we're, we're gonna hit a really big cliff with anesthesiologists. I think the CRNAs are gonna be able to fill in the majority of that, uh, but it's gonna, it's gonna come to a point where you're gonna have to say like, "We either can't do cases today, or you're gonna have to not have an anesthesiologist." So, um, that, that's gonna be a big problem. Now, we, we are doing a few things here in Indiana with GME. There's a couple of private practices that are, that are generating their own anesthesiologists, um, which is, which was again unheard of 10 years ago, right? It was all- Oh, wow … it was all ACGME from the s- from CMS, not, uh, not local- Of course local companies. So that, that's helping a little bit, but you're also talking about, you know, six or eight a year, um, as opposed to our, our shortage of, you know, thousands. So, um, I, I think that's gonna be the real issue that comes up five years from now, just like Randy talked about. Uh, but I do agree there's some stabilat- stabilization to the market. Um, and I go back again to the operational efficiencies. If we can get to a point where we get every facility to create these operational efficiencies, I think actually we, we, we may actually have enough anesthesia providers at some point to cover everything. The overarching prevailing narrative of the last, like, 100 years is CRNAs versus anesthesiologists, and no one's talking about that. What we are talking about is how do these organizations, whether it's CCI or North Star or Guide, uh, create the most value with the people they have, right? And then compete on quality at the local level. Yes. And that's how we get, you know, as these markets are beginning to change, you're seeing these local changes, right? Some, y- you know, so for instance, we're in Phoenix and we're in Florida, and they're distinct CRNA cultures. Mm-hmm. And they've, and they've evolved considerably different over the last 10 years because of those changes. So It's just interesting to me. I think, you know, a lot of- we talk a lot about that gets the headlines that, you know, the, the major thing that's been going on for so long. But the real competition in this industry is not really just the headlines, it's between these two or between organizations that figure out how to get the most out of these, uh, professions. And I will say, just for the audience, Brian, you, you said it well, you know, compensation almost never goes down, but, you know, what it will just happen is then, you know, our companies will begin to underbid each other on administrative costs. Yep. Right? It won't be- or on quality of management or on the data management or whatever it else is. It's not like everyone's gonna start making less money, 'cause I think that's the fear, right? Uh, Randy, any last thoughts on this topic? I mean, I've got a lot of thoughts- … some of which will get me in trouble, but especially when, when we start talking about the professional association. So my sense is, and I'm far enough removed maybe that I don't have an informed opinion here, but I think my, my-- the question I ask myself is, are we seeing a growing irrelevance of the national associations, uh- Hey … when, when, when it comes to the stuff that actually- Come on, man. Don't, don't put me in an awkward position here. Yeah. Oh, man. Well, I mean, I-- it's a question, right? It's, it's, it's not a definitive statement. And, and but as you look at, like, the… I, I don't know. I mean, I, I'm a actually a practicing clinician. I walk the halls of a lot of different facilities. Uh, I practice clinically in some of them. Uh, a- and m- maybe I'm in a bubble, but I don't get a sense that anesthesiologists care much what the ASA thinks, and CRNAs- Hmm think much about what the AANA thinks on certain, on a good number of issues. And that seems that, that, that distance, to me, seems greater than it was even five, 10 years ago. And there's- Hmm … and I, I think part of it is that, um, the associations aren't really focusing on what's most important to their members, A, 'cause they're often distracted by stuff that is, you know, geared towards 3% to 5% of their membership, the militant part that gets into senior level leadership in those organizations. Uh, and- Also, the market is moving in a direction where, you know, like I don't have a lot of arguments with the anesthesiologist about CRNA scope of practice. Yeah. Like it's, it's-- I feel like I'm preaching to the choir, and I'm not even have to preach. I don't have a lot of discussions- It sounds like you, you, you're dealing with practical people with CRNAs about anesthesiologists. Like CRNAs- Yeah … like working with anesthesiologists in, in my facilities. Anesthesiologists really respect and like working with CRNAs. They want CRNAs to grow and to develop. They want the CRNAs to go in OB. They want the CRNAs to be doing blocks. And that, that seems, you know-- That juxtaposition between what I'm hearing the professional associations beat their chest on and what's actually happening in the clinical environment, what's happening in the business environment, that is, to me, that's, that distance is getting more and more significant. I verily, very rarely meet a CRNA who says, "I will never work with an anesthesiologist." And I, I always like to point out all these opt-outs that have gone on, anesthesiologist demand has gone up during all this time. Go ahead. So all, all that I ever hear clinicians care about is am I getting paid well and am I getting the time off? And then secondarily, am I treated well by either the, the group or the facility, right? I, I almost never, and I can't think-- And maybe it's, you know, I, I may be a little bit, just like Randy, a little bit hidden from this, um, because of the way our practices work. But I very rarely hear people say anything about scope. "I don't wanna work with this person because they're a X, Y, or Z, anesthesiologist, CRNA." Um, and I, I think part of that comes from-- And I, and I think of this as in, in more broadly in, in the political realm of the United States. Um, you know, when the economy is great, we argue over things like social issues. Um, or I don't wanna have to stay until seven o'clock every night because we don't have enough providers. So I think that the scope issues, when people fight about those, it's usually when we're flush with both or, you know, we're, we're-- The, the supply is outpacing the demand. Yes. Scar- I don't think people- Scarcity can be a, a, a very strong motivator. Yes. Yes. Yeah. Absolutely. Yeah. I want that high-quality person to be providing care for the patients. So that, that's where I stand on it. Uh, you know, I, again, I, I don't push one way or the other. I don't say- It's very practical … we have to go this way or that way, so. Yeah. I think, um, you know, with opt-out and A's and all this stuff, and I think the more we think about clinical quality in terms of a local issue rather than something that can be regulated at the state level, which is where a lot of that tension comes from, I think we will be better served as a broader anesthesia community 'cause that lowers the temperature, right? metadata.author: The Center for Medical Education
metadata.shortDescription:
Ten Most Important Legal Questions Asked by John Bedolla, MD and Dusty Otwell, Esq.

Purchase the self-study course at https://courses.ccme.org/course/hrem.

Designed and taught by emergency physicians and medical malpractice attorneys, this High Risk Emergency Medicine course is a comprehensive review of the medical-legal issues inherent to the practice of Emergency Medicine.
 
Using actual case analysis and a review of the medical literature, this CME course identifies the critical components of the history, physical exam and data collection process that are critical to assuring a well-supported evaluation, treatment and disposition. Important principles in communication, documentation, medical-legal strategies and EMTALA compliance are discussed to help participants develop an effective Emergency Department Risk Management Program.

metadata.title: AMA Advocacy Insights webinar series: Implementing the No Surprises Act
metadata.author: American Medical Association (AMA)
metadata.shortDescription:
The No Surprises Act (NSA) is here. During this AMA Advocacy Insights webinar, experts discuss the implementation of the NSA, including many of the issues addressed in the AMA’s surprise billing toolkit. Speakers also tackle enforcement challenges and the interaction between state and federal surprise billing requirements.

https://www.ama-assn.org/delivering-care/patient-support-advocacy/implementation-no-surprises-act#toolkit-for-physicians

metadata.title: Ep. 61 - Breaking down the impacts of the TMA 3 ruling
metadata.author: Fulcrum Strategies
metadata.shortDescription:
Source:
https://www.podbean.com/eau/pb-ny4zi-1491651

Matthew Handley and Fulcrum Strategies president and CEO Ron Howrigon discuss the recent rulings in the third Texas Medical Association case against the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), commonly known as TMA 3.  Judge Jeremy Kernodle ruled that CMS violated the No Surprises Act by publishing guidelines on the Qualified Payment Amount that contradicted the law in several ways.  However, Judge Kernodle ruled against the plaintiffs by deciding that the QPA does not have to be transparent.  Matthew and Ron discuss what this means for physicians, hospitals, and the general public.
Follow Matthew and Ron on X.

metadata.title: The Surprise Bill Ban: What the No Surprises Act Actually Covers — and the One Ambulance It Does Not
metadata.author: Covered USA
metadata.shortDescription:
A bill from a doctor you never chose, at a hospital you did choose — is it legal? Since January 1, 2022, the federal No Surprises Act bans balance billing in three situations: most emergency services, non-emergency services from an out-of-network provider at an in-network facility, and covered air ambulance services. Your cost sharing is capped at the in-network level and counts toward your in-network deductible and out-of-pocket maximum.

In this video: why anesthesiology, pathology, radiology and neonatology can never be waived with a form; the strict 72-hour notice-and-consent rule for other non-emergency waivers; the ground ambulance gap the federal law does not cover; and the good faith estimate rule for uninsured and self-pay patients — dispute within 120 days if the bill is at least $400 more than the estimate. Help Desk: 1-800-985-3059.

This video uses AI-generated narration and visuals with original research and commentary. Sources are official CMS guidance, linked below.

- CMS, No Surprises: Understand your rights against surprise medical bills: https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/no-surprises-understand-your-rights-against-surprise-medical-bills
- CMS, Overview of Key Consumer Protections (No Surprises Act): https://www.cms.gov/files/document/nsa-keyprotections.pdf
- CMS, Requirements Related to Surprise Billing, Part I interim final rule: https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/requirements-related-surprise-billing-part-i-interim-final-rule-comment-period

metadata.title: The No Surprises Act Cut Your ER Bill Already — Did You Pay $1,300 Too Much? (2026)
metadata.author: Problem Solved Lab
metadata.shortDescription:
Fix it yourself and save the service call — new practical fixes every week.
Subscribe to Problem Solved Lab so the next fix finds you.

Got a surprise medical bill after an ER visit? The No Surprises Act already caps your emergency bill at in-network rates — learn how to dispute a surprise hospital bill, check your itemized bill for errors, and use your health insurance appeal rights to cut what you owe.

The No Surprises Act already caps your emergency bill at your in-network cost-sharing rate. If you got a surprise out-of-network bill, you may owe far less than the number printed on it. Here is the exact 5-step dispute sequence: request the itemized bill, check every line for duplicates and upcoding, compare prices on FAIR Health Consumer, dispute in writing, and escalate to your insurer or a federal complaint.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Your ER bill may already be capped
1:11 What the law covers and what it does not
2:54 Read every line of the itemized bill
4:03 Compare the price before you negotiate
5:09 The dispute ladder that actually works
6:30 Your five step checklist

5 STEPS TO DISPUTE A MEDICAL BILL
1. Do not pay on arrival. Request the full itemized bill and your explanation of benefits.
2. Check every line for duplicates, upcoding, services you never received, wrong dates, and wrong units.
3. Compare each disputed line to the FAIR Health area estimate and the Medicare reference rate.
4. Call billing, dispute in writing, and ask about self-pay discounts and financial assistance.
5. Escalate in order: insurer appeal, then a federal complaint for a covered surprise bill, then the 400 dollar dispute path if you are uninsured or self-pay.

Q: Is this video sponsored?
A: No. This video is not sponsored.

FAQ — PART B: ABOUT THIS TOPIC
Q: What is the No Surprises Act?
A: A federal law in effect since January 2022 that protects patients from surprise bills for emergency care and for most out-of-network care at in-network facilities, including air ambulances.
Q: What does the law cover?
A: Emergency services from out-of-network providers and facilities, out-of-network care you did not choose at an in-network hospital, and most air ambulance services. Ground ambulances are still exempt.
Q: What does it not cover?
A: Ground ambulances, non-emergency care you choose from an out-of-network provider, and care outside the United States. You can also be asked to sign a notice and consent form to give up protection for some scheduled non-emergency care.
Q: What should I do first if I get a surprise bill?
A: Do not pay it right away. Ask for the itemized bill and your explanation of benefits, then compare the charge against the FAIR Health Consumer estimate and the Medicare reference rate before you call billing.
Q: How does the $400 patient-provider dispute process work?
A: If you are uninsured or self-pay and the final bill is at least $400 more than the good faith estimate, you can ask for a patient-provider dispute. You file with the federal program, pay a $25 fee, and an independent reviewer decides the amount.

The No Surprises Act Went Into Effect on January 1, 2022.

Approximately 20% of ER Visits and 9%-16% of Hospitalizations Results in a Surprise Out-of-Network Medical Bill to Patients.

The No Surprises Act Requires Health Insurance Companies to Apply Out-of-Network Bills to Member's In-Network Deductible and Co-Insurance.

The No Surprises Act Also Requires Out-of-Network Doctors to Not 'Balance-Bill' Patients for Any Additional Payment.

The No Surprises Act States that Insurance Companies and Providers Must Negotiate a Payment Amount for Out-of-Network Bills Using the Qualifying Payment Amount (QPA) as Guidance.

The QPA is the Medical In-Network Allowed Amount an Insurance Company Pays Providers for a Medical Service in a Particular Geographic Area.

The Texas Medical Association Recently Sued Regarding the QPA and a Federal Judge Sided with them Saying that the QPA Cannot be the Sole Determinant of the Amount Paid by the Insurance Company to the Provider.

Sources:
https://www.statnews.com/2022/02/23/federal-court-strikes-down-hhs-surprise-billing-rules/

https://energycommerce.house.gov/newsroom/press-releases/pallone-murray-voice-support-for-biden-administration-s-surprise-billing

https://www.kff.org/health-reform/issue-brief/no-surprises-act-implementation-what-to-expect-in-2022/#:~:text=The%20No%20Surprises%20Act%20(NSA,providers%20they%20did%20not%20choose.

metadata.title: Surprise medical billing will be banished in Texas starting Jan. 1
metadata.author: WFAA
metadata.shortDescription: Experts say surprise medical billing happens to one in three Texans. But beginning Jan. 1, it will be banished.

The No Surprises Act is supposed to protect you from surprise medical bills—but only if you know how to use it.

In this video, Satra Taylor breaks down the No Surprises Act in plain language, including what protections are in place, where the loopholes are, and what steps to take when a medical bill should be illegal under the law.

You’ll learn when out-of-network charges are prohibited, what counts as a covered emergency, how good faith estimates work for uninsured or cash-pay patients, and how to dispute bills that violate the law. The video also explains what the No Surprises Act does not cover—and why documentation matters.

You’ll learn:

•What the No Surprises Act actually protects
•When surprise medical bills are illegal
•Which providers and services are covered
•What to do if a bill violates the law
•How to file a complaint or dispute
•Why good faith estimates and the $400 rule matter

This video is part of AFT’s Fight for Affordability series, which explains how financial systems are stacked against working people—and how to fight back with clear, practical tools.

👉 Get more affordability tools and support:
https://www.aft.org/affordability

metadata.title: Revenue Cycle Management in Healthcare Explained
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) in Healthcare Explained.

Revenue Cycle Management means 'getting the bills paid' for hospitals, doctors and other healthcare providers.

The video explains the steps in RCM: 1) Pre-Registration, 2) Registration, 3) Charge Capture, 4) Utilization Review, 5) Coding, 6) Claim Submission, 7) Remittance Processing, 8) Follow Up and 9) Patient Collections.

RCM is a $29B a year industry and Becker's Hospital Review has a list of 354 healthcare RCM companies in America.

Accordingly, the RCM industry is highly fragmented meaning 1) there are low barriers-to-entry for starting an RCM company and 2) the competence/performance of RCM companies is highly variable.

RCM effectiveness is measured in Accounts Receivable (AR) Days.  Hospital AR Days range from 30 to 70, which for a $3B per year hospital system is a difference of $328M in cashflow.

RCM is so complicated that many physicians are selling their practices to hospital systems so that the hospital can take over the RCM and do a better job with it.

metadata.title: [ANSWERED] What is Front-End Revenue Cycle Management?
metadata.author: Etactics
metadata.shortDescription:
We talk a lot about healthcare revenue cycle management (RCM) on this channel, and rightfully so! The topic is quite broad and has so many different moving parts. Overall, you should know that having an airtight RCM system is key for streamlining your organization’s administrative and clinical functions.

This system consists of three different parts. All of which hold different, but equally important roles. These parts are the: front-end, mid-cycle, and back-end. And each of these parts are made up of even more further divided stages… but we will get into that in a bit. Every point acts like a gear in a watch. So long as all cogs are turning, there’s no worries! However, if any of the gears experience issues, the entire cycle is affected. 

Neglecting even one part of the revenue cycle management system can be detrimental. So much of the focus tends to go to the mid-cycle and back-end stages. Some examples of these functions are coding and billing. As well as denials management, and payment posting. But what about the front-end services? The work before the clinical encounter is just as important! Let’s take a look at this part of the cycle, the functions it is made up of, and how it affects revenue cycle efficiency.

Front-end revenue cycle management encompasses quite a few important processes. All of which involve capturing important patient information. These functions occur at the first point of patient interaction and scheduling. They then carry on through registration and eligibility verification. Making sure that these initial processes run smoothly is essential for timely revenue collection. Here are some key components of the front-end to know.

All which lay the groundwork for a smooth financial workflow:

1. Scheduling and Appointments. The process of recording patient appointments. As well as managing the timeframe of the visits. Having proper scheduling and maintaining your providers’ schedules is the name of the game. By booking a patient with the correct provider, you are ensuring that the following services provided are properly billed.

2. Patient Registration. Pretty self explanatory. You need to collect patient information when scheduling an appointment. Things like demographics, contact information, insurance information and all that jazz. Any necessary authorization or consent forms, too, to ensure compliance on your part.

3. Insurance Verification. To determine the extent of a patient’s insurance coverage, front-end staff must first verify their benefits. Healthcare organizations should check this before rendering services. By doing so, you can avoid claim denials as well as other billing issues down the road. 

4. Prior Authorization. Some medical procedures or treatments may need something called a “prior authorization”. Another front-end process that is crucial when it comes to running a smooth RCM system. This means that your team may need to reach out to a patient’s insurance provider to receive the prior authorization before rendering services.

5. Financial Counseling. Helping your patients understand their part in the RCM cycle is also important. Insurance coverage, financial help, and payment options can be overwhelming to those working in the healthcare field. Imagine how your patients must feel! Offering insight on cost estimation and coverage can prevent payment surprises and reduce the amount of bills sent to collections.

6. Copay and Deductibles. Collecting a patient’s part of the healthcare costs before or right after the appointment. Getting this taken care of as soon as possible ensures that payments are met. It also prevents any possible revenue leakage.

7. Charge Capture. This front-end component ensures that all billable items from a patient encounter are captured. Documenting procedures and treatments administered helps to verify that services are reimbursed properly.

The common denominator for each of these components? They all involve the patient. You can also think of front-end services as part of the overall “patient access” experience. Having a smooth revenue cycle makes navigating the healthcare system easier for your patients, and therefore means better financial health for your business.

segments.text: When people hear the term Revenue Cycle Management, many of them think it's simply Medical
Billing. As a result, many candidates answer this question by explaining only the billing process.
But in reality, RCM is much bigger than billing. In fact, one of The biggest mistakes candidates
make in interviews is treating Revenue Cycle Management and Medical Billing as the same thing.
But, Medical Billing is just one part of Revenue Cycle Management.
RCM is the complete process that helps healthcare organizations get paid accurately
and on time for the services they provide. So, Your answer should be like this:
Revenue Cycle Management is the complete process of managing a patient's account
from the moment an appointment is scheduled until the provider receives the final reimbursement and
the account reaches a zero balance. It starts with patient registration,
insurance verification, and eligibility checks. Then it moves through charge capture,
medical coding, claim submission, payment posting, denial management, AR follow-up,
appeals, and patient collections. From my experience, the real purpose of
RCM is not just submitting claims. It's protecting revenue at every stage of the healthcare journey.
A lot of people think revenue is lost only when a claim is denied. But in reality,
revenue can be lost much earlier due to incorrect insurance information,
missing authorizations, coding errors, documentation issues, or missed follow-ups.
For example, a small mistake during eligibility verification, authorization, coding,
or claim submission can lead to denials, delayed payments, increased AR aging, and revenue loss.
That's why every department in the revenue cycle is connected.
If one step fails, it impacts the entire reimbursement process.
A strong RCM process helps reduce denials, improve clean claim rates,
accelerate cash flow, maximize reimbursement, improve operational efficiency, and enhance the
overall financial health of the organization. From an AR and Denial Management perspective,
RCM is not just about getting claims paid. It's about identifying problems early,
preventing revenue leakage, resolving denials efficiently, and ensuring that
providers receive every dollar they are entitled to for the services they deliver.
In simple words, Revenue Cycle Management is the engine that keeps a healthcare organization
financially healthy while ensuring accurate and timely reimbursement for the services provided.

How does a hospital turn the care it delivers into cash? This complete course walks the revenue cycle end to end — from patient access to final payment.

▶ Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLwIePcdH28rc7B72Clqc9M4doLG2vf2g5

Revenue cycle management (RCM) is how health systems document, bill, and collect the revenue that sustains care. In this full walkthrough you'll follow the money through every hand-off: scheduling and financial clearance, coding and charge capture, the chargemaster, claims and scrubbing, A/R follow-up, denials, self-pay, and customer service — plus the KPIs and dashboards leaders use to run it all, illustrated by a real five-hospital turnaround.

🎯 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
• Why every service becomes an account receivable — and why collection speed decides financial health
• The three segments (front, middle, back end) and the four phases of cycle activity
• Fee-for-service vs. capitation — and how financial risk shifts between payer and provider
• Coding, charge capture, and the chargemaster (CDM) behind every claim
• Clean claims, A/R follow-up, and managing hard vs. soft denials by root cause
• The KPIs and dashboards top systems track — and the Big City Medical Center turnaround

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 Introduction & Roadmap
0:55 Part 1 — Foundations
2:45 Part 2 — Structure & Phases
4:55 Part 3 — Reimbursement Models
6:15 Part 4 — Front End & Middle: Access, Coding & Charges
8:45 Part 5 — The Back End: Claims, Denials & Resolution
12:35 Part 6 — Measuring Performance & the Big City Turnaround
18:15 Part 7 — The Future of RCM
20:15 Part 8 — Putting It Together

👤 WHO THIS IS FOR
Healthcare administration and HIM students, medical billers and coders, patient access and patient financial services teams, practice managers, and anyone who wants to understand how providers actually get paid.

📚 KEY SOURCES
• NCHS/CMS (2025). ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines for Coding and Reporting, FY 2026
• CMS. Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04). Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
• Cleverley WO, Cleverley JO (2017). Essentials of Health Care Finance, 8th ed. Jones & Bartlett Learning

⚠️ This video is for education and general information only — it is not medical, legal, or financial advice. It does not replace clinical judgment, local policy, or regulatory guidance.

🔔 Subscribe to MedConsults for new healthcare education videos every week.

#RevenueCycleManagement #HealthcareFinance #MedicalBilling #MedConsults #HealthcareEducation

segments and phases.
Part three covers how providers actually
get paid. Parts four and five walk the
cycle front to back, access, coding and
charges, then claims, denials and
resolution.

turnaround case. Part seven looks at the
future and part eight puts it all
together. Let's start with the
foundations, what the revenue cycle
actually is and the cash problem it

the set of recurring business activities
and information processing needed to

services provided. A well-run cycle
guarantees three things. Patients are
correctly categorized by payment
obligation, billing is correct and
timely, and the correct payment is
promptly received. Why does it matter?
Because hospitals and practices wait
about 50 days on average to collect from
third-party payers while paying for
facilities, supplies and labor long
before that money arrives. As margins
tighten, faster, cleaner collection is
mission critical. Here's the core
problem in one picture. Care is
delivered first, payment comes later.
So, the provider is effectively
extending an interest-free loan to the
payer. It covers the cost of the service
and waits days or weeks to be repaid.
The faster that loan is repaid, the
healthier the provider.
And notice the ripple effect. A problem
early in the cycle, like a missed
pre-certification, can surface weeks
later as a full claim denial.
Because care precedes payment, every
service creates an account receivable,
money owed to the provider, mostly by
third-party payers.
Managing those receivables is arguably
the most critical part of the whole
cycle.
The aging schedule is the classic tool.
It breaks receivables down by how long
they have been outstanding.
In this example, about half the money is
less than 30 days old and highly
collectible. But 12% has aged past 90
days, where collectibility drops
sharply.
Keep this scoreboard in mind. The rest
of the video is about keeping money out
of that last bucket.
Now, let's see how the cycle is
organized. Three segments from front to
back and the activities that happen
before, at, and after service.
Organizationally, the revenue cycle has
three segments. The front end is patient
access, scheduling, pre-registration,
insurance verification, authorizations,
upfront collections, and financial
counseling.
The middle is revenue integrity, charge
capture, clinical documentation, coding
quality, the charge description master,
and strategic pricing.
The back end is patient financial
services, claims and billing, AR
follow-up, denials and appeals, payment
posting, and customer service.
Different teams, one pipeline, and a
handoff between each.
By timing, the highest leverage work
happens before the patient ever arrives.
First, verify insurance immediately
after scheduling. Confirm the coverage
actually exists. Second, if the payer
requires pre-certification, get it now.
Skipping it risks denial even when the
care was appropriate. Third, counsel the
patient financially. Explain what the
payer covers and what the patient will
owe. It isn't fair to surprise anyone
with a large bill afterward.
And remember, registration data,
demographics plus insurance, is among
the most critical information the
organization collects.
At the time of service, three things.
Re-verify insurance because status may
have changed since booking.
Document the services in a way that
supports a correct claim. And collect
co-pays and balances on the spot. Money
collected now never becomes a
receivable.
After service, the chase begins. If no
payment arrives within about 30 days,
follow up with the payer. Manage any
denials and resubmit promptly. And when
payment does arrive, post it correctly.
That finally closes the account.
The fourth phase, continuous monitoring,
gets its own chapter later in the video.
Before we walk the cycle in detail, we
need one piece of context. How providers
actually get paid and who bears the
financial risk. Payment methods fall
into two broad families. Fee-for-service
means more services, more reimbursement,
with three main variants. Cost-based,
where the payer reimburses allowable
costs after the fact. Charge-based,
which pays from the charge master,
usually discounted 20 to 50%. And
prospective payment, where rates are set
in advance per procedure, per day, or
per case.
Capitation flips the model. A fixed
payment per enrolled member per period,
no matter how many services are used.
That shifts utilization risk onto the
provider and shifts the incentive toward
prevention and efficiency. Line the
methods up and you can see the risk
transfer. Under cost-based payment, the
provider's costs are essentially
guaranteed. The payer bears the risk.
Charge-based payment adds a little
exposure through discounts.
Prospective payment is the middle
ground. The rate is fixed, so the
provider keeps the difference or absorbs
the overrun.
And capitation puts the most risk on the
provider. One fixed payment per member
regardless of utilization.
Where you sit on this spectrum shapes
how you run the entire cycle.
Chapter 4 The front end and the middle
Getting the patient in the door and
turning the care delivered into billable
charges.
Access management is the front door.
Scheduling books the appointment and
manages capacity. Financial clearance is
the heavy lifting. Pre-registration,
insurance verification, referrals and
authorizations, pre-service collections,
and counseling.
Registration captures demographics for
scheduled patients and walk-ins alike.
Admissions handles bed management and
inpatient placement. One detail worth
remembering. Registration generates the
medical record number and the encounter
number, the two identifiers that anchor
every downstream transaction in the
cycle.
Coding translates the services provided
into billable charges. It is the
foundation of fee-for-service payment.
Diagnosis codes describe what was wrong.
Internationally, that's the WHO's ICD
system. Procedure codes describe what
was done. The specific sets vary by
region. CPT in the United States, for
example. And many systems group an
entire inpatient stay into a single
case-based payment group based on
diagnosis and severity. DRG type
grouping.
Accurate, compliant coding at the time
of service is critical to getting paid
on time. Charge capture is where
clinical practice meets billing. Making
sure every service delivered is actually
recorded and billed. Follow the flow.
Registration starts the encounter.
Clinical departments document and charge
for services. Health information
management codes them, and patient
financial services bills the bill and
receives payment.
The objectives are simple to state and
hard to do.
Complete and accurate coding. Charges
that comply with patient, third-party,
and government rules. And effective
billing, collection, and reimbursement.
Every charge comes from somewhere. The
charge description master or charge
master. It is the comprehensive list of
every billable item with the codes and
prices needed to build a claim.
Read one radiology line. The revenue
code groups the charge by category on
the claim. The procedure code identifies
the exact service.
A modifier adds detail, like left or
right side. And the charge is the unit
price.
Keeping the CDM current is a discipline
of its own. An error here multiplies
across thousands of claims.
Chapter five, the back end. Building
clean claims, chasing payment, managing
denials, and bringing every account to
zero.
One encounter often produces two
separate bills. The institutional or
facility claim covers the building,
equipment, nursing, and supplies. The
technical side. In the US, that's the
UB-04 form. The professional claim
covers the clinician's own work during
the encounter. The CMS-1500 in the US.
The split is essentially universal, even
though the exact forms and codes differ
by country. Keep it in mind whenever
you're tracing where a charge ended up.
The billing pipeline looks like this.
Charges captured, then the claim
scrubber. Automated edits that catch
errors before submission. Then the claim
goes to the payer.
Flagged claims land in work queues for
review, which feeds learning back into
the process.
The goal is the clean claim, accepted on
the first pass. No edits, no denial.
Embedded scrubbing limits the number of
touches and handoffs, and fewer touches
mean a lower cost to collect and faster
cash.
Once a claim is out and the payer's
processing time has elapsed, follow-up
begins. Accounts are assigned by logic,
aged accounts first, high dollar
amounts, payer source, or a simple alpha
split by name. Resolution means driving
the balance to zero through one of three
doors: cash collection, an
administrative or contractual
adjustment, or referral to bad debt
placement. Best practice is concrete.
Work 40 to 60 accounts a day and
document every effort in the system
notes.
Denials are a major impediment to prompt
payment, and most trace back to improper
pre-certification or incomplete or
erroneous claims.
There are two kinds. A hard denial means
payment is refused. The claim is not
accepted or is rejected line by line,
and it is subject to timely filing
limits. Overturning it takes a formal
appeal.
A soft denial means the payer will not
pay yet. It needs more information or a
corrected claim. Supply the missing data
or resubmit, and it can still be paid.
Mature denials management is not just
recovering cash. It is prevention. Five
steps. Identify denied claims and read
the payer's reason and remark codes.
Analyze root causes and trends by payer
and service.
Resolve. Appeal the hard denials.
Resubmit the soft ones.
Redesign the upstream process that
caused the problem, and monitor the
denial rate to confirm the fix held.
Those standardized reason codes attached
to every adjustment are your starting
point. They explain exactly why a claim
paid differently than billed.
When the patient side goes unpaid, it
lands in one of three buckets. Bad debt,
the patient could pay but did not, a
measure of collection effectiveness with
a common target under 3% of gross
revenue.
Charity care, patients genuinely unable
to pay, written off intentionally. Some
states even mandate minimums for
nonprofits.
And uncompensated care is the umbrella
total. Bad debt plus charity plus
uninsured discounts.
Watch all three. They tell different
stories about your counseling and your
community role.
The last step is also the safety net.
Patient financial services fields the
phone line, takes payments, sends
statements and correspondence, and
reconciles insurance and patient
balances.
Why it matters. Customer service is
where errors and confusion from every
earlier step get resolved. When a
patient does not understand a bill, a
responsive team prevents the delay that
confusion would cause. Even a day or two
to return a call multiplied across
thousands of accounts adds up to real
cash.
So, how do you know the cycle is
actually working?
Chapter 6, measurement, KPIs,
dashboards, and the lessons of a real
turnaround.
Two tools keep managers on top of the
cycle. Key performance indicators are a
limited set of metrics that measure what
is critical to success. They assess the
current state, track progress toward
goals, and prompt corrective action.
Few enough to stay focused, enough to
cover every critical area, and reviewed
on different rhythms. Some daily, some
monthly or quarterly.
The dashboard presents those KPIs like a
car's instruments. Easy to read gauges
and color codes that let a manager spot
problems at a glance.
Here are the workhorse management KPIs.
Net days in AR, overall collection
performance. Around 50 days or better is
the common benchmark.
Aged AR as a percentage of billed,
collectibility across the aging buckets.
You want it trending down.
Cash collection percentage, how well net
revenue converts to cash.
Bad debt as a percentage of gross, a
read on self-pay collection and
counseling, under 3%.
Cost to collect, the efficiency of the
whole operation.
And case mix index, which reflects
acuity and documentation quality.
These benchmarks are illustrative
orientation, not contract.
One level deeper sit the revenue
integrity indicators. Discharged not
final billed, DNFB, measures how fast
claims are generated after discharge.
About 4 days is a common goal.
Denial write-offs as a percentage of net
revenue capture what is finally lost
after appeals are exhausted.
Aged AR over 90 days by payer group
shows which payers are slow. Late
charges flag capture problems in
clinical departments. And net days of
revenue in credit balances tracks
compliant handling of overpayments.
DNFB and its cousin DNSP are leading
indicators. They move before the AR
numbers do.
A single number means little. The trend
tells the story.
Here a provider starts at 60 days in AR,
well above the 50-day best practice
line, and works it down quarter by
quarter. 58, 55, 53, 51, and finally 48,
under the benchmark.
That is six quarters of steady
operational work. And every day shaved
off is cash pulled forward into the
provider's hands.
Averages hide the action, so break the
denial rate down by payer. In this
example, public payers run around 4 to
5% standard private plans about 6 and
1/2 and managed care plans over 9% with
self-pay close behind. That is where
improvement effort returns the most
cash. Focus the root cause work on the
payers and services actually driving the
number. Let's make it real. Big City
Medical Center, a five-hospital system
with more than a billion dollars in
revenue, was collecting from third-party
payers in about 60 days while the
average hospital collected in roughly
50. At $2.7 million of billing per day,
that 10-day gap tied up serious cash.
Their response, create a chief revenue
officer to own the whole cycle, build a
system-level RCM team across all five
hospitals including IT, open continuous
dialogue with major payers, and
establish roughly 50 performance metrics
driven by reporting and employee
accountability.
Of those 50 metrics, six received the
most attention, the Big City Six.
Days in AR, the average collection
period, the proportion of receivables
over 90 days old, claim rejections as a
percentage of revenue,
final denials as a percentage of
revenue, cash as a percentage of
revenue, and revenue per revenue cycle
staff member.
Each was compared against a management
goal and a best practice benchmark with
variances reported numerically and as
percentages.
That is the pattern to copy. Few
metrics, clear goals, visible variances.
Where does revenue actually leak? Six
classic pitfalls. Missing
pre-certification. Services rendered
without required authorization become
denied claims.
Inaccurate registration data poisons
everything downstream.
Late charge capture. Charges posted more
than three days late inflate DNFB and
delay cash.
Coding errors trigger rejections and
rework. Slow AR follow-up lets accounts
drift past timely filing limits and
become uncollectible.
And resolving denials without root cause
analysis guarantees the same denial
comes back next month.
Flip those pitfalls and you get the
playbook. Get it right at the front
door. Verify, pre-certify, and counsel
before service. Collect at the point of
service. Money taken on site never
becomes a receivable.
Automate edits and scrubbing so errors
are caught before claims leave the
building.
Manage denials by root cause. Fix the
upstream process, not just the symptom.
Run a focused KPI dashboard. Few
metrics, clear goals, accountable
owners. And give the cycle an executive
owner, a chief revenue officer who
aligns clinical and financial teams.
Chapter 7 Where all of this is heading
from a traditional reactive cycle to a
clinically integrated automated one.
The traditional cycle is reactive.
Front-end denials keep rising. The same
errors get corrected over and over.
Charges post late instead of in real
time. And risks surface only after they
hit.
The clinically integrated cycle inverts
that. A digital front door automates
access. Charge capture and coding become
intelligent. Predictive analytics flag
risk early. And organizations strike a
strategic balance between in-house teams
and vendors.
The payoff spans four fronts: a
frictionless patient experience, cleaner
claims and faster cash, recovered
margin, and lower compliance risk.
Walk the automated cycle end to end.
Pre-service, geo-fenced check-in, kiosk
and video registration, and portal save
data, speed up intake and compliance.
During care and charging, telehealth
visits, service level coding automated
natively in the EMR, and NLP assisting
code selection.
In billing and adjudication, embedded
scrubbing limits touches and denials are
auto routed to their root cause owners
and rebuild fast.
Post service, BI dashboards monitor
claims aging and self-pay, while
patients get plain language statements
through the portal.
Why is the shift happening now? Six
forces, margin pressure. Profitability
is harder to sustain than ever.
Regulatory complexity keeps expanding.
The patient has become a payer as higher
deductibles shift balances onto
individuals.
Technology has matured. Automation and
analytics are finally viable at scale.
Value-based care ties reimbursement
increasingly to outcomes
and cost reduction.
Eliminating administrative waste frees
capital to reinvest in care itself.
Let's put it all together. The people
who run the cycle, the terms you'll
heal, and the takeaways that matter
most. The cycle is a team sport. The
chief revenue officer owns it end to end
and aligns clinical and financial teams
toward best practice results.
Patient access staff runs scheduling,
registration, verification, and
financial clearance at the front.
Coders and CDI specialists translate
documentation into accurate, compliant,
billable codes.
The billing and AR team produces clean
claims, works follow-up, and resolves
denials.
Physicians and clinicians actually start
the billing process with their diagnoses
and documentation. And customer service
protects the final collection step. A
quick glossary you can screenshot. AR,
accounts receivable. CDM, the charge
master, the master list of billable
items.
CDI, clinical documentation integrity.
ICD, the WHO's diagnosis codes.
Diagnosis codes say what was wrong,
procedure codes say what was done, and
case-based groups bundle an inpatient
stay into one payment.
DNFB, discharged not final billed.
Facility versus professional claims, the
two bills from one encounter.
Capitation, a fixed payment per member
per period.
And the clean claim, accepted on the
first pass.
That's the vocabulary of this whole
video. If you remember five things, make
them these.
One, the cycle is end-to-end, scheduling
to final payment, not just the business
office.
Two, front-end accuracy is everything.
Most denials are born at registration
and pre-certification.
Three, cash speed is financial health.
Every day off AR is cash back in the
provider's hands.
Four, measure relentlessly. A focused
KPI dashboard turns data into
accountable action.
Five, the future is integrated and
automated. Clinical and financial
workflows are converging on one
platform.
That's revenue cycle management, turning
the care delivered into the revenue that
sustains it, accurately, compliantly,
and faster.
If this video helped you, give it a like
and subscribe for more healthcare
finance lessons. Thanks for watching.
I'll see you in the next one.

Identify denied claims and read the payer's reason and remark codes. Analyze root causes and trends by payer and service. Resolve. Appeal the hard denials. Resubmit the soft ones. Redesign the upstream process that caused the problem, and monitor the denial rate to confirm the fix held. Those standardized reason codes attached to every adjustment are your starting point. They explain exactly why a claim paid differently than billed. When the patient side goes unpaid, it lands in one of three buckets. Bad debt, the patient could pay but did not, a measure of collection effectiveness with a common target under 3% of gross revenue. Charity care, patients genuinely unable to pay, written off intentionally. Some states even mandate minimums for nonprofits. And uncompensated care is the umbrella total. Bad debt plus charity plus uninsured discounts. Watch all three. They tell different stories about your counseling and your community role. The last step is also the safety net. Patient financial services fields the phone line, takes payments, sends statements and correspondence, and reconciles insurance and patient balances. Why it matters. Customer service is where errors and confusion from every earlier step get resolved. When a patient does not understand a bill, a responsive team prevents the delay that confusion would cause. Even a day or two to return a call multiplied across thousands of accounts adds up to real cash. So, how do you know the cycle is actually working? Chapter 6, measurement, KPIs, dashboards, and the lessons of a real turnaround. Two tools keep managers on top of the cycle. Key performance indicators are a limited set of metrics that measure what is critical to success. They assess the current state, track progress toward goals, and prompt corrective action. Few enough to stay focused, enough to cover every critical area, and reviewed on different rhythms. Some daily, some monthly or quarterly. The dashboard presents those KPIs like a car's instruments. Easy to read gauges and color codes that let a manager spot problems at a glance. Here are the workhorse management KPIs. Net days in AR, overall collection performance. Around 50 days or better is the common benchmark. Aged AR as a percentage of billed, collectibility across the aging buckets. You want it trending down. Cash collection percentage, how well net revenue converts to cash. Bad debt as a percentage of gross, a read on self-pay collection and counseling, under 3%. Cost to collect, the efficiency of the whole operation. And case mix index, which reflects acuity and documentation quality. These benchmarks are illustrative orientation, not contract. One level deeper sit the revenue integrity indicators. Discharged not final billed, DNFB, measures how fast claims are generated after discharge. About 4 days is a common goal. Denial write-offs as a percentage of net revenue capture what is finally lost after appeals are exhausted. Aged AR over 90 days by payer group shows which payers are slow. Late charges flag capture problems in clinical departments. And net days of revenue in credit balances tracks compliant handling of overpayments. DNFB and its cousin DNSP are leading indicators. They move before the AR numbers do. A single number means little. The trend tells the story. Here a provider starts at 60 days in AR, well above the 50-day best practice line, and works it down quarter by quarter. 58, 55, 53, 51, and finally 48, under the benchmark. That is six quarters of steady operational work. And every day shaved off is cash pulled forward into the provider's hands. Averages hide the action, so break the denial rate down by payer. In this example, public payers run around 4 to 5% standard private plans about 6 and 1/2 and managed care plans over 9% with self-pay close behind. That is where improvement effort returns the most cash. Focus the root cause work on the payers and services actually driving the number. Let's make it real. Big City Medical Center, a five-hospital system with more than a billion dollars in revenue, was collecting from third-party payers in about 60 days while the average hospital collected in roughly 50. At $2.7 million of billing per day, that 10-day gap tied up serious cash. Their response, create a chief revenue officer to own the whole cycle, build a system-level RCM team across all five hospitals including IT, open continuous dialogue with major payers, and establish roughly 50 performance metrics driven by reporting and employee accountability. Of those 50 metrics, six received the most attention, the Big City Six. Days in AR, the average collection period, the proportion of receivables over 90 days old, claim rejections as a percentage of revenue, final denials as a percentage of revenue, cash as a percentage of revenue, and revenue per revenue cycle staff member. Each was compared against a management goal and a best practice benchmark with variances reported numerically and as percentages. That is the pattern to copy. Few metrics, clear goals, visible variances. Where does revenue actually leak? Six classic pitfalls. Missing pre-certification. Services rendered without required authorization become denied claims. Inaccurate registration data poisons everything downstream. Late charge capture. Charges posted more than three days late inflate DNFB and delay cash. Coding errors trigger rejections and rework. Slow AR follow-up lets accounts drift past timely filing limits and become uncollectible. And resolving denials without root cause analysis guarantees the same denial comes back next month. Flip those pitfalls and you get the playbook. Get it right at the front door. Verify, pre-certify, and counsel before service. Collect at the point of service. Money taken on site never becomes a receivable. Automate edits and scrubbing so errors are caught before claims leave the building. Manage denials by root cause. Fix the upstream process, not just the symptom. Run a focused KPI dashboard. Few metrics, clear goals, accountable owners. And give the cycle an executive owner, a chief revenue officer who aligns clinical and financial teams. Chapter 7 Where all of this is heading from a traditional reactive cycle to a clinically integrated automated one. The traditional cycle is reactive. Front-end denials keep rising. The same errors get corrected over and over. Charges post late instead of in real time. And risks surface only after they hit. The clinically integrated cycle inverts that. A digital front door automates access. Charge capture and coding become intelligent. Predictive analytics flag risk early. And organizations strike a strategic balance between in-house teams and vendors. The payoff spans four fronts: a frictionless patient experience, cleaner claims and faster cash, recovered margin, and lower compliance risk. Walk the automated cycle end to end. Pre-service, geo-fenced check-in, kiosk and video registration, and portal save data, speed up intake and compliance. During care and charging, telehealth visits, service level coding automated natively in the EMR, and NLP assisting code selection. In billing and adjudication, embedded scrubbing limits touches and denials are auto routed to their root cause owners and rebuild fast. Post service, BI dashboards monitor claims aging and self-pay, while patients get plain language statements through the portal. Why is the shift happening now? Six forces, margin pressure. Profitability is harder to sustain than ever. Regulatory complexity keeps expanding. The patient has become a payer as higher deductibles shift balances onto individuals. Technology has matured. Automation and analytics are finally viable at scale. Value-based care ties reimbursement increasingly to outcomes and cost reduction. Eliminating administrative waste frees capital to reinvest in care itself. Let's put it all together. The people who run the cycle, the terms you'll heal, and the takeaways that matter most. The cycle is a team sport. The chief revenue officer owns it end to end and aligns clinical and financial teams toward best practice results. Patient access staff runs scheduling, registration, verification, and financial clearance at the front. Coders and CDI specialists translate documentation into accurate, compliant, billable codes. The billing and AR team produces clean claims, works follow-up, and resolves denials. Physicians and clinicians actually start the billing process with their diagnoses and documentation. And customer service protects the final collection step. A quick glossary you can screenshot. AR, accounts receivable. CDM, the charge master, the master list of billable items. CDI, clinical documentation integrity. ICD, the WHO's diagnosis codes. Diagnosis codes say what was wrong, procedure codes say what was done, and case-based groups bundle an inpatient stay into one payment. DNFB, discharged not final billed. Facility versus professional claims, the two bills from one encounter. Capitation, a fixed payment per member per period. And the clean claim, accepted on the first pass. That's the vocabulary of this whole video. If you remember five things, make them these. One, the cycle is end-to-end, scheduling to final payment, not just the business office. Two, front-end accuracy is everything. Most denials are born at registration and pre-certification. Three, cash speed is financial health. Every day off AR is cash back in the provider's hands. Four, measure relentlessly. A focused KPI dashboard turns data into accountable action. Five, the future is integrated and automated. Clinical and financial workflows are converging on one platform. That's revenue cycle management, turning the care delivered into the revenue that sustains it, accurately, compliantly, and faster. If this video helped you, give it a like and subscribe for more healthcare finance lessons. Thanks for watching. I'll see you in the next one.

Want to understand the complete US Healthcare RCM Cycle in just 5 minutes?
This quick video explains the end-to-end Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) process from patient appointment to billing, payment, collections, and denial management — in a simple and easy-to-understand way.

This video is perfect for:
✔️ Beginners in US Healthcare RCM
✔️ Medical Billing & Coding freshers
✔️ Professionals who want a quick RCM revision

🔍 Topics Covered Quickly:

• Appointment & Registration
• Eligibility & Coding
• Charge Entry & Claim Submission
• Payment Posting
• AR Follow-up, Collections & Denials

metadata.shortDescription:
Understanding the 13 Steps of U.S. Medical Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) is crucial for healthcare providers to ensure financial stability and smooth operations. In this video, we break down each step of the RCM process, from patient pre-registration to final revenue reconciliation, highlighting their importance in reducing claim denials, improving cash flow, and optimizing medical billing efficiency.

Whether you're a healthcare administrator, medical biller, or provider, this detailed guide will help you navigate the complexities of RCM with ease. Don't forget to like, share, and subscribe for more healthcare finance insights!

In medical billing, CARC (Claim Adjustment Reason Code) and RARC (Remittance Advice Remark Code) are standardized codes used to explain adjustments made to claims, especially when a payment is denied, reduced, or changed. Here's a breakdown:

🔹 CARC (Claim Adjustment Reason Code)
What it does: CARCs explain why a payment amount differs from what was billed.

Used for: Identifying reasons for claim denials or adjustments on an ERA (Electronic Remittance Advice) or EOB (Explanation of Benefits).

Format: Typically a numeric or alphanumeric code (e.g., 45, 96, CO-18).

Example:

CARC 45: Charge exceeds fee schedule/maximum allowable or contracted/legislated fee arrangement.

CARC 96: Non-covered charge(s).

🔹 RARC (Remittance Advice Remark Code)
What it does: Provides additional explanation related to the CARC or the payment.

Used for: Giving more context to help understand the CARC or the payment decision.

Format: Usually starts with a letter followed by a number (e.g., N20, M15).

Example:

RARC N20: Service not payable with other service rendered on the same date.

RARC M15: Separately billed services/tests have been bundled.

🔄 How They Work Together
CARC explains the main reason for the adjustment.

RARC gives supplemental detail.

Example scenario:

Claim denied with:

CARC 96 – Non-covered charge(s).

RARC N115 – This decision was based on a National Coverage Determination (NCD).

✅ Why It Matters
Understanding CARCs and RACRs helps medical billers:

Appeal denied claims correctly.

Fix billing errors.

Communicate clearly with insurance companies.

metadata.author: Inlera University
metadata.shortDescription:
Have you ever struggled with understanding an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) or the Electronic Remittance Advice (ERA)? If so, today’s video is for you! We're breaking down real-life examples of claim processing, so you can confidently interpret when an insurance company is processing a claim toward the deductible versus outright denying a claim.

🔔 Subscribe & Stay Connected!
https://inlerauniversity.com/ 

💡 In This Video, You’ll Learn:
✔️ The difference between a denial and a claim applied to a deductible
✔️ How to read insurance EOBs and ERAs from different clearinghouses
✔️ What key codes (like PR1 and CO-45) mean for patient responsibility
✔️ How to determine what the patient actually owes after insurance processing
✔️ Why the allowed amount is different from your billed charges
✔️ How to verify that a claim has been processed correctly

📌 Key Takeaways:

A zero payment from insurance doesn’t always mean denial—it may mean the claim was applied toward the deductible.
PR1 = Patient Responsibility for Deductible → The patient owes this amount.
CO-45 = Contractual Obligation → The practice must write off this amount and cannot bill the patient.
Always cross-check your EOB/ERA formats, as different software systems display the same information differently.

metadata.title: Michigan’s Surprise Billing Law:  What Providers and Health Plans Need to Know
metadata.author: Miller Johnson
metadata.shortDescription:
At the end of 2020, Michigan passed the Surprise Medical Billing law to address billing by out of network physicians. Join us to learn about the law’s disclosure requirements, payment limitations and dispute resolution process and how it will impact providers and health plans.

Tim Gutwald and Tripp VanderWal discuss key issues providers and employers must know.

metadata.title: The Law Stops Surprise Medical Bills. Why Not the Ambulance?
metadata.author: AS DESIGNED | Risk & Insurance Stories
metadata.shortDescription:
Line 1: In December 2024 a family drove eight hours to a reunion, called 911 for a ten-year-old in pain, and did the only thing available to them.

Line 2: Six weeks later, two envelopes arrived in the same week — and one of them was supposed to be illegal.

Composite Disclaimers: This case is a composite constructed to illustrate a documented systemic pattern. It does not describe a specific real individual.

Body Paragraph 1: A family did the textbook right thing in a ninety-second emergency and still received a bill — because the federal law that bans surprise medical bills never covered the one vehicle that got them to the hospital.

Body Paragraph 2: This episode explains, with sources, why ground ambulance transport was left out of the federal surprise-billing protections, why state fixes often cannot reach self-funded employer plans, and how a plan year can charge the same deductible twice.

Practical takeaway in brief: Three questions, not answers: is your plan fully insured or self-funded; does your state limit ground ambulance balance billing and which plans does it cover; and how does your plan treat care that crosses 31 December. This is general education, not advice about your bill — for anything that decides real money, talk to your own plan in writing and to a licensed professional.

Sources / Further Reading:

“Know your medical bill rights when using insurance” — Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) — https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/know-your-rights/insurance

“Consumers Still Face Surprise Bills for Ground Ambulances — States Are Trying to Protect Them” — The Commonwealth Fund, 18 February 2026 — https://www.commonwealthfund.org/blog/2026/consumers-still-face-surprise-bills-ground-ambulances-states-are-trying-protect-them

“Ground ambulance rides and potential for surprise billing” — Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker — https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/ground-ambulance-rides-and-potential-for-surprise-billing/

“Action Plan: Ground ambulance bill” — Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) — https://www.cms.gov/medical-bill-rights/help/plan/insurance-ground-ambulance-bill

“Report of the Advisory Committee on Ground Ambulance and Patient Billing” — Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) — https://www.cms.gov/files/document/report-advisory-committee-ground-ambulance-and-patient-billing.pdf

Escalation route: For bills involving services the No Surprises Act covers: the CMS No Surprises Help Desk, 1-800-985-3059, and the complaint form at https://www.cms.gov/medical-bill-rights/help/submit-a-complaint. For a ground ambulance bill on a state-regulated plan, contact your state insurance department.

AI Disclosure Note: Disclosure: the visuals in this episode are AI-generated illustrations and the narration is synthetic. Nothing in this video is archival or documentary footage.

metadata.title: Fixing the No Surprises Act: Scaling Back and Reforming the Federal Arbitration System
metadata.author: Paragon Health Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
Join Paragon for a virtual discussion on how the No Surprises Act’s federal arbitration system is reshaping out-of-network payment disputes. Our panelists will examine why dispute volume and arbitration awards have grown far beyond initial expectations, how the current process may be affecting provider contracting incentives and health care costs, and what reforms policymakers can pursue to preserve protections from surprise bills while avoiding cost increases for American families. The event will feature two panels with experts from the American Enterprise Institute and Brookings Institution, as well as representatives of employers and physicians, discussing the IDR process and its consequences.

The event is based on a new Paragon research paper, Fixing the No Surprises Act: Scaling Back and Reforming the Federal Arbitration System. The paper shows that federal IDR disputes have surged, providers prevail in the large majority of cases, and arbitration awards often substantially exceed typical in-network rates—giving providers greater incentives to remain out of network and greater leverage to demand higher in-network rates. The paper contains Paragon’s recommendations, which include removing elective services from arbitration and placing limits on arbitration awards for emergency services.

Panelists:

    Jackson Hammond—Senior Policy Analyst, Paragon Health Institute
    Brian Blase, PhD—President, Paragon Health Institute

First Panel

    Loren Adler—Senior Fellow of Economics and Associate Director of the Center on Health Policy, Brookings Institution
    Ben Ippolito—Senior Fellow, American Enterprise Institute

Second Panel

    James Gelfand—Chief Executive Officer and President, ERISA Industry Committee (ERIC)
    Randy Pilgrim, MD—Emergency Physician; Chief Medical Officer for SCP Health; Chair, EDPMA Federal Health Policy Committee


Paragon Health Institute is a policy research center focused on improving health care and lowering prices by empowering patients, expanding competition in the market, reforming government, and increasing innovation. 

Learn more at paragoninstitute.org

videos.full_text: All right, we are extremely excited for today's Paragon Health Institute virtual event fixing [snorts] the No Surprises Act. My name is Brian Blaze. I am the president of Paragon Health Institute. Paragon focuses on evaluating how government health programs are actually working and making recommendations consistent with maximizing choice, competition, and improving incentives that emanate from those programs. Today, we have a two-panel event. We're going to go for an hour and 15 minutes. The event will be recorded and will be available later today on Paragon's YouTube channel. The first panel features three policy experts, my colleague Jackson Hammond, a senior policy analyst at Paragon who authored our paper on the No Surprises Act, which contained a very rich data analysis for how the arbitration system in at the core of the act is working, as well as Paragon's policy recommendations. Joining Jackson are really the two leading academic experts in the country on surprise medical billing. Loren Adler is a fellow and associate director at the Brookings Institution's Center on Health Policy. He serves as an associate editor of Health Affairs Scholar. Loren has been working on this issue for at least a decade. In fact, I remember when he met with me when I was in the White House in 2017 on this issue. Ben has also been working on this issue for at least a decade, often doing work jointly with Loren. Ben Ippolito is a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute in the economic policy studies. He currently serves as a member of the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission and is an associate editor of Health Affairs scholar. Ben, Lauren, thank you for joining Paragon for this virtual event. And Ben, I'm going to start with you. And before we get into how the No Surprises Act is working, tell us what Congress was trying to do when it passed the No Surprises Act. >> Yeah, thanks Brian. Thanks for having me. It is a little scary to think just how long we've been we've been at this. I was just looking at some slides that that we did for a member briefing in in 2017, I think. So, um you know, this whole issue really emanated from what was viewed as a sort of deeply unfair situation facing patients. Essentially, patients were unexpectedly, and that was key, unexpectedly getting treated by providers that did not accept their insurance. The canonical examples we always talked about were emergencies. You get rushed to the nearest emergency room, that facility may or may not be in your network. Or you go give birth at your in-network hospital with your in-network OB, but the anesthesiologist you didn't choose happen to not accept your insurance. And the key was that these were cases where patients could not reasonably avoid being treated by an out-of-network provider, and they could then be so-called balance billed. In essence, they they had high financial exposure. Whatever their insurer didn't pay of the provider's full bill charges could be billed to the patient. And so, I think there was I don't want to speak for Congress, but I I think it was unanimous agreement that that was both unfair and not really how we want a market to function. Patients did not have any choice. metadata.title: Surprise Bills Are Illegal — So Why Did Arbitration Just Hit $15 Billion?
metadata.author: Top Hospitals USA
metadata.shortDescription: Surprise medical billing has been illegal in America since January 2022. So how did arbitration under the No Surprises Act award nearly $15 billion to providers in a single year? This investigation follows the money: the law that protected patients, the arbitration machine that grew out of it, the enforcement record, and the two bills fighting over its future in Congress in October 2026 — plus a practical guide to what you can do if a surprise bill lands in your mailbox. CHAPTERS 0:00 The $15 Billion Question / 1:06 The Law: What the No Surprises Act Bans / 2:05 The Arbitration Money Trail / 3:26 The Enforcement Record / 4:55 The October 2026 Fight in Congress / 6:15 What To Do If You Get a Surprise Bill. THE FACTS: The No Surprises Act took effect in January 2022. It bans surprise bills for emergency care, for non-emergency care from out-of-network providers at in-network facilities, and for air ambulance services. Patients pay only their normal in-network cost sharing. Arbitration (independent dispute resolution) awarded $14.85 billion to providers in 2025, up from $4.08 billion in 2024, according to a Wall Street Journal analysis of federal data. Arbitration firms collected about $1.3 billion in fees. Providers prevailed in about 85% of second-half 2025 determinations, and the winning offer was above the insurer benchmark in about 87% of cases, according to CMS. CMS enforcement report (June 2026): nearly 40,000 complaints since 2022; 15,145 closed; 14,799 about the No Surprises Act; 11,417 against providers, facilities, or air ambulance services. Most common complaint: surprise billing for non-emergency care at an in-network facility (4,806). Nearly $30 million in direct relief. October 2026: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the Lower Premiums, Faster Payments Act (Oct 8) to end arbitration for care from January 1, 2028, and pay a benchmark based on median in-network rates. Rep. Gregory Murphy's No Surprises Act Enforcement Act would keep arbitration and raise penalties for late payment after an arbitrator rules. WHAT TO DO IF YOU GET A SURPRISE BILL: Do not pay it right away. Compare it with your insurer's explanation of benefits and check whether the service is one the law covers. You can report it to the No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059, or file a complaint online through the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. If you have no insurance, ask for a good faith estimate before scheduled care. If the final bill is at least $400 more than the estimate, you may be able to dispute it within 120 days of the first bill, for a $25 fee. Ground ambulance rides are generally NOT covered by the federal protections — check your state law. Keep your bill, insurance card, explanation of benefits, and any estimate you were given. This video describes general rights and complaint channels; it is not legal or financial advice. Check your own plan and state rules, and verify details with CMS or your insurer. RELATED VIDEO: The most common surgeries in America — video #77: https://youtu.be/4EONO6rThLk SOURCES: Wall Street Journal analysis via Becker's Payer Issues (July 22, 2026): https://www.beckerspayer.com/payer/no-surprises-arbitration-payouts-hit-15b-in-2025-alone-wsj/ ; CMS enforcement report via Becker's Payer Issues (June 5, 2026): https://www.beckerspayer.com/policy-updates/cms-bulk-of-no-surprises-complaints-filed-against-providers/ ; Georgetown Center on Health Insurance Reforms (CHIR): https://chir.georgetown.edu/implementing-the-no-surprises-act-updated-complaint-data-from-2022-to-2025/ ; The Fiscal Times on the Pallone bill (Oct 8, 2026): https://www.thefiscaltimes.com/2026/10/08/Key-Democrat-Introduces-Surprise-Medical-Billing-Reform ; Becker's ASC on the Pallone bill (Oct 12, 2026): https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-news/inside-the-bill-that-wants-to-get-rid-of-no-surprises-arbitration/ ; Becker's ASC, "The No Surprises Act's $15B reckoning" (Oct 16, 2026): https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/the-no-surprises-acts-15b-reckoning/ ABOUT THIS CHANNEL: Top Hospitals USA explains American hospitals, health rankings, and the systems behind your care — as a documentary guide, using verified public sources. The footage in this video is AI-generated illustrative B-roll, not real footage of any hospital, person, or proceeding. No medical advice is given in this video.
