hands in 1 year in a system that was
supposed to stop surprise medical bills.
In 2025, arbitration under the No
Surprises Act awarded nearly $15 billion
to hospitals, doctors, and air ambulance
companies.
That is more than three times the $4.08
billion awarded the year before.
And here's the part that does not add
up. Surprise billing has been illegal in
America since January 2022. The law says
so. Patients are protected. The bill you
used to get after an emergency room
visit, the one from a doctor you never
chose at a price nobody told you about,
that bill is banned.
So, how did a law that worked for
patients turn into a $15 billion fight
money?
The answer is not in your mailbox. It is
in a back room where insurers and
providers argue over who pays what,
while you were told you owe nothing
extra.
This is the story of a law that
protected patients and an arbitration
machine that grew out of control. In
2020, Congress passed the No Surprises
Act and it took effect in January 2022.
It's a rule of simple. If you go to an
emergency room, you cannot be billed
extra because the hospital or the doctor
was out of your insurance network. If
you have surgery at a hospital that is
in your network, but the
anesthesiologist or the assistant
surgeon is not, you cannot be billed
extra for that either.
Air ambulance rides are covered, too.
In all of these cases, you pay only what
you would have paid in network, your
normal copay, co-insurance, or
deductible.
The rest of the bill becomes a fight
between your insurer and the provider,
and you are not in it.
Before this law, the fight landed on
you. A patient could do everything
right, choose an in-network hospital,
and still get a bill for thousands of
dollars from a doctor they never met.
The law ended that. The patient
protection part worked.
What nobody planned for was what
happened next when the providers and the
insurers started fighting each other.
When an insurer and a provider cannot
agree on a price, the law sends them to
arbitration called independent dispute
resolution.
Each side submits one final number and
the arbitrator must pick one of the two.
No middle ground.
Congress expected about 22,000 of these
disputes a year.
Instead, certified arbitrators issued
about 2.2 million payment decisions in
2025 alone.
Providers won about 85% of the decisions
in the second half of the year. And the
winning offer was above the insurer
benchmark in about 87% of cases.
The money followed.
$4.08 billion in awards in 2024 became
$14.85 billion in 2025.
The arbitration firms themselves
collected about $1.3 billion in fees.
Just three filers, Hello MD, Team
Health, and SCP Health, accounted for
about 38% of disputes in the second half
of last year.
Committee Democrats say 10 provider
groups filed about 67% of the 2.5
million disputes in 2025.
United Healthcare says the average
payout runs 11 times Medicare rates.
The Congressional Budget Office once
projected this law would lower premiums
by about 1%.
In June 2026, the Budget Office said the
emerging evidence suggests otherwise.
So, is the law actually being enforced?
The federal agency in charge, the
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid
Services, published an enforcement
report in June 2026.
Since 2022, it has received nearly
40,000 complaints. It has closed 15,145
of them.
Almost all of those, 14,799,
were about the No Surprises Act. 11,417
were filed against providers,
facilities, or air ambulance services.
The single most common complaint, 4,806
cases, was surprise billing for
non-emergency care at an in-network
facility.
The second most common, 2,363,
was surprise billing for emergency care.
In 2,086 closed cases, investigators
found a violation.
Enforcement has produced nearly $30
million in direct relief.
But nearly 25,000 complaints were still
open when the report was published.
And the complaint numbers look small
next to the scale of the system.
Researchers at Georgetown note that
insurers process close to a million
covered claims a month.
Fewer than 1% of them produce a
complaint.
Either the law is working or many people
who get a wrong bill never complain.
On October 2nd, 2026, the agency called
the leaders of 17 arbitration firms to a
meeting about rising costs, ineligible
disputes, and delayed payments. No new
rule was announced.
That brings us to October 2026, when
Congress split into two camps.
October 8th, Representative Frank
Pallone of New Jersey, one of the
original authors of the No Surprises
Act, introduced the Lower Premiums,
Faster Payments Act.
His bill would end arbitration for care
delivered on or after January 1st, 2028
and replace it with a benchmark, the
median in-network rate for the same
service.
Insurers would have to pay within 30
days of a claim.
Pallone says a few bad actors, largely
backed by private equity, are gaming the
system, creating backlogs, and driving
up premiums.
The competing bill comes from
Representative Gregory Murphy of North
Carolina, a doctor himself.
His No Surprises Act Enforcement Act
would keep arbitration, but raise the
penalties for plans and providers that
miss payment deadlines after an
arbitrator rules.
It has 36 bipartisan co-sponsors,
but 58 employers and employer groups
wrote to Congress in July opposing it,
arguing the system itself needs fixing,
not just tougher enforcement.
The stakes are your premiums.
Arbitration awards are paid by insurers,
and those costs can flow into the
premiums that employers and workers pay
every year.
With federal funding set to expire on
December 11th, a year-end spending
package could carry a narrower fix.
Nothing is decided yet.
So, what should you do if a surprise
bill arrives in your mailbox?
First, do not pay it right away.
Compare it with the explanation of
benefits from your insurer, and check
whether the service is one the law
covers. Emergency care, care from an
out-of-network provider at an in-network
facility, or an air ambulance.
If the bill charges you more than your
normal in-network cost sharing for one
of those, it may be a surprise bill, and
you can report it.
Call the No Surprises Help Desk at
59, or file a complaint online through
the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid
Services.
Keep your bill, your insurance card,
your explanation of benefits, and any
estimate you were given.
If you have no insurance, ask for a good
faith estimate before scheduled care.
If the final bill is at least $400 more
than the estimate, you can dispute it
within 120 days of the first bill for a
$25 fee.
One gap to know about, ground ambulance
rides are generally not covered by the
federal protections. So, check your
state law.
The law worked for patients. Whether the
money fight behind it gets fixed is now
up to Congress.
If this helped, watch our video on the
most common surgeries in America, linked
below, and subscribe for the next
investigation.

metadata.title: The Truth Is in the Data: Myths, Reality & What’s Next in IDR Under the NSA | Becker’s x HaloMD
metadata.author: HaloMD
metadata.shortDescription:
What does the data reveal about independent dispute resolution (IDR) under the No Surprises Act (NSA)—and what does it mean for healthcare organizations’ financial sustainability?

In this Becker’s Healthcare x HaloMD webinar, Alla LaRoque, Megan Rausch and Patrick Velliky examine six common IDR myths, evaluate the evidence behind competing narratives, and discuss what’s next for providers.

Drawing on CMS data, published research and industry surveys, the discussion explores:

• Dispute volumes, provider win rates and the context behind the headlines
• The qualifying payment amount (QPA) and how to interpret IDR awards
• Reimbursement trends and their implications for providers
• The assumptions behind widely cited IDR cost estimates
• Payer payment delays, accountability and enforcement proposals
• The IDR Operations Final Rule and upcoming implementation milestones

For hospital and health system executives, physician group leaders, and revenue cycle and managed care teams, this conversation connects the data to reimbursement strategy, operational readiness and informed decision-making.

Learn more about HaloMD: halomd.com

#NoSurprisesAct #IDR #HealthcareFinance

metadata.title: Are Ambulances Covered Under Surprise Billing Laws?
metadata.author: Law & Business
metadata.shortDescription:
A detailed legal analysis of ground and air ambulance coverage under the federal No Surprises Act and state level healthcare legislation. This video examines the statutory exclusions passed by Congress, the impact of Employee Retirement Income Security Act preemption on self funded employer plans, and specific consumer protections in states like California, Texas, and New York. Learn how to verify plan types, navigate itemized billing, and execute internal insurance appeals to contest unexpected out of network transport charges.

segments.text: Emergency medical transportation often
exposes health insurance policy holders
to unexpected financial liabilities
after a sudden medical crisis because
out-of-network emergency transit
providers are not fully restricted by
federal legislation, leading to massive
balance bills for unsuspecting patients
nationwide. The federal No Surprises Act
took effect in 2022 to prevent
unexpected balance billing for emergency
medical care. But its statutory reach is
limited, leaving certain critical
sectors of the emergency response
landscape completely open to aggressive
out-of-network provider charges. This
comprehensive piece of legislation
successfully protects consumers from
unexpected out-of-network charges at
conventional hospitals, freestanding
emergency rooms, and behavioral health
facilities, ensuring that patients only
pay their standard in-network
cost-sharing responsibilities under
their health plan. The federal statute
also explicitly covers air ambulance
transport services, restricting patient
out-of-pocket costs to their standard
in-network rates, regardless of whether
the helicopter operator maintains a
formal contractual agreement with the
consumer health insurance company or
network. However, ground ambulance
vehicles were completely omitted from
these federal consumer protection laws
during the legislative drafting process
in Congress due to intense lobbying and
complex jurisdictional disputes over
local government funding models and
municipal ambulance service rate-setting
frameworks. Consequently, ground
ambulances remain the single largest
source of out-of-network emergency bills
for insured Americans today, creating
widespread financial vulnerability and
forcing patients to pay massive,
unexpected expenses after relying on
emergency services for transport to a
hospital facility. National data
indicates that over 50% of all emergency
ground ambulance transports involve an
out-of-network provider, exposing
patients to severe billing risks because
consumers cannot choose their ambulance
operator during a life-threatening
medical emergency situation.
Balance billing occurs when an
out-of-network ambulance service charges
a total rate higher than the health
insurance plan agrees to pay for care,
and the insurer refuses to cover the
remaining cost under the standard terms
of the policy.
The ambulance operator then bills the
patient directly for the remaining
financial balance, which can easily
reach hundreds or thousands of
out-of-pocket dollars, causing
significant economic distress for
individuals who believed their health
insurance would fully cover emergency
transit.
Congress excluded ground ambulances from
federal protections because the
emergency medical transport industry is
incredibly decentralized and complex
across different states and
municipalities, making a uniform federal
reimbursement standard exceptionally
difficult to implement without
disrupting local emergency response
systems.
Ground ambulance systems are operated by
an intricate mixture of municipal fire
departments, county governments, private
companies, and volunteer emergency
squads with entirely different
operational costs, capital structures,
funding mechanisms, and local regulatory
oversight frameworks that vary
dramatically by state.
Local governments frequently establish
and regulate ambulance rates via
specific local ordinances to fund their
public safety infrastructure, which made
comprehensive federal rate setting
politically and logistically difficult
during the negotiations for the original
No Surprises Act legislative package.
Private equity firms have also acquired
many private ambulance operators over
the last decade, often choosing not to
participate in insurance networks to
maximize their corporate revenue streams
and exploit the lack of federal consumer
billing protections in this sector.
Air ambulances were treated differently
by federal lawmakers because they are
legally governed under federal aviation
laws instead of localized municipal
statutes or ordinances, allowing
Congress to utilize interstate commerce
powers to regulate their billing
practices without interfering with local
government authority. To address this
specific regulatory gap, Congress
created the Advisory Committee on Ground
Ambulance and Patient Billing to analyze
industry practices, evaluate consumer
data, and recommend statutory solutions
to protect patients from unfair and
exorbitant balance billing practices
nationwide. The Federal Advisory
Committee formally recommended that
future federal legislation should cap
patient cost-sharing at their standard
in-network deductible and copayment
amounts, ensuring that ground ambulance
trips are treated identically to other
protected emergency medical services
under the law.
They also proposed that health insurance
companies should pay ground ambulance
providers according to locally
established public fee schedules
whenever those schedules are available
or utilize a standardized benchmark rate
to prevent long disputes between
insurers and transit operators over fair
payment. Despite these comprehensive
formal recommendations, federal
lawmakers have not yet passed a
nationwide statutory solution to ban
ground ambulance surprise billing across
the country, leaving consumers entirely
dependent on the specific laws enacted
within their individual home states for
legal protection. Because federal
protections are missing, individual
state legislatures have taken
independent action to pass localized
consumer protection statutes to defend
their residents from surprise bills.
But these state laws vary widely in
their scope, definition, and operational
effectiveness across boundaries.
Approximately 14 states have implemented
specific statutory frameworks that
directly restrict ground ambulance
companies from balance billing
vulnerable consumers within their state
boundaries, providing varying levels of
relief depending on the specific type of
health insurance coverage the patient
maintains.
For example, California passed Assembly
Bill 716
to comprehensively limit out-of-network
ground ambulance charges for state
regulated health insurance policies,
ensuring that consumers are not
penalized financially for out-of-network
transport during emergencies.
The California statute caps patient
out-of-pocket costs at the exact rate
they would pay for an equivalent
in-network medical service and prohibits
ambulance companies from reporting
delinquent bills to credit bureaus for
at least 12 months after billing.
Texas implemented its own statutory
framework that shields consumers from
surprise ambulance bills by utilizing
state mandated reimbursement benchmarks
for out-of-network services and
requiring arbitration to resolve payment
disputes between insurance companies and
emergency medical service providers
directly. New York state insurance law
requires commercial health insurers to
pay a standardized rate directly to
non-preferred local ground ambulance
corporations to protect consumers from
receiving a balance bill after transport
by an out-of-network emergency vehicle
operator.
Other states with notable protections
include Colorado, Florida, Maryland,
Ohio, and several additional proactive
jurisdictions working to eliminate these
unexpected out-of-network bills through
state-level legislation targeting
insurance reimbursements and provider
billing limitations within their local
borders. However, state laws suffer from
a major constitutional limitation known
as federal preemption under the Employee
Retirement Income Security Act of 1974,
which severely curtails the ability of
states to protect a significant portion
of their insured population.
This federal statute prevents state
governments from regulating self-funded
employer health insurance plans, which
currently cover the vast majority of
working individuals nationwide,
meaning state ambulance billing bans
cannot legally apply to these federally
overseen corporate benefit plans.
Approximately 60% of commercially
insured workers are enrolled in these
self-funded employer plans, completely
exempting them from any state-level
ambulance protections, and leaving them
exposed to balance billing, despite
living in a state with active consumer
laws. This creates a highly fragmented
legal system, where two neighbors in the
same town can face completely different
financial outcomes for using the same
ambulance service, based entirely on how
their employer chooses to structure and
fund their corporate health benefits
package. If a consumer is covered by a
self-funded employer plan, state-level
ground ambulance billing protections
will generally not apply to their
situation, meaning they must rely on
internal insurance appeals or personal
negotiation with the emergency medical
provider.
When an unprotected patient receives an
expensive out-of-network ground
ambulance bill, the provider can
initiate standard debt collection
actions to recover funds, including
sending the account to collection
agencies or initiating legal proceedings
to secure payment for services rendered.
Unpaid medical debt can severely damage
a consumer's credit score. If the
delinquent account is eventually
transferred to an aggressive third-party
collection agency and reported to major
credit reporting repositories, impacting
the consumer's ability to secure loans
or housing.
Major national credit bureaus have
removed paid medical debt from credit
reports, but unpaid balances over $500
can still remain for years under current
credit reporting regulations, creating
long-term financial consequences for
patients facing unprotected ambulance
bills.
To contest an unfair ground ambulance
charge, patients should immediately
request a fully itemized bill to check
for potential coding errors, duplicated
charges, or compliance issues that could
invalidate portions of the total amount
demanded by the transit operator.
Patients should then contact their
health insurance company to request an
administrative review or a formal
out-of-network exception for the
emergency transit, arguing that they had
no choice of provider during the acute
medical crisis.
In some circumstances, insurance
companies will voluntarily negotiate
directly with the ambulance company to
settle the disputed balance on behalf of
the insured to avoid litigation or
protect the policy holder from
aggressive collection actions by the
medical provider. Consumers can also
check if their local municipality has a
specific ordinance limiting what
city-operated ambulance providers can
legally collect from local residents, as
some town councils explicitly prohibit
balance billing for taxpayers within
their municipal borders.
It is essential to examine your physical
health insurance card to determine
whether your specific plan is classified
as fully insured or self-funded because
this distinction dictates which
regulatory body governs your health
coverage benefits and consumer
protection remedies. This legal
distinction determines whether
state-level consumer protection laws can
successfully shield your family from an
unexpected out-of-network ground
ambulance charge or if you are left
vulnerable to federal regulatory
exclusions under the current framework.
Comprehensive resolution of this
persistent healthcare loophole requires
coordinated federal legislation to
uniformly protect all insured patients
across the entire United States
landscape, eliminating the confusion
caused by overlapping state regulations
and federal preemption exceptions.

The federal No Surprises Act took effect in 2022 to prevent unexpected balance billing for emergency medical care. But its statutory reach is limited, leaving certain critical sectors of the emergency response landscape completely open to aggressive out-of-network provider charges. This comprehensive piece of legislation successfully protects consumers from unexpected out-of-network charges at conventional hospitals, freestanding emergency rooms, and behavioral health facilities, ensuring that patients only pay their standard in-network cost-sharing responsibilities under their health plan. The federal statute also explicitly covers air ambulance transport services, restricting patient out-of-pocket costs to their standard in-network rates, regardless of whether the helicopter operator maintains a formal contractual agreement with the consumer health insurance company or network. However, ground ambulance vehicles were completely omitted from these federal consumer protection laws during the legislative drafting process in Congress due to intense lobbying and complex jurisdictional disputes over local government funding models and municipal ambulance service rate-setting frameworks. Consequently, ground ambulances remain the single largest source of out-of-network emergency bills for insured Americans today, creating widespread financial vulnerability and forcing patients to pay massive, unexpected expenses after relying on emergency services for transport to a hospital facility. National data indicates that over 50% of all emergency ground ambulance transports involve an out-of-network provider, exposing patients to severe billing risks because consumers cannot choose their ambulance operator during a life-threatening medical emergency situation. Balance billing occurs when an out-of-network ambulance service charges a total rate higher than the health insurance plan agrees to pay for care, and the insurer refuses to cover the remaining cost under the standard terms of the policy. The ambulance operator then bills the patient directly for the remaining financial balance, which can easily reach hundreds or thousands of out-of-pocket dollars, causing significant economic distress for individuals who believed their health insurance would fully cover emergency transit. Congress excluded ground ambulances from federal protections because the emergency medical transport industry is incredibly decentralized and complex across different states and municipalities, making a uniform federal reimbursement standard exceptionally difficult to implement without disrupting local emergency response systems. Ground ambulance systems are operated by an intricate mixture of municipal fire departments, county governments, private companies, and volunteer emergency squads with entirely different operational costs, capital structures, funding mechanisms, and local regulatory oversight frameworks that vary dramatically by state. Local governments frequently establish and regulate ambulance rates via specific local ordinances to fund their public safety infrastructure, which made comprehensive federal rate setting politically and logistically difficult during the negotiations for the original No Surprises Act legislative package. Private equity firms have also acquired many private ambulance operators over the last decade, often choosing not to participate in insurance networks to maximize their corporate revenue streams and exploit the lack of federal consumer billing protections in this sector. Air ambulances were treated differently by federal lawmakers because they are legally governed under federal aviation laws instead of localized municipal statutes or ordinances, allowing Congress to utilize interstate commerce powers to regulate their billing practices without interfering with local government authority. They also proposed that health insurance companies should pay ground ambulance providers according to locally established public fee schedules whenever those schedules are available or utilize a standardized benchmark rate to prevent long disputes between insurers and transit operators over fair payment. Other states with notable protections include Colorado, Florida, Maryland, Ohio, and several additional proactive jurisdictions working to eliminate these unexpected out-of-network bills through state-level legislation targeting insurance reimbursements and provider billing limitations within their local borders. However, state laws suffer from a major constitutional limitation known as federal preemption under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, which severely curtails the ability of states to protect a significant portion of their insured population. This federal statute prevents state governments from regulating self-funded employer health insurance plans, which currently cover the vast majority of working individuals nationwide, meaning state ambulance billing bans cannot legally apply to these federally overseen corporate benefit plans. Approximately 60% of commercially insured workers are enrolled in these self-funded employer plans, completely exempting them from any state-level ambulance protections, and leaving them exposed to balance billing, despite living in a state with active consumer laws. This creates a highly fragmented legal system, where two neighbors in the same town can face completely different financial outcomes for using the same ambulance service, based entirely on how their employer chooses to structure and fund their corporate health benefits package. metadata.title: Empowering Plans: P254 – Fixing the No Surprises Act: Will Congress Repair IDR?
metadata.author: The Phia Group, LLC
metadata.shortDescription: In this episode of the Empowering Plans podcast series, Attorneys Brian O’Hara and John Gresh explore challenges surrounding the federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process, from rising dispute volume and administrative costs to payment enforcement and errors. They also discuss potential reforms that could balance provider protections with a more transparent and efficient process.

videos.full_text: [music] >> Healthcare is too expensive. Employers are offsetting costs onto their employees. Who will make health benefits [music] affordable for hardworking Americans and their families? >> You will. This is the Empowering [music] Plans podcast, a show dedicated to helping you once again emphasize the benefit in your benefit plan. [music] Now prepare to learn, >> plan, >> save, >> and protect with The Fia Group. >> Hello and welcome to another episode of the Empowering Plans podcast with The Fia Group. I'm John Gresch, a senior attorney in the Provider Relations department, and I am joined by a director in the Provider Relations department, Brian O'Hara, who specifically handles No Surprises Act claims. And with Halloween behind us, you know, the only thing more scary than ghosts and goblins and so forth is politics. So we have the midterms right around the corner, and so we thought we would give you a little bit of an update about the different approaches that that may be in play politically and in kind of the current state of the NSA and kind of give you a little bit. Brian? >> It's my my least favorite topic, John. I'm not going to lie to you, but but here we are talking politics. Make sure that that, you know, you don't listen to this podcast around the dinner table because you don't talk politics around the dinner table. That's right. >> That's right. That's right. I think a good place to start even talking about this is, you know, where is the NSA at today? Where's it at right now? What are the issues? What are the problems? And then what potential fixes might be on the way depending on whether, you know, Democrats you know, win win large at the midterms or Republicans retain control, stuff like that. And I think that the first thing to note is that the No Surprises Act really did accomplish its goal of preventing surprise balance bills members, to patients. Uh and as we know that it was a bipartisan uh uh legislation that was passed to to create this, but the interesting aspect about that is that uh just because it was a bipartisan piece of legislation does not mean both sides agree on how it should be implemented or what how to fix the problems or how to enforce uh certain things that may stem from the No Surprises Act as well. Uh until so we'll get into that. Uh do you have any comments on that at all? >> Yeah, I I mean like you said, John, this is uh the No Surprises Act was a bipartisan um kind of achievement and it has done uh it's really done its job of protecting patients. I don't think that that there's, you know, a a Republican side or a Democrat side in this. I think that that both sides realized that Americans needed help uh being protected from these bills and uh I don't know that until recently, you know, members of either political party realized how bad the IDR uh dispute resolution process is going cuz that's that's really the main issue, right? There's there's two kind of components to it. There's that patient protection aspect of it which is going great and then there's the actual dispute resolution part part of it that is really uh problematic. And, you know, performing the IDR does not mean weakening patient protections, right? Uh we want to preserve those protections without shifting growing costs back to patients. And that's kind of what's happening right >> Yeah, no, it's it's a good point. And yeah, I think we both agree there that that reforming it should shouldn't be about weakening it, it should be about strengthening it. And the question is just how do you do that? Uh you know, and to to know how to do it, you have to know what the problems are currently. You know, what what what are the issues facing uh plans and and you know, decision makers uh that deal with the NSA process as it as it currently is. Uh and so uh do you have any thoughts on on you know, what's what would you say is wrong uh with with the current IDR process in general? >> So John, >> I could talk to you for the rest of the day, the rest of the week, the rest of the month about all of the things that are wrong with the NSA. We don't have time to go through all of them, but I would like to go through some some some of the high level things that um you know that we see on a day-to-day basis and um and then we can kind of talk about some of the changes that that might need to occur. So, you know number one I would say is just the sheer volume of disputes. When this was initially passed, this legislation, CMS indicated that they expected around you know 17,000 disputes a year. Well, right now the dispute numbers are in the 8 millions. I don't know if that actually means that 8 million disputes have been brought. I don't know if they if they go you know one by one by one, but we are way past what anyone ever expected in terms of um you know just the the sheer volume of disputes. And what does that mean? Well, that means that there's a significant administrative burden uh that's uh having people you know process these, that's having people uh negotiate them, that's paying IDR fees, uh additional payments on these disputes or on these negotiations. Uh you know and it's a small number of provider groups who have really turned this you know what was meant to be a process to address genuine payment disputes into just a a a standard you know revenue cycle management process. So, you know all of that adds to uh administrative costs which goes downstream to uh you know the individual the individual patient in terms of their you know member contributions or in terms of their deductibles or in terms of their uh you know patient responsibility, things of that nature. I would say one of the the other biggest issues with the No Surprises Act right now is just the deluge of ineligible claims that are being put with no meaningful way to stop them. You know, in theory, there is one set of eligibility rules, right? Claim either should or should not be eligible. Well, unfortunately, we have 16 17 IDREs. They're they're kind of adding and subtracting some you know seemingly on on a daily basis, but 16 to 17 different independent dispute resolution entities. And really in practical terms, you're dealing with 16 to 17 different sets of eligibility rules. One IDRE might deem a claim eligible, another one might not, another one might ask for information. We're currently dealing with a claim right now that had I think it's 15 different CPT codes. The provider brought 15 different disputes one per CPT code. They're all ineligible, but they've gone to I think seven or eight different IDREs. Some IDREs have dismissed disputes, some are letting them go through, some we haven't heard back from. We're dealing with all sorts of different rules and no real meaningful way to address it. You know, you can make your eligibility argument at the IDRE selection stage, but a lot of times these things clearly aren't being reviewed. And if your eligibility argument is not sustained, really it's it's impossible to get in in contact with anyone to actually talk about this meaningfully. One of the biggest problems with this too is the fact that the IDRE entities these are for-profit entities and they only get paid if a claim is deemed eligible. So the entity that is determining eligibility has a vested financial interest in deeming these claims eligible. So while there technically is no burden of proof on either party to you know prove a claim is eligible or or is not eligible. The practical reality is that uh there's a significant burden of proof on health plans to prove beyond some sort of you know standard of evidence. I don't know what it is, if it's clear and convincing, if it's beyond a reasonable doubt, whatever it is, uh to prove that a claim is is not eligible. You know uh >> That's a good that's a good point. I just wanted to piggy back off off of that if I can interject, is that it it kind of highlights the other major flaw of that as well and it's just an overall lack of transparency on how how the determinations are reviewed, you know, which criteria they're they're weighing and how they're doing it. Who who is doing the review? Uh things like that uh just just makes it difficult to know. >> it exactly. I mean I think you hit the nail on the head there. I was going to say, you know, 16 to 17 different kind of eligibility review standards. Well it's also 16 to 17 different standards for substantively deciding these cases. You know, we have factors that are completely detached from like the amount of money that uh that should be paid for a particular dispute or for for a particular claim. For example, I mean, you know, patient acuity or the quality of the provider or whatever. IDREs are accepting arguments about a provider's training by just saying, oh okay, well, you know, this provider gave me their curriculum vitae and they proved that they're a doctor and they they gave me copies of their diploma. So therefore they're a doctor and therefore they get whatever amount of money they want. It's you know and and unfortunately um I would say kind of my my last one that I want to talk about and once again I could go on about this for for days and days, but really one of the the last ones I want to talk about is the fact that there's no real appeal procedure. There's nobody in charge. There's no one at home. If you go, listen, I can prove that there's all sorts of different standards uh of evidence for eligibility uh for, you know, substantive uh readings of these uh evidentiary briefs. There's no one to complain to. There's literally no one in charge who's making sure that there's, you know, any kind of uniformity in these decisions. So it's a real problematic process and ultimately what it comes down to is that it's costing millions, if not billions, in administrative costs and uh it's resulting in just inordinate awards for providers. Uh those awards have to be paid and all of that all of those costs they're being passed down to you, to me, uh to the average American who uh gets, you know, receives their health insurance through their employer. >> Yeah, and I think that that raises the important distinction that that the member of the patient can be protected from that surprise balance bill, but they might not be protected from the costs. Uh as as you note they they'll trickle down and that that'll be an issue that they'll deal with eventually. So is is the law really accomplishing what it set out to do? Uh you know, it does on the surface, but not when you look at it a little bit deeper. Uh so the I think it's a good place to to go from here is, you know, what are the different approaches? What what are, you know, Republicans saying? What's their approach? Democrats and and we also know that this is bipartisan, so I'm sure that there's kind of an in between or something they could work on uh together. Uh but the the two big approaches out there right now are the the Greg Murphy approach which I'll I'll cover and I'll let you kind of cover the other side. But the the highlight of Greg Murphy who's a Republican uh senator from uh North Carolina was a physician uh and his solution is to keep the independent dispute resolution process in place, so not to touch it there, but to to create an enforcement mechanism for the decisions themselves. And I think that would be a pretty provider favored approach, right? Because they're winning the vast majority of those decisions. So there's various issues with that that we could we could talk about. Uh but writers are arguing that uh that the successful, getting a a successful arbitration award is kind of meaningless if there's not a mechanism by which they can collect payment on that. Are you are you seeing that on your end? >> Yeah, and I think that uh I think that it makes sense uh what they're saying. You know, if you were to bring a a lawsuit against someone, you know, for personal injury or breach of contract or whatever and you were to get uh a judgment in your favor, if there's no way to enforce it, then certainly like what's the point of going through the entire process? The problem with this approach, of course, is that it assumes that the IDR process is working and it's not. If you're a reasonable objective person, and I understand I'm coming from the payer side, so I can't say that that I'm completely 100% objective, but if you are a reasonable objective person, you cannot look at the results of six years of the No Surprises Act and say that this process is working. You can't do it. And if we were to just simply say, well, the solution is to enforce all these determinations and to provide penalties and interests in what not, it it's just going to take a major problem and snowball it and make it worse. The plans are reeling right now in terms of the uh financial distress that this has caused. And you know, I think it's important to note that while uh Greg Murphy is is a Republican, I don't think that this is necessarily a a Republican stance. I think this has more to do with the fact that he's a uh physician by trade and uh you know, probably has that uh that backing. Uh so, you know, I think that's kind of the way to look at his approach. It's it's very much looking at it from from the standpoint of let's enforce these awards, let's get as much money from these plans as possible regardless of the the uh behind the the actual IDR process itself. >> Well, and as you talked about earlier with eligibility, there's you know, a lot of claims that are not eligible that are getting to this IDR stage and and even having awards rendered on them and that if you don't fix eligibility, I don't know how you can then enforce the the arbitration awards on top of that if you have claims that are that are getting these awards that that aren't that shouldn't even be there in the first place. >> There are plans that don't know about final payment determinations until months after they've been rendered because they never got notice which John, as an attorney, you know, I mean, like notice is is one of the most fundamental aspects of due process in in American law, right? If if if you're going to you know, if you're going to get sued, you get your day in court. You get to make your arguments. The this this process that we have right now where a provider can just use whatever random email address and one notice goes out and that's all you get in terms of notice and this process can go all the way to the end without a plan ever getting notice. Um and and I don't want to go too far off the rails, but uh there actually has been guidance published about correcting these exact type of technical errors and the IDREs are taking the stance that if they the IDRE themselves didn't make the error, meaning the provider is the one that used the wrong email address, for example, well, that's not the IDRE's error, so therefore they don't have to overturn these even if they know one of the parties never got an opportunity to uh present their side. And this is not outlier. We're not we're not talking about one case every now and then. This is all the time. This is probably, you know, cases with eligibility issues are probably half the cases. So if you just start saying we are going to blanket enforce these determinations without any kind of meaningful appeals process or review process, it it could spell disaster. >> Right. Absolutely. And that's kind of contrasted by Frank Pallone's approach, which is to replace arbitration with a payment benchmark entirely. It would change the process quite significantly. He's a Democrat from New Jersey. It's more of a structural response to some of the problems that we've seen. Lower premiums, faster payments. The difficulty I see with that is how do you agree on on which metric is the payment benchmark? What is that based on? Do you have any thoughts on how they might implement something like that? >> My initial reaction when I hear this is yes, absolutely. That that that works. But again, I I have to admit I'm coming from the payer side. I am not completely objective here. The problems with with calculating the QPA and things like that, these are real problems. There could be, you know, nefarious actors who purposely pay way too low. And if a provider can't balance bill and they can't go to arbitration, it essentially allows the payer side to unilaterally set rates. That also wouldn't be fair. You know, as an aside, I would mention too, this New Jersey politician, he's coming from New Jersey where for whatever reason, rates are just astronomical. Like way more than anywhere else in the country you see. A provider is expecting to to get, you know, $10,000 to $15,000. They'll regularly bill and expect $100,000, $200,000, $500,000. I've seen claims for assistant surgeons at over a million dollars. And what they say is that that's the usual and customary amount, which technically is not a permissible factor in the NSA, but these things get through anyway. So it makes sense that it's coming from a New Jersey politician because I think he's seen a lot of plans and a lot of employers in his area really get hit hard by these just ridiculous determinations that are completely untethered from market rates, really untethered from reality. >> Right, and that kind of highlights the the the differences between those two approaches. You know, one seems to be a little bit more provider central that keeps the IDR process the way it kind of currently is, but then requires these prompt payments. And then the the second approach is more let's let's do away with that I don't say farce, but let's do let's do away with that structure entirely and put put a benchmark in place so that everybody knows and it's it's transparent and and you can kind of predict a little bit more about what your costs might be. And I think that approach as well has things for prompt payment in it as well. And so I think that's kind of the one thing they agree on is that there there is going to be some reform related to how quickly these arbitration awards are paid if if the arbitration process exists after the reform. So I think that's kind of where they're at and it'll depend on and we know how Washington is in general is that nothing may happen, right? It may just be gone out and go back and forth and you know, no change at all, but it's important to note kind of which two proposals are on the table and what it might yield. >> And and I think really what can you draw from this? Like this these are two completely diametrically opposed you know, solutions to perceived problems. But really what does it show? It shows that there is a complete lack of enforcement. There's a complete lack of of control. Like there's nobody at the wheel. From the provider standpoint, they're saying we can't get anybody to actually enforce these awards. As we know, most courts have have stated that they're not going to get involved in enforcing these awards because they're saying that that the law doesn't prescribe any private right of action to enforce them in court. So, you know, from the provider's perspective they're saying, hey, there's no one at the wheel to actually steer this thing and make sure that that these determinations are paid. From the payer perspective, you know, we're saying, hey, listen, like this process is I I wouldn't even call it a kangaroo court because I would be afraid of defaming every kangaroo court in the world. Uh there's no standards. The determinations are completely untethered from reality. There's no appeals process. There's really no meaningful review of these claims. I mean, we receive final payment determinations where the language is is clearly just cut and paste. You know, we can we can show them like over and over again. It's just the same language used over and over again regardless of what evidence you propose. So these aren't getting meaningfully reviewed. So I think from both sides it shows that there's nobody at the helm guiding this ship. So do I think that IDR is going away? No. I don't think that's possible. Uh I do think that the powers that be recognize that there are significant problems with the IDR process and that changes need to be made. Uh you know, I think that that some things that they could focus on, that they should focus on, you know, creating some sort of genuine eligibility gate before arbitration, maybe a department within CMS that reviews these because it would allow for there to be some sort of uniformity. It would also take the decisions away from the IDR entities who have a vested pecuniary interest in finding these disputes eligible, making sure that claims can't be broken up by CPG code because it makes it seem like one surgery was 10 different surgeries. There's all sorts of problems with that. Uh requiring actual reasons determinations, uh you know, actually citing to the evidence that was presented in the briefs. There's a number of changes that I think that they can make, but you know, I guess I'm going to choose to be positive and say that that I'm hopeful that this is a sign that the powers that be in Washington are actually seeing that this process is in need of very serious reform. I just hope that they talk to people uh who actually know what they're talking about uh before before they go and make any changes. >> Yeah, I think that's the optimistic view is that they that they recognize that there are gaps there and that they they correct the gap around eligibility or uh the the transparency aspect of these decisions uh and it may become to some sort of agreement on on how to correct those things going forward. But I think the biggest thing is that we know we all agree that the patient protections should stay the same, should should remain. And protecting patients also means, you know, paying attention to those costs that are generated behind the scenes that the plans are dealing with every single day, the difficulty of of being as you said, having your day in court, making your case uh being heard uh is another way to put that. Uh the excessive awards, the ineligible disputes, uh you know, hopefully the whatever they do come up with as I said, if something occurs in general uh is is and will recognize those those problems. Uh and and I think the other thing that you mentioned as well about enforcing the IDR awards because of all these problems is that you really can't just enforce the IDR awards. You know, you can't that it can't just be well we got to enforce it, you got to pay it quick and there's going to be a bunch of penalties because as you said, that puts even greater strain on these already strained health plans. And and I think, you know, we reviewed the approaches, we reviewed the the problems. I think that that leads us in a pretty good spot to end here today. Did you have any closing thoughts or anything like that, Brian? >> Just that um you know, it's a very interesting time uh in our country right now with these elections um and you know, that there could be some significant changes coming and it could have a profound impact on our uh on our industry. So it it remains to be seen. >> Yeah, and certainly uh Fia will be looking out and keeping track of it and passionate people like yourself, Brian will be uh making sure they know every development along the way. And with that, I would like to say thank you for joining us for another episode of Empowering Plans. Thank you.

segments.text: The No Surprises Act achieved its
primary legislative goal, shielding
millions of patients from unexpected
out-of-network medical bills. But behind
the scenes, the mechanism built to
enforce it has triggered an
administrative crisis for healthcare
providers. When federal regulators
drafted the law, they projected a very
specific volume of provider-payer
conflicts. They estimated approximately
17,000 independent dispute resolution,
or IDR, filings per year across the
entire country.
This line graph shows a massive gap
between that initial projection and

Got a surprise medical bill from a doctor you never even met? There's a federal law that can wipe it out — and most Americans have no clue how to use it.

In this video, a 15-year medical billing advocate breaks down the No Surprises Act in plain English, so you know exactly what's protected, what's not, and the steps to take when a sketchy bill lands in your mailbox.

🎯 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
→ What the No Surprises Act actually covers (and the big gaps it doesn't)
→ How to spot an illegal surprise bill the moment it arrives
→ The exact phone scripts to use with your insurer and the provider
→ How to file a federal complaint that gets results — for free
→ When you can (and can't) waive your protections by signing a form
→ How the Independent Dispute Resolution process works behind the scenes
→ Real-world examples of bills that got reduced from thousands to zero

📚 SOURCES:
• Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF) — Surprise Billing Research
• CMS.gov — No Surprises Act Consumer Protections
• Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) — Medical Debt Reports
• U.S. Department of Health & Human Services — NSA Complaint Portal (1-800-985-3059)

metadata.title: Unlocking Hidden Revenue: The No Surprises Act Strategy Providers Are Missing
metadata.author: Apex IONM Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
Healthcare revenue cycle management is no longer just about submitting claims—it’s about understanding how the system is actually deciding what gets paid, reduced, or disputed.

Since the introduction of the No Surprises Act, providers have been operating under a new set of rules designed to protect patients, but which have also quietly reshaped how out-of-network reimbursement is determined and recovered. For many organizations, the real financial impact of this shift is still being underutilized.

In this episode of The Revenue Fix, Laura Trotter, CFO of Axis Neuromonitoring, breaks down what is really happening behind the scenes in today’s revenue cycle environment—and why providers are unintentionally leaving revenue on the table.

From arbitration strategy to shifting payer behavior, this conversation focuses on how revenue cycle teams can move from reactive billing to a more intentional, structured approach to revenue recovery.

What you’ll learn:
• How arbitration is actually impacting reimbursement outcomes
• Why payer behavior has shifted in recent years
• Where revenue is commonly lost in the process
• How operational structure influences financial performance

The environment has changed—but the opportunity is in how you respond.
🎧 Listen now to Episode 2 of The Revenue Fix

metadata.title: Federal IDR Changes Nov. 1, 2026: Radiology Batching & Deadlines
metadata.author: Xpert Billing Talk
metadata.shortDescription:
Federal IDR rules are changing on November 1, 2026, bringing important updates to batched out-of-network payment disputes.

In this episode, we break down the changes and what they mean for radiology billing and dispute workflows:

The new 50-line-item limit for eligible batched disputes

The 30-business-day cooling-off period

The four-business-day filing window after the cooling-off period ends

How the open negotiation start date determines which rules apply

Radiology batching under eligible Category I CPT code sections

How to track payment determination dates and filing deadlines

The separate January 15, 2027, transition away from most IDR web forms

These changes do not apply identically to every dispute. Single and bundled disputes, as well as certain older batched disputes, continue to follow different timelines.

Review the dispute type, open negotiation start date, line-item count, and filing deadline before submitting a case. The $15 administrative fee took effect earlier, on June 11, 2026, and is not a new November 1 change.

Federal IDR rules are changing, and the updates may affect how out-of-network payment disputes are filed, tracked, and managed.

In this video, we explain the key changes starting with disputes linked to open negotiation periods beginning November 1, 2026:

New Federal IDR Gateway portal

Batching limit increasing from 25 to 50 line items

Administrative fee reduced from $115 to $15 per party

New 5-business-day eligibility decision timeline

Open negotiation deadlines based on portal submission

New payer ID registration requirements

Steps to update your billing and follow-up workflow

These changes may affect out-of-network billing, dispute tracking, documentation, and payment recovery.

metadata.title: Benefit Verifications 101 - Let your clients check their own out-of-network coverage!
metadata.author: Reimbursify
metadata.shortDescription: A Reimbursify Office Hours presentation: everything you wanted to know about verifying both out-of-network AND in-network benefits using the Reimbursify practice portal.  Learn about copays vs. coinsurance, low vs. high deductible (consumer directed) health plans, specific coverage for mental health benefits, and finally, to see if a particular service requires a pre-authorization or pre-certification.  This will be one of the most informative 15 minutes you've ever spent!  A great overview for ALL health care practitioners, both in and out of network!

Your provider may have different information so please refer to your specific form (superbill) for the values you need for your own reimbursement.  Not all insurance plans have out of network benefits so please consult your specific insurance prior to receiving any out of network care.

metadata.title: Quick Take: No Surprises Act: Out of Network Charges
metadata.author: HealthWatch Wisconsin
metadata.shortDescription:
The No Surprises Act went into effect January 1, 2022. It aims to stop certain kinds of "surprise" medical bills with historic, new consumer protections. We’re taking a closer look at some of the protections relating to out-of-network charges. 
---
0:00 NSA - Out of Network
0:28 Emergency Treatment
1:14 In-Network Rate
1:52 Exceptions
---
No Surprises Act Hotline at 1-800-985-3059

For broader background on the No Surprises Act, our video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Isv_cU74BBk

Fighting Forward: Your Guide to Challenging Medical Debt:
https://www.safetyweb.org/healthwatchwi/medical-debt.html

Support HealthWatch Wisconsin with a tax deductible donation:
https://www.paypal.me/healthwatchwisconsin

Visit our official website:
https://healthwatchwisconsin.org

Want to get in touch with us? Send an email:
info@healthwatchwisconsin.org

About HealthWatch Wisconsin:
HealthWatch Wisconsin is a nonprofit subsidiary of ABC for Health, Inc. working to promote improved access to health care coverage and services. HealthWatch Wisconsin actively shares materials, education, and trainings with health care professionals and consumers.

On our YouTube channel, you will find content about health insurance and coverage programs like Medicaid, social security programs, and private health insurance. We stay on top of current events, policy, and rule changes. We also cover topics that intersect with health coverage for vulnerable populations, such as food, energy, and housing assistance programs. You will also find content on programs specific to Wisconsin such as: BadgerCare Plus eligibility, enrollment, and program rules and disability program rules and features for adults as well as children with special health care needs (CYSHCN). Finally, we share some tips and advocacy strategies.

segments.text: The No Surprises Act took effect on
January 1st of 2022.
It tried to stop some of those tragic
surprise medical bills that patients
were receiving. We're going to take a
look at some of the consumer protections
included in the No Surprises Act
starting with some out-of-network
protections. This applies to individuals
with private insurance because there
were other protections already in place
for individuals that have coverage that
comes from either Medicaid or Medicare.
Let's talk about emergency treatment
first. For somebody getting emergency
services, most providers cannot bill you
more than you would have paid for
in-network treatment even if you're at
an out-of-network facility. There is a
notable exception and that is ground
ambulances. The No Surprises Act
included some new protections for folks
getting air ambulance bills, but it did
not include protection for ground
ambulance bills. There is some talk of
other legislation that might tackle that
in the future. Behind the scenes, there
are some rules determining how much your
insurance is actually going to pay the
provider for this emergency care that
you are receiving. But the bottom line
for patients is that your out-of-network
emergency treatment costs what it would
have been had you been at an in-network
facility. Let's talk about in-network
rates. The No Surprises Act tackled the
issue of out-of-network providers being
at in-network hospitals. Not all
providers working at an in-network
facility that you go to may be in your
network. Under the No Surprises Act,
charges for treatment by an
out-of-network provider at an in-network
facility cannot be more than had that
provider been an in-network provider in
the first place. So it tries to level
the playing field a little bit where
your expectation going to an in-network
facility is that all of the physicians
at the facility would be in-network as
well. Now, there are some exceptions to
some of the consumer protections in the
No Surprises Act. The first one is the
ground ambulance that we talked about.
Secondly, the emergency services
protections don't apply to all of the
follow-up or ancillary treatment that
individuals might get after that
emergency has concluded. For
non-emergency services, you can waive
your No Surprises Act protections under
some conditions, and we talk about that
in a separate video. And remember, there
is the No Surprises Act hotline. If you
have a complaint or dispute with the any
of the bills that you get that you
consider to still be a surprise bill,
you can run it through the hotline and
learn what some of your rights might be.

segments.text: My name is Rich Heller
and this is surprise medical billing and the No Surprises Act.
More surprises than you think. Part one.
So in his State of the Union address this year, President Biden proudly proclaimed
that we're already stopping 1 million surprise bills per month.
This received applause from both sides of the aisle, deservedly so.
Surprise Medical billing is not a partizan issue.
In fact, the law that President Biden was talking about, the No Surprises act
was passed with bipartisan support.
It's one of the few things that Speaker Pelosi and Donald Trump both agreed on
and that both parties agreed needed to be addressed.
The problem of surprise medical bills.
But much went left unsaid in the State of the Union address.
For example, President Biden did not mention
that his own administration's report showed that the program itself
was overwhelmed and suffering operational difficulties.
Furthermore, the president did not mention that the day before
the State of the Union address, his administration lost their second
straight lawsuit on their implementation of the law.
But let's first take a step back.
What is surprise medical billing?
Well, for starters, it's kind of a misnomer.
It's much more accurately termed a surprise insurance gap
because that's what it is.
It's a surprise gap in people's health insurance.
So here's how I explain that surprise insurance gap.
Using the language of my children emojis.
So this is Emmy the emoji.
Now, Emmy has private health insurance.
She gets it through work.
So when Emmy got hurt, she knew just what to do.
Emmy went to the nearest in-network hospital.
They took good care of Emmy.
They made me feel all better.
But then a few weeks later, Emmy got a big bow in the mail.
It turns out that one of the doctors at that in-network
hospital was not in network with Emmy's health plan.
And because they were out of network with Emmy’s health plan
Emmy owes a lot more money out of pocket than she was expecting.
That's the surprise insurance gap or surprise medical billing.
Somebody who has private health insurance gets unexpected out-of-network care.
And because it's at a network,
they may end up owing more money out of pocket than they were expecting.
Now, there was consensus within the House of Medicine
that this was a problem and it needed to be addressed.
But what not everybody recognized was that laws to address
surprise medical billing can do two things.
The first one's intuitive.
It addresses surprise medical billing.
That's not controversial.
That's patient protective.
But what it can also do is that laws to address
surprise medical billing if crafted in a certain way,
they can disrupt those good faith network contract negotiations
that take place between insurance companies
and medical providers, such as physician practices or hospitals.
In many ways, the issue of surprise medical billing legislation
can be seen as a Trojan horse of sorts, meaning
that you took the very real issue of surprise medical billing,
but it was used to push through legislation to disrupt the good faith
contract negotiations that take place between medical organizations
and insurance companies for the benefit of the insurance companies.
But we're left with this.
We do need to address surprise medical billing.
And what are a few basic principles that we should consider as we address them?
Well, insurance products need to have network adequacy standards.
There needs to be a reasonable number of different types of physicians
in each health plan.
And it needs to be obvious, transparent to patients,
which physicians, which hospitals are in-network,
and that if a patient gets unexpected out-of-network care,
they should be held financially harmless,
meaning that they simply pay their normal in-network cost sharing amount
and that the insurance companies then reimburse the providers for the balance.
Now, there are two approaches to determine what that balance should be
or how we should determine what that value is.
And the first one was benchmarking.
The idea of benchmarking was really, how are we going to value that service?
What about Medicare?
Well, people were quickly moved off using Medicare as a benchmark.
Medicare is not a market based rate, nor was it intended to be a market based rate.
But then somebody I'm going to assume
from insurance company I actually don't know had an idea.
They go, I'll tell you what.
Why don't we, the insurance company,
pay you the median of our in-network rates?
Go on.
What they said was what we the insurance company for out-of-network care.
We're not going to pay you
the best rate that we have contracted for that item or service.
But we're not going to pay you the worst either.
We'll give you the median, the 50th percentile rate for that service.
Well, that seems reasonable, said lots of people.
I even had physicians tell me, look, Rich, I know that you're interested
in this surprise insurance gap, but I got to tell you, our practice.
We're like 98% in network.
We're a good practice.
We invest in quality improvement.
We've got good contracts.
So if I get a median rate
for 2% of my claims, buddy, I got bigger fish to fry.
And what I had to
tell that person was, you're missing the point.
They're not going after the 2%.
They're going after the 98%.
Let me walk you through this figure in this slide on the left hand side.
You see a tall blue box that represents the spectrum of rates
an insurance company would have contracted for a given item or service.
Let's put some numbers on it.
Let's say the median rate they have for that item or service is $50.
And then the top rate, the 100 percentile rate they have is $100.
Now, imagine that you're in a good medical practice.
You invest in quality improvement.
You do all the right stuff.
You've negotiated a rate of $60.
What would happen to that $60 rate
if Congress passed a law benchmarking off the median in network?
Well, you would get a letter from the insurance company
and it would read something like this dear valued provider.
And now I'm going to paraphrase.
You got two choices.
And we, the insurance company, we are cool either way.
You just let us know which way you want to go.
Option one, you go out and network.
Now, if you go out of network, you're not going to get paid quickly
because frankly, we have your money invested that we would pay you.
We're getting interest on it and gosh darn it, we like getting that money.
We like getting that interest.
So we're going to make you an out of network provider.
You're going to have to jump
through a lot of hoops to get that money as an out of network provider.
But at the end of the day, you're going to get your money, but it won't be $60.
Or, you can stay in network.
Now, if you stay in network, frankly, it's going to be easier for you to get paid.
It's going to be faster, more reliable.
It's going to be less expensive for you to get your money,
but you're not going to get to keep your $60 rate.
You're probably not going to get $50.
There's usually some discount to being in network.
Let's say it's $47.
Now, I made up the numbers. They're completely made up.
But the intuition is there. Benchmarking at the median

segments.text: Hi, I'm Lindsay Bennett, healthcare
finance executive. And in today's video,
I'm going to tell you about five
hospital metrics that you need to know
if you're a clinical leader, or revenue
cycle leader, or a healthcare finance
professional. Today, I'm going to tell
you about patient days, average daily
census, average length of stay, adjusted
discharges, and the case mix index.
Patient days are simply the total number
of days of care that are provided to
inpatients. And they're important to
know because you often express revenue
and expenses in relation to patient
days. So, revenue per patient day,
expenses per patient day, salaries and
benefits per patient day, drug costs per
patient day, medical supplies per
patient day. And that gives you a way to
compare actual and budget, or to compare
against industry benchmarks.
This is just a simple example of how
patient days are calculated. So, we have
three patients in this example, and we
have their admission date and their
discharge date.
The way that we count patient days, we
count whether there's a head in a bed at
midnight. So, in the example of patient
three down here, they're admitted on
July the 3rd.
So, they're in the bed at midnight on
that day, that day counts. So, we have
the 3rd, the 4th, the 5th, the 6th, the
7th, and the 8th. That's six patient
days because they're discharged on the
9th. So, that day is not going to count
as a patient day because they're not in
the bed at midnight.
So, our patient days for this one
patient, patient number three, are six.
Patient number one had four days,
patient number two had nine days,
patient number six had six days. So, if
these were our only patients, we would
just sum up these patient days here.
That would give us 19 patient days.
We can calculate the average daily
census for a period of time. So, for
example, if we want to calculate the
average daily census for a year, what we
need to do is take the total patient
days for that period of a year and
divide it by 365 days in the year.
Another example would be if we had 9,300
patient days in a month with 31 days in
that month. We would divide 9,300
divided by 31 days to
to get an average daily census of 300
patients.
The average daily census is important
because it's used often to allocate
resources. For example, staffing models
are often based on average daily census.
So, we might staff a certain number of
RNs or LPNs or technicians to a medical
or surgical floor in a hospital based on
its average daily census.
The average length of stay tells you how
long on average your in patients are in
the hospital. And the way that we
calculate average length of stay is to
take the patient days divided by the
discharges for a period of time. So, we
could calculate this for the year, we
could calculate it for a month, or we
could even calculate it for a week.
Now, average length of stay matters in
the hospital world because hospitals are
paid by DRG or diagnosis-related group.
That means that the hospital gets a
fixed payment for each discharge, which
means that if you have a longer length
of stay, you're going to incur more
costs because every additional day of
stay has nursing labor costs associated
with it. It has supply costs, lab tests,
etc. So, a lower length of stay tends to
be more desirable because you're more
efficient, you're getting your patients
discharged sooner, which is limiting
your cost and preserving your profit
margin from that payment that you're
getting for that patient's stay.
Now, if your average length of stay is
too short, that can be an indicator of
quality problems, which you would likely
see reflected in other measures such as
avoidable readmissions.
We often look at our average length of
stay versus benchmarks, and if our
length of stay is longer, then we have
an opportunity to be more efficient and
put certain process improvements in
place to reduce that average length of
stay and then all the costs that are
associated with it. So, typically, if
you can reduce your average length of
stay even by a fraction of a day, it's
going to increase your profit margin if
you're hospital.
Adjusted discharges. We all know what a
hospital discharge is. It's when you
send the patient home, but what's an
adjusted discharge? An adjusted
discharge is we are taking our inpatient
discharges and we are applying an
adjustment factor to adjust for
outpatient business. Now, this is really
important in the hospital world because
the trends that we're seeing over the
last several years are a shift from
inpatient to outpatient settings. So,
outpatient care can be a big portion of
a hospital's business. So, what we're
doing is we're reflecting that by
adjusting our inpatient discharges. The
way that we do that is we take our
inpatient discharges and we multiply
them by an adjustment factor. That
adjustment factor is your total gross
revenue divided by your total inpatient
revenue.
And then our final hospital metric is
the CMI or case mix index.

metadata.title: Agentic Automation And Why It's Transforming Healthcare RCM - AGS Health
metadata.author: AGS Health
metadata.shortDescription:
AGS is transforming RCM with agentic AI—intelligent digital workers that collaborate, adapt, and deliver real results. From fewer denials to faster clean claims, learn how AI agents are transforming healthcare ops. Hear more from our CIO, Thomas Thatapudi:
https://www.agshealth.com/videos/agentic-automation-and-why-its-transforming-healthcare-rcm/

📌 Key discussion points include:
1️⃣ Real-world applications, including AI agents managing accounts receivable (A/R) calls, predicting denials, and performing autonomous coding with speed and accuracy.
2️⃣ Operational and financial benefits, including faster collections, reduced denial rates, improved coding accuracy, and increased staff productivity.
3️⃣ Implementation strategies using AI-ready data and high-ROI applications with an agile mindset for testing and aligning efforts for outcome-focused results.

Watch all AGS Health Videos: https://www.agshealth.com/videos/
Website: https://www.agshealth.com/
Blog: https://www.agshealth.com/blog/
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/ags-health/

#AgenticAI #AgenticAutomation #ArtificialIntelligence #AIInnovation #IntelligentAgents #AIAutomation #AutonomousAI #AIRevolution #AITransformation #futureofai #HealthcareAI #RCMAutomation #AIInHealthcare #AgenticAIinHealthcare #AIForHealth #healthtech #healthcareautomation  #RCM #HealthcareInnovation #AutomationInHealthcare #FutureOfHealthcare #HealthTech #DigitalHealth #AIAutomation #SmartHealthcare #HealthIT #RCMLeaders #HealthcareExecutives  #RevenueCycleManagement

metadata.title: What Is CMS-1500 Form in Medical Billing? How to Read It for Denial Handling? #medicalbilling #rcm
metadata.author: JobRath
metadata.shortDescription:
What is the CMS-1500 form in medical billing, and how do experienced AR callers read it while handling claim denials?

In this video, I explain the CMS-1500 claim form in simple language and show you how to understand its boxes for faster denial handling in US Healthcare RCM.

A medical service may be provided correctly, but a claim can still be rejected or denied because of missing, incorrect, or inconsistent claim information.

That is why understanding the CMS-1500 form is extremely important for medical billers, AR callers, denial handlers, and anyone preparing for a career in US Healthcare Revenue Cycle Management.

In this video, you will learn:

• What is the CMS-1500 form?
• How is CMS-1500 used in medical billing?
• CMS-1500 vs UB-04 claim form
• Why CMS-1500 is important in RCM
• How to understand the 33 numbered CMS-1500 Item Numbers
• Patient and insurance information in Boxes 1–13
• Clinical and claim information in Boxes 14–20
• Diagnosis codes in Box 21
• Resubmission information in Box 22
• Prior authorization or referral information in Box 23
• Why Box 24 is important for service-line review
• Place of Service in Box 24B
• CPT/HCPCS codes and modifiers in Box 24D
• Diagnosis pointer in Box 24E
• Charges and units in the service-line section
• Rendering provider information in Box 24J
• Billing provider information in Box 33
• How to read CMS-1500 while handling denials
• Which CMS-1500 boxes to check based on the denial

The most important lesson is simple:

While handling denials, you do not always need to read the complete CMS-1500 form from Box 1 to Box 33.

You need to understand the denial first and then review the relevant claim information.

For an eligibility-related issue, review the patient and insurance information.

For an authorization denial, review the authorization information and verify the payer's authorization records.

For a diagnosis-related denial, review Box 21 and the diagnosis pointer in Box 24E.

For a CPT or modifier-related denial, review Box 24D.

For a place-of-service issue, review Box 24B.

For a rendering provider issue, review Box 24J.

And for a billing provider issue, review Box 33.

This is how denial handlers start connecting the denial reason with the relevant claim information.

The CMS-1500 is not just a claim form.

It tells the story of a professional medical service through patient information, insurance details, diagnosis codes, procedure codes, modifiers, service-line information, and provider details.

Once you understand this claim map, reading the CMS-1500 form becomes much easier and faster.

This video is useful for:

Medical Billing Beginners
AR Callers
Denial Management Executives
RCM Professionals
Medical Billing Interview Candidates
Healthcare Revenue Cycle Professionals
Prior Authorization Professionals
US Healthcare Job Seekers

From eligibility and prior authorization to claims, denials, payment posting, follow-up, and reconciliation, IRIS is designed to take on the repetitive, high-volume work that slows revenue cycle teams down.

Instead of forcing your organization to replace the systems it already depends on, IRIS works within your existing revenue cycle environment. It can connect with practice management systems, payer portals, clearinghouses, APIs, and other healthcare platforms to move work across the revenue cycle.

ONE PLATFORM. MULTIPLE WAYS TO AUTOMATE.

• Automated revenue cycle workflows

That is why IRIS is built to support configurable automation rather than forcing every organization into the same workflow.

Whether you are a hospital or health system, provider group, or RCM company, Innobot Health works with your team to identify high-impact opportunities for automation and build workflows around the way your revenue cycle actually operates.
