For example, it flagged an auth not obtained denial spike of 18% for Aetna in July compared to the prior three-month average. Opening the deep dive on a trend like this shows how it developed over time, the root causes the model identified, the impact, its recommended actions, and a sample of affected claims, along with the model's confidence rate for that trend. The task execution breakdown shows automated tasks, manual tasks, in progress, not started, completed today, and every rule active on the platform. Clicking into any of these gives an in-depth breakdown. The account performance tracker shows how every bot is performing, including any errors, alongside every manual user and their assigned tasks, queued, assigned, completed, and in progress. Clicking a specific user expands to show exactly which task queues they've been assigned. Finally, there's an issue log where clients can report issues for admins to resolve. And an SOW tracker, scope of work, showing an overview, client information, contacts on both the InoBot and client teams, the work scope and protocols delivered for that client, and the issue logs that have been resolved. This is our AI assistant, available right inside Iris. It can give you performance insights, drill into individual visits and claims, explain its own reasoning, and pick up right where a past conversation left off. Say, I want to know how we've performed this year. I can just ask the chatbot directly. Iris pulls up a full snapshot, how many tasks it's handled, the average resolution time, how many were successfully automated, and the AI confidence scores behind them. I can also look up an individual visit the same way. Let's pull up visit ID 45612. If I expand this, Iris shows me everything tied to this task, the payer, the outcome, when it was completed, the AI's confidence score, and its suggested next steps. It also surfaces follow-up suggestions I can click into to dig deeper. For instance, why does this case require human review? Clicking that gives me the model's actual reasoning for why this particular task needs a human in the loop. So Iris chatbot isn't just a status checker. It's there to help you figure out the best next step, get a recommendation, and know when someone else needs to be brought in. So that's the full picture from the moment a claim leaves your practice management system through extraction and standardization into Iris's decision engine and task routing out to a live agent, human, bot, or voice working that claim to resolution and finally into the dashboards that show you exactly what all of that delivered. Every task you saw today, whether it moved through an API, a bot, a human, or a conversational AI, followed the same rules and dispositions we walked through, which means the same visibility, the same reporting, and the same accountability, no matter which channel actually did the work. That's Iris.

metadata.title: Eligibility Verification in Healthcare with Agentic AI | #RCM #AIinHealthcare #HealthcareAutomation
metadata.author: OpenBots
metadata.shortDescription:
Nearly 12% of healthcare claims get denied, and a staggering 24% of those denials stem from registration and eligibility errors — driven by coordination of benefits, coverage lapses, and benefit maximums.

In this session, healthcare automation leaders unpack how Agentic AI is transforming eligibility and registration—reducing manual errors, accelerating patient access, and improving first-pass claim rates.

📌 What You’ll Learn:
1️⃣ Why eligibility remains the #1 cause of claim denials
2️⃣ How Agentic AI validates patient coverage in real time across multiple payers
3️⃣ Ways providers are using AI Agents to prevent registration and eligibility errors before submission
4️⃣ Measurable ROI: faster intake, fewer denials, and better cash flow visibility

🎙️ Speakers:
🔹 Gabriel Skelton – Head of Artificial Intelligence Solutions, OpenBots
🔹 Ranodeb Banerjee – Associate Director, Healthcare Automation Solutions, OpenBots

#HealthcareAI #HealthTech #RCM #EligibilityVerification #HealthcareAutomation #AgenticAI #DigitalHealth #SmartHealthcare #AIAutomation #RevenueCycleManagement #FutureOfHealthcare

metadata.title: Explaining the Independent Dispute Resolution Process in New Hampshire
metadata.author: New Hampshire Insurance Department
metadata.shortDescription:
https://insurance.nh.gov
Chapter 143 of the New Hampshire laws of 2024 created new consumer protections against balance billing by out-of-network (OON) healthcare providers and established a new, state-level process called independent dispute resolution (IDR), which is managed by the New Hampshire Insurance Department.

This process is available to healthcare providers and facilities as an alternative to the federally administered IDR process that was established under the federal No Surprises Act. Providers and facilities can use the state process to settle disputes with health plans about the payment rates for OON items and services that are subject to the prohibition on balance billing patients.

More information and all forms are available at https://www.insurance.nh.gov/consumers/health-insurance/independent-dispute-resolution

If you have insurance questions or complaints, our Consumer Services Division is here to help providers and consumers by calling (800) 852-3416 or emailing consumerservices@ins.nh.gov.

Transcripts available upon request by emailing communications@ins.nh.gov

metadata.title: How to Generate Revenue for Out-of-Network Medical Claims: Insights with Thomas J. Force
metadata.author: Patriot Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Join Thomas J. Force, owner of Patriot Group and Force Law Firm, as he discusses the current state of out-of-network medical claims in the U.S. In this insightful episode, Tom shares expert advice on navigating the complexities of out-of-network billing, from creating effective workflows to managing appeals and combating insurance audits. With over 30 years of experience in healthcare law and revenue cycle management, Tom provides actionable tips for maximizing reimbursement and overcoming the challenges faced by medical providers.
🎙️ Key Topics Covered:
The decline in revenue for out-of-network providers
Effective vetting processes for claims
The importance of plan documents and appeals
Addressing Fee Forgiveness Audits and other challenges
📌 Don’t miss this essential guide to thriving as an out-of-network provider!
#MedicalBilling #OutOfNetwork #RevenueCycleManagement #HealthcarePodcast

metadata.title: Out of Network Therapist | Superbills and Health Insurance
metadata.author: Nate Page
metadata.shortDescription:
In our therapy practice we often get phone calls where the immediate question is, "Do you take my health insurance"? If we say no, most people assume that they can't meet with us. The reality is many health insurance plans offer "out of network" benefits, which means that you can get reimbursement for meeting with an out of network provider. This video will help you know how to find your out of network benefits, and also navigate the process of using your health insurance to cover some of the costs of meeting with an "out of network" therapist. 

The first step is to decide if you WANT to use your health insurance. Most people do, but some don't want their mental health diagnosis to become part of their permanent health record. 

Most people are ok with their mental health diagnosis becoming part of their record, and so the next step is to contact your insurance company and find out the exact rate they will reimburse you for meeting with an out of network therapist. Each plan is different. Some have excellent out of network benefits, some don't have any. 

Questions to ask your health insurance company about your out-of-network benefits

(1) What is my out-of-network coverage for outpatient mental health visits?
(2) Is there a deductible that needs to be met prior to  services? How much of my deductible has been met this year?
(3) Is there a limit on the number of sessions my plan will cover per year?
If Yes, How many?
(4) Do I need a referral from an in-network provider or a primary care physician to see someone out-of-network?
(5) How do I submit claims for out-of-network reimbursement?
(6) Are virtual outpatient mental health visits (or teletherapy) covered by my plan?
(7) Is there anything else I need to know about utilizing my out of network benefits (limitations, rules, or other "small print" things to know). 

Nate Page, PhD, LP, CGP
northfielddynamictherapy.com
grouptherapycentral.com

metadata.title: My In-Network Doctor Sent My Labs Out-of-Network… Now I Owe $2,000?
metadata.author: Insured and Informed
metadata.shortDescription:
You went to an in-network doctor… so how did you still end up with a $2,000 medical bill?

In this video, I break down a real Reddit health insurance question involving an out-of-network lab bill, surprise medical billing, and the No Surprises Act. We’ll talk about when patients are protected from unexpected out-of-network charges, when those protections may not apply, and what steps you can take if you receive a large medical bill after visiting an in-network provider.

If you’ve ever been confused about health insurance, medical bills, out-of-network charges, or healthcare billing, this video will help you better understand your rights as a patient.

Whether you’re self-employed, approaching retirement, changing health plans, navigating the ACA marketplace, or just trying to avoid expensive healthcare mistakes, understanding how surprise medical billing works can potentially save you thousands.

⭐️ About me ⭐️

Hi, I'm Shamy. I'm a healthcare finance consultant, and a Certified Healthcare Finance Professional. I break down health insurance and policy jargon into simple and easy-to-understand language to help you understand your health plan better, and make more informed financial decisions with your healthcare. Healthcare can be complicated, but I've got you! 

--

⭐️ Sources & Links ⭐️

https://www.dfs.ny.gov/consumers/health_insurance/home

https://www.cms.gov/files/document/nsa-at-a-glance.pdf

https://www.cms.gov/files/document/nsa-notice-and-consent-decision-tree.pdf

https://www.cms.gov/files/document/nsa-notice-and-consent-guidelines.pdf

⭐️ Disclaimers & Disclosures ⭐️

I am not an insurance agent, insurance broker, patient navigator, or patient advocate. Views expressed here are my own. I create videos for informational and educational purposes only and watching them does not create a professional relationship between you and I. Nothing on this channel is financial or medical advice nor can it replace receiving advice from a professional that is familiar with your personal circumstances.

 #medicalbills  #healthinsurancepolicy  #patientrights #healthcarecosts #healthinsurance

Superbills in Private Practice | Out of Network Billing

My experience being on insurance panels:

When I first started in private practice, I had never heard of a superbill or out-of-network billing.. But it turns out that superbills are incredibly useful in private practice and are simple to use. In today’s video I share with you everything you need to know about superbills so you’re set up for out of network billing.

LINKS
*Some links are affiliate links. A percentage of purchases come back to me and help my channel immensely!
👉 How to DIY a Therapist Website that Fills your Practice: https://privatepracticeskills.teachable.com/
👉 Private Practice Skills Merch: https://teespring.com/stores/private-practice-skills
👉 All my filming gear: https://kit.co/privatepracticeskills/all-my-gear
👉 Music I use: https://www.epidemicsound.com/referral/c7m5mj/

This video is geared for therapists of all kinds, including psychologists, MFTs, LPCCs, social workers, and others in the clinical counseling field.

Welcome to Private Practice Skills! I’m Dr. Marie Fang, psychologist in private practice. I post videos offering tools I learned the hard way about starting and growing private practice so that you don’t have to.

www.privatepracticeskills.com
Facebook: www.facebook.com/PrivatePracticeSkills/
Insta: PrivatePracticeSkills

Music Credit:
"Throwback" by Ikson
https://soundcloud.com/ikson

This video is not intended as professional or legal advice. Be sure to seek the services of a professional if you are in need of them.

So what the heck is a superbill? A superbill is a detailed itemized receipt that healthcare providers like us use to reflect the services we offer. These receipts are most often used to submit claims for reimbursement from third party payers, like insurance companies.

So how are superbills different than a CMS-1500 form?

For those of you not familiar, the CMS-1500 is a form used by insurance companies that healthcare providers fill out in order to bill insurance. 

For the most part, the CMS-1500 form primarily only applies to providers who are in-network on insurance panels.

To really understand what I’m saying, I think I need to break down the difference between in-network and out-of-network providers.

To avoid any possible insurance fraud, the superbill involves some key information beyond simply your name and how much you charge the client. In fact, I’ve found even in just the last 12 months that insurance companies have really been cracking down on the information they require in a superbill in order to avoid cases of fraud.

So the superbill must also reflect key information about who you are to demonstrate that you are licensed in your field and that you are who you say you are.

Here are the key items required from the superbill receipt:
-Your basic information (name, address, phone number)
-Your professional information (Tax ID, NPI, License #)
-Your client’s name, ICD-10 code, and date of birth
-An itemized list of services including date of service, CPT code, description of service, and cost of service.

I also like to make sure I include:
-Place of service code
-A statement that the client has already paid the balance in full

Lastly, I sign and date the superbill for good measure.

Often clients are not aware that they may qualify for out-of-network benefits, so I always cover this when going over payment options during the initial phone screen. Sometimes clients have been surprised to find that their insurance will cover most of the cost!

As far as frequency, many therapists offer superbills at the end of every month, others every session. You can decide on a reasonable frequency that fits you and your practice.

Once you pass the superbill to the client, it’s up to them to coordinate with their insurance to ask about how they submit for reimbursement. Your work is done!

Superbills are a quick and easy way to make care more accessible to your clients while also allowing you to receive your full fee. It’s definitely worth considering offering them to clients you’re seeing in your practice.

Everyone has their own formatting for their superbill. If you’d like to borrow mine as a template, you can snag it for free at the link in the description box.

metadata.title: Ch # 3- What is Out-of-Network Billing | How to resolve Out-of-Network denial in medical billing
metadata.author: Azeem khan Watanyar Official
metadata.shortDescription:
What is Out-of-Network (OON) Billing in Medical Billing?**

**Out-of-Network (OON) billing** refers to healthcare services provided by a **provider who is not contracted with a patient's insurance plan**. Since there’s no negotiated rate between the provider and insurer, billing and reimbursement work differently.

#### **Key Points:**
- **Higher patient responsibility**: Patients may pay more out-of-pocket.
- **No contracted rates**: Provider charges full fee; insurance may reimburse partially or not at all.
- **Balance billing**: The provider may bill the patient for the difference not covered by insurance.

### **Examples of OON Billing Scenarios:**
- A patient goes to a specialist not listed in their insurance network.
- Emergency services rendered at a non-network hospital.

### **What are Out-of-Network Denials?**

**Out-of-network denials** occur when an insurance company **refuses to pay or limits payment** for services rendered by a non-network provider.

#### **Common Denial Reasons:**
1. **Lack of Prior Authorization**  
2. **Out-of-Network Benefits Not Covered**  
3. **Missing Medical Necessity Documentation**  
4. **Incorrect or incomplete claim submission**  
5. **Patient out-of-pocket limit not met**


 **How to Handle OON Denials:**
- Verify if OON benefits exist for the patient.
- Submit appeal with medical necessity documentation.
- Request single-case agreement or gap exception.
- Educate patients about OON benefits and balance billing risks.

الذين لديك! في باكستان، لديك شركات أيضاً. يمكنك التواصل معهم؛ فلديك معرفة جيدة بذلك. يمكنك العمل خارج الشبكة؛ فهناك الكثير من العمليات للشباب. لديك الكثير من الإرشادات للشباب، والكثير من القوانين والفرص. لذا، أنا لدي الإرشادات فقط ؛ فلديك الكثير من الشباب لذلك. يمكنك العمل مع شركات جديدة هنا. نعم، يمكنك العمل في الفوترة خارج الشبكة. آه. الفرق الرئيسي بين داخل الشبكة وخارجها. يقبل مقدم الخدمة جدول الرسوم الخاص بالتأمين عن جميع الخدمات التي يقدمها. في حالة داخل الشبكة، يقوم مقدم الخدمة بمراقبة التأمين. قبول جميع الخدمات المقدمة. التأمين يحدد الأسعار المسموح بها ولا يطلب الطبيب أو مقدم الخدمة دفع مبالغ تتجاوز المعدل المتعاقد عليه ، حيث تلتزم شركة التأمين ومقدم الخدمة باتفاقية، أما خارج الشبكة فلا يوجد عقد بينهما، ويتم التفاوض على سعر متفق عليه لكل خدمة بين الطبيب وشركة التأمين. ماذا يحدث عند تقديم مطالبة خارج الشبكة؟ المريض لديه مزايا خارج الشبكة. والحالة الثانية هي أن المريض ليس لديه مزايا خارج الشبكة. ستفتح شركة التأمين باب التفاوض مع مقدم الخدمة، وستدفع المطالبة في النهاية بمجرد الاتفاق على سعر وتوقيعه من قبل مكتب مقدم الخدمة. آه. مزايا الرعاية المنزلية خارج الشبكة. أو. ما هو التفاوض؟ يُرسل التفاوض المطالبة إلى أطراف ثالثة مثل "داتا إنسايد" أو "ملتي بلان" أو ممثلين يرسلون عروضاً مختلفة لمقدم الخدمة بشأن المطالبة. إذا لم يوافق مقدم الخدمة على المبلغ، فسيقوم بإعادة العرض مع ملاحظاته والمبلغ الذي يتوقعه. وسيستمر هذا حتى يوافق مقدم الخدمة ويوقع على اتفاقية التفاوض. تتم مفاوضات المطالبات عبر البريد الإلكتروني أو البوابات الإلكترونية ، وللمفاوضات مع أطراف خارجية حد أقصى للعرض، وإذا لم يوافق مقدم الخدمة عليه، تُعاد المطالبة إلى جهة الدفع. يحق لمقدم الخدمة تقديم استئناف إذا أُعيدت المفاوضات إلى جهة الدفع، وقامت جهة الدفع بسداد مبلغ عشوائي لا يقبله مقدم الخدمة. والآن، فيما يخص مفاوضات التأمين، لديك كل المطالبات التي حصلت عليها من الأطراف. أدخل البيانات، وتوفر لدينا العديد من الأمثلة، وهذا مثال محلي يوضح كيفية الحصول على طبيب. بخصوص العرض، انتظر معي لحظة. أنا في رحلة بحث، ورغم أننا نقدم طبيباً جيداً، إلا أننا نتفق على جانب الطبيب. عليك بالرد، تأكد من حصولي على الطبيب مع السجل الصحي ، واتفق معي على الأمر. بخصوص العرض، أرسله مجدداً إلى الطرف المعني، وتواصل مع شركة التأمين، مع إضافة التعليقات المناسبة على السجل. يجب أن تكون التعليقات واضحة، تابع كتابة المقالات، وتابع المفاوضات، واجعل الأمور واضحة. باختصار ، في جوهر المفاوضات، ربما نقدم عرضاً أكبر بين الطبيب الذي اتفقت معه والحكومة. باختصار ، لدينا مبلغ لمشكلة الطبيب الذي لديه تأخير سيسمح للآخرين بالتدخل. لنفترض أننا وافقنا على الدفع للطبيب للاستئناف لأن المفاوضات واضحة. باختصار، يجب أن نوافق على دفع المبلغ للطرف المعني، أو الدفع لتسوية المطالبة، أو أن يوافق الطبيب بوضوح على ما يجب القيام به بخصوص المطالبة. الدفع للطرف المعني، والمفاوضات مع الطرف المعني، والبريد الإلكتروني للطرف المعني، والبوابة الإلكترونية للطرف المعني. في حالة خاصة، شركات GHI أو Emblem لا تفتح باب التفاوض مع مقدم الخدمة. بدلاً من ذلك، يسددون المطالبة باستخدام معدلات الرعاية الصحية العادلة والمعتادة والمعقولة. شركات GHI أو Emblem أو أي تفاوض مع طبيب، بدلاً من التفاوض، سندفع أو سيدفعون معدلات الرعاية الصحية العادلة باتباع تلك الإرشادات. توفر "Fair Health" تقديراً لمعدل الخدمة بناءً على مجموعة بيانات تضم 40 مليار مطالبة رعاية صحية لأكثر من 10,000 خدمة في جميع أنحاء الولايات المتحدة. توفر "Fair Health" معدلاً تقديرياً في الولايات المتحدة لأكثر من 10,000 خدمة. هل يمكنك تحديد معدل مسموح به لخفض التكلفة؟ هل "Fair Health" هو الحد الأدنى للمعدل الذي يمكن لمقدم الخدمة توقعه من GHI؟ يمكن لمقدم الخدمة الحصول على أكثر من ذلك المبلغ. في الواقع ، جودة العمل في GHI تتعرض لخفض في الدفع إذا كانت المطالبة مدفوعة بأقل من قيمتها . يمكن إنشاء نموذج من بوابة مزودي خدمة Emblem Health باستخدام نموذج تفويض المزايا (AOB). نموذج للمطالبات مرفق في ملف PDF تم دفعه مباشرة. بصفتي مقياس مزايا GHI، لنفترض أن GHI تدرك أنه يجب تخصيص مزايا من الرعاية الصحية، وما أهتم به هو أنك ستكون مستعداً للتعامل مع رعاية تخصيص المزايا هنا. تخصيص المزايا، هو نموذج يمكن لمريضي تقديم توقيع موافقة عليه، والذي يمثل جوهر التوقيع الذي تراه لتمثيل ما سيقوم به مقدمو الخدمة خارج الشبكة، وما ستفعله شركة التأمين الخاصة بي، وما ستدفعه مقابل الرعاية، وكيف ستتم معالجة الرعاية خارج الشبكة. ماذا لو لم يكن لدى المريض مزايا خارج الشبكة؟ إذا كان طبيب الجهاز الهضمي، على سبيل المثال، ضمن الشبكة مع شركة التأمين وتم رفض مطالبة التخدير بسبب طبيب تخدير خارج الشبكة، فإن المطالبة ستوجه نحو المريض، لكن المريض ذهب إلى مقدم خدمة داخل الشبكة وقام بإحالته إلى مقدم خدمة خارج الشبكة لسبب ما، مثل عدم توفر طبيب تخدير داخل الشبكة. وبالتالي، المريض غير مسؤول عن الدفع. يسمى هذا شرط الفواتير المفاجئة. تعريف شرط الفواتير المفاجئة هو حدوث فاتورة مفاجئة عندما يتلقى المريض دون قصد أو دون علم رعاية صحية من مقدمي خدمة خارج شبكة شركة التأمين الخاصة به ويتم محاسبته مباشرة على تلك الرعاية. الخدمات التي تلقت رعاية خارج شبكة شركة التأمين. رمز التأمين. هل من التجاري مطابقة طبيب داخل الشبكة المتاح في الطلب فقط؟ المفاوضات للحصول على طبيب، هل يمكنك الحصول على ذلك أو هل تم تخفيض معدل الوظيفة؟ سيحرصون على حصولهم على ذلك. قانون عدم المفاجأة هنا. قانون عدم المفاجأة هو قانون تم إقراره في عام 2020 و 2022. يحمي هذا القانون المستهلك أو المريض الذي لديه معظم أنواع تغطية التأمين الصحي الخاص ضد بعض الفواتير الطبية المفاجئة. تم توقيعه ليصبح قانوناً في عام 2020 ودخلت معظم الحماية حيز التنفيذ اعتباراً من يناير 2022. تم إقرار هذا القانون في عام 2020. يناير 2022. تنفيذ الفواتير المفاجئة للمرضى لحماية التأمين، يمكن للمريض الاستئناف، حماية المريض والطبيب داخل الشبكة. سيرسل المريض استئنافاً إلى شركة التأمين مع الفاتورة الطبية المستلمة من مكتب مقدم الخدمة، وستفتح شركة التأمين مفاوضات مع مقدم الخدمة للدفع. في النهاية، سيكون المريض محمياً من أي تكاليف. تكلفة المريض ستكون. هناك بعض الأهداف السهلة للاستئناف والاستفسارات. أي تأمين؟ سيتم إرفاق كشف حساب الفواتير لجميع الأطراف استفسار من البوابة الإلكترونية قد أقدم لك مثالاً لنموذج PDF لمطالبة تم دفعها بشكل صحيح. نموذج فاتورة مفاجئة من يونايتد هيلث كير، أو هو كشف حساب أو فاتورة. مطلوب وثائق استئناف، نموذج فاتورة مفاجئة وكشف حساب، أو يمكنك الاتصال بالعضو لإجراء مكالمة استئناف لكي نتمكن من الحصول على...

metadata.title: Superbills for Therapists: How Out-of-Network Reimbursement Actually Works
metadata.author: Craft Your Practice
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to Craft Your Practice Method™
The place where the art of therapy meets the business of practice.

If you are out of network, the question you hear more than any other is "will my insurance pay me back?" A superbill is a receipt, not a guarantee, and this episode explains exactly what happens after your client sends one in, so their expectations match what their plan will really do.

Go deeper with The Superbill and Out-of-Network Guide ($27): https://www.craftyourpractice.com/the-practice-library/p/the-superbill-and-out-of-network-guide?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=superbill-oon&utm_content=ep40
Want credentialing, billing and getting paid handled start to finish? The Get Paid course: https://www.craftyourpractice.com/accelerator?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=superbill-oon&utm_content=ep40
Prefer a book? Credentialing, Insurance and Getting Paid: https://www.craftyourpractice.com/books?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=superbill-oon&utm_content=ep40

A superbill is an itemized receipt. The client pays your full fee at the session, you give them the superbill, and they submit it to their own plan. You are not filing a claim, and any money that comes back goes to the client.

Then the part almost nobody explains. Out of network benefits usually have their own deductible, often higher than the in network one, and nothing comes back until it is met. After that the plan pays a percentage of its allowed amount, which is often well below your fee. With round numbers: a $150 fee, a $100 allowed amount and 60 percent back means $60 returned and a real cost of $90 a session, and only once the deductible is met. Many HMO and EPO plans have no out of network benefits at all.

It also covers what has to be on a superbill so it doesn't bounce back, what to say when a client asks whether insurance will cover it, the four questions your client asks their own insurer, the diagnosis code conversation, and three things that catch people: Medicare, good faith estimates and submission deadlines.

Get free therapist tools & resources:
https://www.craftyourpractice.com/start

Explore Private Practice Foundations, your first 90 days:
https://www.craftyourpractice.com/launch

Follow Craft Your Practice:
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/craftyourpractice

Pinterest: https://www.pinterest.com/craftyourpractice

Website: https://www.craftyourpractice.com

About Lisa Reidsema, LMHC
Lisa Reidsema is a therapist, author, and mentor helping new and emerging therapists build aligned, sustainable, profitable private practices without burnout.

metadata.title: Out-of-network 101 for therapists
metadata.author: Alicia Murray | The Therapist HQ 🪩
metadata.shortDescription:
IN THIS EPISODE, ALICIA MURRAY SHARES A PRACTICAL, REAL-WORLD DEEP DIVE INTO OUT-OF-NETWORK BENEFITS FOR THERAPISTS, INCLUDING HOW TO SIMPLIFY BILLING, IMPROVE CLIENT ACCESSIBILITY, AND BUILD SYSTEMS THAT SUPPORT BETTER RETENTION AND CONVERSIONS.

WHAT WE COVER

* Why consistency matters more than perfection in podcasting and business

* The difference between super bills and courtesy/complementary out-of-network billing

* How super bills work and what clients need to submit them to insurance

* How complementary billing works in a practice setting

* What extra admin tasks come with out-of-network billing

* How to use your website and onboarding flow to make out-of-network benefits easier to understand

* Why a benefits checker can increase conversions

* How to explain insurance language in plain English

* Common out-of-network realities, including W-9 requests and diagnosis code limitations

* How to decide which system is realistic for your practice right now


Key takeaways

* You do not need to do out-of-network “perfectly” to make it work well.

* Super bills are the lowest-lift option and can still be valuable for clients.

* Complementary billing can improve client experience, but it adds more operational work.

* Clear website language, onboarding steps, and benefits education can reduce friction and increase follow-through.

* The best system is the one that fits your current bandwidth, resources, and practice model.

Insurance Pay vs Out-of-Network: Why One80 Physical Therapy is Different

Dr. Rhett Polka shares into the key differences between using insurance pay and opting for out-of-network care at One80 Physical Therapy. Traditional insurance-based physical therapy comes with many limitations—long wait times, the need for physician referrals, and restrictions on treatment. On the other hand, the out-of-network model at One80 PT offers a more flexible, personalized experience focused solely on your health and recovery.

Dr. Polka discusses how being out-of-network means no more waiting for authorization from insurance companies or being limited by a number of sessions. With One80 PT, you get direct access to physical therapy without the hassle of insurance interference. This model allows us to focus on what’s best for your treatment, offering longer, more detailed sessions to get you back to doing what you love.

You’ll discover how this patient-centered approach leads to faster recovery times, more effective treatments, and a better overall experience. If you’re tired of insurance red tape and want faster, personalized care, this is for you!

metadata.title: Autonomy in Medicine: The Path to Fulfillment and Innovation
metadata.author: Andrea Austin
metadata.shortDescription:
In episode 86, I sit down with Dr. Brian Cohen, a practicing anesthesiologist and entrepreneurial innovator in healthcare. We explore his journey from traditional medical practice to founding Miami Anesthesia Services, a concierge ambulatory surgery center anesthesia company.


Dr. Cohen shares his insights on the evolving landscape of anesthesiology, highlighting the shift towards independent practice models and the importance of physician autonomy. He discusses how his experiences in various healthcare settings led him to create a practice that prioritizes physician satisfaction and patient care.


We delve into the world of healthcare technology, examining Dr. Cohen's role as Chief Medical Officer of Adaptrack and his involvement with CMEfy and Learner Plus. These platforms aim to revolutionize continuing medical education by focusing on reflective practice and personalized learning experiences.
Key takeaways from our conversation include:

     
     
  •  The benefits of independent practice models in anesthesiology
     
     
  •  How technology can enhance physician learning and improve patient care
     
     
  •  The importance of reflective practice in medical education
     
     
  •  Strategies for physicians looking to explore entrepreneurial opportunities in healthcare
     
     





Dr. Cohen offers valuable advice for healthcare professionals considering leadership roles or entrepreneurial ventures, emphasizing the importance of finding supportive partners and embracing calculated risks.


"Success is not about agreeing all the time. It's about finding the best path forward for the overall success of the organization or whatever group that you're working in." - Dr. Brian Cohen


Join us for this inspiring conversation that challenges traditional notions of medical practice and education, offering a glimpse into the future of healthcare innovation.




Resources mentioned in this episode:


- Learner Plus (https://learnerplus.com/)  - A platform for personalized medical education and reflective practice

metadata.title: Ed Gaines: How Independent Physicians Finally Got Leverage Against Insurance Companies
metadata.author: The Doctors Lounge
metadata.shortDescription:
*Guest:* Ed Gaines, JD, CPC Vice President of Regulatory Affairs, Zotec Partners Honorary Member, American College of Emergency Physicians



*Episode Summary:*

If you're a hospital-based physician and you don't understand the No Surprises Act, you're missing the biggest shift in payment leverage in decades. Insurance companies estimated there would be 17,000 disputes. The actual number? Over 2.5 million. And physicians are winning 85-90% of them.

Ed Gaines has been fighting for physician payment for 32 years—from the 1990s battle over 1099 independent contractors to today's war over Independent Dispute Resolution. He explains how California's "neutral" stance cost physicians dearly, why Trump's price transparency rule changed everything, and what Anthem's threat to cut hospital payments really means.



0:00 - Introduction & Opening

1:05 - Who is Ed Gaines?

2:25 - The Origin Story: From Healthcare Fascination to Capitol Hill

6:31 - The 1099 Battle: A Five-Year Fight (1997-2002)

14:19 - What is the No Surprises Act?

17:26 - State Laws vs. Federal Action

23:48 - California's Mistake: When the CMA Was "Neutral"

26:44 - The Consolidation Paradox

28:36 - The Legislative Battle: Ways and Means vs. Energy and Commerce

31:43 - Becerra's Sabotage: Four Lawsuits, Four Victories

37:39 - The Current Battle: Insurance Companies Strike Back

40:43 - The Trump Transparency Game-Changer

42:55 - Who's Really Using IDR?

43:50 - Anthem's New Tactic: Going After Hospitals

46:18 - The Antitrust Argument

47:40 - Closing Thoughts



*In This Episode:*

* The 1099 battle (1997-2002): How persistence won a 5-year legislative fight
* Why the California Medical Association regrets being "neutral" on AB 72
* The $50 billion that health plans tried to extract from physicians
* How HHS tried to sabotage the NSA—and lost in federal court four times
* Why CMS was off by 147X in predicting IDR case volume
* Trump's transparency rule: The data that's winning cases for physicians
* Anthem's new strategy: Threatening 10% payment cuts to hospitals
* The antitrust case against insurance company boycotts
* Why 70% of IDR users are independent physicians, not just PE groups

*Key Quotes:*

"CMS estimated 17,000 cases. The actual number was over 2.5 million. They missed by just a touch."

"The judge literally said the agency tried to put their thumb on the scales of justice in favor of health plans."

"The California Medical Association was neutral on benchmarking to 125% of Medicare. To their credit, they realized they'd made a mistake."

"They're losing 85-90% of cases at 6, 7, 8X of Medicare. They didn't see this coming."

"For years they got to unilaterally decide what out-of-network payment would be, then just blame doctors for balance billing."



*About Ed Gaines:* Ed has worked in physician revenue cycle management for 32 years, supporting over 22,000 physicians across all 50 states. He specializes in emergency medicine, radiology, anesthesia, and orthopedics advocacy. The American College of Emergency Physicians made him an honorary member in 2010—rare recognition for a non-physician.



*Subscribe to The Doctor's Lounge:* Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | RSS

metadata.title: SCA 2027 Blueprint: Protect Out-of-Network Revenue Before It Gets Recouped
metadata.author: AR Specialist
metadata.shortDescription:
Out-of-network revenue is under increasing pressure as payers tighten Single Case Agreement requirements, challenge gap exceptions, and retroactively review previously approved claims.
In this SCA 2027 Blueprint, Medical Billing Consultancy examines the risks treatment facilities may face when managing out-of-network claims, including retroactive authorization reversals, recoupments, payer-specific appeal rules, and the 50-mile provider-access requirement.
Using an anonymized California case study, this lesson explains how a previously approved SCA resulted in payment, was later retroactively voided, and became subject to recoupment after the payer determined that an in-network alternative allegedly existed within a 50-mile radius.
You’ll learn how to:
Understand what a Single Case Agreement or gap exception represents
Identify the difference between standard out-of-network billing and SCA-based reimbursement
Document the absence of suitable in-network alternatives
Verify the payer’s 50-mile radius requirement
Research provider availability, capability, and geographic access
Prepare a formal, well-documented appeal
Track the applicable EOB date and appeal deadline
Avoid relying on standard manual-review tickets when a formal appeal is required
Follow payer-specific submission instructions
Manage differences between fax, mail, and provider-portal requirements
Reduce the risk of retroactive recoupment
Build a repeatable 2027 SCA revenue-protection workflow
The video also discusses a case study involving payer-specific procedures, including different appeal channels, claim-by-claim contact rules, and varying submission requirements.
The central message is clear: SCA revenue must be defended proactively, documented carefully, and appealed before the applicable deadline expires.
Payer policies, appeal windows, network standards, provider directories, and submission requirements vary. The 180-day and 365-day periods discussed in the video relate to the case study and should not be treated as universal rules. Always verify the applicable payer contract, EOB instructions, state requirements, and appeal policy for each claim.
For specialized revenue cycle support, visit:
mbcrcm.lovable.app

00:41 The 2027 SCA revenue-protection blueprint
01:06 What is a Single Case Agreement?
02:26 California case study: how an approved SCA became a denial
03:22 Payment, retroactive voiding, and recoupment risk
04:05 SCA approval and the 50-mile provider-access requirement
04:55 Financial consequences and payer administration barriers
05:53 The 2027 step-by-step appeal strategy
06:40 Appeal deadlines and the EOB date
07:17 Payer-specific routing: fax, mail, and portals
07:58 How MBC RCM supports SCA revenue protection
08:51 Final questions for your facility’s 2027 strategy

Operator Insights is a Revenue Cycle Management thought leadership series from Ensemble Health Partners, who was voted Best In KLAS for healthcare revenue cycle outsourcing in 2020. SUBSCRIBE NOW: https://shorturl.at/irRY5 

In this episode, Julie Roberts talks with Elizabeth Estrada about Healthcare Revenue Recovery. What is revenue recovery and what is its value? What skills help someone work in that part of RCM? What organizations NEED support from a revenue recovery team?

metadata.title: In-Network Hospital, Out-of-Network Doctor: The Private Equity Trap
metadata.author: Capital Autopsy
metadata.shortDescription:
You paid for good insurance. You went to an in-network hospital. A few weeks later a bill for thousands of dollars arrives anyway.

It is not a clerical mistake. Over two decades, private equity firms bought the companies that staff America's emergency rooms, and some of them learned that an out-of-network doctor inside an in-network hospital is a source of leverage. This episode traces the money, the debt, and the Envision bankruptcy.

In this episode:
- The in-network promise and how it breaks
- How private equity entered emergency room staffing
- Out-of-network billing as a business model
- Lawsuits against patients
- The Envision collapse and who was paid before it

Capital Autopsy takes apart corporate collapses and finance structures, one case file at a time.

Educational commentary based on public reporting and court filings. Not investment advice.

#CapitalAutopsy #PrivateEquity #SurpriseBilling #Healthcare #FinanceExplained

segments.text: Right now, you probably believe that if you pay twelve
hundred dollars a month for gold-tier health insurance,
and you carefully make sure the ambulance takes you to
an in-network hospital, you are financially protected.
For years, millions of Americans believed exactly that, and learned otherwise.
They followed every rule in their insurance policy.
They went to an in-network building.
They lay in an in-network hospital bed.
They were scanned by an in-network MRI machine.
And then, a few weeks later, an envelope arrived demanding four thousand
four hundred dollars, because the emergency room doctor who
treated them was somehow out-of-network inside an in-network hospital.
It was not a clerical mistake.
It was a business model.
Over the past two decades, private equity firms bought up the
companies that staff America's emergency rooms, and some of those
companies learned that a patient on a stretcher cannot negotiate.
Researchers, insurers and Congress all came to the same conclusion:
the out-of-network bill had become a pricing lever,
pulled against both families and insurance companies.
Today, we are opening up the contracts behind
America's emergency room staffing industry,
and following the money from the trauma bay to Wall Street.
Welcome to Emergency Room Arbitrage.
Let's look at the real data.
To understand how an out-of-network doctor ends up standing over your
bed inside an in-network hospital, you have to understand a structural
fact that most patients never realize: in modern America,
many hospitals do not actually employ the doctors working in their emergency rooms,
their anesthesiology departments, or their radiology suites.
One major study estimated that roughly two thirds of the
emergency physician market is outsourced to staffing companies.
Decades ago, hospitals realized that running a twenty-four-hour
emergency department is a logistical and financial headache.
Patient volume is unpredictable, malpractice liability is high,
and federal law, specifically the Emergency Medical
Treatment and Labor Act of nineteen eighty-six,
requires emergency rooms to screen and stabilize anyone who walks
through the door, regardless of whether they can pay.
To offload that burden, hospitals began outsourcing their
emergency departments to third-party physician staffing companies.
When you walk into your local community hospital,
the nurses and the building belong to the hospital,
but the emergency room doctors, anesthesiologists and radiologists
may actually work for an outside staffing vendor.
For years, many of these vendors were regional, physician-owned groups.
Then private equity spotted a feature of American healthcare
billing that could be worth billions,
because emergency room demand is what economists call price-inelastic.
When you are having a heart attack, or your child is
bleeding in the back of an ambulance, you cannot shop around for prices,
and you cannot ask the ER doctor which
insurance networks he belongs to before he intubates you.
Let us walk through the three-step autopsy of
how this blind spot became a financial engine.
Step One: Cornering the Emergency Staffing Market through Mega-Buyouts.
In late two thousand and sixteen, the private equity giant
Blackstone agreed to buy the physician staffing company TeamHealth
in a deal valued at about six point one billion dollars
including debt, closing in early two thousand and seventeen.
Two years later, in two thousand and eighteen, rival KKR went bigger,
buying Envision Healthcare, the parent of the
emergency staffing giant EmCare, in a leveraged buyout valued at
about nine point nine billion dollars including debt,
with roughly seven billion dollars of that financed by borrowing.
Even before those buyouts, researchers at Yale had found that EmCare
and TeamHealth together accounted for roughly thirty percent of
the outsourced emergency physician market in the United States.
Now both sat inside two of Wall Street's biggest private equity firms.
And at Envision, KKR had loaded around seven billion
dollars of debt onto the company's balance sheet.
Servicing that debt required hundreds of millions of dollars in cash flow every year.
You cannot generate that kind of margin simply by
treating more broken bones at standard insurance rates.
The model needed a pricing lever.
Step Two: The Out-of-Network Squeeze.
Historically, staffing companies stayed in-network with insurers
like UnitedHealthcare, Anthem and Aetna,
accepting negotiated discounted rates in exchange for steady patient volume.
But emergency medicine has a peculiar feature:
an emergency room does not need an insurance network to bring in customers.
The ambulances bring the customers, twenty-four hours a day,
and the patient has no say in which doctor treats them.
The study that documented what happened next was published by
Yale economists Zack Cooper, Fiona Scott Morton and Nathan Shekita,
using insurance claims from twenty eleven to twenty fifteen.
They found that when EmCare took over a hospital's emergency department,
out-of-network billing rates jumped by more than eighty
percentage points, and the doctors' charges roughly doubled.
EmCare also billed more patients at the highest-severity codes,
and admitted more of them to the hospital.
The broader point: an out-of-network doctor inside an in-network hospital holds a threat.
Bill the patient directly, or get a higher rate from the insurer.
Watch how that worked in the billing software.
A patient arrives at an in-network hospital with chest pain.
An out-of-network emergency doctor treats the patient.
Picture a visit that Medicare would pay a few hundred dollars for,
and that a typical in-network contract might pay six hundred dollars for.
The out-of-network bill instead goes out at a list price of, say, five thousand dollars.
The patient's insurer pays its standard six hundred dollars,
and the provider sends what is legally known as a balance bill,
the surprise bill, directly to the patient's
home for the remaining four thousand four hundred dollars.
If the family could not pay, the account could go to collections.
In Memphis, a TeamHealth subsidiary filed more than four
thousand eight hundred lawsuits against patients in Shelby
County courts starting in twenty seventeen,
and in some cases sought to garnish the wages of low-income workers.
After journalists started asking questions in
late twenty nineteen, TeamHealth announced it
would stop suing patients and drop pending cases.
It was a two-way vise.
Either the patient paid, or the threat of those bills pushed
insurers to grant the staffing companies higher in-network rates,
costs that insurers then spread across everyone's premiums.
Step Three: Gaming Federal Arbitration and the Debt Collapse.
By twenty nineteen, public fury over surprise medical
bills had become a bipartisan issue in Washington.
That summer, a group called Doctor Patient Unity flooded the
airwaves with tens of millions of dollars in ads attacking proposals
to cap out-of-network payments at the median in-network rate.
The group did not say who was paying for it.
In September of twenty nineteen, The New York Times
reported that it was backed by TeamHealth and Envision,
the staffing companies owned by Blackstone and KKR.
Bloomberg later put the total ad spending at more than fifty million dollars.
In December of twenty twenty, Congress passed the No Surprises Act,
which took effect in January of twenty twenty-two.
It banned surprise balance bills for emergency care.
But on the question of how much the doctor gets paid,
the final law did not set a hard benchmark rate,
which is what the provider side had lobbied against.
Instead, disputed out-of-network payments go to a federal
arbitration process called Independent Dispute Resolution, or IDR.
Federal regulators estimated the system would
handle about seventeen thousand disputes a year.
Instead, providers filed about six hundred and fifty thousand
in twenty twenty-three, close to six hundred thousand in
just the first half of twenty twenty-four,
and about one point two million in the first half of twenty twenty-five.
Providers have won the large majority of decided cases,
more than eighty percent in recent data, and the biggest filers have won median
awards of roughly three to nine times the median in-network rate.
A handful of filers, mostly private-equity-backed,
account for more than half of all disputes.
TeamHealth is one of them.
But arbitration could not outrun the mathematics of Envision's leveraged buyout debt.
As interest rates rose, Envision was also locked in a long,
bitter payment fight with UnitedHealthcare,
and it said the rollout of the No Surprises Act had delayed
or cut hundreds of millions of dollars in payments.
In May of twenty twenty-three, Envision Healthcare
filed for Chapter Eleven bankruptcy protection,
carrying about seven point seven billion dollars of debt.
KKR's multibillion-dollar equity investment was wiped out,
and Envision's lenders took control of the company.
TeamHealth, still backed by Blackstone, remains one of
the largest emergency staffing companies in the country.
To protect your family from healthcare billing arbitrage, here are three rules.
Rule number one: Never pay an out-of-network emergency room,
anesthesiology or air-ambulance bill at face value.
Under the federal No Surprises Act, if you have private or employer insurance,
an out-of-network provider generally cannot
bill you more than your normal in-network cost-sharing for
emergency care at any hospital, for most care by out-of-network
doctors at an in-network hospital, or for air-ambulance trips.
One important gap: ground ambulances are not covered by the federal law.
Billing systems still make mistakes, so if a bill exceeds
the patient responsibility amount on your insurer's Explanation of Benefits,
dispute it in writing, cite the No Surprises Act,
and contact the federal No Surprises Help Desk.
Rule number two: Read any out-of-network consent form before you sign it.
For some scheduled, non-emergency care at an in-network facility,
an out-of-network provider can ask you to sign a
notice-and-consent form that waives your surprise billing protection.
You are never required to sign it.
The law also says certain doctors cannot ask for that waiver at all,
including emergency medicine, anesthesiology, radiology,
pathology, assistant surgeons, hospitalists and intensivists,
and the form can never be used for emergency care itself.
If someone hands you that form,
you can decline and ask for an in-network provider instead.
Rule number three: If you invest in healthcare companies or hospital bonds,
look at where the profit actually comes from.
A business model whose margins depend on billing disputes,
out-of-network leverage or regulatory gaps,
rather than on delivering care efficiently, can be one law change away
from serious trouble, as Envision's lenders discovered.
When financial engineering enters the trauma bay,
the patient risks becoming a revenue line rather than a person to save.

videos.full_text: Right now, you probably believe that if you pay twelve hundred dollars a month for gold-tier health insurance, and you carefully make sure the ambulance takes you to an in-network hospital, you are financially protected. For years, millions of Americans believed exactly that, and learned otherwise. They followed every rule in their insurance policy. They went to an in-network building. They lay in an in-network hospital bed. They were scanned by an in-network MRI machine. And then, a few weeks later, an envelope arrived demanding four thousand four hundred dollars, because the emergency room doctor who treated them was somehow out-of-network inside an in-network hospital. It was not a clerical mistake. It was a business model. Over the past two decades, private equity firms bought up the companies that staff America's emergency rooms, and some of those companies learned that a patient on a stretcher cannot negotiate. Researchers, insurers and Congress all came to the same conclusion: the out-of-network bill had become a pricing lever, pulled against both families and insurance companies. Today, we are opening up the contracts behind America's emergency room staffing industry, and following the money from the trauma bay to Wall Street. Welcome to Emergency Room Arbitrage. Let's look at the real data. To understand how an out-of-network doctor ends up standing over your bed inside an in-network hospital, you have to understand a structural fact that most patients never realize: in modern America, many hospitals do not actually employ the doctors working in their emergency rooms, their anesthesiology departments, or their radiology suites. One major study estimated that roughly two thirds of the emergency physician market is outsourced to staffing companies. Decades ago, hospitals realized that running a twenty-four-hour emergency department is a logistical and financial headache. Patient volume is unpredictable, malpractice liability is high, and federal law, specifically the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act of nineteen eighty-six, requires emergency rooms to screen and stabilize anyone who walks through the door, regardless of whether they can pay. To offload that burden, hospitals began outsourcing their emergency departments to third-party physician staffing companies. When you walk into your local community hospital, the nurses and the building belong to the hospital, but the emergency room doctors, anesthesiologists and radiologists may actually work for an outside staffing vendor. For years, many of these vendors were regional, physician-owned groups. Then private equity spotted a feature of American healthcare billing that could be worth billions, because emergency room demand is what economists call price-inelastic. When you are having a heart attack, or your child is bleeding in the back of an ambulance, you cannot shop around for prices, and you cannot ask the ER doctor which insurance networks he belongs to before he intubates you. Let us walk through the three-step autopsy of how this blind spot became a financial engine. Step One: Cornering the Emergency Staffing Market through Mega-Buyouts. In late two thousand and sixteen, the private equity giant Blackstone agreed to buy the physician staffing company TeamHealth in a deal valued at about six point one billion dollars including debt, closing in early two thousand and seventeen. Two years later, in two thousand and eighteen, rival KKR went bigger, buying Envision Healthcare, the parent of the emergency staffing giant EmCare, in a leveraged buyout valued at about nine point nine billion dollars including debt, with roughly seven billion dollars of that financed by borrowing. Even before those buyouts, researchers at Yale had found that EmCare and TeamHealth together accounted for roughly thirty percent of the outsourced emergency physician market in the United States. Now both sat inside two of Wall Street's biggest private equity firms. And at Envision, KKR had loaded around seven billion dollars of debt onto the company's balance sheet. Servicing that debt required hundreds of millions of dollars in cash flow every year. You cannot generate that kind of margin simply by treating more broken bones at standard insurance rates. The model needed a pricing lever. Step Two: The Out-of-Network Squeeze. Historically, staffing companies stayed in-network with insurers like UnitedHealthcare, Anthem and Aetna, accepting negotiated discounted rates in exchange for steady patient volume. But emergency medicine has a peculiar feature: an emergency room does not need an insurance network to bring in customers. The ambulances bring the customers, twenty-four hours a day, and the patient has no say in which doctor treats them. The study that documented what happened next was published by Yale economists Zack Cooper, Fiona Scott Morton and Nathan Shekita, using insurance claims from twenty eleven to twenty fifteen. They found that when EmCare took over a hospital's emergency department, out-of-network billing rates jumped by more than eighty percentage points, and the doctors' charges roughly doubled. EmCare also billed more patients at the highest-severity codes, and admitted more of them to the hospital. The broader point: an out-of-network doctor inside an in-network hospital holds a threat. Bill the patient directly, or get a higher rate from the insurer. Watch how that worked in the billing software. A patient arrives at an in-network hospital with chest pain. An out-of-network emergency doctor treats the patient. Picture a visit that Medicare would pay a few hundred dollars for, and that a typical in-network contract might pay six hundred dollars for. The out-of-network bill instead goes out at a list price of, say, five thousand dollars. The patient's insurer pays its standard six hundred dollars, and the provider sends what is legally known as a balance bill, the surprise bill, directly to the patient's home for the remaining four thousand four hundred dollars. If the family could not pay, the account could go to collections. In Memphis, a TeamHealth subsidiary filed more than four thousand eight hundred lawsuits against patients in Shelby County courts starting in twenty seventeen, and in some cases sought to garnish the wages of low-income workers. After journalists started asking questions in late twenty nineteen, TeamHealth announced it would stop suing patients and drop pending cases. It was a two-way vise. Either the patient paid, or the threat of those bills pushed insurers to grant the staffing companies higher in-network rates, costs that insurers then spread across everyone's premiums. Step Three: Gaming Federal Arbitration and the Debt Collapse. By twenty nineteen, public fury over surprise medical bills had become a bipartisan issue in Washington. That summer, a group called Doctor Patient Unity flooded the airwaves with tens of millions of dollars in ads attacking proposals to cap out-of-network payments at the median in-network rate. The group did not say who was paying for it. In September of twenty nineteen, The New York Times reported that it was backed by TeamHealth and Envision, the staffing companies owned by Blackstone and KKR. Bloomberg later put the total ad spending at more than fifty million dollars. In December of twenty twenty, Congress passed the No Surprises Act, which took effect in January of twenty twenty-two. It banned surprise balance bills for emergency care. But on the question of how much the doctor gets paid, the final law did not set a hard benchmark rate, which is what the provider side had lobbied against. Instead, disputed out-of-network payments go to a federal arbitration process called Independent Dispute Resolution, or IDR. Federal regulators estimated the system would handle about seventeen thousand disputes a year. Instead, providers filed about six hundred and fifty thousand in twenty twenty-three, close to six hundred thousand in just the first half of twenty twenty-four, and about one point two million in the first half of twenty twenty-five. Providers have won the large majority of decided cases, more than eighty percent in recent data, and the biggest filers have won median awards of roughly three to nine times the median in-network rate. A handful of filers, mostly private-equity-backed, account for more than half of all disputes. TeamHealth is one of them. But arbitration could not outrun the mathematics of Envision's leveraged buyout debt. As interest rates rose, Envision was also locked in a long, bitter payment fight with UnitedHealthcare, and it said the rollout of the No Surprises Act had delayed or cut hundreds of millions of dollars in payments. In May of twenty twenty-three, Envision Healthcare filed for Chapter Eleven bankruptcy protection, carrying about seven point seven billion dollars of debt. KKR's multibillion-dollar equity investment was wiped out, and Envision's lenders took control of the company. TeamHealth, still backed by Blackstone, remains one of the largest emergency staffing companies in the country. To protect your family from healthcare billing arbitrage, here are three rules. Rule number one: Never pay an out-of-network emergency room, anesthesiology or air-ambulance bill at face value. Under the federal No Surprises Act, if you have private or employer insurance, an out-of-network provider generally cannot bill you more than your normal in-network cost-sharing for emergency care at any hospital, for most care by out-of-network doctors at an in-network hospital, or for air-ambulance trips. One important gap: ground ambulances are not covered by the federal law. Billing systems still make mistakes, so if a bill exceeds the patient responsibility amount on your insurer's Explanation of Benefits, dispute it in writing, cite the No Surprises Act, and contact the federal No Surprises Help Desk. Rule number two: Read any out-of-network consent form before you sign it. For some scheduled, non-emergency care at an in-network facility, an out-of-network provider can ask you to sign a notice-and-consent form that waives your surprise billing protection. You are never required to sign it. The law also says certain doctors cannot ask for that waiver at all, including emergency medicine, anesthesiology, radiology, pathology, assistant surgeons, hospitalists and intensivists, and the form can never be used for emergency care itself. If someone hands you that form, you can decline and ask for an in-network provider instead. Rule number three: If you invest in healthcare companies or hospital bonds, look at where the profit actually comes from. A business model whose margins depend on billing disputes, out-of-network leverage or regulatory gaps, rather than on delivering care efficiently, can be one law change away from serious trouble, as Envision's lenders discovered. metadata.title: Collect Rx's 6 Keys to Success in Revenue Cycle Management for Out of Network Providers
metadata.author: Collect Rx
metadata.shortDescription:
Being good at managing the revenue cycle is not easy. It requires a vast amount of knowledge, attention to detail, and expertise in a variety of skillsets. The lack of time and resources to adequately manage the revenue cycle, typically leads providers to issues like poor cash flow, aged receivables, and increased denials.

For providers with complex and out-of-network claims, segments with higher than average denial rates or underpayments, the stakes are even higher. Staying financially healthy is critical and in challenging times, more important than ever. 

Join Collect Rx's Meagan Hanna to learn the how you can optimize your revenue cycle and drive success. In this free webinar, you’ll learn
• Collect Rx’s secret sauce for billing and collections that focuses on payors, not patients
• How to leverage automation, bots, data and workflow to drive improve collections
• The expertise needed to manage complex claims environments 

If you'd like to learn more about Collect Rx's Billing & Collections Solutions, please visit www.collectrx.com/contact

metadata.shortDescription:
Unlock the mystery of the revenue cycle as Ryan O’Hara, Managing Principal of the Denial Research Group, explains basic concepts and how denials and appeals impact YOUR hospital’s revenue cycle. This webinar is tailored for hospital-based healthcare professionals managing insurance denials.  

About the Presenter:

Ryan O'Hara
Managing Principal | Denial Research Group

Ryan O’Hara is an accomplished healthcare executive with a wealth of experience in revenue cycle operations. Throughout his 20+ year career, Ryan has demonstrated a deep understanding of the complexities of healthcare financial management and has worked to develop strategies and solutions to drive efficiency, reduce costs, and improve patient outcomes.

He has spent the majority of his time on the healthcare provider side, working as a revenue cycle operations leader across many hospitals and health systems. He also has spent several years working on the EMR and 3rd party business partner side. This has provided for a diverse and rounded background; but one that is always rooted in being a trusted and value-add contributor for healthcare providers.

https://www.payerwatch.com

Today, medical groups and hospitals are keenly focused on managing costs and maximizing cash flow. A healthy, solid revenue cycle underpins this objective. 

This webinar focuses on five best practices to leverage analytics for revenue cycle improvements, including tactics to manage denials effectively. Additionally, the value of visual analytics technology in identifying recurring registration, coding and billing errors, underpayments, and payer rejection patterns will be examined. 

Presented by two industry experts: Daniel J. Marino, Managing Partner at Lumina Health Partners, and Russell Hendrickson, CEO of Practical Data Solutions.

metadata.title: Revenue Cycle NOW: Strengthening Back-End Performance
metadata.author: HealthLeaders Media
metadata.shortDescription:
Collecting cash at the end of the billing cycle has become increasingly difficult as health plan requirements grow more complex denials accelerate. 

In this HealthLeaders Revenue Cycle NOW webinar, sponsored by Pivotal Health, Terri Meier, Assistance Vice Chancellor of Revenue Cycle at University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, and Michael Haney Associate Chief Revenue Cycle Officer at the Medical University of South Carolina, share practical strategies to resolve back-end bottlenecks.

HealthLeaders is a platform for peer-sourced and solution-focused insights for healthcare executives. Our focus is on giving CEOs, CNOs, CMOs, CFOs, and dozens of other leaders an avenue to connect with one another, build community, and share ideas. 

For daily updates and healthcare analysis, check out our website here: https://www.healthleadersmedia.com/ 

Subscribe to our newsletters: https://interactive.healthleadersmedia.com/subscribe 

Follow us: 
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/healthleaders-media 
X: https://x.com/HealthLeaders

#revenuecyclemanagement #revenuecycle #healthcareinnovation #healthtech #healthcaretechnology

metadata.title: Intro to IDR: What To Know About Income-Driven Repayment (IDR) Plans for Student Loans
metadata.author: Federal Student Aid
metadata.shortDescription:
On March 10, 2026, a court order ended the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) Plan. The U.S. Department of Education will contact affected borrowers, who can explore and apply for other repayment plans. For more information, visit https://StudentAid.gov/courtactions


------------------------------

Income-driven repayment (IDR) plans are intended to be the most affordable repayment plans.  

This video explains what IDR plans are and how they adjust based on your income and family size. IDR plans change with you as life changes, unlike fixed payment repayment plans, which base your monthly payment amount on your total loan balance.  

Want to know if an IDR plan is right for you? Try Loan Simulator to compare different plans, check your eligibility, and get an estimate of your monthly payment amount and repayment period: 
https://www.StudentAid.gov/loan-simulator 

Apply for an IDR plan today at:  
https://www.StudentAid.gov/idr 

To find contact information for your loan servicer, log in and view your Dashboard at: 
https://www.StudentAid.gov

Watch the full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL5C43A3FD801FDF45

00:00 – Intro
00:39 – IDR Plan Benefits
00:58 – List of IDR Plans
01:26 – IDR Repayment Periods
01:53 – IDR Plan Recertification Requirement
02:36 – Adjustable Payments
03:10 – Fixed Payment Repayment Plans
03:23 – Interest and IDR Plans
03:48 – IDR Loan Forgiveness
04:07 – Use Loan Simulator
04:51 – Consider Financial Goals & Outro

segments.text: Income-driven repayment plans,
commonly referred to as IDR plans,
are a group of student loan repayment plans.
These plans are flexible and are meant to be affordable,
so they can adjust to you and your life.
The four different income-driven repayment plans each
use your income and family size to determine your monthly payment amount.
This is different from fixed payment repayment plans,
which calculate your monthly payment amount using your total loan balance.
Income-driven repayment plans offer many benefits for eligible borrowers,
like loan forgiveness, lower payments,
and Public Service Loan Forgiveness, or PSLF, eligibility.
Additionally, each of the income- driven repayment plans
have their own unique benefits.
The four income-driven repayment plans
are the Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE, Plan;
the Income-Based Repayment, or IBR, Plan;
the Pay As You Earn, or PAYE, Plan;
and the Income-Contingent Repayment, or ICR, Plan.
Each plan has specific loan eligibility requirements,
so be sure to check and see
which income-driven repayment plans your loans are eligible for.
Income-driven repayment plans also have different repayment periods,
but all the plans can lead to loan forgiveness
if your loans are not fully repaid at the end of the repayment period.
In some cases, you may be eligible for more than one
income-driven repayment plan,
but it’s important to know that each plan calculates your monthly payment amount
differently by using a different percentage of your discretionary income.
Every year, you’re required to recertify your income-driven repayment plan.
This means you’ll provide your updated income and family size information.
You can either provide consent for us to securely access your tax information
so we can automatically recertify your plan for you,
or you can manually update this yourself yearly.
If your monthly payment amount changes,
we’ll notify you before any changes go into effect.
Income-driven repayment plans aim to help you pay what you can afford
so if your situation changes, you can update your income information
at any time before your annual recertification date.
Income-driven repayment plans also aim
to keep payments adjustable, so if your income goes down
or your family size goes up,
your monthly payment could decrease.
But this also means that if your income goes up
or your family size goes down,
your monthly payments could increase instead.
If paying the same amount every month throughout your repayment
period works better for your goals, then adjustable payments
on an income-driven repayment plan might not be the best choice for you.
Consider instead enrolling in one of the fixed payment repayment plans.
These plans include the Standard Repayment Plan,
the Graduated Repayment Plan, and the Extended Repayment Plan.
Another thing to consider is that some income-driven repayment plans
could lead to you paying more interest over time.
If your monthly payments are considerably low,
your total balance could grow due to unpaid interest.
The SAVE Plan offers an interest subsidy
which can prevent your loan balance from growing due to unpaid interest.
Watch our SAVE Plan video to learn more.
However, as long as you successfully make qualifying monthly payments,
then any remaining loan balance
will be forgiven at the end of the repayment period.
Keep in mind that loan forgiveness could lead to potential tax charges,
meaning you may have to pay income tax on your forgiven loan balance.
If you’re not sure if an income-driven repayment plan
is right for your repayment goals,
then try Loan Simulator to see your eligibility
and your estimated monthly payment amount and repayment period.
To use Loan Simulator and see if an income-driven
repayment plan meets your repayment goals,
visit StudentAid.gov/loan-simulator.
When you’re ready to apply for an income-driven repayment plan,
you can visit StudentAid.gov/idr
to fill out an application.
After you submit the application,
we’ll need a few weeks to process your request.
You can also contact your loan servicer
to help you choose the right repayment plan for you.
Before changing repayment plans,
consider your financial goals, how long you aim to be in repayment,
what you can afford, and what plans you’re eligible for.
Visit StudentAid.gov/idrplans

videos.full_text: Income-driven repayment plans, commonly referred to as IDR plans, are a group of student loan repayment plans. These plans are flexible and are meant to be affordable, so they can adjust to you and your life. The four different income-driven repayment plans each use your income and family size to determine your monthly payment amount. This is different from fixed payment repayment plans, which calculate your monthly payment amount using your total loan balance. Income-driven repayment plans offer many benefits for eligible borrowers, like loan forgiveness, lower payments, and Public Service Loan Forgiveness, or PSLF, eligibility. Additionally, each of the income- driven repayment plans have their own unique benefits. The four income-driven repayment plans are the Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE, Plan; the Income-Based Repayment, or IBR, Plan; the Pay As You Earn, or PAYE, Plan; and the Income-Contingent Repayment, or ICR, Plan. Each plan has specific loan eligibility requirements, so be sure to check and see which income-driven repayment plans your loans are eligible for. Income-driven repayment plans also have different repayment periods, but all the plans can lead to loan forgiveness if your loans are not fully repaid at the end of the repayment period. In some cases, you may be eligible for more than one income-driven repayment plan, but it’s important to know that each plan calculates your monthly payment amount differently by using a different percentage of your discretionary income. Every year, you’re required to recertify your income-driven repayment plan. This means you’ll provide your updated income and family size information. You can either provide consent for us to securely access your tax information so we can automatically recertify your plan for you, or you can manually update this yourself yearly. If your monthly payment amount changes, we’ll notify you before any changes go into effect. Income-driven repayment plans aim to help you pay what you can afford so if your situation changes, you can update your income information at any time before your annual recertification date. Income-driven repayment plans also aim to keep payments adjustable, so if your income goes down or your family size goes up, your monthly payment could decrease. But this also means that if your income goes up or your family size goes down, your monthly payments could increase instead. If paying the same amount every month throughout your repayment period works better for your goals, then adjustable payments on an income-driven repayment plan might not be the best choice for you. Consider instead enrolling in one of the fixed payment repayment plans. These plans include the Standard Repayment Plan, the Graduated Repayment Plan, and the Extended Repayment Plan. Another thing to consider is that some income-driven repayment plans could lead to you paying more interest over time. If your monthly payments are considerably low, your total balance could grow due to unpaid interest. The SAVE Plan offers an interest subsidy which can prevent your loan balance from growing due to unpaid interest. Watch our SAVE Plan video to learn more. However, as long as you successfully make qualifying monthly payments, then any remaining loan balance will be forgiven at the end of the repayment period. Keep in mind that loan forgiveness could lead to potential tax charges, meaning you may have to pay income tax on your forgiven loan balance. If you’re not sure if an income-driven repayment plan is right for your repayment goals, then try Loan Simulator to see your eligibility and your estimated monthly payment amount and repayment period. To use Loan Simulator and see if an income-driven repayment plan meets your repayment goals, visit StudentAid.gov/loan-simulator. When you’re ready to apply for an income-driven repayment plan, you can visit StudentAid.gov/idr to fill out an application. After you submit the application, we’ll need a few weeks to process your request. You can also contact your loan servicer to help you choose the right repayment plan for you. Before changing repayment plans, consider your financial goals, how long you aim to be in repayment, what you can afford, and what plans you’re eligible for. Visit StudentAid.gov/idrplans for details about each of the income-driven repayment plans.

{"type":"IBR","borrowerEligibleIndicator":"Y","loanEligibleIndicator":"Y","qualifyingPaymentCount":214

Here's a breakdown of the new IDR (Income-Driven Repayment) Plan landscape for those navigating paying off student debt. These changes went into affect July 1, 2026. This includes elimination of the SAVE plan, which was the most generous option, which has been replaced by RAP. We went through it all in our recent Student Loan Repayment Strategies webinar to help you decide the best student loan strategy moving forward. Watch the full webinar here: https://zurl.co/ASzni 

Need additional help navigating your student loans? Our financial advisors are here to help you on your journey to financial freedom. Book a free consultation now! https://zurl.co/hkSWh
