segments.text: It's 7:14 on a Friday evening and you're
alone in your office staring at an email
that could unravel your practice. The
computer screen illuminates your
favorite coffee mug and a slightly
wobbly desk plant you've named Phil.
You're ready to close out the week, but
a chime from your inbox has stopped you.
The subject line reads, "Problem with
insurance again." The message is from
Sarah. She's been a client for nearly a
year. You open the email and a knot
forms in your stomach as you read. Her
insurance company has denied her
reimbursement claim for the third time.
She attached the denial letter. She
sounds frustrated asking if it's even
worth the effort to keep submitting the
super bills you provide. A super bill is
a detailed receipt you give
out-of-network clients so they can seek
reimbursement from their insurer.
You started your own practice to give
clients like Sarah better, more
personalized care.
You left the paperwork and paneling of
the agency world behind for freedom.
You never wanted to create more
financial stress for the people you
help. You close your laptop without
replying. The question hangs in the
quiet office. All weekend it follows
you. On Saturday morning, you pull up
the super bill template you downloaded a
year ago. It looks so professional with
neat fields for your practice name, your
national provider identifier, and the
client's diagnosis. You spend hours
searching online for out-of-network
claim denials. You fall down a rabbit
hole of forums and articles, each with a
different opinion.
You learn the difference between a
rejection and a denial. A claim
rejection happens when a claim is sent
back right away because of a simple
error, like a typo in a name. A claim
denial is when the insurance company
processes the claim and then refuses to
pay.
Sarah's issue is a denial. It's more
complicated. On Monday morning, you call
Sarah and get her permission to speak
with her insurance company on her
behalf. After 45 minutes on hold
listening to repetitive music, a
representative finally answers. You
explain the situation. The
representative is polite but firm. They
can't discuss the details of the claim
with you. You are an out-of-network
provider. Before they end the call, they
vaguely mention an issue with the place
of service and an unspecified diagnosis.
You hang up the phone feeling more
powerless than before. You lean back in
your chair and stare at the wobbly
leaves of your desk plant. You pull up
the super bill you created for Sarah's
last session. You've looked at this
document a dozen times. This time you
look closer, remembering the
representative's words, "Place of
service." You see the place of service
code you entered. A place of service
code is a two-digit number on a claim
that shows where the service happened.
The code on Sarah's form is 11 for an
in-person office visit. Your heart
sinks. Sarah's last several sessions
were via telehealth. You do a quick
search. Telehealth sessions often need a
different code, like 02 or 10, depending
on the payer. Then you remember the
other phrase, "Unspecified diagnosis."
You look at the diagnosis code on the
super bill. A diagnosis code represents
a client-specific diagnosis and tells
the insurance company why the care was
needed. You've been using a general code
for anxiety that you thought was good
enough. Your clinical notes, however,
support a much more specific diagnosis.
You realize the template you downloaded
isn't enough. It's just a blank form. It
doesn't know if a session was online or
person. It can't read your notes and
suggest the most accurate code. You're
beginning to understand that a clean
claim is what matters. A clean claim is
a claim with all the correct information
needed for an insurer to process it
automatically without any human having
to look at it. Your super bills were not
generating clean claims. A chilling
thought surfaces. How many other clients
are quietly struggling with this? You've
issued dozens of these super bills since
you opened. You do some quick math on a
notepad. Your session fee is $150.
If a client like Sarah expects to get
60% of that back from her insurance,
that's $90 she is counting on. If she
can't get that reimbursement, she might
have to reduce her sessions from weekly
to bi-weekly. She might have to stop
coming altogether. This isn't just a
client's problem. It's a threat to your
practice's cash flow. Cash flow is the
movement of money into and out of your
business. If your clients can't afford
to continue care, your income becomes
unstable. The freedom you wanted when
you started your practice suddenly feels
very fragile. Just then, another email
notification chimes. You glance at the
screen. It's from Mark, a new client you
saw for the second time this week. The
subject line is simple, super bill
request. He's asking for a super bill
for his first few sessions so he can
submit them to his insurance. The
problem is no longer a mystery from last
week. It's sitting in your inbox, a
ticking clock demanding a real solution
right now. You can't send him the same
flawed document you sent Sarah.
You look from Mark's email back to the
still unanswered message from Sarah. You
think about the pride you felt hanging
your diploma on the wall, the excitement
of choosing the furniture, the
satisfaction of helping people on your
own terms. None of that matters if your
clients are being punished by a system
you don't understand. The hidden costs
of being out of network aren't just
about lower reimbursement rates. They
are the hours you lose to research, the
trust you risk with your clients, and
the financial instability that creeps in
when your billing process fails. The
story ends as it began. It's Friday
night. You are alone in your office, the
room lit by your computer screen. Your
coffee in its mug is now cold. Phil, the
plant, is still wobbly. This time, you
don't close the laptop. You pull it
closer. You open a new document. You
begin drafting a reply to Sarah
explaining what you've learned and
promising to send her a corrected super
bill on Monday. You tell her you will
help her appeal the denials. Then you
start building a new smarter template
for Mark. You're not just a therapist
anymore. You're a business owner.
Additionally, tonight you're finally
taking control of your business. This is
a fictional story created for
educational purposes. The situations and
characters are illustrative. The story
is not a testimonial and does not
represent the experience of any specific
person or practice. The operational
details described are meant to explain
how behavioral health billing can work,
not to provide financial or legal
advice.

metadata.title: Healthcare Underpayments Explained: Causes, Costs, and How to Recover
metadata.author: MD Clarity
metadata.shortDescription:
Healthcare underpayments are partial payments from insurance payers that fall short of the rate your contract requires. The claim gets paid, so no denial code appears, and the shortfall hides in the gap between your contracted rate and the deposited amount. Underpayments cost providers 1% to 3% of net patient revenue every year, and some estimates reach as high as 11%.

This video explains what healthcare underpayments are, how they differ from denials and write-offs, what they cost at different practice sizes, why they happen, and the detect-recover-resolve workflow you use to find and fix them at the source.

KEY FACTS COVERED
- Underpayments are paid claims that fall short of the contract, so they never appear on a denial report.
- The industry benchmark is a 1% to 3% loss of net patient revenue per year. A 100-physician group earning $66.9M loses $669K to $2M annually.
- The AMA reports a 19.3% commercial-insurer claims-processing error rate, a $17 billion annual inefficiency.
- The AHA found Medicare and Medicaid underpaid U.S. hospitals by $130 billion in 2023.
- A federal judge approved a $2.8 billion Blue Cross Blue Shield underpayment settlement in August 2025, and UnitedHealthcare was ordered to pay $91.2 million to Envision Healthcare.
- Contract-anchored appeals that cite exact contract language recover 70% to 85% of underpaid claims.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Introduction
0:41 What are healthcare underpayments?
1:32 Underpayments vs. denials vs. write-offs
2:53 How bad is the situation? The numbers
4:11 Financial impact by practice size
5:31 Why the system breeds underpayments
7:12 Payer-driven causes
8:39 Revenue-cycle causes
9:54 The detect-recover-resolve workflow
11:52 Key takeaways

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

What are healthcare underpayments?
Healthcare underpayments occur when a payer reimburses a provider less than the contracted or expected amount for a covered service. The claim is paid, just not paid correctly, and it arrives without a denial code, which is why it hides in remittance data.

What is the difference between an underpayment and a denial?
A denial is an outright refusal to pay all or part of a claim, marked by an explicit denial code. An underpayment is a claim that was paid at less than the contracted rate with no denial signal. Denials show up on standard reports. Underpayments only surface through contract-based variance reconciliation.

What is the difference between an underpayment and a write-off?
An underpayment is recoverable through appeal inside the timely filing window. A write-off is a balance the provider has accepted as lost. Underpayments mislabeled as routine contractual adjustments often become permanent write-offs because nobody investigated them.

How much do underpayments cost providers?
Industry benchmarks place commercial-payer underpayments at 1% to 3% of net patient revenue annually. A regional health system with 500 physician FTEs loses $3.3M to $10M per year.

What are the main causes of healthcare underpayments?
Causes fall into three buckets: payer-driven (contract misinterpretation, fee schedule errors, improper bundling, missed escalators, lesser-of clauses), revenue-cycle-driven (coding errors, missing modifiers, incorrect DRG assignment, trailer billing), and industry-driven (plan complexity, RCM staffing shortages, inadequate technology).

How do you recover an underpayment?
Recovery follows three phases. Detect the variance by comparing every payment to the contract at the claim-line level. Recover it with contract-anchored appeals prioritized by dollar value and filing deadline. Resolve the root cause through trend analysis and contract renegotiation so the same leakage does not return.

RESOURCES
Read the full guide: https://www.mdclarity.com/blog/healthcare-underpayments
See underpayment detection in action: https://www.mdclarity.com/revfind
Get a demo: https://www.mdclarity.com/request-a-demo

ABOUT MD CLARITY
MD Clarity is an AI-powered revenue cycle management platform that helps healthcare provider organizations detect payer underpayments, recover lost revenue, and optimize their managed care contracts. RevFind, MD Clarity's underpayment detection software, compares every payment against your contract terms automatically, flags variances by payer, CPT code, location, and physician, and tracks your recovery over time.

segments.text: Hello everyone and welcome back. Today
we're going to talk about one of the
most overlooked sources of lost revenue
in all of healthcare finance,
underpayments. Now, if you work in
revenue cycle, you already spend a lot
of time thinking about denials. Denials
are loud. They show up on reports. They
have codes attached and our team chases
them every day. But underpayments,
underpayments are quiet. And by the end
of this lesson, you'll understand
exactly why that quietness makes them so
expensive and what a disciplined
organization does about it. We'll cover
five things today. What payments
actually are, how they differ from
denials and write-offs, what they cost,
why they happen, and the three-phase
workflow for finding and fixing them at
the source. Let's start with a precise
definition because precision matters in
this subject. A healthcare underpayment
occurs when an insurance payer
reimburses a provider less than the rate
stipulated in the provider's contract.
The key word here is less. The claim was
not rejected, it was paid, just not paid
correctly. And I want you to really sit
with that distinction because it
explains that follows. When a claim is
denied, the remittance arrives with an
explicit denial code. Your system flags
it. Your denial report catches it.
Somebody works it. When a claim is
underpaid, the remittance lands, the
claim closes as paid in your patient
accounting system, and the shortfall
buries itself in the gap between the
contracted amount and the deposited
amount. No alarm goes off. No report
flags it. The money simply never arrives
and nobody notices. That is why I call
underpayments the hidden leak in the
revenue cycle. They are structurally
invisible to the tools most

metadata.title: Out-of-Network Reimbursement: Why Paid Claims Can Still Hide Lost Revenue
metadata.author: Vee Healthtek
metadata.shortDescription:
A paid out-of-network claim does not always mean accurate reimbursement. Payment adjustments, missed variances, and disconnected recovery workflows can leave recoverable revenue hidden after posting. This video explains how healthcare providers can distinguish complete reimbursement from unresolved exposure and prioritize recovery that justifies its cost.

In this video, you will learn:

Why payment status and denial rates cannot confirm reimbursement accuracy
How claim-level review and recurring small-dollar variances reveal hidden recovery opportunities
Which measures connect paid-claim variance with net recovery, cash timing, and prevention

Read the full article: https://www.veehealthtek.com/why-us/points-of-view/out-of-network-reimbursement-missed-revenue

Relevant Vee Healthtek capabilities:

Underpayment Recovery and Payer Variance Resolution : https://www.veehealthtek.com/how-we-deliver/back-office/underpayment-recovery-and-payer-variance-resolution
Payment Posting and Reconciliation : https://www.veehealthtek.com/how-we-deliver/back-office/payment-posting-and-reconciliation
Accounts Receivable Follow-Up : https://www.veehealthtek.com/how-we-deliver/back-office/accounts-receivable-follow-up

About Vee Healthtek
Vee Healthtek is a practitioner-led, technology-powered revenue cycle partner helping healthcare providers identify payment variances and convert credible recovery opportunities into cash. We connect remittance data, expected reimbursement, specialist review, and accountable follow-up to reduce recurring revenue leakage.

metadata.title: What is the difference between overpayment and underpayment in medical billing
metadata.author: Azeem khan Watanyar Official
metadata.shortDescription:
Overpayment in medical billing refers to a situation where a healthcare provider receives more money than they are owed for a service, often due to billing errors, duplicate payments, or incorrect insurance processing.

Underpayment occurs when a provider receives less than the amount due for a service, which may result from coding errors, incorrect insurance adjustments, or payer reimbursement issues.

Here are **20 keywords** and **20 hashtags** related to **overpayment and underpayment in medical billing**:

जब इंश्योरेंस या पेशेंट जो अलाउड अमाउंट होती है उनसे अगर ज्यादा अमाउंट पे कर दें तो उसको ओवरपेमेंट बोलते हैं। एग्जांपल क्या है? अ क्लेम इज़ बिल्ड फॉर $100 बट द इंश्योरेंस पेज़ $120। एग्जांपल में कहा जा रहा है भाई कि अगर हम बिल कर देते हैं $100 और इंश्योरेंस उससे ज्यादा पे कर देता है यानी $120 पे कर देते हैं। उसको और पेमेंट कहते हैं। मस्ट बी रिफंडेड और एडजस्टेड टू कॉम्प्लाई विथ लीगल एंड कॉन्ट्रैक्टेड ऑब्लिगेशन। यह जो और पेमेंट अमाउंट है यह दोबारा रिफंड करने होंगे ताकि जो है वह कॉन्ट्रक्चुअल ऑब्लिगेशन जो है उसके मुताबिक पे हो और लीगल जो है वह इशू से बचा जा सके। अब अंडर पेमेंट क्या हैपेंस व्हेन द पेयर और पेशेंट पेज़ लेस देन द बिल्ड और एक्सपेक्टेड अमाउंट। अंडर पेमेंट के बारे में कहा जा रहा है कि यह पेयर या पेशेंट जो है वह बिल्ड अमाउंट से या एक्सपेक्टेड अमाउंट से कम पे कर दे तो उसको फिर अंडर पेमेंट बोलते हैं। एग्जांपल क्या है? क्लेम इज़ बिल फॉर $100 बट द इंश्योरेंस पेज़ ओनली $60। अगर हम इंश्योरेंस को $100 बिल भेजें और इंश्योरेंस उसकी $60 पे कर दें तो उसका जो है वह उसको अंडर पेमेंट के थ्रू क्लेम को प्रोसेस किया है उन्होंने। रिक्वायर्ड फॉलो अप और अपील टू कवर द मिसिंग अमाउंट इफ जस्टिफाइड। अगर वो अमाउंट जो है वह जस्टिफायबल है तो हम उनके लिए अपील भेजेंगे। उनके साथ फॉलो अप करेंगे। इंश्योरेंस को कॉल करेंगे कि भाई आपने जो यह पेमेंट की है यह लो की है। जबकि स्टैंडर्ड गाइडलाइंस के मुताबिक इसका ज्यादा होना चाहिए। तो उसके अपील भेजते रिप्रोस करवाते हैं। की डिफरेंसेस क्या है? नंबर वन है पेमेंट स्टेटस पेड मोर देन एक्सपेक्टेड। ओवर पेमेंट में जबकि अंडर पेमेंट है पेड लेस दैन एक्सपेक्टेड। एक्शन रिक्वायर्ड क्या है? रिफंड और एडजस्टमेंट। अगर जो है वह ज़्यादा अमाउंट हो जाए तो रिफंड करने होंगे और एडजस्टमेंट की तरफ़ जाना होगा। लेकिन अगर अंडर पेड है तो अपील और रीसबिमिट द क्लेम। हम ज़्यादा अमाउंट के लिए क्लेम को भेजेंगे। अपील भेजेंगे कि भ आपने कम पे की है। जो फी स्केजुअल है उसके मुताबिक आप क्लेम को पे कर दे तो उसके लिए अपील भेजना होता है। इंपैक्ट क्या है? फाइनेंशियल लायबिलिटी रिफंड और पेमेंट। उसमें फाइनेंशियल लायबिलिटी या रिफंड की शक्ल में उनको हमें क्या करना होगा? वह रिफंड करना होगा। वह फाइनेंशियल जो है वह लायबिलिटी के तौर पर कंसीडर किया जा सकता है। इसके अलावा अंडर पेमेंट में क्या है? रेवेन्यू लॉस इफ नॉट करेक्टेड। अगर कोई करेक्टेड पेमेंट या क्लेम नहीं भेजा जाता तो वह जो है वो मनी लॉस होगा उस इंडस्ट्री के लिए डॉक्टर के लिए। अच्छा हमारे पास कुछ एग्जांपल्स हैं और पेमेंट के हवाले से। नंबर वन है डुप्लीकेट पेमेंट बाय इंश्योरेंस। इंश्योरेंस या डुप्लीकेट पेमेंट की है। अ क्लेम फॉर अ प्रोसीजर इज़ सबमिटेड एंड पेड करेक्टली ड्यू टू अ सिस्टम एरर द इंश्योरेंस पेज़ अगेन फॉर द सेम क्लेम रिजल्टिंग इन ओवर पेमेंट द प्रोवाइडर मस्ट रिफंड द एक्सेस अमाउंट और नोटिफाई द पेयर्स। अच्छा यहां पे ये किया जा रहा है कि ये क्लेम जो है वो एक प्रोसीजर बिल की अगेन इंश्योरेंस को और उसने करेक्टली पे कर दिया है लेकिन सिस्टम एरर होने की वजह से जो है वो इंश्योरेंस ने क्लेम को दोबारा प्रोसेस करके पे कर दिया है। अब डबल अमाउंट एक ही क्लेम के लिए पे कर दिया है। तो प्रोवाइडर जो है उसको नोटिफाई करना चाहिए इंश्योरेंस को कि आपने जो है वो एक क्लेम दो दफा पे किया है। जो दूसरी दफा पे किया है उसको रिफंड करना होगा। तो रिफंड रिक्वेस्ट या तो फ्यूचर क्लेम में एडजस्टमेंट की शक्ल में होनी चाहिए या जो है वो डॉक्टर अपने अ अकाउंट से जो है वो इंश्योरेंस को रिफंड करेगी और उसको अमाउंट जो है वो इंश्योरेंस को उसको भेजना होगा। ठीक है? एग्जांपल नंबर टू हमारे पास है इनकरेक्ट पेशेंट रिस्पांसिबिलिटी पेशेंट इज़ बिल्ट अ को पे ऑफ़ $20 बट मिस्टेकली पेज़ $50। द एक्स्ट्रा 30 इज़ कंसीडर्ड एन ओवर पेमेंट एंड मस्ट बी रिफंडेड और क्रेडिटेड टू द पेशेंट्स अकाउंट। नाज़रीन यहां पे कहा जा रहा है कि एक पेशेंट को जो है वह उसको कोपे के लिए $20 के लिए बिल किया गया। लेकिन उस पेशेंट ने मिस्टेकनली $50 पे किए तो एक्स्ट्रा $30 जो है वह ओवर पेमेंट की शक्ल इख्तियार कर गई है जो कि डॉक्टर को रिफंड करने होंगे पेशेंट को और पेशेंट के अकाउंट में उसकी एडजस्टमेंट हो सकती है। अगर इन केस पेशेंट की कोई और अकाउंट में कॉपे पड़ा है तो यह अमाउंट जो है वो जो एक्सेसिव अमाउंट है यह वहां पे उसकी एडजस्टमेंट हो सकती है। क्योंकि वह जो अमाउंट है वह कॉप पे वह पेशेंट ने पे करना होता है दूसरे अकाउंट्स में। तो वहां पे जाके दूसरे विजिट्स में उनको क्या होगा? यह वाला जो ओवर पेमेंट अमाउंट होगी वह वहां पे एडजस्टमेंट करनी होगी। उनको वहां पे एंट्री पास करनी होगी और पेशेंट को जो है वह जब स्टेटमेंट जाएगा तो वो अमाउंट नहीं जाएगी। वो ऑलरेडी एडजस्टमेंट हो चुकी होगी उन अमाउंट्स के लिए। अब हमारे पास एग्जांपल फर्स्ट है अंडर पेमेंट के लिए। वो क्या है? इनकरेक्ट इंश्योरेंस एडजस्टमेंट अ सर्विस इज़ बिल्ट एट $2 अलाउड अमाउंट इज़ $150। अच्छा इंश्योरेंस पेज़ ओनली $100 इनकरेक्टली एडजस्टिंग द रिमेनिंग $50 प्रोवाइडर आइडेंटिफाई इट एज़ एन अंडर पेमेंट एंड मे अपील द एडजस्टमेंट। अच्छा यहां पे क्या है? सर्विस जो है वह बिल किया गया है 200 अमाउंट के लिए अलाउड अमाउंट है $150। इंश्योरेंस ने $100 पे किए इनकरेक्टली जबकि एडजस्टमेंट जो है रिमेनिंग कितनी होगी? $50 होगी। इंश्योरेंस के मुताबिक अलाउड अमाउंट 150 है। लेकिन इंश्योरेंस ने उसको गलती से $100 जो है वो पे किए जिसके मुताबिक $50 जो है वो क्या करने होंगे? यह लो पे कर दिए हैं। मतलब यह कि लेस देन अलाउड अमाउंट। प्रोवाइडर जो है वह आइडेंटिफाई करेगी और अंडर पेमेंट के बारे में और उसके लिए बाकी एडजस्टमेंट के लिए अपील सेंड करने होंगे इंश्योरेंस को ताकि वह जो रिमेनिंग $50 वह पे कर सके। नंबर टू है मिसिंग मॉडिफायर और कोड अ प्रोसीजर रिक्वायर्ड्स अ मॉडिफायर फॉर द फुल रिइबर्समेंट द क्लेम इज़ सबमिटेड विदाउट द मॉडिफायर एंड द इंश्योरेंस स्पेस ओनली पार्शियली द मिसिंग मॉडिफायर लीड्स टू अंडर पेमेंट रिक्वायरिंग क्लेम करेक्शन एंड रीस सबमिशन अच्छा यहां पे ये बात की जा रही है कि जो प्रोसीजर्स हैं उसके लिए मॉडिफायर चाहिए था जो कि नहीं भेजा गया और उस केस में क्या होगा कि जो क्लेम सबमिट किए विदाउट मॉडिफायर तो इंश्योरेंस उसको पार्शियली पे किया है और उस पार्शियल पेमेंट के मुताबिक जो है वह क्लेम अंडरपेड में आ गया। अब क्या होगा जो मिसिंग मॉडिफायर करेक्टेड क्लेम भेजना होगा और उसमें जो वही मॉडिफायर है वह सीपीटी के साथ लगाएंगे। वो दोबारा क्लेम भेजेंगे तो क्लेम जो है वो क्या हो जाएगा? वो प्रोसेस हो के पे हो जाएगा। ठीक है? आज के लिए इतना ही नाज़रीन। उम्मीद है आपको यह लेक्चर की समझ में आया होगा और अपने कीमती राय जरूर पेश करें। अगले लेक्चर के लिए सजेशन पेश करें और वीडियोस को शेयर करें। थैंक यू सो मच। अल्लाह हाफिज़।

videos.full_text: You went to an in network hospital, so why did you just get a $3,000 bill from a doctor you never chose? I'm Maya. That bill might be illegal. Since 2022, the No Surprises Act protects you from exactly this. Here's how it works. Balance billing happens when an out of network provider bills you for the difference between their charge and what your insurer paid. It can add thousands to your bill. The No Surprises Act bans balance bills in three cases: emergency care from an out of network provider, non-emergency services by an out of network doctor at an in network facility, and out of network air ambulance. Under the law, your cost sharing is calculated as if the provider were in network. The insurer pays the rest, and the provider cannot bill you for the balance. Example: Mark has surgery at an in network hospital. The out of network anesthesiologist charges $3,500. The in network allowed amount is $1,800. Mark's 20% co-insurance is $360. The anesthesiologist tries to balance bill Mark for $1,340, the difference. That $1,340 comes from $3,500 - $1,800 - $360, and it's prohibited under the No Surprises Act. Mark pays only $360. Don't pay it. Contact your insurer to confirm the claim was processed under No Surprises Act rules. If the provider keeps billing, file a complaint with the CMS No Surprises Help Desk at 1-800-985-3059. For some scheduled non-emergency care, a provider can ask you to waive these protections, but only with written notice 72 hours ahead and your informed consent. It can never be used for emergency, anesthesia, radiology, or pathology. Quick recap. Simply, the No Surprises Act bans balance bills for emergency care, out-of-network providers at in-network facilities, and air ambulance. You pay only in-network cost sharing. Call 1-800-985-3059 if a provider balance bills you in a protected situation. I'm Maya. If this helped, hit subscribe and I'll see you in the next one. Let's make insurance simple.

metadata.title: S1 Ep161: The No Surprises Act's new payment dispute rule, with Anders Gilberg of MGMA
metadata.author: Medical Economics TV
metadata.shortDescription:
When a patient is treated by an out-of-network physician at an in-network hospital, the resulting payment dispute is supposed to be settled through the No Surprises Act's independent dispute resolution process. A newly finalized rule is meant to make that process work better, and for practices, the headline change is significant: the fee to initiate a dispute has dropped from $115 to just $15. 


In this episode, Physicians Practice Managing Editor Keith Reynolds sits down with Anders Gilberg, senior vice president of government affairs at MGMA, to unpack what the rule actually changes, where administrative burden still weighs on practices and why so many physicians win in arbitration only to never see payment from insurers. Gilberg also responds to the insurance industry's criticism of the process, explains which specialties are most affected and lays out the regulatory developments practices should be watching through the rest of the year, from two pending HIPAA rules to the physician fee schedule.

Editor's note: Episode timestamps and transcript produced using AI tools.

0:00 – 0:23 | Sponsor message Copic medical liability insurance (https://www.copic.com/) .


0:23 – 0:56 | Cold open Gilberg previews one of the episode's central frustrations: physicians win the vast majority of payment disputes through arbitration, only to never receive payment.


0:56 – 1:46 | Introduction Austin Littrell introduces the episode and guest, previewing what the new independent dispute resolution rule changes for practices.


1:46 – 4:06 | What the IDR rule is and where it came from Keith Reynolds opens the conversation, and Gilberg recaps how the independent dispute resolution process grew out of the No Surprises Act to settle out-of-network payment disputes, often involving specialties like emergency medicine, radiology, pathology and anesthesia.


4:06 – 5:17 | What the final rule changes Gilberg explains the two biggest wins: the fee to initiate a dispute dropped from $115 to $15, and new remittance codes will tell practices which claims actually fall under the No Surprises Act.


5:17 – 6:12 | What the delay cost practices With the rule under regulatory review for more than two years, Gilberg says the lag kept fees high and left practices to navigate ambiguity over which claims were even eligible.


6:12 – 8:20 | Where the administrative burden still sits New transparency codes will help, but Gilberg says the process remains cumbersome and points to a bigger problem: physicians win arbitration more than 80% of the time and still go unpaid, with enforcement legislation needed to make payers actually pay.


8:20 – 11:01 | The payers' pushback Responding to insurers who say the rule does too little to stop ineligible claims, Gilberg argues they are hiding behind a handful of egregious cases while ignoring how often physicians legitimately prevail, and acknowledges that a few profit-driven ownership arrangements are rare exceptions.


11:01 – 11:52 | P2 Management Minute Keith Reynolds shares practice management tips and invites listeners to submit their own workflow ideas.


11:52 – 14:08 | What it means for administrators Gilberg notes the IDR process mainly affects hospital-based specialties like emergency medicine, anesthesia and radiology, but advises any administrator to treat denials more seriously now: the path from a 30-day negotiation to baseball-style arbitration is clearer, cheaper and tends to favor the practice.


14:08 – 16:41 | What practices should watch for next Gilberg doesn't see the rule as a signal of broader change, but flags a busy regulatory year ahead: two pending HIPAA rules on privacy and security, the physician fee schedule due in early July and payment issues set to expire at year's end, with a post-election lame-duck session likely to determine the rest.

metadata.title: The No Surprises Act - What You Need to Know
metadata.author: First Healthcare Compliance
metadata.shortDescription:
First Healthcare Compliance hosts Rachel V. Rose, JD, MBA, principal with Rachel V. Rose – Attorney at Law, P.L.L.C., Houston, TX, for an interactive discussion on “The No Surprises Act - What You Need to Know.” Effective January 1, 2022, the No Surprises Act has implications for patients, providers, and insurance companies alike. The impetus behind the legislation, as well as the regulations, is to prevent patients from receiving bills for certain services that were performed or delivered by providers out of their plan's network. The scope is limited and providers and plans alike need to take steps to understand the appeal process when a payment or claim is challenged. 

The purpose of this presentation is to provide a brief overview of the evolution of the United States' healthcare system and its relevance to the No Surprises Act. From there, the No Surprises Act and regulations will be explained, along with the appeal process. Finally, compliance tips will round out the presentation.

This webinar will cover the following objectives:

1. Understand the No Surprises Act
2. Appreciate the steps and timing of the NSA's appeal process
3. Appreciate the need to educate staff and patients on the NSA

Our flexible and scalable solutions allow organizations to share, track, and manage their compliance processes with ease, view compliance in real time across all locations, and have peace of mind that they are current in all federal healthcare regulatory areas.

Administrators using the First Healthcare Compliance platform are able to share, track, and manage their compliance processes with ease, view compliance in real time across all locations, and have peace of mind that they are current in all areas.

metadata.title: No More Surprise Medical Bills: 5 Things To Know about the No Surprises Act Taking Effect in 2022
metadata.author: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
metadata.shortDescription:
New Year. New Law. Beginning January 1, 2022, new federal protections championed by the Biden-Harris Administration will shield millions of consumers from surprise medical bills. 

Surprise medical bills – unexpected bills from an out-of-network provider, out-of-network facility or out-of-network air ambulance provider – is common among those with private insurance. Nearly one in five patients who go to the emergency room, have an elective surgery, or give birth in a hospital receive surprise bills, with average costs ranging from $750 to $2,600 per episode.
Learn about how the No Surprises Act can protect you from surprise medical billing. 

--

U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) | http://www.hhs.gov

http://www.Twitter.com/HHSGov | http://www.Facebook.com/HHS http://www.Instagram.com/HHSGov
http://www.LinkedIn.com/company/us-department-of-health-and-human-services

HHS Privacy Policy: http://www.hhs.gov/Privacy.html
keywords: Department of Health and Human Services

segments.text: After seeking medical care, the last thing you need is an eye-popping surprise bill.
Effective January 1, 2022, yes, that means now, hardworking Americans will no longer
need to worry about surprise medical bills.
Here are 5 Things to Know about the No Surprises Act taking effect.
First, we have banned surprise billing for emergency and certain non-emergency services.
This means when you go to an emergency room, even if the anesthesiologist isn’t in your
insurance network, the hospital can no longer balance bill you for their out of network fees.
In other words, no surprise bill.
Second, our rules now in effect, will remove patients from the middle of out-of-network
payment disputes that should be settled between providers and payers.
We have set in place rules for providers and payers to settle out-of-network service costs
in a manner that is transparent and focuses on the patient.
Third, the new law ensures price transparency requirements and protections for uninsured
or self-pay individuals.
Our regulations outline requirements for health care cost estimates to be provided to patients
who are uninsured or self-pay.
Further, an arbitration process has been established for uninsured or self-paying individuals to
negotiate with providers should their final bill exceed cost estimates previously provided.
Fourth, we are here to help.
We have created a consumer-friendly complaint help desk
to guide patients through the dispute process.
The help desk is open from 8am - 8pm Eastern time, 7 days a week to help you with the payment
arbitration process or other questions.
Fifth, with the No Surprises Act in effect, you have the protection and assurance that
life-saving care will not unexpectedly cost your life’s savings.
Learn more by visiting CMS.gov/Nosurprises.

metadata.title: Unexpected Medical Bill? Know Your Rights Under the No Surprises Act
metadata.author: The On-Air Advocate
metadata.shortDescription:
Have you ever been shocked by the cost of a medical bill? The No Surprises Act (NSA) is a federal law that protects you from unexpected medical bills. This act covers emergency care and out of network doctors, so you are not stuck with surprise bills.

What the Law Covers:

✅ Emergency room care at in-network hospitals — even if the doctors are out-of-network
✅ Out-of-network specialists (like anesthesiologists, radiologists, or pathologists) working at in-network facilities
✅ Uninsured or self-pay patients — must receive a Good Faith Estimate before scheduled non-emergency care

⸻

❗ What Is Balance Billing?

Balance billing happens when a provider charges you the difference between what your insurance paid and their full rate.
⚠️ This practice is now illegal in most cases covered under the No Surprises Act.

⸻

✅ Who Can Take Action?

Whether you are:
– Privately insured
– Covered through your employer
– Uninsured or self-pay

You may file a free complaint with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) if you believe your rights were violated.

⏱ You have 120 days from the date on your bill to act.
📍 File online: https://www.cms.gov/nosurprises/consumers
📞 Call: 1-800-985-3059

⸻

🔍 Not Sure If Your Rights Were Violated? Here Are Some Signs:

You should file a complaint if:
– You got a surprise bill from an out-of-network provider during an emergency visit
– You were billed by an out-of-network doctor at an in-network hospital, and you didn’t knowingly consent ahead of time
– You were charged out-of-network cost-sharing (higher deductible or coinsurance) for a protected situation
– You were balance billed for any of the services this law protects
– Your insurance didn’t follow the law properly (e.g., denied a covered claim or misapplied pricing)

If any of these happened, you have the right to report it—and CMS will investigate for free.

⸻

⚠️ The $400 Rule — Applies ONLY to Uninsured/Self-Pay Patients

If you are uninsured or paying out of pocket, you must be given a Good Faith Estimate before scheduled care.
If your final bill is $400 or more higher than that estimate, you can file a formal dispute with CMS.

📌 This process does not apply if you used insurance—but you can still file a complaint as noted above.

⸻

Advocacy Tip:

Ask these 3 questions before any appointment or procedure:
 1. Is this provider in-network for my plan?
 2. Will I receive a Good Faith Estimate if I’m uninsured or self-pay?
 3. What are my rights if I get a surprise bill?

⸻

📌 Best Ways to Connect with The On-Air Advocate

Free resources & downloads: www.onairadvocate.com/resources
Instagram: www.instagram.com/theonairadvocate

⚠️ Disclaimer

This content is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical or legal advice. For help with your specific situation, contact CMS, your provider, or your insurance plan directly.

segments.text: All right, let's jump right in. Today we're talking about RCM, or as I like to call it,
the healthcare payment game. I mean, have you ever really stopped to think about it? How do
hospitals actually get the money for the care they provide? It's definitely not a simple bill in the
mail. It's not magic, that's for sure. It's a high stakes game where the prize is payment and every
single move counts. The name of this game, revenue cycle management. So, let's get started. Section
one, the game begins with patient info. This is ground zero where everything kicks off. Okay,
so in simple terms, this is patient scheduling and registration. When you book an appointment,
someone collects your basic details, right? Your name, date of birth, insurance info. That's the
first move on the board. But watch out. Here's the first risk. One tiny typo. Just a single wrong
digit in a birth date. And what's the result? a guaranteed claim denial later on. Seriously,
you ignore this step and the payment is gone. All right, the info is in, but now we hit our first
major challenge. Section two, getting approval. This step is called insurance verification,
and it's exactly what it sounds like. We're checking before any treatment if the patients
insurance is even active and what it actually covers. This is the moment that decides if the
hospital will see any money at all. And right after that comes a special mission, something
called pre-authorization. Trust me, this part is a real gamecher. So, here's the deal. If a service,
let's say an MRI, needs pre-authorization, and you skip it, what happens? A 100% claim denial,
no approval, no money. It's that simple. This is exactly where the game changes.
Now for the next level, section three, cracking the code, the language of money. This part can
get a little technical, but it's where everything gets translated into cash.
So medical coding is basically a translation service. Every single thing the hospital does,
every diagnosis, every procedure, it all gets converted into these universal alpha
numeric codes. It's literally how the hospital speaks to the insurance company and says, "Hey,
this is what we did." Take a look at this screen. It's a perfect example. A patient has a fever,
that gets an ICD code. The doctor's visit itself, that's a service, so it gets a CPT code. Every
little thing has its own unique code. Now, here's where the problem comes in. Use the wrong code,
even by a little bit, and the result, the claim either gets underpaid or just denied flat out.
One tiny mistake with a code can bring the whole payment process to a halt. The codes are set. The
bill is ready. And now the claim officially starts its journey. Welcome to section 4. Check out this
flow on the screen. The hospital creates the bill. It's then submitted to a place called a clearing
house. Think of it like a digital post office that sorts everything out. And from there, the clean,
sorted claim is finally sent to the insurance company. But hold on. Before it goes out, there's
a critical power up called claim scrubbing. It's an automated quality check, a final scan to catch
any last minute errors. This one step massively boosts the chances of getting paid on the first
try. Okay, the claim is on its way. This is the moment of truth. Section five, judgement day. Is
it going to be paid or is it going to be denied? And this chart really shows you what happens next.
The insurance company reviews the claim in a process called adjudication. As you can see,
it's not always a happy ending. About 65% get paid in full, but a quarter are only partially paid,
and a solid 10% are just denied. So, what happens when a claim gets denied? Do you just give up?
No way. You fight back. This comeback is called denial management. And what this means is when a
claim gets rejected, you fix it and you send it right back in. First, you figure out why it was
denied. Second, you correct the error. And third, you resubmit the corrected claim for another shot.
Okay, the claim has been resubmitted and hopefully paid. But wait, the game isn't
over just yet. Now we face section six, the final boss, getting to a zero balance. This
is all about AR follow-up and patient billing. It's chasing down those last pending payments
from insurance and then billing the patient for their share, you know, co-pays and deductibles.
The game is only truly won when that account balance hits zero. So after all that, what's the
game plan to win? Let's quickly recap. Accurate data is your absolute superpower. Always, always
get approval first. Clean coding means fast cash. Think of every denial as a lesson. And finally,
you follow up relentlessly until that balance is zero. Because when you boil it all down,
the end goal of this entire complex process is just one thing, payment. Mastering this cycle is
what keeps hospitals doors open. And understanding that, well, that's where the whole game changes.

segments.text: Greetings, friends of the revenue cycle.
I am Professor Riemer. Today we are
going to read an 835 remittance an ERA
line by line. By the end, you will know
exactly where your money went.
An 835 is the electronic remittance
advice. It is the insurance company's
explanation of what they paid, what they
adjusted, and why. It looks like
gibberish, but it is really just short
lines called segments. Each one ends
with a little squiggle called a tilde.
The first lines are the envelope. ISA,
GS, and ST simply say who sent the file,
who it is for, and that it is an 835.
You can mostly wave your wand past them.
BPR is the payment line. This one says
the payer sent $1,250 by a CH on
November 5th. That is the total of the
whole check or EFT.
TRN is the trace number. That is the
check or EFT number, and it is how you
match this ERA to the deposit in your
bank.
N1 PR is the payer. N1 PE is the payee.
That is you, the practice with your NPI
number.
Now the claims. CLP starts each claim,
your account number, status one, which
means processed as primary. You charged
$200. They paid 120 and the patient owes
NM1 QC is the patient's name, here Jane
Doe.
SVC is a service line, procedure 99213,
an office visit, charged 200, paid 120.
CAS lines are the adjustments, the most
important lines on the page. CO45 means
$60 over the contracted fee, and the
practice writes it off. PR2 is $20 of
coinsurance that the patient owes.
AMT B6 is the allowed amount, $140.
That is what the payer says the visit is
worth under your contract.
Let us check the magic. 200 charged 60
contractual leaves 140 allowed. 120 paid
plus 20 from the patient is 140. It
balances.
And watch for PLB near the end. It takes
money from the whole payment like this
$25 overpayment recovery.
It is easy to miss and it is why a check
can be smaller than its claims.
That is an 835 line by line. Follow the
money and it always adds up. Next time
we will decode the 10 denial codes that
cost practices the most money. Subscribe
for more billing magic and may your
claims always be clean.

metadata.title: How Air Ambulances Actually Work
metadata.author: Hospital Decoded
metadata.shortDescription:
The golden hour is the most famous rule in emergency medicine, and in 2001 two researchers went looking for the study behind it. They could not find one.
Follow one 60-minute countdown from a 911 call on a rural road to a hospital rooftop, then to the bill that arrives weeks later.

Who is allowed to call a medical helicopter? Who decides whether it flies, and why is the pilot told nothing about the patient? Where did the idea come from, from Korea and Vietnam to a Maryland State Police helicopter on the Baltimore Beltway in March 1970? What does the evidence actually say about helicopters and survival? And why did an air ambulance bill once run to tens of thousands of dollars, until a federal law changed the rules in 2022?

CHAPTERS
0:00 The hour nobody measured
3:04 Who is allowed to call a helicopter
5:51 Baltimore, 1970: Helicopter 108 and Cowley's shock lab
10:35 Thirteen minutes to the first ambulance
14:54 Korea: the pilot who flew alone
19:58 Who owns the helicopters, and what the pilot is told
23:41 "Unable. Weather." The no that nobody can overrule
32:55 Building a runway in a field
37:29 The golden hour on trial
44:32 Six minutes to the roof
49:03 The envelope: a $36,400 question
58:10 The state where the bill never comes

Have you ever watched a medical helicopter land, on a highway or a hospital roof? And if you fly as a pilot, flight nurse, flight paramedic or communications specialist: what did we get wrong?

This is a documentary explainer, not medical advice. Recreated scenes are AI illustrations of invented people.
June Avery, the county paramedic and the two helicopter bases in this episode are a composite built from published data. They are not real people or real operators.

SOURCES
- Maryland State Police Aviation Command: 50th anniversary release (2020); history page
- EMS1: how the "death lab" evolved into a modern trauma system (R Adams Cowley)
- MIEMSS: EMS News (1974, 1988)
- Lerner and Moscati: The golden hour: scientific fact or medical "urban legend"?, Acad Emerg Med (2001)
- Galvagno et al.: helicopter vs ground EMS and survival, JAMA (2012); Cochrane review (2015)
- Bledsoe et al.: helicopter scene transport meta-analysis, J Trauma (2006)
- Mell et al.: EMS response times, JAMA Surgery (2017)
- Branas et al.: Access to trauma centers, JAMA (2005)
- American College of Surgeons: National Guideline for the Field Triage of Injured Patients (2021)
- U.S. Army: Army helicopters in Korea, 1950-53; Army Medical Department, Dustoff in Vietnam
- National Academy of Sciences / NRC: Accidental Death and Disability (1966)
- NTSB: Special Investigation Report on EMS Operations (2006)
- FAA: Helicopter Air Ambulance final rule, 79 FR 9932 (2014); 14 CFR 135.617 and 135.619
- GAO: GAO-17-637 (2017); GAO-19-292 (2019)
- MedPAC: Ambulance Services Payment Basics (2024)
- CMS: No Surprises Act consumer protections; Qualifying Payment Amount methodology
- ASTNA / ENA: Responsible Helicopter Shopping (2025)
- Fox Baltimore: "Bipartisan support for socialized medicine at 2,000 feet" (2017)

IMAGE CREDITS
Archival images: U.S. National Archives, U.S. military photographs, Wikimedia Commons, MIEMSS and others; licenses and authors listed in the pinned comment and on screen. Stock: Pexels and Pixabay. Diagrams: Hospital Decoded. AI illustrations are labeled on screen and show invented people only.

metadata.shortDescription:
How the No Surprises Act Impacts your Practice | Good Faith Estimate

Sign up for TherapyNotes and get two months FREE:
https://www.therapynotes.com/r/private%20practice%20skills/

Ready for a deep dive? Check out Ken Clark's Webinar on the No Surprises Act:
https://www.semiprivatepractice.com/a/2147502742/zgh2pLSB
(This is an affiliate link)

UPDATED 2-14-22: Kate & Katie of The Private Practice Startup put together a FREE bundle of templates and educational information about the No Surprises Act. I've used it myself and it's super helpful! Here is a link:
https://www.privatepracticestartup.com/good-faith-estimate

FREE Guide: Start a Private Practice in Counseling:
https://tinyurl.com/y9ek9en8

The No Surprises Act seemed to appear out of nowhere and it can be a little fuzzy trying to understand when and how we're expected to offer a Good Faith Estimate to our clients.

In this video, I give an overview of the No Surprises Act and I teach you the details of how to go about implementing it properly in your private practice, including when and how to complete a Good Faith Estimate.

Links to the sources/references from the video:

CMS Good Faith Estimate Template:
https://www.cms.gov/files/document/good-faith-estimate-example.pdf

CAMFT Sample Good Faith Estimate Notice (post to your website and in your office):
https://www.camft.org/Portals/0/Docs/forms/Sample-Good-Faith-Estimate-Notice.docx?ver=2021-12-30-111629-873

CMS Website on the No Surprises Act:
https://www.cms.gov/nosurprises

ASPE Article: "Evidence on Surprise Billing: Protecting Consumers with the No Surprises Act"
https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/acfa063998d25b3b4eb82ae159163575/no-surprises-act-brief.pdf

APA Article: "New billing disclosure requirements take effect in 2022"
https://www.apaservices.org/practice/legal/managed/billing-disclosure-requirements?fbclid=IwAR2-O_7vxewLd8z0Wi7xCebWHB7BKKYfYZbGa1tkCAZN0W4XMX9gF-Q2d_U

AMA Article: "Implementation of the No Surprises Act"
https://www.ama-assn.org/delivering-care/patient-support-advocacy/implementation-no-surprises-act

CAMFT Article: "The No Surprises Act : What MFTs Need to Know"
https://www.camft.org/Resources/Legal-Articles/Chronological-Article-List/the-no-surprises-act-what-mfts-need-to-know

LINKS
*Some links are affiliate links. A percentage of purchases come back to me and help my channel immensely!
👉 How to DIY a Therapist Website that Fills your Practice: https://privatepracticeskills.teachable.com/
👉 Private Practice Skills Merch: https://teespring.com/stores/private-practice-skills
👉 All my filming gear: https://kit.co/privatepracticeskills/all-my-gear
👉 Music I use: https://www.epidemicsound.com/referral/c7m5mj/

This video is geared for therapists of all kinds, including psychologists, MFTs, LPCCs, social workers, and others in the clinical counseling field.

Welcome to Private Practice Skills! I’m Dr. Marie Fang, psychologist in private practice. I post videos offering tools I learned the hard way about starting and growing private practice so that you don’t have to.

www.privatepracticeskills.com
Facebook: www.facebook.com/PrivatePracticeSkills/
Insta: PrivatePracticeSkills

Music from Epidemic Sound:
https://www.epidemicsound.com/track/1CtdB8usjS/

This video is not intended as professional or legal advice. Be sure to seek the services of a professional if you are in need of them.

metadata.title: How the No Surprises Act solved balance billing but created a pricing problem | Loren Adler
metadata.author: Health Tech Nerds
metadata.shortDescription:
Loren Adler, Fellow and Associate Director at the Brookings Institution, joins to assess the No Surprises Act four years in after recent coverage in NYT sparked discussion.

The good news: patients have largely been removed from balance billing. The harder news: the IDR arbitration process that replaced rate-setting has pushed prices to nearly 4x historical in-network rates in radiology, with those costs flowing to employers and likely eventually back to patients through higher premiums. Arbitration was always risky — it's opaque, and human arbitrators tend to be more sympathetic to physicians than insurers.

Loren walks through what may have been a cleaner approach: a benchmark price tying out-of-network payments to a percentage of Medicare, or regulating contract design directly by making it illegal for anesthesia and surgical groups to hold discordant network status from the hospitals they work in. Both solutions had appeal but neither got far in Congress.

On the near-term outlook, Loren is candid: no big picture changes are likely because the winners are concentrated — a handful of PE-backed emergency medicine and anesthesia groups dominating the IDR process — and the losers are diffuse. This dynamic makes congressional action very unlikely in the near term.

For more from Health Tech Nerds, subscribe to our weekly newsletters: https://www.healthtechnerds.com/subscribe

Brought to you by:

Ursa Health: Helping value-based care organizations unlock the full value of their data. Learn more at ursahealth.com
 
Nashville Healthcare Sessions: join HTN and 1,400 execs from across the ecosystem Sep 13-15 in Nashville. Register at nashvillehealthcaresessions.com/register/

Referenced:

No Surprises Act: https://www.brookings.edu/articles/no-surprises-act-arbitration-databook/

Loren Adler, Brookings: https://www.brookings.edu/people/loren-adler/

Loren Adler on X: https://x.com/LorenAdler

Right, we're talking about folks with commercial insurance here. This isn't sort of Medicare or Medicaid. And it turns, you know, the hospital's in network, but it turns out the emergency physician group is not in your insurer's network. And basically, you know, there's no contract there. So, the insurer pays something. The provider group bills you, bills the patient for the difference between what the insurer pays and and what they what they're sort of like dream list price is for this issue. And basically it's kind of get stuck in the middle. I think the Right, the good parts are Right, the No Surprises Act pretty clearly protected the patient from those one-off large bills. metadata.title: Medical Billing Denials: The 45-Minute Strategy That Gets Results
metadata.author: MBC RCM
metadata.shortDescription:
Have you ever faced a medical billing denial requesting records—even when the payer previously paid a similar claim for the same patient and episode of care?
In this practical medical billing case study, we break down how an accounts receivable specialist challenged inconsistent denials using documented evidence, including prior authorization, a single case agreement, verified out-of-network benefits, and paid claim history.
You’ll learn how to:
Identify inconsistencies between paid and denied claims
Use prior authorization and single case agreement details as leverage
Understand the difference between a home plan and a host plan
Prepare for a strategic payer call
Request a plan-to-plan clarification review
Establish follow-up deadlines and accountability
Track EOBs, reference numbers, representatives, and call notes
Separate genuinely disputable denials from valid records requests
Submit only the minimum necessary documentation
Protect psychotherapy notes and maintain appropriate compliance boundaries
The key lesson: not every denial is wrong—but every denial should be investigated with the full evidence available.
Whether you work in medical billing, healthcare revenue cycle management, accounts receivable, behavioral health billing, or payer relations, these cross-referencing tactics can help you approach challenging denials with greater confidence and precision.
Chapters:

00:00 Introduction

00:35 The inconsistent denial problem

01:46 Gathering evidence before calling the payer

02:31 Understanding home plans and host plans

03:15 What documentation the payer requested

03:38 The psychotherapy-notes compliance boundary

04:03 The 45-minute tactical payer call

05:40 Outcomes and next steps

06:35 Key lessons for AR specialists

07:28 Final takeaway
This video is provided for educational purposes only. Always verify applicable payer policies, contracts, privacy requirements, and legal or compliance obligations before submitting records or disputing a claim.
If you found this breakdown helpful, subscribe for more practical medical billing, denial management, and revenue cycle strategies.

Medical billing software is essential for hospitals, clinics, and healthcare providers to manage insurance claims, reduce errors, and improve revenue cycles.

Platforms like Kareo, AdvancedMD, DrChrono, Athenahealth, and eClinicalWorks are widely used in the US healthcare system for billing automation and claims processing.

If you are planning to build a healthcare SaaS platform or a revenue cycle management system, this guide will help you understand everything.

Healthcare billing software must meet strict regulatory standards.

✔️ Advanced claims management platform: $120,000 – $300,000

It typically costs between $50,000 and $800,000+ depending on features and compliance.

Usually 4 to 12 months based on complexity.

EHR systems, insurance payers, clearinghouses, and payment gateways.

Yes, HIPAA and other regulations are mandatory.

Welcome to RCMOpsPro. To operate at an executive level in healthcare finance, you must know how to read the actual architecture of a medical claim.

In this session, we tear down the two primary claim forms in US Healthcare: the CMS-1500 (Professional Billing) and the UB-04 (Institutional/Facility Billing). We break down critical Form Locators (FL), Place of Service (POS) codes, and Revenue Codes. An elite RCM Analyst doesn't just rely on billing software, they can read a raw claim and spot a formatting failure before it ever reaches a clearinghouse.

This is Video 3 of our 100-Video RCM Masterclass Curriculum. Hit SUBSCRIBE to get advanced, executive-level healthcare finance training.

segments.text: Welcome back to RCM ops pro.
Today we are looking at the actual
architecture of a medical bill. If you
want to be an elite analyst, you need to
read these forms like the Matrix.
Every single claim in the US healthcare
system falls into one of two distinct
buckets, professional billing or
institutional billing.
Professional billing represents the
physician's actual time and clinical
expertise. These claims go out on a CMS
1500 form.
Institutional or facility billing covers
the massive overhead of the hospital
itself, the operating room, the medical
equipment, and the nursing staff. These
go on a UB-04 form.
To the untrained eye, these forms look
like a confusing wall of boxes, but an
RCM expert knows exactly which form
locators or FLs drive the revenue.
On a CMS 1500, the most critical box is
the place of service or POS code. This
two-digit number tells the payer exactly
where the doctor was standing when they
delivered the care.
On a UB-04, everything revolves around
revenue codes. These three-digit numbers
categorize the hospital's massive
expenses into neat departments like the
ER or the pharmacy.
If a doctor bills a CMS 1500 with an
inpatient POS code, but the hospital
forgets to bill the matching UB-04, the
payer will flag the mismatch and deny
both claims instantly.
A basic data entry clerk relies on the
software to catch these errors. An elite
RCM analyst can spot a formatting
failure on a raw claim before it ever
reaches the clearinghouse.
Master the architecture of the CMS 1500
and the UB-04, and you control the cash
flow. Hit subscribe, and in our next
session, we will crack open the EDI
pipeline.

segments.text: Welcome back to RCMpro. In today's
video, we're going to break down the CMS
1500 health insurance claim form, one of
the most important forms you'll work
with in US medical billing. We'll go
through it section by section, so you
understand not just what each field is,
but why it matters and how it all
connects to create a clean, professional
claim. By the end of this video, you'll
be able to look at a CMS 1500 and know
exactly what belongs where. Let's get
started. Before we jump into individual
fields, let's look at the overall
structure of the form. This will make
everything easier to follow. The CMS
1500 is organized into four main
sections. Fields 1 through 13 cover the
patient, the insured person, and the
insurance information, including
signatures and authorizations. Fields 14
through 23 cover important dates, the
referring provider, diagnoses, and other
claim details. Field 24 is the service
line section. This is where you list the
actual services provided, dates,
procedure codes, diagnosis pointers,
charges, and the rendering provider.
Fields 25 through 33 cover the billing
side. Tax ID, account information, total
charges, signatures, the service
facility, and the billing provider. Now
that you have the big picture, let's go
through each section carefully. This
section tells the payer who the patient
is, who is insured, and which insurance
plan is being billed. Field 1 Insurance
type. Field 1 shows the type of
insurance you're billing. Medicare,
Medicaid, Tricare, ChampVA, group health
plan, or other. Always select the
correct one based on the patient's
coverage. Field 1A Insured's ID number.
This is the member ID or policy number
assigned by the insurance plan. Use
exactly what appears on the insurance
card or eligibility response. Field 2
Patient's name. Enter the patient's full
name, last name, first name, and middle
initial if available. Make sure it
matches the insurance and registration
records. Field three, patient's date of
birth and sex. Accurate demographic
information reduces claim rejections.
Enter the date of birth and the sex as
required. Field four, insured's name.
The insured is the person whose
insurance is being used. It could be the
patient, a parent, or a spouse. Field
five, patient's address and telephone
number. Enter the patient's complete
address and phone number. Field six,
patient's relationship to the insured.
Select self, spouse, child, or other.
Field seven, insured's address and
telephone number. Enter the insured
person's address and phone number when
it is different from the patient's.
Field eight, reserved for NUCC use. This
field is reserved by the National
Uniform Claim Committee. Do not enter
routine information here. Field nine,
other insured's name. Use this when the
patient has another insurance and you
need to report the other insured person.
Field nine A, other insured's policy or
group number. Enter the policy or group
number for the other insurance. Fields
nine B and nine C, reserved for NUCC
use. These are also reserved and not
used for normal claim entry. Field nine
D, insurance plan name or program name.
Enter the name of the other insurance
plan. Field 10 A, employment related
condition. Indicate whether the
condition is related to the patient's
job, current or previous. Field 10 B,
auto accident. Indicate whether the
condition is related to an auto
accident. If yes, enter the state where
it occurred. Field 10 C, other accident.
Indicate whether the condition is
related to any other type of accident.
Field 10 D, claim codes used only for
specific claim codes designated by the
NUCC when required. Field 11, insured's
policy, group, or FECA number. Enter the
policy or group number for the insurance
being billed. Field 11A, insured's date
of birth and sex. This is the insured
person's date of birth and sex, not the
patient's, unless they are the same
person. Field 11B, other claim ID used
for another claim identification number
when designated by the NUCC. Field 11C,
insurance plan name or program name.
Enter the name of the insurance plan.
Field 11D, another health benefit plan.
If the insured has another health plan,
check yes and complete the related other
insurance fields. Field 12, patient's or
authorized person's signature. This
authorizes the release of information
needed to process the claim and requests
payment of benefits. Field 13, insured's
or authorized person's signature. This
authorizes payment of medical benefits
directly to the physician or supplier.
Teaching tip, field 12 is about
releasing information and requesting
payment. Field 13 is specifically about
assigning payment to the provider. That
covers fields 1 through 13. Field 14,
date of current illness, injury, or
pregnancy. Enter the relevant date and
use the correct qualifier so the payer
knows what the date represents. For
example, onset of symptoms or last
menstrual period. Field 15, other date.
Enter any other required date and its
qualifier. Field 16, dates patient was
unable to work. Enter the from and two
dates if the patient was unable to work
because of the condition. Field 17, name
of referring physician or other source.
Enter the name of the referring,
ordering, or supervising provider. Use
the correct qualifier before the name.
Field 17A, other provider identifier.
Enter another provider identifier if
required with the proper qualifier.
Field 17B, national provider identifier.
Enter the referring provider's NPI.
Field 18, hospitalization dates. Enter
the admission and discharge dates if the
services are related to a hospital stay.
Field 19, additional claim information.
Use this field only for information
designated by the NUCC or required by
the payer. Field 20, outside laboratory.
Indicate whether outside lab services
were used and enter the charges if
applicable. Field 21, diagnosis or
nature of illness or injury. This is one
of the most important fields on the
form. Enter the patient's diagnosis
codes, ICD-10-CM,
in positions A through L. Put the
primary diagnosis first. The ICD
indicator, zero for ICD-10, tells the
payer which code set you're using. These
diagnosis letters are linked to the
services in field 24 through diagnosis
pointers. Field 22, resubmission code
and original reference number. Use this
when you are replacing or voiding a
previously submitted claim. Follow the
payer's specific instructions. Field 23,
prior authorization number. Enter the
prior authorization number when one is
required. Having an authorization number
does not automatically guarantee
payment. That completes fields 14
through 23. Field 24 is the service line
section. Each line represents one
service. You can use multiple lines on
the same claim. Field 24A, date or dates
of service. Enter the from and two dates
for the service. Field 24B, place of
service. Enter the place of service code
that shows where the service was
performed, for example, office or
hospital. Field 24C, EMG. This is the
emergency indicator. Check it only if
the service was an emergency. Note, EMG
here does not mean electromyography.
Field 24D, procedures, services, or
supplies. Enter the CPT or HCPCS code
for the service along with any
appropriate modifiers.
This field describes what you are
billing.
Field 24E, diagnosis pointer. This links
the service line back to the diagnosis
in field 21. Enter the letter or letters
A, B, C, and so on that correspond to
the diagnosis that supports this
service.
Field 24F, charges. Enter the charge for
this specific service line. Field 24G,
days or units. Enter the number of days
or units for the service. Field 24H,
EPSDT or family planning. Complete this
field when required for early and
periodic screening, diagnostic, and
treatment or family planning services.
Field 24I, ID qualifier. This identifies
the type of provider identifier you are
reporting.
Field 24J, rendering provider ID. Enter
the NPI of the provider who actually
performed the service. The rendering
provider may be different from the
billing provider.
Teaching tip. Field 21 lists the
diagnoses, field 24D lists the
procedures, and field 24E connects them.
Getting this connection right is
critical for clean claims. That
completes field 24.
Field 25, federal tax ID number. Enter
the federal tax identification number,
EIN preferred, and indicate whether it
is an SSN or EIN. Field 26, patient's
account number. Enter the account number
your practice uses to identify this
patient or claim.
Field 27, accept assignment. Indicate
whether the provider accepts assignment
according to the payer's rules. Field
28, total charge. Enter the total of all
the service line charges from field 24.
Field 29, amount paid. Enter any amount
already paid, if applicable. Field 30,
reserved for NUCC use. Do not enter
routine information here. Field 31,
signature of physician or supplier. The
provider signs and dates this field,
certifying the information on the claim.
Field 32, service facility location
information. Enter the name and address
of the facility where the services were
performed if it is different from the
billing provider location. Include the
facility NPI in field 32A when required.
Field 33, billing provider information
and phone number. Enter the billing
provider's name, address, and phone
number. This is the entity submitting
the claim and receiving payment-related
communication.
Enter the billing provider's NPI in
field 33A.
Teaching tip, field 32 is the service
facility. Field 33 is the billing
provider. They are not always the same.
Let's quickly review. Fields 1 through
13, patient, insured, and insurance
information plus signatures. Fields 14
through 23, dates, referring provider,
diagnoses, and claim details. Field 24,
service lines, procedure codes,
diagnosis pointers, charges, rendering
provider. Fields 25 through 33, tax ID,
charges, signatures, service facility,
and billing provider.
Three fields are especially important to
master. Field 21, diagnosis codes, the
why. Field 24D, procedure codes, the
what. Field 24E, diagnosis pointer, the
connection between them. Understanding
these fields helps you complete claims
more accurately and spot common billing
errors faster.
That's it for today's video. If this
explanation helped you understand the
CMS 1500 form, like the video and
subscribe to our CM Pro for more
practical lessons on US healthcare
revenue cycle management.

metadata.title: How AI Is Transforming High-Volume Document Workflows at Scale in Healthcare RCM
metadata.author: LandingAI
metadata.shortDescription:
* An RCM (Revenue Cycle Management) automation team is processing 120,000+ pages/day and needs a more accurate and scalable way to handle complex healthcare documents—handwritten forms, checkboxes, mixed layouts, and degraded scans that traditional OCR and LLM pipelines couldn’t reliably process.

In this webinar, we’ll share how they improved accuracy from less than 60% to over 90%, achieved HIPAA-compliant Zero Data Retention, and built an extraction engine prepared to scale to 240,000 pages/day.

*Goals*
In this webinar, you’ll learn:
* Why OCR/LLM pipelines fail on real healthcare documents
* How visual document understanding improves accuracy & reliability
* Key technical challenges: checkboxes, handwritten text, tables, strikethroughs, mixed layouts
* How confidence-based routing reduces manual review volume
* Enterprise Security: HIPAA, BAA, Zero Data Retention (ZDR)
* 2-week POV framework used to validate extraction performance
* Scale outcomes: predictable throughput across 120K–240K pages/day
* Lessons for RCM, PA, patient access, claims, and CDI teams handling high-volume documents

* Audience* 
This webinar is designed for leaders in revenue cycle operations, automation, AI/engineering, prior authorization, patient access, and coding/CDI who want to modernize document-heavy workflows with reliable AI extraction.

*Chapters*
00:00: Intro to Agentic Document Extraction
06:58: How ADE can solve challenges in healthcare document processing (overview)

12:10: Case Study: Scaling prior authorization processing

16:15: Parsing demo

29:49: Extraction demo
33:50: Documentation & Discord
37:09: Pricing
37:56: Benchmarks

47:54: Q&A - round 2

metadata.title: 6 Keys to Success in Out of Network Reimbursement
metadata.author: Collect Rx
metadata.shortDescription:
With patient volume down by as much as 90% in some practice areas and facilities, it's more important than ever to ensure that you're being paid correctly by insurance companies.  But over the last 12 months, payors have become more and more aggressive in their tactics to deny, delay and underpay out-of-network claims.  

View this on-demand webinar to learn about the Collect Rx 'secret sauce' for combating payor efforts to reimburse significantly below usual and customary rates and avoid paying fairly to providers across all specialties.  Ryan Ellison, Vice President at Collect Rx will will provide insights into how we navigate roadblocks to achieve higher payments that significantly improve collections from payors.

metadata.author: Bill Fighter
metadata.shortDescription:
Got hit with a shocking out-of-network medical bill you never saw coming? Before you pay a single penny, watch this — because most of these bills are negotiable, and some are flat-out illegal under federal law.

In this video, we break down the exact playbook to fight back against out-of-network charges and slash what you owe — even if the bill is in the thousands.

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN
→ Why you got an out-of-network bill (even though you showed your insurance card)
→ How the No Surprises Act protects you from balance billing in 2024 and beyond
→ The first 3 phone calls to make BEFORE you negotiate a single dollar
→ How to request and decode your itemized bill to spot overcharges
→ The exact counteroffer script that works on out-of-network providers
→ A real case study: how one viewer knocked an $8,472 bill down to under $1,000
→ When to dispute, when to appeal, and when to call your state insurance commissioner

SOURCES
→ Kaiser Family Foundation (KFF) — Surprise Medical Bills Research
→ CMS.gov — No Surprises Act Consumer Protections
→ Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) — Medical Debt Reports
→ Commonwealth Fund — Out-of-Network Billing Studies

DISCLAIMER: This video is for educational purposes only and is not legal, financial, or medical advice. Always consult a qualified professional about your specific situation.

0:00 - Introduction
0:07 - Hook

5:50 - Step 1: Verify Every Charge

8:55 - Real Example: Sarah's Story
9:39 - Step 1: No Surprises Act check

metadata.title: Episode 29: Revenue Cycle Management Explained: Remittances, ERAs, and Portals
metadata.author: The Claim Game X Practice Solutions
metadata.shortDescription: Jeremy breaks down the critical distinction between an EOB (what the patient sees) and a Remittance Advice (the professional version for the provider). He walks through the "detective work" required to audit these documents, highlighting why the Allowed Amount—not just the paid amount—is the number that determines if you’re being underpaid. The episode also explores the "digital pipeline," comparing the speed of ERAs to the "snail mail" of paper and warning about the hidden dangers of "set-and-forget" auto-posting. Finally, Jeremy shares a real-world case study where forensic remittance auditing recovered significant underpayments for a large agency.

metadata.shortDescription:
EPISODE SUMMARY


Jeremy breaks down the critical distinction between an EOB (what the patient sees) and a Remittance Advice (the professional version for the provider). He walks through the "detective work" required to audit these documents, highlighting why the Allowed Amount—not just the paid amount—is the number that determines if you’re being underpaid. The episode also explores the "digital pipeline," comparing the speed of ERAs to the "snail mail" of paper and warning about the hidden dangers of "set-and-forget" auto-posting. Finally, Jeremy shares a real-world case study where forensic remittance auditing recovered significant underpayments for a large agency. 





KEYWORDS


Revenue Cycle Management, RCM, Remittance Advice, Explanation of Benefits, EOB, Electronic Remittance Advice, ERA, 835 File, Contractual Obligation, CO Codes, Patient Responsibility, Payer Portals





TAKEAWAYS


The Remittance as a Scorecard: A deposit without a remittance is like a box without a packing slip; you can’t post the money accurately without knowing the patient, date of service, and CPT code. 


The Trap of the "Paid Amount": Never stop at the paid amount. You must audit the contractual adjustments (CO codes) and patient responsibility (PR codes) to ensure you aren't writing off money you should have collected. 


ERAs vs. EOBs: Electronic Remittance Advice (ERA) files (835 files) arrive days or weeks faster than paper. However, always look for the PLB segment (provider level adjustments) to find "missing" money buried in recoupments. 


Portals are a Fast Pass: Use payer portals like Availity or Optum to skip the 45-minute hold times. Portals allow for instant remittance downloads and "correction speed" for fixing claim modifiers in days rather than months.





CHAPTERS

02:48 Remittance vs. EOB: Knowing the Difference


06:48 From Paper to Digital: Understanding ERAs


09:56 The Secret Weapon: Payer Portals


12:20 Case Study: Finding Hidden Underpayments


15:47 Conclusion: The Winning Formula for Remittances and Portals

metadata.title: 3 Unpaid Claims, 3 Different Next Actions | A/R Audit Walkthrough
metadata.author: Talisman Solutions
metadata.shortDescription:
An aging report tells you how much money is outstanding. But does it tell your team why each claim is still unpaid?

In this illustrative A/R walkthrough, we look at three claims that need three different actions:

Claim A: Obtain missing supporting documentation before resubmission.

Claim B: Refer a possible coding inconsistency for specialist review.

Claim C: Review the payer's decision and check the appeal deadline.

The takeaway is simple: claims in the same aging bucket don't necessarily need the same follow-up.

Talisman's UAE A/R audit offering uses intelligent review of revenue cycle, documentation and compliance processes to help identify recovery opportunities and accuracy issues.

A useful audit output should help your team understand the issue, supporting evidence, recommended next step, deadline and responsible owner.

Book a FREE Talisman A/R audit. Turn a sample aging list into an action list.

Explore Talisman's healthcare AI solutions:
https://talismansolutions.com/uae-healthcare-ai-solutions/

Note: The claims shown are illustrative examples using a synthetic workflow, not actual patient or payer records.

metadata.title: Revenue Cycle for OBLs: Payer Contracts, 2026 Coding and Denials | OEIS Annual Meeting
metadata.author: Outpatient Endovascular & Interventional Society
metadata.shortDescription:
Most OBLs let their payer contracts renew year after year at the same rates. This session covers how to renegotiate them, code the 2026 lower extremity set correctly, and stop losing revenue to prior authorization denials.

In the Revenue Cycle session from the 2026 OEIS Annual Meeting, speakers walk through the business side of running an outpatient lab: building a payer mix and CPT utilization profile, benchmarking negotiated rates against the market with transparency in coverage data, defining the ask and modeling the return on a modest rate increase, the new lower extremity revascularization codes (37254 to 37299) and what they do to physician RVUs and OBL payment, preventing prior authorization denials and writing appeals that work, and one physician's path from a payer refusal to commercial rates well above CMS. The panel closes with audience questions on negotiation and coding.

0:00:00 Renegotiate, Don't Just Renew
0:03:20 Understanding Your Payer Mix and CPT Utilization
0:07:25 Benchmarking Your Rates Against the Market
0:13:11 Defining the Ask and Measuring ROI
0:17:14 2026 IR Coding: What Changed This Year
0:22:18 The New Lower Extremity Codes: 37254 to 37299
0:32:38 Physician RVUs and OBL Payment, 2025 vs 2026
0:41:33 Preventing Prior Authorization Denials
0:50:53 Denial Appeals: Best Practices
0:55:11 How I Beat CMS: Negotiating Commercial Rates
0:56:44 80% vs 185% of CMS: What It Means for Your Practice
1:01:43 A Framework for Payer Negotiations
1:10:27 Panel Discussion and Audience Q&A

This is what the Annual Meeting is for: practical answers from peers who run outpatient labs themselves and will tell you what worked and what didn't. OEIS members get that network all year, along with the education, advocacy, and registry that support outpatient endovascular care.

Join us in person for the 2027 OEIS Annual Meeting in Orlando. Register here to join sessions like this one live: https://oeisweb.com/2027-annual-meeting-attendee-registration

#RevenueCycle #PayerContracting #MedicalCoding #OBL #OEIS
